title: Security Deposit Amount Limits
bodyText: North Dakota caps the security deposit at one month's rent, with two distinct paths to two months: you may choose to accept up to two months from a tenant with a felony conviction, as an incentive to rent to them, or you may demand up to two months from a tenant who has a prior judgment against them for violating a previous rental agreement. This is different from a general "poor credit" exception — several online guides get this wrong.

title: Separate Pet Deposit Cap
bodyText: You may charge a separate pet security deposit, capped at the greater of $2,500 or two months' rent. This deposit cannot be charged for a service or companion animal required as a disability accommodation.

title: Deposit Must Be Held in an Interest-Bearing Account
bodyText: North Dakota requires you to hold the security deposit in a federally insured, interest-bearing savings or checking account for the tenant's benefit. If the tenant occupied the property nine months or longer, you must pay them the accrued interest when the deposit is returned.

title: A New Owner Inherits Your Deposit Obligations
bodyText: If you sell or transfer the property, the security deposit and accrued interest transfer to the new owner. You aren't released from liability until that transfer actually happens, and the new owner is bound by North Dakota's deposit rules even though they didn't originally receive the deposit.

title: Penalty for Withholding the Deposit Without Justification
bodyText: If you withhold security deposit money without reasonable justification, North Dakota law makes you liable for treble (triple) damages.

title: Self-Help Eviction Is Prohibited
bodyText: North Dakota law imposes treble (triple) damages on anyone who forcibly ejects or excludes another person from possession of real property. This applies to a landlord who locks out a tenant, shuts off utilities, or otherwise forces a tenant out without going through the court eviction process — you're exposed to three times the tenant's actual damages.

title: What North Dakota's Entry Rules Require
bodyText:
North Dakota lets you enter at any time, with no notice at all, in three situations: an emergency, or where you reasonably believe the tenant has abandoned the premises, or where you reasonably believe the tenant is in substantial violation of the lease. Outside those three, North Dakota doesn't set a specific number of hours of advance notice. Instead, unless it's impractical, you must first notify the tenant and get their consent — which can't be unreasonably withheld — and your notice must identify a specific time. If the tenant doesn't object after receiving notice of that time, consent is presumed.

Notice may be given personally, by posting it conspicuously in or about the unit for a reasonable period, or by any other method that results in actual notice.

Entry is limited to reasonable hours and manner, and only for specific purposes: inspecting the premises, making necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supplying necessary or agreed services, or showing the unit to prospective purchasers, insurers, mortgagees, agents, tenants, workers or contractors. You may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass or intimidate the tenant.

title: Retaliation Protection Is Narrower Than in Other States
bodyText: North Dakota has no general law protecting tenants from retaliation for exercising ordinary lease or habitability rights -- unlike Colorado, Kansas, and Nebraska. A tenant who simply reports a maintenance problem or code violation has no statutory retaliation protection. Two narrower protections do exist. Under the housing discrimination chapter it is a discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with anyone for exercising or enjoying a right granted by that chapter, or for having aided or encouraged someone else to do so. And separately, a narrow protection applies to tenants and applicants connected to a domestic violence lease termination -- see the guidance on domestic violence information and non-disclosure for that duty and the damages a court may award for breaching it.

title: Notice Required Before Filing for Nonpayment
bodyText: If a tenant hasn't paid rent within three days of the due date, you may pursue eviction — but you must first give three days' written notice of intention to evict before filing in district court (N.D.C.C. 47-16 and 47-32). The notice has no prescribed wording. It may be served and returned the way a summons is, or, if the tenant can't be found, by the sheriff or a process server posting it conspicuously on the premises. Note what the three days are not: North Dakota gives the tenant no statutory right to cure by paying within them. The notice tells the tenant you intend to evict; it is not a pay-or-quit notice, and nothing obliges you to accept late payment once it has run. No North Dakota court rule adds a further pre-filing condition. Federal law may: if the property has a federally backed mortgage or takes part in a covered federal housing program, you may need to give a 30-day notice to vacate before filing (see the federal CARES Act notice row).

title: North Dakota Adds Protected Classes Beyond Federal Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Beyond the federal Fair Housing Act's protected classes (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin, disability), North Dakota law also prohibits housing discrimination based on age, marital status, and receipt of public assistance.

title: Cannot Refuse Applicants Receiving Public Assistance, Including Vouchers
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to a prospective tenant because they receive public assistance, and North Dakota defines that to expressly include a tenant receiving federal, state, or local rental subsidies, rental assistance, or rent supplements -- which covers housing choice vouchers. This is a source-of-income protection under the fair housing law, not a requirement that you enrol in HUD's voucher programme, but you cannot decline an applicant for planning to pay with one. It is subject to the small-landlord exemptions in the same chapter.

title: Cannot Charge a Fee for Accepting Cash, Check, or Money Order
bodyText: You may not charge a tenant a fee just for accepting cash, a check, or a money order as payment of rent or any other payment required under the lease. This is separate from a returned or bounced-check fee, which is a different topic governed by general banking law, not this section.

title: Double-Letting a Room Is Prohibited
bodyText: If you rent out a room as a dwelling to more than one tenant, the first tenant you rented any part of it to is entitled to the whole room for their full term. Every other tenant in the building under your ownership is relieved of all rent obligations for as long as the double-letting continues.

title: Grounds for Early Termination Outside the Eviction Process
bodyText: Beyond the formal eviction process, North Dakota law gives each party an independent right to end the lease early in narrow circumstances. You may terminate if Tenant uses the property in a way contrary to the lease, or fails to make repairs Tenant is responsible for within a reasonable time after a request. Tenant may terminate if you don't fulfill your obligations (quiet possession, habitable condition, repairs) within a reasonable time after a request, or if the greater or most important part of the property is destroyed through no fault of Tenant.

title: Eviction Grounds and Which Ones Require Notice
bodyText: North Dakota law lists eight grounds for eviction. Only four of them require you to give notice first: holdover or nonpayment of rent, holdover after a sale or contract-for-deed cancellation, wrongful possession after a partition judgment or judicial sale, and violation of a material term of a written lease. For those four you must give three days' written notice of intention to evict before filing. The other four grounds -- forcible or fraudulent entry, turning out the occupant by force, holding possession by force or threats, and a tenant or their guest acting in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment -- require no advance notice at all. In no case does North Dakota law give the tenant a right to cure: the three-day notice is a notice of intention to evict, not a notice to fix the problem.

title: Carbon Monoxide Alarm Requirement
bodyText: If a dwelling unit has a fuel-fired appliance installed, or has an attached garage, an approved carbon monoxide alarm must be installed outside each sleeping area in the immediate vicinity of the bedrooms, on every habitable level, and in each bedroom or its attached bathroom containing a fuel-fired appliance. If more than one alarm is required in a unit, they must be interconnected so that one activating sets off all of them. Alarm systems must be installed under the supervision of a master or class B electrician.

title: A Lease Induced by Fraud Can Be Terminated
bodyText: If a tenant entered into this lease based on fraudulent misrepresentations, they may terminate the lease and are entitled to the return of their security deposit plus any accrued interest.

title: Tenants Can Petition to Seal Eviction Records
bodyText: A tenant subject to an eviction order for nonpayment of rent or damage to the premises, who has resolved all nonpayment and damage claims, may move to seal the eviction court records seven years after the order has been satisfied -- provided they have not been evicted from another property during the seven years following the eviction. Separately, a tenant who was subjected to domestic violence during the tenancy and was evicted because of a domestic violence incident may move to seal immediately, once the assailant is convicted of domestic violence or becomes subject to a disorderly conduct restraining order, sexual assault restraining order, or domestic violence protection order. Sealing is the tenant's motion to make; it imposes no duty on you.

title: Returned Check: Collection Fee and Civil Penalty
bodyText: If a tenant's check is returned for insufficient funds you may recover collection fees or costs of up to $40, on top of the amount of the instrument itself. That $40 carries no advance-notice or disclosure precondition. A larger civil penalty is available but only if you first mail the statutory notice of dishonor and the tenant fails to pay the instrument plus your collection fee within ten days of receiving it -- then you may sue for the lesser of $200 or three times the amount of the instrument. Two traps: if you knowingly accepted a postdated check, or agreed not to present a check until a specified time, the statute does not apply at all and none of these remedies are available to you. And if you use the ACH network to collect the fee, you must comply with that network's rules.

title: Holdover Damages: Two Statutory Double-Damages Measures
bodyText: If a tenant gave you notice they intended to leave and then failed to give up the premises, the measure of damages is double the rent they would otherwise owe. Separately, if a tenant willfully holds over after the end of the term, and after you have duly given notice of intention to evict and made demand for possession, the measure is double the yearly value of the property for the time of withholding, plus compensation for the detriment caused. Outside those two specific situations an evicted tenant simply remains liable for rent for the remainder of the term, and your duty to mitigate applies throughout.

title: The Court Can Stay Execution for Hardship
bodyText: If the court rules for you it must enter judgment for immediate restitution of the premises. But if the tenant shows that immediate restitution would work a substantial hardship on them or their family, the court may stay the special execution for up to five days. That stay is unavailable if the eviction judgment rests in whole or in part on a disturbance of the peace.

title: No Separate Utility-Shutoff Penalty (But Shutoff Is Still Exposure)
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute making a landlord's utility shutoff its own offence with its own penalty. That does not make it safe: cutting utilities to force a tenant out is exposure under the general forcible-exclusion measure, which is treble damages. You also have an affirmative duty to supply running water, reasonable hot water, and reasonable heat.

title: After the Writ: What You May Do With Belongings Left Behind
bodyText: North Dakota imposes no post-writ inventory, storage, notice, or care-standard duty on you or the sheriff for a tenant's remaining belongings. The abandoned-property rules govern instead. One provision applies specifically after eviction: if you remove abandoned property from the unit after obtaining a judgment of eviction and after the special execution has been served, you have a lien on that property for the reasonable amount of storage and moving expenses, and may keep possession until those charges are paid. That lien does not have priority over a prior perfected security interest in the property.

title: No Statutory Procedure for Animals Left After an Eviction
bodyText: North Dakota law says nothing about what happens to a tenant's animals after an eviction -- no animal-control notification route, no notice-posting requirement, no unattended-animal rule, and no duty assigned to you or the sheriff.

title: Domestic Violence Information: Non-Disclosure Duty and Damages
bodyText: If a tenant gives you information documenting domestic violence in support of a lease termination, you may not disclose it. It may not be entered into any shared database or given to any person. You may use it as evidence in an eviction proceeding, in a claim for unpaid rent or damages arising out of the tenancy, or where the law otherwise requires. You also may not refuse to rent to someone, refuse to negotiate for a rental with them, otherwise make a dwelling unavailable to them, or retaliate, solely because they or a household member exercised this termination right. That duty reaches applicants, not just current tenants, so it applies at the screening stage as well as during a tenancy. A court may award $1,000 in statutory damages for a violation, plus actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, costs, and disbursements.

title: Deposit Return Timing After a Domestic Violence Termination
bodyText: When a tenant terminates under North Dakota's domestic violence provision, the clock for returning the security deposit does not start the way it normally would. If the departing victim is the only tenant (counting their minor children), the deposit timing is triggered on the first day of the month following the date they vacate. If other tenants remain bound by the lease, it is triggered on expiration of the lease instead.

title: Weekly and Room Tenancies Follow Different Rules
bodyText: North Dakota does not treat every residential tenancy the same way. If you rent lodgings for an unspecified term, the tenancy is presumed to run for whatever period you use to set the rent -- rent at a weekly rate presumes a one-week tenancy. Termination notice for an unspecified-term lease is measured by the length of the term itself, capped at one calendar month, so a weekly tenancy takes roughly a week's notice, not a month's. Only where there is no agreement about the rent period does the tenancy default to monthly. The automatic-renewal notice rule applies only to leases with a specified term of two months or more, and the mid-tenancy term-change right applies only to month-to-month tenancies.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses Require 30 Days Written Notice
bodyText: If your lease has a specified term of two months or more and contains an automatic renewal clause, you cannot enforce that clause unless you notified the tenant in writing of the automatic renewal provision -- personally or by first-class mail -- at least thirty days before the current lease expires. If you don't give that notice, the lease simply expires and the terms convert to a month-to-month tenancy.

title: Changing Lease Terms Mid-Tenancy
bodyText: In a month-to-month tenancy you may change the terms of the lease -- including rent -- effective at the expiration of the month, by giving written notice at least thirty days before the end of that month. Notice may be served in any reasonable manner that actually informs the tenant of the changes. If the tenant stays past the end of the month, the new terms become part of the lease. A tenant who receives such a notice may instead terminate at the end of the month by giving at least twenty-five days' notice.

title: You May Be Exempt From Parts of North Dakota Fair Housing Law
bodyText: North Dakota's housing discrimination chapter exempts some small landlords. If you rent rooms or units in a building with no more than four families living independently, and you occupy one of those units as your own residence, the sale-or-rental prohibitions do not apply to you. There is also an owner-occupied single-family exemption: it covers an owner of no more than three single-family houses who does not use a broker or agent, and it is limited to one sale or rental in any twenty-four-month period where you were not the most recent resident. Two warnings. The advertising prohibition is NOT exempted -- you may not publish a notice or advertisement indicating any discriminatory preference, whatever your exemption. And federal fair housing law applies separately and does not necessarily exempt you on the same terms.

title: Victims in State Housing Programs Cannot Be Denied or Evicted On That Basis
bodyText: If your rental is part of a state housing program, you may not deny admission to, deny assistance under, terminate participation of, or evict an applicant or tenant on the basis that they are or have been a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking, provided they otherwise qualify.

title: Reasonable Modifications and Accommodations for Disability
bodyText: You may not refuse to permit a reasonable modification of the premises made at the tenant's own expense where it may be necessary for them to fully enjoy the property -- though in a rental you may, where reasonable, condition permission on the tenant restoring the interior to its prior condition afterwards, ordinary wear and tear excepted. Separately, you may not refuse a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies, practices, or services where the accommodation may be necessary to give the tenant equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling. Neither duty requires you to house someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety.

title: What a Fair Housing Violation Actually Costs
bodyText: A tenant or applicant can complain to the Department of Labor and Human Rights within one year of the discriminatory practice, or file a civil action in district court within two years. In court, a judge may award actual and punitive damages, reasonable attorney's fees, and court costs. Through the administrative route the Department may order actual damages, fees and costs, and on top of that assess civil penalties rising with your history of prior findings. Using force or threat of force to intimidate or interfere with someone exercising these housing rights is a class A misdemeanour, and coercing, intimidating, threatening or interfering with anyone exercising rights under the chapter is itself a discriminatory practice.

title: When You Are Exempt From the Visual Alarm Requirement
bodyText: You must provide an approved visual smoke detection system or other visual fire alarm if a deaf tenant requests one in writing. You are exempt from that requirement only if your rental property does not exceed one building and that building does not exceed four residential dwelling units. Both conditions must be met -- owning a single six-unit building does not exempt you, and neither does owning two four-unit buildings. Separately, lodging establishments and assisted living facilities are outside this statute altogether and follow the Department of Health's rules instead.

title: Accepting a Postdated Check Forfeits Your Bad-Check Remedies
bodyText: If you knowingly accept a postdated rent check, or agree with the tenant that a check will not be presented until a specified time, North Dakota's bad-check statute does not apply to that check at all. You lose the $40 collection fee, the civil penalty, and the ability to refer the matter for criminal prosecution. If you want those remedies available, do not agree to hold a check.

title: Alarm Requirements Differ by Building Type
bodyText: North Dakota's electrical code sets alarm requirements that vary with the kind of building you own. Smoke alarms are required in each sleeping room, outside each separate sleeping area near the bedrooms, and on each additional story including basements and habitable attics; where more than one is required in a unit they must be interconnected. If you own a two-family dwelling -- a duplex -- each unit must additionally have a notification device connected to the smoke alarm system in the other unit. Apartment houses, hotels, and congregate residences must have a manual and automatic fire alarm system. In new construction, an approved heat alarm must be installed in an attached single-tenant garage and interconnected with the residence's smoke alarms.

title: What You Must Do With an Unclaimed Security Deposit
bodyText: A security deposit, including its interest, that stays unclaimed for more than one year after the lease ends is presumed abandoned and you become a holder under North Dakota's unclaimed property act. That carries real duties. If you have a usable address for the tenant and the deposit is worth $25 or more, you must mail them notice by first-class mail no more than 120 days before you file your report, using the wording the statute prescribes. You must file the report electronically before November 1 each year, covering the twelve months ending the previous July 1, and pay the money over when you file. You must keep the records for ten years. If you miss the deadlines the state can charge interest and a civil penalty for each day you are late, and deliberately evading the duty carries far steeper penalties. Paying over in good faith after giving proper notice releases you from further liability to the tenant.

title: North Dakota Moved Its Protection Order Law in 2025
bodyText: North Dakota's domestic violence protection order provisions were repealed from the domestic violence chapter in 2025 and now live in the civil protection orders chapter. The definition of domestic violence itself did not move and still sits in the domestic violence chapter, so a lease that cites it remains correct. If you rely on any guidance written before 2025 that cites the old protection order sections, those citations are dead.

title: Rent Receipts: Give One When the Tenant Asks
bodyText: North Dakota's landlord-tenant chapter does not make you hand over a receipt for every rent payment unasked. But a general contract rule lets anyone paying what they owe demand a written receipt (N.D.C.C. § 9-12-22). So if a tenant asks for a receipt for rent, cash or otherwise, give one. Giving one unasked is worth doing too: without a receipt a cash payment leaves no record either party can produce, and in a nonpayment dispute the absence cuts against whoever carries the burden on that point.

title: No Statutory Duty to Give the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: North Dakota does not require you to deliver a copy of the signed lease to the tenant, and failing to do so is not a defence the tenant can raise against enforcement. You are separately required to provide a signed statement describing the condition of the premises at the time the rental agreement is entered into.

title: A Disclosure Failure Does Not Block Your Eviction
bodyText: North Dakota has no general rule that failing to make a required disclosure bars you from bringing an eviction. Chapter 47-32 also gives the tenant no rent-withholding defence: a tenant cannot resist a nonpayment eviction just because you failed to make repairs. But § 47-16-13 lets a tenant who gave you notice of dilapidations you ought to repair, and waited a reasonable time while you neglected them, repair them and deduct the expense from the rent. Rent lawfully deducted that way is not unpaid rent, so check for a § 47-16-13 deduction before you serve a nonpayment notice. The one statutory exception is narrow and concerns mobile home parks.

title: What "Fire Marshal Standards" Actually Means
bodyText:
When North Dakota law says your smoke detection system must comply with fire marshal standards, that resolves to the State Fire Code: the fire-safe construction and operation provisions of the State Building Code, plus the International Fire Code, 2021 edition, as modified by the state. Those are privately published model codes -- you obtain them from the International Code Council or the National Fire Protection Association, not from a free state webpage. The fire code supplements the statutes rather than replacing them, and where the two conflict the Century Code wins.

Two points worth knowing: sprinklers are not required in single-family dwellings or residential buildings of no more than two dwelling units with no higher-risk occupancy in the same building; and a condition that was lawful when the code was adopted may continue even if it no longer strictly complies, but only so long as the state fire marshal does not consider it a distinct hazard to life or property.

title: Military Lease Termination: Federal Law, Extended to State Active Duty
bodyText: North Dakota has no lease-termination statute of its own for servicemembers, and federal law does the main work. Under the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, a tenant gives written notice with a copy of the orders, and termination takes effect thirty days after the next rent due date. North Dakota adds one thing. A member of its National Guard or militia called to state active duty for thirty consecutive days or longer gets all of the federal Act's protections as state law (N.D.C.C. §§ 37-01-01(2), 37-01-43). That reaches state call-ups, such as a disaster response, that the federal Act may not cover. The state right follows the federal Act as it stood on December 31, 2024, so later federal changes do not carry over automatically. Treat a tenant on such orders as you would a federal servicemember. North Dakota adds no shortened notice period for periodic tenancies.

title: Electronic Notice: No Landlord-Tenant Regime, But the Transactions Act Applies
bodyText:
North Dakota's landlord-tenant chapter says nothing about electronic notice — there is no affirmative-consent requirement, no pre-consent disclosure, no hardware and software statement and no re-consent when your systems change. But do not read that as a free hand, because the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (N.D.C.C. ch. 9-16) applies to a lease like any other contract.

Three things follow. First, it works only by agreement: the chapter applies only between parties each of which has agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means, judged from the context and the parties' conduct, so get that agreement in the lease. Second, if a law requires you to give the tenant something in writing, an electronic record satisfies it only if the record is capable of retention by the recipient at the time of receipt — and if you or your system inhibit the tenant's ability to print or store it, the record is not enforceable against the tenant. That requirement may not be varied by agreement, except where the other law itself allows its writing requirement to be varied, which North Dakota's landlord-tenant sections do not.

Third, some notices cannot go electronically at all: an automatic-renewal notice must be “delivered personally or by first-class mail” (§ 47-16-06.1), and a domestic violence termination notice may be delivered by mail, facsimile or in person (§ 47-16-17.1(3)) — neither list includes email. Where the statutes are permissive they are genuinely permissive: a change-of-terms notice may be served in any reasonable manner that actually informs the tenant (§ 47-16-07).

title: Some Duties Are Frozen to a Specific Edition of an Outside Standard
bodyText: Several North Dakota requirements are defined by reference to an outside technical standard fixed at a particular edition rather than to whatever the current version happens to be. Accessible-design requirements for covered multifamily dwellings are measured against the 1986 ANSI standard, and the state fire code adopts the 2021 edition of the International Fire Code. Reading the current edition of one of those standards can give you the wrong answer about what North Dakota actually requires.

title: No Separate Ban on Asking About Protected Characteristics
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute separately prohibiting you from asking an applicant about a protected characteristic, or from recording one. What is prohibited is discriminating on the basis of one, and publishing any notice, statement, or advertisement indicating a preference or limitation. The practical effect is much the same: an inquiry that has no lawful purpose is evidence of the discrimination itself, and a written record of the answer is evidence a complainant can use. The absence of a separate inquiry ban is not permission to ask.

title: The Small-Landlord Exemption and the Assistance Animal Rules
bodyText: The small-landlord exemption in North Dakota's housing discrimination chapter does not switch off the state's assistance animal documentation rules, because those rules sit in a different title and the exemption only lists sections of its own chapter. But the two do not actually collide. The documentation rules govern how you may verify a request for an assistance animal that some other law requires you to consider -- they apply where a tenant asserts an accommodation is required under any provision of law. If you are genuinely exempt from both the state and federal accommodation duties, there is no request you are obliged to grant, and the documentation limits have nothing to operate on. If you are not exempt, they apply in full. Do not treat the exemption as a general licence around assistance animals: the federal exemption is drawn differently from the state one, and this has not been analysed.

title: Signed Condition Statement Required at Move-In
bodyText: North Dakota requires you to provide the tenant, at the time the rental agreement is entered into, a statement describing the condition of the facilities in and about the premises to be rented. The statement must be agreed to and signed by both you and the tenant. **It then constitutes prima facie proof of the condition of the facilities and the premises at the beginning of the rental agreement** — which makes it the single most useful document you will have in any later dispute about damage, because without it you are arguing about the starting condition from memory while the tenant does the same. The statute fixes no form, no itemisation standard, and no penalty for skipping it; the consequence of omission is evidentiary, and it falls on you. Complete it carefully and specifically rather than treating it as a formality, keep a signed copy with the lease, and give the tenant one.

title: Service-Animal Misrepresentation Penalty Is Conviction-Gated
bodyText: North Dakota makes it an infraction to knowingly claim a pet is a service or assistance animal, or to knowingly submit fraudulent supporting documentation, in order to obtain a reasonable accommodation (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.6(1)). The penalty that actually matters practically is separate and conditional: only where the tenant pleads guilty to, or is convicted of, that infraction may the landlord evict the tenant and recover a damage fee of up to $1,000 (§ 47-16-07.6(2)) -- a landlord cannot simply assess this fee based on their own belief that a claim is fraudulent; a criminal disposition has to happen first. Read narrowly, subsection (2)'s fee is tied to a tenant who "provides fraudulent disability documentation" specifically, which is narrower than subsection (1)'s two grounds (a false claim OR fraudulent documentation) -- on the statute's own words, the $1,000 fee may not be available for a bare false claim that isn't accompanied by fraudulent paperwork. No North Dakota authority resolves that gap; treat it as an open drafting question rather than a settled one.

title: What North Dakota Law Will Not Let the Lease Do
bodyText: North Dakota has no list of prohibited residential lease terms inside its landlord-tenant chapter, and it is easy to conclude from that the lease can say whatever you want. That is wrong. Five sections of Chapter 9-08 void whole categories of contract term, and a lease is a contract like any other. A provision is unlawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law, contrary to the policy of express law though not expressly prohibited, or otherwise contrary to good morals (§ 9-08-01). A provision whose object is, directly or indirectly, to exempt anyone from responsibility for their own fraud, for willful injury to another person or their property, or for violation of law -- whether the violation is willful or negligent -- is against the policy of the law (§ 9-08-02). Penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (§ 9-08-03). A clause fixing damages in advance is void to that extent, unless it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage (§ 9-08-04). And a clause that restricts a party from enforcing its rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or that shortens the time in which it may enforce them, is void unless a North Dakota statute specifically permits it (§ 9-08-05). What this means in practice: a flat "Landlord is not liable" sentence will not protect you where the loss came from your own violation of a statute or building code; a flat early-termination, short-notice, or administrative fee is exposed as a contractual penalty rather than a damages estimate; and Chapter 47-16's own unconscionability section (§ 47-16-13.3) sits on top of all of it as a case-by-case backstop.

title: The Tenant Can Repair and Deduct, or Just Leave
bodyText:
North Dakota gives a tenant three routes when you do not repair, and none of them requires going to court first. If, within a reasonable time after the tenant's notice of dilapidations that you ought to repair, you neglect to do so, the tenant may repair the premises and deduct the expense of the repair from rent; recover that expense from you in any other lawful manner; or vacate the premises -- and a tenant who vacates on that ground is discharged from further payment of rent and from performing the lease's other conditions (§ 47-16-13).

There is no escrow mechanism, no statutory dollar cap on the deduction, no requirement that the tenant get your approval of the repair or the contractor, and no notice period fixed in days.

Two consequences to plan around. First, a deduction properly made under this section is not unpaid rent, so treating it as a nonpayment default and filing on it is a real risk. Second, on any claim under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 the court may award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party (§ 47-16-13.6), so a small repair dispute can carry your opponent's fees. Answering a written repair request promptly, in writing, with a date, is the only reliable way to keep this section from being used against you.

title: Selling a Property With a Tenant in It
bodyText: North Dakota imposes no duty to tell your tenant you are selling, and no statutory notice period before a sale -- but four other things bind you. The security deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to the buyer; you are not released from liability until that transfer actually happens, and the buyer is bound by North Dakota's deposit rules even though the buyer never received the deposit (§ 47-16-07.1(5)). The buyer steps into your rent remedies (§ 47-16-28), your tenant's remedies under the lease run against the buyer (§ 47-16-29), and your remedies run against anyone the tenant assigned to, for claims accruing while they held the assignment -- except where the assignment was security for a loan and was not accompanied by possession (§ 47-16-30). Separately, selling triggers seller-disclosure duties in Chapter 47-10 that have nothing to do with the lease. For a residential dwelling of four or fewer units you must give the buyer a written disclosure of all material facts you are aware could adversely and significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment, before final acceptance of the purchase agreement -- and that applies whether or not a real estate licensee is involved, subject to nine exemptions including foreclosure, fiduciary and immediate-family transfers (§ 47-10-02.1). Since 2025 you must also disclose in writing any knowledge you have of radon concentrations, give the buyer the prescribed radon warning to acknowledge by signature, and hand over any prior test results and evidence of mitigation reasonably available to you; comply and you are immune from radon-based claims (§ 47-10-02.2). And if the property sits in a homeowners' association or condominium project, you have ten days from executing the agreement to deliver the association's governing documents, budgets, assessments, litigation and violation history -- and if you do not, the buyer may void the purchase contract until they are delivered and for five days afterwards, or until the sale closes, whichever comes first (§ 47-10-02.3(6)).

title: No Radon Disclosure Duty When You Rent -- But There Is One When You Sell
bodyText: North Dakota requires no radon disclosure, testing, or warning from a landlord to a tenant, even though the EPA places the whole state in its highest-risk zone. The one mandatory disclosure at the start of a North Dakota tenancy is the signed condition statement (§ 47-16-07.2), and it says nothing about radon. The picture changes the moment you sell rather than rent: since 2025 a seller of residential real property must disclose any knowledge of radon concentrations in writing, give the buyer a prescribed radon warning to acknowledge by signature, and provide any prior test results and evidence of mitigation (§ 47-10-02.2). Testing and disclosing voluntarily to a tenant is still worth considering, since a habitability claim under § 47-16-13.1 does not require a disclosure statute to exist.

title: No Mold Disclosure Duty
bodyText: North Dakota has no mold disclosure requirement, no statutory mold standard, and no remediation timeline. Mold is not therefore risk-free: visible mold or the water intrusion behind it can put you in breach of the duty to keep the premises fit and habitable and to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (§ 47-16-13.1(1)(a)-(b)), and a tenant who gives you notice and gets no repair in a reasonable time can repair and deduct, or vacate and stop paying rent (§ 47-16-13). Treat a moisture complaint as a habitability matter on a clock rather than a disclosure question.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure or Treatment Rule
bodyText: North Dakota imposes no bed bug disclosure duty, no treatment timeline, and no allocation of treatment cost between landlord and tenant. An infestation is handled under the general duties instead: your obligation to keep the premises fit and habitable and to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (§ 47-16-13.1(1)(a)-(b)), against the tenant's obligation to keep the occupied part of the premises as clean and safe as its condition permits (§ 47-16-13.2(2)). Because nothing divides the cost by statute, whatever your lease says about pest treatment is what will govern -- so say it.

title: No Duty to Change the Locks for a Domestic Violence Victim
bodyText: North Dakota's domestic violence tenancy statute gives a victim one thing: the right to terminate the lease early on written notice, without penalty, paying the month of termination plus one additional month's rent subject to your duty to mitigate (§ 47-16-17.1). It does not give the tenant a right to require you to change the locks, and it does not give you a deadline, a cost allocation, or any immunity for doing so. If a tenant asks, you are deciding under the lease and under your own judgment, not under a statute -- and you still owe every remaining tenant on that lease quiet possession (§ 47-16-08) and the confidentiality duty in § 47-16-17.1(4), which bars you from disclosing the documentation the tenant gave you and carries statutory damages of $1,000 plus actual damages, fees and costs. A court order changes the picture, though. A civil protection order may exclude the abuser from the tenant's home (N.D.C.C. §§ 14-07.7-06(1)(b), 14-07.7-07(2)(b)). If a person excluded by an order asks you for keys or a new code, do not give them. Breaking the order is a class A misdemeanor and contempt of court (§ 14-07.7-17), and the police must arrest for it without a warrant (§ 14-07.7-18). Ask to see the order and follow what it says about the home. Your quiet-possession duty runs only against persons 'lawfully claiming' possession (§ 47-16-08). Send any dispute about who may be in the unit back to the court that issued the order. The order itself does not make you re-key, pay for a re-key, or act by any deadline.

title: No General Late Fee Cap (Except Mobile Home Parks) -- But Do Not Read That as No Limit
bodyText:
North Dakota sets no cap on late fees for ordinary residential tenancies, and no statutory grace period. Mobile home parks are the exception. A park may not charge a monthly late fee above ten percent of the monthly rent, or a daily late fee above five dollars a day (N.D.C.C. § 47-10-28(11), added in 2025). A violation carries a civil penalty of at least $2,500 plus attorney's fees (§ 47-10-28(12)). It is also a defense to the park's eviction case (§ 47-32-01.1).

For other rentals, the legislature has declined a general cap three times: bills to cap late rent fees were introduced in 2021 (HB 1440, HB 1442) and again in 2025 (SB 2236, which would have amended § 47-16-20 to cap a late fee at eight percent of the overdue rent). None became law.

The absence of a cap is not the absence of a limit. Two general contract sections reach a late fee directly: penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (§ 9-08-03), and a clause fixing damages in advance is void unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (§ 9-08-04). A late fee set at a level that looks punitive rather than like a genuine estimate of what a late payment actually costs you is therefore attackable in North Dakota on grounds that have nothing to do with a cap -- and § 47-16-13.3 unconscionability sits behind that. Keep the figure defensible and keep a reason for it.

Separately, North Dakota has no statute setting the order in which you must apply a tenant's payment, so whether a payment goes to rent first or to fees first is a contract question here, not a statutory one.

title: Stating the Purpose of the Lease Gives You Two Extra Remedies
bodyText: North Dakota attaches a specific consequence to a lease that states what the property is leased for. When real property is leased for a particular purpose the tenant must not use it for any other purpose, and if the tenant does, you may either hold the tenant responsible for the safety of the property during that use in all events, or treat the contract as rescinded (§ 47-16-11). The first of those is unusual and worth understanding: it is not a negligence standard. During a use outside the stated purpose the tenant answers for the property's safety whatever the cause, which shifts a category of loss you would otherwise carry. The second lets you treat the lease as at an end without waiting on the eviction chapter's grounds. Both depend on the lease actually stating a purpose -- which the residential-use clause does -- so this is a right you either capture in the drafting or forfeit silently.

title: When a Tenant Leaves Early: What You Can Collect and What You Must Do
bodyText:
North Dakota's rules here are narrower than they look, and they differ depending on how the tenancy ended. If you evict, the tenant stays liable for rent for the remainder of the term, and that section expressly does not relieve you of the duty to mitigate damages (§ 47-16-13.7). If the lease is terminated, you have a claim for possession and for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach (§ 47-16-13.4). If a lease ends before the time originally agreed, the tenant must pay the due proportion for the use actually made, unless that use was merely nominal and of no benefit to the tenant (§ 47-16-21).

What North Dakota does not have is a general statutory duty to mitigate covering every tenant who simply leaves: the mitigation section is written into the habitability group, applying to a party aggrieved under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 (§ 47-16-13.5), and the duty otherwise appears only in § 47-16-13.7 for an evicted tenant and § 47-16-17.1(5) for a domestic violence termination.

Do not treat that as licence to sit on an empty unit and bill the departed tenant: your own lease promises reasonable mitigation efforts, common law may supply the rest, and a flat early-termination or lease-break fee is separately exposed as a contractual penalty under § 9-08-03 or as liquidated damages under § 9-08-04. Re-rent, document the effort, and charge actual loss.

title: Deposit Return Deadline and Unclaimed Deposits
bodyText: Within 30 days after the lease ends and the tenant delivers possession, or after a different starting point North Dakota law sets (such as a domestic-violence termination), return the deposit with any interest the law requires, less lawful deductions, and a written itemization of anything you kept (N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.1). If the deposit goes unclaimed for a year after the lease ends, report and remit it under North Dakota's unclaimed property law (47-30.2-04). See the notes on interest, penalties and domestic-violence timing.

title: If a Tenant Dies
bodyText: If a tenant dies, a surviving co-tenant or the tenant's estate may choose to end the lease. It then ends on the last day of the month after the month of death, unless the term would have ended sooner, and the estate owes rent through that date (N.D.C.C. 47-16-18).

title: Fire or Casualty: When the Lease Ends
bodyText: If the greater part of the property, or the part that was the tenant's material reason for leasing it, is destroyed or damaged through no fault of the tenant, the tenant may end the lease (N.D.C.C. 47-16-17(2)). If the property is destroyed, the leasing terminates automatically (N.D.C.C. 47-16-14(4)) — and that provision has no fault exception, so a total loss the tenant caused still ends the lease and leaves you a damages claim rather than a continuing tenancy. North Dakota has no statutory rent abatement while repairs are made. But the money is not all or nothing. When a lease ends before the agreed time, the tenant pays only the due proportion of the rent for the use actually made of the property (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-21). The tenant pays nothing for that use if it was 'merely nominal and of no benefit' to the tenant.

title: Domestic Violence: Tenant's Right to End the Lease
bodyText: A North Dakota tenant who is a victim of domestic violence by a family or household member, or who fears imminent domestic violence against themselves or their minor children by such a person if they stay, may end the lease without penalty or liability (N.D.C.C. 47-16-17.1). The tenant must give you advance written notice, by mail, fax or in person before the tenancy ends, stating that they fear imminent domestic violence from a person named in a court order, an order prohibiting contact, a civil protection order or another record filed with a court; that they need to end the tenancy; and the date it will end. The tenant owes rent for the full month in which the tenancy ends plus one more month's rent, subject to your duty to mitigate, and must pay that on or before termination to be released from the rest of the term; rent and other amounts already owed remain due. The tenancy, including the right of possession, ends on the date in the notice, and it continues for any other tenants. See the notes on confidentiality and deposit timing.

title: Your Basic Habitability Duties
bodyText: North Dakota requires you to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; make all repairs needed to keep the property fit and habitable; keep common areas clean and safe; maintain the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply in good and safe working order; provide waste receptacles and arrange removal; and supply running water and reasonable hot water and heat, unless the building isn't required by law to have them or the heat or hot water is under the tenant's exclusive control through a direct utility connection (N.D.C.C. 47-16-13.1). See the note on the tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy.

title: Termination Notice Periods
bodyText: In North Dakota, either party may end a month-to-month tenancy by giving at least one calendar month's written notice, unless the parties agreed in writing to a longer period or a different notice time; rent is due through the termination date. If a lease doesn't specify its term, notice must be at least as long as the term itself, up to one calendar month. A lease that converts to month-to-month ends on the last day of a month with at least one calendar month's notice (N.D.C.C. 47-16-15). A lease notice requirement longer than one month only binds the tenant if they initial it (see the initialing clause). One asymmetry to plan around: the agreed period binds either party, so if you write a longer period into the lease you are bound to give it too — but the initialling rule that lets a tenant escape a longer period has no equivalent for you.

title: No Just-Cause Rule — the End of the Term Does End Possession
bodyText: North Dakota has no just-cause or good-cause eviction regime. Holding over after the termination of the lease or the expiration of the term is itself a ground for eviction (N.D.C.C. § 47-32-01(4)), so a lease that says possession ends when the term ends states North Dakota law rather than contradicting it, and you do not need a reason beyond the expiry. Four situational limits are worth knowing. The material-breach ground applies only to “a material term of the WRITTEN lease agreement” (§ 47-32-01(8)), so an oral North Dakota tenancy gives you no material-breach ground at all — you are left with nonpayment, holdover, or the disturbance ground. A tenant in a mobile home park may defend an eviction by showing you violated § 47-10-28, and the court may then refuse to order eviction (§ 47-32-01.1). On a showing that immediate restitution would work a substantial hardship on the tenant or the tenant's family, the court may stay the special execution for up to five days — except where the judgment rests wholly or partly on a disturbance of the peace (§ 47-32-04). And a tenant who exercised the domestic violence termination right is protected from retaliation in the rental of a dwelling (§ 47-16-17.1(10)).

title: Does North Dakota’s Consumer Fraud Law Reach a Lease? Unsettled
bodyText: North Dakota's consumer fraud statute (N.D.C.C. ch. 51-15) has no list of unfair practices — nothing about leaving blank spaces to be filled in after signing, nothing about giving the tenant a copy at signing, and no plain-language requirement. What it does have is a broad general standard: § 51-15-02 makes unlawful any deceptive act, fraud, false pretense, false promise or misrepresentation, with the intent that others rely on it, whether or not anyone was in fact misled. Separately, it makes unlawful any act or practice “which is unconscionable or which causes or is likely to cause substantial injury to a person which is not reasonably avoidable by the injured person and not outweighed by countervailing benefits to consumers or to competition.” Both limbs apply only “in connection with the sale or advertisement of any merchandise.” Whether that reaches renting a home is genuinely open. “Merchandise” is defined to include “real estate.” But “sale” is defined as a sale, offer for sale, or attempt to sell merchandise for consideration, and the definition never mentions a lease, a rental or leasing. So the act plainly covers selling a house and plainly does not list renting one; nothing in the chapter mentions a lease or rental of a dwelling anywhere. The advertising limb leans toward coverage, though. “Advertisement” includes any attempt to induce a person “to enter into any obligation or acquire any title or interest in any merchandise” (§ 51-15-01(1)), and a lease is arguably both. So treat your rental listings and ads as within reach. Treat it as a live risk rather than a settled exposure. The attorney general enforces the chapter, and a court may add a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation (§ 51-15-11). A tenant can also sue to recover money or property taken by an unlawful practice. If the court finds you acted knowingly, it may award up to three times actual damages, and it must award costs and attorney's fees (§ 51-15-09). Claims must be brought within four years of discovery (§ 51-15-12). The unconscionable limb needs no intent. North Dakota's own lease-specific unconscionability rule (§ 47-16-13.3) applies regardless.

title: No Plain-Language Requirement for a Lease
bodyText: North Dakota has no plain-language statute for consumer contracts, and none for residential leases. There is no readability standard, no required type size, no rule about defined terms, and no sanction for a lease a tenant finds hard to read. Writing plainly is still worth doing — § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision, and how a term was presented is part of what a court looks at — but nothing requires it.

title: Shifting Your Repair Duties to the Tenant Needs More Than a Lease Clause
bodyText:
North Dakota lets you move some of your own maintenance duties onto the tenant, but the route differs by property type and one of the two cannot be done in the lease at all. For a single-family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant performs your waste-receptacle and water-and-heat duties, and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodelling — but only if the transaction is entered into in good faith (§ 47-16-13.1(4)).

For any other dwelling unit, the tenant may agree to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodelling only if all four of these hold: the agreement is in good faith; it is set forth in a SEPARATE WRITING signed by the parties and supported by ADEQUATE CONSIDERATION; the work is not needed to cure a failure of your waste-receptacle duty; and the agreement does not diminish or affect your obligations to other tenants (§ 47-16-13.1(5)).

Because the statute requires a separate signed writing supported by its own consideration, a paragraph inside the lease cannot supply it. And you may not treat the tenant's performance of a single-family agreement as a condition of any obligation under the rental agreement (§ 47-16-13.1(6)) — so it cannot be a condition of renting. Your building-and-housing-code duty is never shiftable: where it is greater than any other duty in the list, it governs (§ 47-16-13.1(3)).

title: Where North Dakota Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: North Dakota's leasing chapter leaves six things to the lease, and a lease that is silent takes the statutory default instead of the choice. (1) The products of the property during the term belong to the tenant “in the absence of any agreement to the contrary” (§ 47-16-04), so if a garden, fruit trees or standing hay matter to you, say so. (2) A lease with an automatic renewal clause escapes the holdover-converts-to-month-to-month presumption (§ 47-16-06) — see "Automatic Renewal" clause. (3) A single-family residence may shift some of your maintenance duties to the tenant (§ 47-16-13.1(4)) — see tenant-duty-shift-single-family-nd. (4) Any other dwelling unit may do so only in a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration (§ 47-16-13.1(5)), which the lease cannot be. (5) A month-to-month tenancy takes one calendar month's notice “unless the parties have otherwise agreed in writing to a longer notice period or a different notice time” (§ 47-16-15(2)) — and a longer period binds the tenant only if initialled (§ 47-16-15(4)). (6) Double-letting of a room cannot be agreed around at all: the first tenant takes the whole room “notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary” (§ 47-16-26). Two further terms are lawful but not offered in this library. A landlord's own right to terminate after a fire or casualty: North Dakota gives you none, and nothing bars the lease from creating one, but it has to be drafted against § 47-16-14(4), which already ends the lease on destruction, and against § 47-16-17(2), which is the tenant's right and cannot be taken away. A clause reserving the products of the property: lawful under § 47-16-04, but it belongs in an agricultural or rural lease rather than a dwelling lease. If you want either, add your own clause and take advice first.

title: North Dakota Writes a Covenant of Quiet Possession Into Every Lease
bodyText: North Dakota does not leave quiet possession to the lease's wording. An agreement to lease real property binds the lessor to secure to the lessee the quiet possession of the property during the term, against all persons lawfully claiming the same (§ 47-16-08). The duty runs against lawful claims — a mortgagee, a buyer, a co-owner, a superior title — rather than against a trespasser or a noisy neighbour, and it is yours whether or not the lease mentions it. Two consequences for you. A tenant whose possession you fail to secure may terminate if you do not fulfil the obligation within a reasonable time after a request (§ 47-16-17(1)). And it is the reason the tenant must pass on any notice of a proceeding against the property and may not recognise anyone else as landlord without your consent or a court judgment (§ 47-16-25) — your duty and that one are two halves of the same arrangement.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent Setting
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute addressing algorithmic or software-assisted rent setting, and no ban on using a third-party pricing service or on sharing rent data with one. Federal antitrust law still applies to agreements among competing landlords, and § 47-16-02.1 separately bars a political subdivision from controlling what you may charge — so neither a local rent cap nor a state rule stands in the way, and the exposure such a service creates is a federal one rather than a North Dakota one.

title: No Rule on Calling Fees “Rent”
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute that lets you designate fees as additional rent, and none that stops you. Nothing in the leasing chapter defines rent, and no provision restricts what a lease may treat as rent. That silence matters most at eviction: the nonpayment ground is “fails to pay rent for three days after the rent is due” (§ 47-32-01(4)), and whether an unpaid fee the lease calls rent supports that ground has not been settled in North Dakota. Treat it as unsettled rather than available. This library's shared payment clause applies each payment to rent first and only then to other charges, which keeps an unpaid fee from turning into an apparent rent shortfall — the practical protection, whatever the label question turns out to be.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix the Tenant’s Breach and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: North Dakota gives you no URLTA-style right to remedy a tenant's breach yourself and recover the cost as rent. What the chapter gives you instead is a termination right: you may terminate the lease and reclaim the property before the end of the term if the tenant uses it contrary to the agreement, or does not make the repairs the tenant is bound to make within a reasonable time after a request (§ 47-16-16). You may also sue for the cost — the tenant must repair deteriorations or injuries caused by the tenant's ordinary negligence (§ 47-16-10), and a terminated lease leaves you a separate claim for actual damages (§ 47-16-13.4). What you cannot do is treat the repair cost as rent and evict for nonpayment of it; that route does not exist in North Dakota, and trying it risks the eviction.

title: No Rule Against Blank Spaces in the Lease
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute requiring a written lease to have every blank space completed, and no provision making an incomplete lease a breach or unenforceable. Leaving blanks is still a bad idea — § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision, and a term filled in after signing invites exactly that argument — but there is no North Dakota rule to point at, and no consumer-protection list of unfair practices that names it.

title: Statutory Forms North Dakota Supplies
bodyText: North Dakota supplies no form for a residential lease and no form for an eviction notice — the three days' written notice of intention to evict has no prescribed wording (§ 47-32-02). Two forms are set out verbatim in statute, and only one is likely to touch you. If a tenant's cheque is dishonoured and you want the civil penalty rather than just the collection fee, § 6-08-16(4) prints the notice of dishonour you must mail, including its demand that the tenant pay within ten days; the notice itself is optional, but the penalty depends on it. The other, § 47-16-36, prints a notice for cancelling a forfeited oil, gas or mineral lease and has nothing to do with a dwelling. The move-in condition statement § 47-16-07.2 requires is a mandatory document with no prescribed form — the statute says what it must describe and who must sign, and leaves the layout to you.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute about a tenant installing a security camera, a video doorbell or a monitoring device at a rented home — nothing permitting it, nothing banning it, and no rule about recording common areas or a neighbour's door. So the lease governs. Two limits are worth knowing anyway: a camera or doorbell that is screwed, drilled or wired into the property is an alteration under this library's alterations clause and needs your written consent, while a device that simply sits on a shelf or plugs in is not; and a request to install one as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is a fair housing question rather than an alterations question, which North Dakota law does reach.

title: Medical Cannabis and Your Smoking Ban
bodyText:
North Dakota allows medical marijuana for registered qualifying patients and has not legalised recreational use. Its medical chapter says almost nothing about renting. It expressly does not require “a landlord to allow production or processing on rental property” (§ 19-24.1-34(1)(c)) — production and processing only, not possession or use by a patient. It bans consumption on school, correctional and child-care grounds, and where the smoke or vapour would be inhaled by a minor who is not the patient (§ 19-24.1-33), but not in a rented home. And it protects a registered qualifying patient from “arrest or prosecution or the denial of any right or privilege” (§ 19-24.1-32(1)) without saying whether housing is among those privileges.

The result is an untested gap: your flat lease ban on smoking marijuana is not void — nothing in North Dakota law voids it, and there is no constitutional cannabis provision here — but whether it can be enforced against a registered qualifying patient's medical use has not been decided. A ban on smoking of any kind, applied to every tenant alike and justified by odour, damage and fire risk, is the stronger ground than one aimed at marijuana; and a patient who asks to use a non-smoked form is making a request worth considering on its own.

title: Renting a Property With a Second Dwelling Unit
bodyText:
North Dakota has no accessory-dwelling-unit statute, so nothing in state law gives a tenant the right to an accessory unit and nothing in state law stops a city from forbidding one. But N.D.C.C. § 47-16-27 says a tenant "may ... [o]ccupy the buildings" and "has no rights to the property other than such as are given the tenant by the agreement ... or by the provisions of this section" - buildings, plural. If the lease rents "the property" without naming the structures, a tenant can argue § 47-16-27(1) lets them occupy every building on it, the accessory unit included. The lease clause on the scope of the premises is what keeps the accessory unit out of the tenancy.

CAUTIOUS COURSE on the zoning question, which state law leaves to local ordinance: North Dakota zoning is delegated to cities (N.D.C.C. ch. 40-47), counties (ch. 11-33) and townships (ch. 58-03), which may regulate "the location and use of buildings, structures, and land for trade, industry, residence, or other purposes" (§ 40-47-01). None of those chapters mentions accessory units. Do not assume an accessory unit may lawfully be rented at all. Confirm with the city or county zoning office in writing before advertising a second unit, and do not rely on the lease clause to legalise a unit the ordinance does not permit - the clause allocates the unit between landlord and tenant, it does not create a right to use it.

title: No Alarm-Tampering Fee - and Check § 23-13-15 Before Assuming You Have No Alarm Duty
bodyText: Default rule: North Dakota has no alarm-tampering fee. There is no provision authorising a charge for removing or disabling a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm and no figure to put in the lease, so there is no Oregon-style ORS 90.302(2)(c) analog here. North Dakota does impose the alarm DUTY, in section 23-13-15. All residential rental property, other than lodging establishments and assisted living facilities covered by section 23-09-02.1, "must be equipped with smoke detection systems or other approved alarm systems". In a single-family rental the tenant maintains and inspects the system. In other dwellings you install it and ensure it works "upon the occupancy of each new tenant", and the tenant maintains it during the tenancy. On a deaf tenant's written request you must provide a visual alarm, unless you rent out only one building of four or fewer units. Willfully failing to install a system is a class B misdemeanor. Building and housing codes add to this through section 47-16-13.1(1)(a). You still have a remedy for tampering, and you already have it without a lease clause: section 23-13-15(1) makes the tenant responsible for maintaining the system during the tenancy, section 47-16-13.2(6) obliges the tenant not to destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises deliberately or negligently, section 47-16-09 requires the tenant to use ordinary care to keep the property in good condition, section 47-16-10 makes the tenant repair deteriorations or injuries caused by the tenant's ordinary negligence, and section 47-16-07.1(3)(a) lets you apply the security deposit to damage caused by the tenant's negligence. What you may not do is set a figure. Section 9-08-03 voids a penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance and section 9-08-04 voids -- to that extent -- an amount fixed in advance as the measure of damages, unless the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. The cost of restoring an alarm is an invoice, so it is neither impracticable nor extremely difficult to fix, and a flat "$250 alarm tampering fee" is the textbook void term. Note what the legislature did do: section 47-16-07.6(2) authorises a fixed "damage fee" of up to one thousand dollars, and only for fraudulent service-animal disability documentation after a plea or conviction. That is the one flat landlord fee North Dakota has created, which shows it knows how, and it did not create one here. What to do: put the duty not to disable or remove an alarm in your rules, test and document the alarms at move-in on the section 47-16-07.2 condition statement, and when tampering happens charge the actual cost of parts and labour against a receipt -- not a stated fee.

title: No animal-care entry right in North Dakota — what to do when a pet is shut in an empty unit
bodyText:
The default rule in North Dakota is that a landlord has no entry right tied to an animal. Nothing in the North Dakota statutes gives a landlord a right — or a duty — to enter a dwelling unit to feed, water, check on or remove a tenant's animal, and nothing lets a lease create one. Your only entry authority is N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.3: you may enter at any time in an emergency, or on a reasonable belief that the tenant has abandoned the premises, or on a reasonable belief that the tenant is in substantial violation of the lease; otherwise you may enter only during reasonable hours and in a reasonable manner, and only after notifying the tenant of a time certain and obtaining consent (consent is presumed if the tenant does not object to that notice). An animal shut in an empty unit will usually be evidence that supports a reasonable belief of abandonment or an emergency, and that is the lawful basis to go in — not any animal-care provision, because North Dakota has none.

What to do. (1) Document first: dated photographs, the notice you gave, what the neighbours reported, how long the rent and the mail have gone untouched. Write down the belief and the facts behind it before you enter, because § 47-16-07.3(1) protects a reasonable belief, not a hunch. (2) Call animal control or law enforcement rather than taking the animal yourself. Chapter 36-21.2 gives the job to the officer. Under § 36-21.2-08 'A law enforcement officer may take custody of an animal if the officer has reasonable cause to believe that the animal has been abandoned', must provide care, and notifies the owner; an unclaimed animal may be sold, adopted or destroyed after five days, and the owner gets it back only by showing it was not abandoned and paying the costs of care. Abandonment, a class A misdemeanor for the owner (§ 36-21.2-04), means giving up custody 'without placing the animal into the custody or control of another person' able and willing to care for it. Nothing in the chapter gives a landlord a role. (3) Do not dispose of, rehome or sell the animal, and do not treat it as abandoned property under your lease — the North Dakota statutes do not authorise a landlord to do any of that. (4) At signing, collect an emergency contact for the animal and the name of someone who may care for it if the tenant is away or hospitalised. That costs nothing and is the only thing that reliably prevents this problem.

If the unit is in a mobile home park, § 47-10-28 adds nothing about animals, but it does require you to acknowledge a tenant complaint within two business days and to have an emergency contact number manned at all times — a neighbour's call about a distressed animal is such a complaint. A violation of § 47-10-28 carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and is a defence to an eviction.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText:
In North Dakota the landlord's maintenance duty is keyed to what the landlord supplied. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(d) requires the landlord to "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord." There is no North Dakota statute presuming that an appliance which is merely present was supplied by the landlord - but there is also nothing stopping a tenant arguing it was. The record is what decides it, and the record is the signed statement N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.2 already makes you give.

What the landlord should actually do: fill in both lists, and fill in the § 47-16-07.2 statement of condition on the same day, item by item. An excluded appliance that Tenant installs stays Tenant's: under N.D.C.C. § 47-06-04 a tenant may remove anything affixed "for the purpose of trade, manufacture, ornament, or domestic use" at any time during the term if removal can be done without injury to the premises, unless it has become an integral part of them - so do not write a clause claiming Tenant's appliances become yours. Do not try to exclude an appliance you actually supply in order to escape the § 47-16-13.1(1)(d) duty; that is a duty shift, not an exclusion, and in anything other than a single-family residence it needs everything § 47-16-13.1(5) requires: good faith, a separate writing signed by both parties, **adequate** consideration, work that is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subdivision (e) of subsection 1 (the waste-receptacle and removal duty), and no diminution of Landlord's obligations to other tenants. Note also that § 47-16-13.1(6)'s bar on treating performance as a condition of the lease refers by its words to 'the separate agreement described in subsection 4', the single-family provision; the cautious course, taken here, is to observe the bar for a subsection 5 agreement too.

title: What You May Charge an Applicant Before the Lease Exists
bodyText: Default rule: North Dakota does not regulate application or screening money at all. There is no fee cap and no CPI adjustment, no refund right if the fee goes unused or if an earlier applicant takes the unit, no exemption for a minor household member, no duty to disclose estimated rent, fees, availability date or screening criteria before you take the money, no unit-count threshold, and no closed list of permitted up-front money. Chapter 47-16 carries no list of prohibited lease terms of any kind. That is not a free hand -- three provisions still bind you. First, labels do not control: section 47-16-07.1(1) reaches money required as security "however denominated", so any up-front amount you hold against rent, damage or the unit itself is a security deposit, capped at one month's rent, payable into a federally insured interest-bearing account for the tenant's benefit, and recoverable in treble damages if withheld without reasonable justification (section 47-16-07.1(4)). A fee that is genuinely consumed by screening and never credited back is outside that section. Second, you may not charge any fee to accept cash, a check or a money order for the application money or for anything else payable under the lease (section 47-16-20.1). Third, under section 9-08-01 a contract provision is unlawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law or to the policy of express law; sections 9-08-03 and 9-08-04 void a penalty, and void -- to that extent -- a sum fixed in advance as the measure of a loss, unless the actual loss would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. A screening fee charged before any tenancy is not a charge for breach, so that pair does not reach it, but it does reach any "application fee" you keep as a forfeiture when an approved applicant walks away. What to do: set the fee at your actual screening cost and keep the invoice; state in writing, before you take the money, that it is nonrefundable and what it pays for; never credit it toward rent or the deposit; and if you take money to hold a unit off the market, treat it as a deposit under section 47-16-07.1, not as a forfeitable fee.

title: North Dakota has no asbestos disclosure duty for landlords - but its asbestos rules bind you when you renovate a building of five or more units
bodyText:
Default rule first: nothing in the North Dakota statutes implies an asbestos warranty, an asbestos disclosure or an asbestos testing duty into a residential lease, and no statute requires a lease to say anything about asbestos. What the lease statute does impose is N.D.C.C. 47-16-13.1(1)(a): the landlord must "comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and subsection 3 says that where that duty is greater than any other duty in the subsection, the landlord's duty is determined by reference to it. That makes a requirement living in the building code a binding lease obligation. The State Building Code, enforced locally under 54-21.3-05, consists of the international building, residential, mechanical and fuel gas codes adopted by rule (54-21.3-03(1)); no North Dakota statute or state rule ties an asbestos duty to a lease. So the accurate statement is: the North Dakota statutes and state rules impose no asbestos disclosure duty on a landlord, and the asbestos duties they do impose arise when you renovate or demolish.

Where North Dakota does legislate about asbestos, the duty sits on someone other than the landlord. N.D.C.C. 23.1-06-05 licenses asbestos and lead-based-paint contractors, certifies their workers and has the department set abatement standards at least as stringent as the federal ones; chs. 32-46, 32-46.1 and 32-46.2 govern asbestos successor liability, asbestos bankruptcy trust transparency and asbestos civil actions; 28-01-47 limits the time to bring an asbestos claim. None of those is a landlord duty and none mentions a lease. North Dakota's one environmental-condition disclosure statute is 47-10-02.1, whose written form must cover "latent defects, general condition, environmental issues, structural systems, and mechanical issues" - but it applies only to "a transaction for the sale, exchange, or purchase of real property", and its sibling 47-10-02.2(1)(a) defines a "buyer" as a person acquiring, or acquiring the right to acquire, title. A tenant is not a buyer. Chapter 47-16 carries exactly one lease-accompanying document requirement, the condition-of-premises statement in 47-16-07.2, and asbestos is not in it.

What to do: do not print an asbestos rider as though North Dakota required it - that invites the tenant to believe a state right exists. If you know of asbestos-containing material, either record it in the 47-16-07.2 condition statement or disclose it voluntarily, and use a contractor licensed under 23.1-06-05 for any disturbance. If you own a residential building of five or more units, North Dakota's own asbestos rule applies when you renovate or demolish. Before work starts you must 'thoroughly inspect the affected facility' for asbestos, and above set quantities you must give the Department of Environmental Quality written notice, at least ten working days ahead for a demolition (N.D. Admin. Code ch. 33.1-15-13, subsection 6 of the asbestos standard). Buildings of four or fewer units are excluded from that rule. Before relying on this absence, check your municipal code and the locally enforced State Building Code.

title: You Owe a Buyer Association Documents, Not a Tenant
bodyText: Default rule: North Dakota requires no association disclosure to a tenant.
