A lease of a unit in a condominium or a homeowners' development need not disclose the association's obligations, attach or summarise the declaration, bylaws or rules, carry the owner's statement that the owner knows the condominium law and bylaws, send a copy of the lease to the board, or carry any tenant statement for an access-controlled community. There is no Montgomery County-style Maryland rule and no Puerto Rico-style required statement. The disclosure duty North Dakota does have runs the other way, to a purchaser, and it is new. Under section 47-10-02.3, created by Senate Bill 2229, 2025 Session Laws chapter 422, effective August 1, 2025, a seller of a property subject to the rules and regulations of a homeowners' association or condominium project must disclose fifteen specified items in writing to a prospective buyer by an agreed date or within ten days of executing the agreement to sell -- among them the periodic assessment and unpaid assessments, approved special assessments, a copy of the bylaws, amendments, supplemental declarations, rules or regulations and the minutes of the last two meetings, reserve and budget information, insurance documents, unsatisfied judgments and pending suits, uncured violations relating to the unit, transfer fees, the remedies for nonpayment, the collection policy, "Notice of any homeowners' association or condominium project restrictions related to the leasing of a unit", the amenities, and the association's contact details. The association must furnish those documents within ten days of the seller's request and may charge a reasonable fee for them, disclosed before final acceptance. None of that is owed to a tenant. What to do: because nothing makes you disclose and the association's rules reach your tenant only through your lease, hand the tenant the current rules at signing, attach them to the lease and have the tenant initial them, and identify the association and its contact. Where the association restricts leasing, say so in the lease rather than leaving the tenant to discover a cap that could cost them the tenancy. If you bought the unit on or after August 1, 2025, your own section 47-10-02.3 packet is the fastest source of the rules, budget and leasing restrictions to pass on. If you did not, section 47-04.1-07(3) requires all bylaws, rules and regulations to be reduced to writing and made available to every owner of any interest in the project, so you can demand them from the association as owner; and section 47-04.1-07(1) requires a true copy of the bylaws to be annexed to the recorded declaration, so a recorder search is your fallback.

title: Attorney's Fees: Left to Your Agreement, With Two Statutes to Watch
bodyText: North Dakota leaves attorney's fees in civil actions to the agreement of the parties, express or implied (N.D.C.C. § 28-26-01(1)), so a lease fee clause is permitted - and this library's default clause makes fees mutual, recoverable by whichever party prevails. Two statutes sit around that. First, whatever the lease says, a court must award reasonable actual and statutory costs including attorney's fees to the prevailing party on a finding that a claim was frivolous, where there is such a complete absence of actual facts or law that a reasonable person could not have thought a court would rule for the claimant, and only if the prevailing party pleaded the claim's frivolous nature in a responsive pleading (§ 28-26-01(2)). Second, § 28-26-04 voids a provision for an attorney's fee on default or collection in any note, bond, mortgage, security agreement or other evidence of debt. A residential lease is not one of those instruments, so a lease fee clause is not void on its face - but a clause aimed at collecting rent arrears sits closer to that line than one aimed at recovering possession. Separately, on a habitability claim the court may award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party (§ 47-16-13.6), and a domestic-violence violation carries fees and costs (§ 47-16-17.1(11)).

title: North Dakota has no balcony or deck inspection law - the duty you owe runs through the code and the common-area rule
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a landlord to have balconies, decks, stairways, landings or other exterior elevated elements inspected - not on a cycle, not by a licensed professional, not before a sale or a refinance, and not at all. There is no report to file, no record-retention period, no unit-count threshold and no penalty. "Balcony", "exterior elevated element", "load-bearing", "cantilever", "railing", "porch" and "weight limit" produce nothing in any North Dakota statute searched. The only time the word "structural" appears in any statute chapter in this research is 47-10-02.1(2), which makes a SELLER's written disclosure form cover "latent defects, general condition, environmental issues, structural systems, and mechanical issues" - a seller-to-buyer duty in a sale transaction, and the sibling that proves the negative here, since 47-10-02.2(1)(a) defines a buyer by reference to acquiring title and a tenant is not a buyer.

Two real duties fill the gap, and both are already implied into every lease, which is why this is education rather than a clause. First, 47-16-13.1(1)(c): the landlord must "keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition". A shared balcony, exterior stair, landing or walkway is a common area, so its safety is your statutory obligation without any inspection statute. Second, the code route, and it is the one that changes this answer: 47-16-13.1(1)(a) requires compliance with "applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety" and 47-16-13.1(3) makes that duty controlling where it is the greater one - so a guard-height, live-load, flashing or inspection requirement living in the State Building Code is a binding lease obligation. The State Building Code, ch. 54-21.3, consists of the international building, residential, mechanical and fuel gas codes adopted by rule, enforced by the city, township or county that elects to (54-21.3-03(1), (6)); the chapter itself sets no balcony inspection duty, and any guard or load figure lives in those model codes. So the honest statement is that the statutes impose no balcony inspection duty, not that North Dakota has no balcony rule. Also relevant: 47-16-13.1(1)(b) requires all repairs necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable, and 47-16-13.1(1)(d) requires landlord-supplied facilities to be kept "in good and safe working order and condition".

The enforcement machinery that does exist is in ch. 18-01, the State Fire Marshal Department chapter: 18-01-04 (rules for prevention of fires to be issued), 18-01-14 (abatement of fire hazards), 18-01-15 (abatement of conditions dangerous to persons - order - failure to comply - penalty), 18-01-16 (order of abatement - to whom directed - contents - how served - service by publication), 18-01-17 and 18-01-18 (appeals), 18-01-19 to 18-01-26 (court proceedings and judgment) and 18-01-27 (costs and the lien for them). So North Dakota's answer to a dangerous fire condition is a fire marshal's abatement order against the property, enforceable in district court with a cost lien - a regulatory route, not a lease term and not a disclosure. Those sections were read whole. Section 18-01-15 lets the fire marshal order 'the immediate removal or correction' of 'any condition which is a danger or a menace to the safety of life and limb of the occupants', and an owner, agent or occupant who fails to comply within the time set commits a class B misdemeanor. The order may be made against 'the owner, lessee, or occupant' (18-01-16), and enforcement costs become a lien on the premises (18-01-27).

What to do: inspect anyway, on a schedule you set, and keep dated records with photographs - a failed balcony is a catastrophic-injury exposure and 9-08-02 means you cannot contract out of responsibility for your own willful injury or violation of law, which includes a breach of the 47-16-13.1 duties. Do not print an exculpatory clause for balcony collapse and do not print a tenant waiver of inspection rights: North Dakota has no inspection right to waive, so the waiver is empty and it tells the tenant they gave something up. Do not shift structural inspection to the tenant: in anything other than a single-family residence, 47-16-13.1(5) reaches only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, needs good faith plus a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration, must not diminish your obligations to other tenants, and 47-16-13.1(6) bars making performance a condition of the lease. A sensible lease rule - no overloading, no grills, no attaching anything to a railing, report damage immediately - is fine as a house rule, but it is yours, not the statute's. Finally, check the locally enforced building code and your municipal ordinance, which are outside this research and are where a real inspection requirement would sit.

title: Do not put a binding arbitration clause in a North Dakota lease until one statute is read
bodyText:
THE DEFAULT RULE FIRST, AND IN NORTH DAKOTA IT STARTS FROM VOIDNESS. N.D.C.C. s 9-08-05: 'Every stipulation or condition in a contract by which any party thereto is restricted from enforcing that party's rights under the contract by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals or which limits the time within which that party thus may enforce that party's rights is VOID, EXCEPT AS OTHERWISE SPECIFICALLY PERMITTED BY THE LAWS OF THIS STATE.' A binding arbitration clause is exactly a stipulation restricting a party from enforcing rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals. So in North Dakota the starting point is NOT 'arbitration clauses are enforceable'. The starting point is that the clause is VOID unless a statute specifically permits it.

THE PERMISSION EXISTS: CHAPTER 32-29.3. North Dakota's Uniform Arbitration Act says in s 32-29.3-06(1): 'An agreement contained in a record to submit to arbitration any existing or subsequent controversy arising between the parties to the agreement is valid, enforceable, and irrevocable except upon a ground that exists at law or in equity for the revocation of a contract.' That is the specific permission s 9-08-05 asks for, and it has no exception for leases, consumers or tort claims. Under s 32-29.3-03(3) it governs an agreement to arbitrate 'whenever made'. Under s 32-29.3-04(2), before a dispute arises a party may not give up the motion procedure (s 32-29.3-05(1)), the validity rule (s 32-29.3-06(1)), provisional remedies (s 32-29.3-08), subpoenas (s 32-29.3-17(1)-(2)), jurisdiction (s 32-29.3-26), appeals (s 32-29.3-28), or the right to a lawyer (s 32-29.3-16).

(1) 'Does a statute let the parties agree in the lease to binding arbitration of tenancy disputes, and what must stay in court (possession actions) or be preserved (the right to counsel)?' (the Alaska shape, AS 34.03.345(b), 09.43.310(b)). Yes, through the general act: s 32-29.3-06(1) covers 'any existing or subsequent controversy'. North Dakota has NO landlord-tenant arbitration provision -- nothing in chapter 47-16, 47-32 or 47-10 -- so there is no statutory carve-out for possession. The right to counsel is preserved: s 32-29.3-16 says 'A party to an arbitration proceeding may be represented by a lawyer', and s 32-29.3-04(2)(d) forbids waiving it before a dispute. (2) 'Does the state arbitration act exclude personal injury or tort claims?'. No: s 32-29.3-03 sets only dates of application, and chapter 32-29.3 has no tort or consumer exclusion.

THE ONE PLACE NORTH DAKOTA LAW DOES EXPRESSLY PERMIT BINDING ARBITRATION IN HOUSING -- AND IT IS NOT YOUR LEASE. s 14-02.5-22 ('Conciliation'): where a discriminatory housing practice complaint has been filed with the department, 'A conciliation agreement between a respondent and the complainant is subject to departmental approval. A CONCILIATION AGREEMENT MAY PROVIDE FOR BINDING ARBITRATION or another method of dispute resolution. Dispute resolution that results from a conciliation agreement may authorize appropriate relief, including monetary relief.' That is a specific statutory permission -- but it is confined to a department-approved conciliation agreement reached after a complaint, it is not something a lease can invoke, and it says nothing about a term agreed at the start of a tenancy. Read for what it is worth and no further.

WHAT STILL APPLIES. (a) POSSESSION. North Dakota's eviction is a statutory proceeding 'maintainable in the proper DISTRICT COURT' (s 47-32-01), with a summons, a court-set appearance of not fewer than three nor more than fifteen days (s 47-32-02), and sheriff or process-server service. An arbitrator cannot issue a writ of possession, and nothing in this research suggests an eviction may be arbitrated. Keep possession out. (b) s 9-08-03 still voids contractual penalties and s 9-08-04 still voids damages fixed in advance, whoever decides the dispute. (c) s 47-16-13.3 (unconscionability) still applies, including to a settlement waiving a right under ss 47-16-13.1 to 47-16-13.6. (d) s 47-16-13.6 lets a court award reasonable attorney's fees to 'the prevailing party' in a habitability action, which cuts both ways and which an arbitration clause might inadvertently give away. (e) IN A MOBILE HOME PARK, arbitration is the wrong instinct outright: s 47-10-28(14) provides that 'the district court of the county in which the dispute arose has original jurisdiction', and that for civil damages under subsection 12 'the tenant may ELECT to commence the action in small claims court or district court'. A statutory election between two COURTS is not easily squared with a lease term sending the matter to an arbitrator, and s 47-10-28(12)'s civil penalty of not less than $2,500 plus actual fees and costs, with s 47-32-01.1 making a violation a defence to the eviction, is not worth risking on an untested clause.

WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY DO, AND THIS IS THE PRACTICAL ANSWER. An arbitration clause in a North Dakota residential lease is lawful, but it is rarely worth it. If you use one: keep possession, and a park tenant's small-claims election, out of it; do not limit the right to a lawyer, fees or remedies; and keep it even-handed, because s 32-29.3-06(1) still lets a court refuse an agreement 'upon a ground that exists at law or in equity for the revocation of a contract', and s 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse an unconscionable term. Whether an eviction could be compelled to arbitration only case law could settle, so carve it out. If you want the benefit of staying out of court without that risk, use the notice-and-informal-resolution clause instead (see the informal-dispute-resolution row), which is drafted expressly NOT to restrict either party's access to the ordinary tribunals and so does not engage s 9-08-05 at all. Because the general act is the specific permission § 9-08-05 asks for, a clause that keeps those protections is valid. The library now offers an optional clause, "Binding Arbitration of Money Claims" clause, built on these limits: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury and emergency claims kept in court, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you.

title: Do Not Write an Automatic Carpet-Cleaning Charge into a North Dakota Lease
bodyText: Default rule: North Dakota has no carpet statute. The word "carpet" appears nowhere in the landlord-tenant law. There is no provision letting you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, no condition precedent such as Alaska's requirement that the carpets were professionally cleaned before the tenancy (AS 34.03.120(c)), and no condition-and-age test or ten-year carpet rule of the Colorado kind (C.R.S. section 38-12-103(11)). That absence does not give you a free hand -- it leaves you with a rule that is stricter than most of those statutes. Section 47-16-07.1(3) lets you apply the security deposit to exactly three things: damage from the tenant's pet or from the negligence of the tenant or the tenant's guest; unpaid rent; and "the costs of cleaning or other repairs which were the responsibility of the lessee, and which are necessary to return the dwelling unit to its original state when the lessee took possession, reasonable wear and tear excepted." Two limits in that sentence decide this topic. It is measured against the unit's original state when the tenant took possession, and it excepts reasonable wear and tear. A carpet that is simply older and more walked-on at the end of the term than at the start is wear and tear, so the cost of cleaning or replacing it is not deductible. A blanket clause charging every tenant for professional carpet cleaning regardless of condition is therefore a charge for wear and tear and a sum fixed in advance as the measure of a loss -- void to that extent under section 9-08-04 unless the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, which a cleaner's invoice shows it is not -- and, if you then take it out of the deposit, it is money withheld without reasonable justification, which section 47-16-07.1(4) punishes with treble damages. What to do: use the section 47-16-07.2 condition statement, which the landlord must provide and both parties sign and which is prima facie proof of the condition of the premises at the start of the tenancy. Record and photograph the carpet's condition there, and at move-out charge the actual cost of cleaning only the soiling that goes beyond reasonable wear and tear, itemised within thirty days as section 47-16-07.1(3) requires. If you want the carpet professionally cleaned between every tenancy, pay for it as a turnover cost.

title: Can Your Lease Change the Casualty and Mitigation Rules? Mostly Yes, With Three Limits
bodyText: North Dakota attaches no non-waiver clause to either rule, so both are variable by agreement - within limits. The casualty rules: the leasing terminates by the destruction of the property, with no fault exception, so a total loss the tenant caused still ends the lease (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-14(4)); and the tenant may terminate where the greater part, or the part that was the material inducement, perishes from any cause other than the tenant's ordinary negligence (§ 47-16-17(2)). The mitigation rules: a party aggrieved under the habitability sections has a duty to mitigate (§ 47-16-13.5), and an evicted tenant owes rent for the rest of the term subject to your duty to mitigate (§ 47-16-13.7). Three limits bound what the lease can do with any of it. A court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision, and a settlement waiving a habitability right is itself reviewable (§ 47-16-13.3). A contractual penalty is void and damages fixed in advance are void unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (§§ 9-08-03, 9-08-04) - which is what a clause shifting the whole loss of a casualty onto the tenant looks like. And a clause restricting a party from enforcing its rights by the usual legal proceedings, or shortening the time to do so, is void unless a North Dakota statute permits it (§ 9-08-05). In practice: shifting a tenant-caused loss to the tenant is on solid ground because the statute already carves tenant negligence out of the tenant's exit right; waiving your own mitigation duty after an eviction is the weakest thing you could try, because § 47-16-13.7 states it as a limit on your own recovery. One more rule belongs with these, and the library has been missing it: section 47-16-21. When a leasing of real property is terminated before the time originally agreed upon, the tenant must pay the due proportion of the lease for the use the tenant actually made of the property - unless that use was "merely nominal and of no benefit to the lessee", in which case the tenant pays nothing for it. So a casualty termination is not all or nothing on the money: it proportions what the tenant owes for the period actually used, and can excuse it entirely. That rule carries no non-waiver clause either, so it is variable by agreement within the same three limits.

title: No certificate-of-occupancy disclosure in North Dakota - the phrase is not in the Century Code at all
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a landlord to hold a certificate of occupancy, to show one to a tenant, to attach one to the lease, to state its number or date, or to disclose that the unit has never had one. There is no state rule making rent uncollectable or a lease void for want of a certificate, and no tenant remedy keyed to one.

Here is the whole picture, because it is the opposite of what a lease drafter expects. The phrase "certificate of occupancy" appears in NO section name anywhere in the North Dakota Century Code, and neither does "occupancy permit". Their only occurrences in this research are incidental: a 2025 session law conditioning an agriculture grant on issuance of a certificate of occupancy for the facility, a cannabis-business licensing provision requiring "a current certificate of occupancy, or equivalent document, to demonstrate compliance with the provisions of state and local fire code", and - most tellingly - a nonpublic-school provision requiring the school to "hold a valid occupancy permit IF REQUIRED BY THE SCHOOL'S MUNICIPALITY". That last phrasing is the answer: in North Dakota an occupancy permit is a municipal instrument, and the legislature writes as though it may or may not exist depending on the city. The State Building Code is ch. 54-21.3 and enforcement is elective: a city, township or county that elects to enforce a building code must adopt the state code (54-21.3-03(6)), and a city or township may hand enforcement to the county (54-21.3-05) - so whether a certificate of occupancy exists for your building at all is a local question.

Where North Dakota does require a posted certificate, it is not about residential occupancy. The Boiler Inspection chapter requires a certificate of inspection for each boiler, to be posted, and makes operating a boiler without a valid one a class A misdemeanor for the owner, user or operator (23.1-16-10, 23.1-16-11). It does not apply to a heating boiler 'in a private residence or in an apartment house of less than six family units' (23.1-16-06(3)), so it reaches only larger buildings, and it certifies the boiler, not the dwelling. The lodging-establishment certificate in 23-09-12 that the master index still lists was repealed in 1997 and is not law; 4.1-57-16 is for potatoes.

What does bind you instead, and why a disclosure clause adds nothing: 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes you "comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and 47-16-13.1(3) makes that duty controlling where it is the greater one - so if the local code requires a certificate of occupancy, 47-16-13.1 already requires you to have one, as a term implied into the lease by statute. 47-16-13.1(1)(b) separately requires repairs to keep the premises "fit and habitable", and 47-16-08 entitles the lessee to quiet possession. A tenant whose unit is shut down for want of a certificate has 47-16-13 remedies for an unrepaired dilapidation - uncapped repair-and-deduct, recovery in any other lawful manner, or the right to vacate and be discharged from further rent - and, if the greater part of the property perishes or the landlord fails to put it in good condition after request, 47-16-17(1) and (2) termination rights. That caveat about the code is important enough to repeat: the statutes impose no certificate disclosure, and chapter 54-21.3 sets none either; any certificate requirement comes from the code your city or county enforces.

What to do: do not print a certificate-of-occupancy disclosure or representation as a North Dakota requirement, and in particular do not print a tenant acknowledgment that the unit "has a valid certificate of occupancy" unless you have actually checked with the municipality - an inaccurate representation is a liability you created for no statutory reason. Equally, do not print a tenant waiver of certificate requirements; North Dakota has none to waive, so the waiver is empty and it suggests the tenant gave something up. Confirm locally whether your jurisdiction issues certificates at all, since enforcing a building code is a local choice under 54-21.3-03(6) and 54-21.3-05, and keep whatever the municipality issued in your file.

title: Occupancy Limits and Children
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota imposes no required lease content about children, and no occupancy standard at all. There is no statutory maximum number of occupants, no persons-per-bedroom rule and no floor-area-per-occupant rule anywhere in the North Dakota statutes searched, and no provision pairs a bedroom or a square-foot figure with an occupant. So the only occupancy limit that applies to your unit is the one your lease sets, and the one the locally adopted code sets.

WHAT NORTH DAKOTA DOES PROHIBIT, AND IT IS STATE LAW, NOT JUST FEDERAL. Familial status and age are protected classes in North Dakota's own fair housing act. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-02(1) bars refusing to rent, refusing to negotiate, or in any other manner making unavailable or denying a dwelling because of "race, color, religion, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin, or status with respect to marriage or public assistance", and § 14-02.5-02(2) bars discriminating "in the terms, conditions, or privileges of... rental of a dwelling or in providing services or facilities in connection with a... rental of a dwelling" on the same grounds. Section 14-02.5-01(9) defines familial status as "one or more minors being domiciled with a parent or another person having legal custody of the minor or minors; or the designee of the parent or other person having such custody with the written permission of the parent or other person", and extends the protection to "any person who is pregnant or is in the process of securing legal custody of any minor". Section 14-02.5-03 bars making, printing or publishing any notice, statement or advertisement about a rental "that indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination" on those grounds. Familial status is also protected by the federal Fair Housing Act, but what is set out above is NORTH DAKOTA law and applies on its own terms - do not describe one as the other.

So: no "adults only", no "no children", no "mature building", no limiting children to ground-floor or rear units, no barring children from the pool or laundry at all times, no extra deposit or rent per child, no refusing an applicant who is pregnant. The stakes are not trivial. Under § 14-02.5-41 a court may award "actual and punitive damages, reasonable attorney's fees, court costs" and injunctive relief; under § 14-02.5-32(2) the department may assess a civil penalty of up to $27,000 where the respondent has been found to have committed one other discriminatory housing practice in the five years ending on the filing of the charge, and up to $55,000 where two or more were committed in the preceding seven years - and under § 14-02.5-32(3) those figures may be imposed without regard to those periods where the same individual committed the earlier acts. The lowest tier, $11,000, is printed in the Century Code as applying "if the respondent HAS been found... to have committed a prior discriminatory housing practice", which cannot be right as it stands, because that is also the condition for the higher tiers; the federal provision this chapter follows applies its lowest tier where the respondent has NOT been so found. Treat the exposure as at least $11,000 for a first violation, and do not rely on either reading of that tier; § 14-02.5-44 lets the court or the department award fees to the prevailing party; and under § 14-02.5-39 an aggrieved person has until "the second year after the date of the occurrence or the termination" of the practice to sue.

WHAT THE LANDLORD SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. Write the limit in persons, not in children, and record in your file the code figure or unit size you derived it from - that record is the whole defence. Keep the same rule and the same screening for every household. Review your advertising wording as well as your lease, because § 14-02.5-03 reaches advertisements independently.

TWO EXEMPTIONS, AND A TRAP INSIDE THEM. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-09(1) exempts "[s]ections 14-02.5-02 through 14-02.5-08" for the sale or rental of a single-family house by an owner who does not own more than three single-family houses at a time, but only if the house is let without a real estate broker or agent or a person in the business of selling or renting dwellings, and without publishing a notice prohibited by § 14-02.5-03, and the exemption "applies only to one sale or rental in a twenty-four-month period, if the owner was not the most recent resident of the house"; subsection 1(c) treats anyone owning a dwelling intended for or occupied by five or more families as in the business of renting. Section 14-02.5-09(2) exempts a dwelling of "not more than four families living independently of each other, if the owner maintains and occupies one of the living quarters as the owner's residence" - and here is the trap: subsection 2 exempts "Section 14-02.5-02 and sections 14-02.5-04 through 14-02.5-08", DELIBERATELY OMITTING § 14-02.5-03. So an owner-occupied duplex, triplex or fourplex is exempt from the rental bar but is still fully bound by the ADVERTISING bar - a "no children" advert from an owner-occupied fourplex is unlawful even though the refusal itself may not be. Section 14-02.5-11 is the separate elderly exemption: the chapter's familial-status and age provisions do not apply to housing determined by HUD or by the department to be designed and operated to assist elderly individuals under a federal or state programme, housing "intended for, and solely occupied by, individuals sixty-two years of age or older", or housing "intended and operated for occupancy by at least one individual fifty-five years of age or older for each unit as determined by department rules", with the rules required to demand at least that "eighty percent of the units are occupied by at least one individual fifty-five years of age or older per unit" and "[t]he publication of, and adherence to, policies and procedures which demonstrate an intent by the owner or manager to provide housing for individuals fifty-five years of age or older". Subsection 2 protects pre-1 October 1999 residents who do not meet the age requirement and unoccupied units reserved for qualifying occupants. If you are relying on the 55-plus exemption, the published policy and the 80 per cent figure are the two things that are checked.

CAUTIOUS COURSE on the point only a court could settle. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-12(1) says the chapter "does not affect a reasonable local or state restriction on the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling or a restriction relating to health or safety standards." On its face that saves a LOCAL OR STATE restriction - it does not say it saves a landlord's own lease limit. Whether a private occupancy term takes shelter under it is not settled by the words, and no state code supplies a figure: the State Building Code consists of the international building, residential, mechanical and fuel gas codes (§ 54-21.3-03(1)), and no housing or property-maintenance code is among them. If your city has adopted one, that is the code to derive the number from. Take the cautious course: do not set a lease limit lower than any limit in a code adopted in your city, derive the number from that code or from the unit's bedroom count and record the derivation, and apply it identically to every household. A limit you can trace to a code figure sits inside § 14-02.5-12(1) on any reading; a number you chose does not.

title: No Winter or Cold-Weather Notice Rule in North Dakota - Put It in the Lease
bodyText:
The default rule first: a North Dakota tenant ends a month-to-month tenancy by giving at least one calendar month's written notice, at any time of year, and the rent runs to and including the termination date (N.D.C.C. 47-16-15(2)); a fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term (47-16-14(1)). The month of the year makes no difference to any of it.

North Dakota has no cold-weather rule of any kind. There is no duty on a tenant to tell you before vacating in winter, no duty to leave the heat on, no winter shut-off or eviction moratorium, and no seasonal utility rule in the statutes. The statutes do not use the words 'cold weather', 'winter' or 'heating season' in any landlord-tenant provision.

What does carry the risk is the ordinary maintenance split. You must supply reasonable heat and running and reasonable hot water at all times, unless the building is not required by law to be equipped for it, or the unit is built so that heat or hot water is generated by an installation in the tenant's exclusive control on a direct public utility connection, or supply fails at the utility (47-16-13.1(1)(f)). In a building other than a single-family residence that duty cannot be shifted to the tenant by any agreement. The tenant must use the heating and plumbing facilities reasonably (47-16-13.2(5)), must use ordinary care to preserve the property and keep it in good condition (47-16-09), and must repair deteriorations caused by the tenant's own ordinary negligence (47-16-10).

So the practical answer is that frozen and burst pipes in a unit the tenant left are settled by 47-16-09 and 47-16-10 and by whatever your lease says, not by a statute. Do this: write the winter duty into the lease - the tenant keeps the heat at a stated minimum temperature whenever the unit is unoccupied in cold weather, tells you in writing before being away more than a stated number of days between stated dates, and does not shut off heat or utilities before the end of the term. In a single-family residence you may also agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant performs the 47-16-13.1(1)(f) heat and water duty (47-16-13.1(4)); in any other dwelling unit you may not. Say nothing in the lease about a statutory winter notice: there is no such rule, and a term that implies the tenant gave one up is empty and misleading.

title: Charging the Tenant for Collection Costs
bodyText: North Dakota sets no general cap on collection costs a lease may pass to a tenant, and no statute authorises them either - with one exception. If a tenant's check or electronic payment is dishonoured, you may recover collection fees or costs of up to forty dollars under the bad-check statute, and that figure and its mechanics are set out separately in this library. Outside that, a stated collection charge is a contract term facing two general rules: a penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance is void (N.D.C.C. § 9-08-03), and damages fixed in advance are void unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (§ 9-08-04). You may not charge any fee simply to accept cash, a check or a money order for rent or any other payment under the lease (§ 47-16-20.1). Recovering what collection actually cost you is the safer course than a stated percentage or flat fee.

title: North Dakota does not require anyone to approve your lease - but tribal trust land is not North Dakota law
bodyText:
North Dakota's default is that a lease of land is a private contract: it takes effect between the parties when they make it, and no state officer approves, registers or confirms it first. There is no North Dakota analogue of the territorial communal-land statutes (for example A.S.C.A. section 37.0221), and no North Dakota statute conditions the validity of a lease of communal, tribal, allotted or trust land on the approval of a governor, a land commissioner, an attorney general or any other officer. Nothing in North Dakota law therefore tells you what happens to rent or possession 'before approval', because the state imposes no approval step to be before.

The reason is jurisdictional rather than accidental, and it is the part worth understanding. North Dakota contains several Indian reservations, but leasing of tribal trust land and of allotted land held in trust is not the state's to regulate: it is governed by federal law and by the law of the tribe whose land it is, and it is administered through the federal government rather than through Bismarck. You will not find the answer in the North Dakota Century Code, and the absence of a state approval requirement is not a licence to treat such a parcel as ordinary fee land.

What to do. First, establish the land status of the parcel before you sign anything, because the status decides which body of law governs the tenancy, not the address. If the parcel is ordinary fee land - including fee land inside reservation boundaries - the North Dakota rows in this library apply in the normal way and no approval is needed. If the parcel is tribal trust or allotted trust land, do not rely on this library's North Dakota rows at all: treat the lease as governed by federal and tribal law, assume an approval or consent step may be required before the lease is effective, do not assume chapter 47-16's terms, chapter 47-17's notice to remove from the premises or chapter 47-32's eviction procedure are available to you, and take advice from counsel who practises in that forum before you take rent or give possession. Second, do not put a clause in your lease reciting that the lease is 'approved' or 'exempt from approval' under North Dakota law; there is no such approval machinery and the recital would be meaningless at best and misleading at worst.

title: North Dakota has no rent bar for condemned premises - but destruction can end the lease outright under 47-16-14(4)
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute says a landlord may not collect rent for a period during which the premises were condemned, placarded, closed or subject to an order to vacate, and none makes rent already collected recoverable, or creates a penalty or a treble-damages claim for collecting it. There is no rent escrow and no rent-into-court procedure in North Dakota either. The whole list of rent-relief triggers in the statutes is three sections, and not one of them is condemnation: 47-16-13(3), where a tenant who gives notice of a dilapidation the landlord neglects may vacate and "shall be discharged from further payment of rent or performance of other conditions"; 47-16-17.1, where a tenant terminating because of domestic abuse is "relieved of any other contractual obligation for payment of rent" subject to the landlord's duty to mitigate and to rent being paid through the termination; and 47-16-26, where an unlawful double letting of a room relieves "all tenants in the building under the same landlord" from all obligation to pay rent while it continues.

But do not stop at the absence, because the general lease statutes may already have ended the tenancy. 47-16-14 says the leasing of real property terminates, among other ways, "4. By the destruction of the property leased." That is automatic - no notice, no election, no court order - and a condemnation following destruction by fire, flood or collapse will often mean the leasing ended by operation of law on the date of destruction, so there is no rent to bar because there is no lease. Where the property is not destroyed but is unusable, 47-16-17 lets the lessee terminate before the end of the term "1. When the lessor does not fulfill the lessor's obligations, if any, within a reasonable time after request, as to placing and securing the lessee in the quiet possession of the property leased, or putting it into a good condition, or repairing it; or 2. When the greater part of the property leased, or that part which was, and which the lessor had reason to believe was, the material inducement to the lessee to enter into the contract, perishes from any cause other than the ordinary negligence of the lessee." A vacate order on a building that is largely unusable fits subsection 2 comfortably and subsection 1 if you were asked to repair and did not. Add 47-16-08's entitlement to quiet possession and 47-16-13's uncapped repair-and-deduct, and the practical result is close to a rent bar even though no statute calls it one. Pointing the other way: 47-16-13.4 gives the landlord, after termination, "a claim for possession and for rent and a separate claim for actual damages", and 47-16-13.7 makes a lessee evicted according to law liable for rent for the remainder of the term subject to the duty to mitigate.

Where North Dakota's condemnation power over unfit housing actually lives: 40-58-18, "Ordinances relating to repair, closing, and demolition of dwellings unfit for human habitation", in ch. 40-58 (the Urban Renewal Law). That is an enabling section - the state authorises municipalities to adopt ordinances, and the operative rules, the inspection, the order, the placard, the hearing and the consequences are all in the municipal code. Read whole, it contains no rule about rent. Note too that in the Century Code "condemnation" as a term of art means eminent domain: every condemnation section the master index names is either ch. 32-15 eminent domain, a highway or water-project taking, a diseased animal, a seized food item or a weighing device. There is no "condemned building" statute at state level at all. The state-level inspection-and-order machinery that does exist is the state fire marshal's: 18-01-14 abatement of fire hazards, 18-01-15 abatement of conditions dangerous to persons - order - failure to comply - penalty, 18-01-16 order of abatement - to whom directed - contents - how served - service by publication, 18-01-17 to 18-01-26 appeals and district court enforcement, and 18-01-27 costs and the lien for them. For a mobile home park there is also 23-10-12 (revocation or suspension of license), 23-10-13 (change in use or closure of a mobile home park) and ch. 23-10.1 (Mobile Home Park Receiver, 23-10.1-02 conditions for appointment of a receiver). For a lodging establishment there is 23-09-11 (inspection - reports), 23-09-18 (failure to comply with chapter - notice - how served) and 23-09-22 (license canceled). None of those sections bars or refunds rent for a closed or condemned period (23-10-13 touches rent only to bar a park rent increase within ninety days before a change-in-use notice).

Mobile home parks checked, and this one cuts against a rent bar rather than for it. 47-10-28 read whole. Subsection 13 lets the district court suspend a park's licence for a violation of the section, assesses a daily civil penalty equal to half the month's rent roll divided by the days in the month - and then provides that "All park tenants must be allowed to continue to reside in the mobile home park through the duration of the license suspension". Subsection 14 goes further: "If an action between a landlord and tenant is commenced, the tenant shall continue paying rent and comply with all park rules and regulations in effect at the time the action was commenced." So in the one North Dakota setting where the legislature has written a detailed shutdown regime, it expressly preserved occupancy and expressly required rent to keep being paid. There is no rent bar in 47-10-28, and nothing elsewhere in it about condemnation or an order to vacate.

What to do: do not keep billing rent for a period the tenant could not occupy. The statute does not forbid it in terms, but 47-16-14(4) may mean the lease is already over, 47-16-17(2) gives the tenant a termination right, and 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes your code non-compliance a breach of a duty the statute wrote into the lease - so a rent claim for a condemned period is weak and expensive, and 47-16-13.6 lets the court award attorney's fees to the prevailing party, which cuts both ways. Account for the rent in writing from the date of the order, return prepaid rent for the unusable period, and settle the security deposit under 47-16-07.1. Do not write a lease clause saying rent continues during a condemnation: it cannot survive 47-16-14(4), which terminates the leasing by operation of law, and under 9-08-01(2) a term contrary to the policy of express law is unlawful even where no statute expressly prohibits it. What the enforcement chapters say, read whole: 40-58-18 has the public officer order the owner to repair or "to vacate and close the dwelling as a human habitation", makes the officer's costs a lien on the land, and provides that "a person affected by an order of the public officer may not recover any damages for action taken pursuant to any order of the public officer, or because of compliance by that person with any order". The fire marshal's orders in 18-01-14 to 18-01-27 and the lodging and park sections in ch. 23-09, ch. 23-10 and ch. 23-10.1 likewise contain no rent bar. And ch. 32-03 sets the damages if a lockout or holdover follows: double rent for a tenant who gives notice and fails to surrender (32-03-27), double the yearly value for a willful holdover (32-03-28), and "three times such a sum as would compensate for the detriment" for forcibly excluding a person from possession (32-03-29). So do not lock a tenant out yourself because of an order; let the order and the court process do it. Local ordinances adopted under 40-58-18 may add rules of their own.

title: Do Not Put a Confession of Judgment in a North Dakota Lease
bodyText: The default rule is section 9-08-05: 'Every stipulation or condition in a contract by which any party thereto is restricted from enforcing that party's rights under the contract by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals or which limits the time within which that party thus may enforce that party's rights is void, except as otherwise specifically permitted by the laws of this state.' A confession of judgment is the purest form of that restriction -- it takes the tenant's defence away before there is anything to defend -- so it is void unless a North Dakota statute specifically permits it. No statute in the landlord-tenant chapters does. The eviction chapter points the other way: section 47-32-02 fixes an appearance date not fewer than three nor more than fifteen days out and sets minimum service periods, and section 47-32-04 contemplates the court finding for the plaintiff and then entering judgment -- a structure that assumes a hearing. The one place North Dakota mentions a confession of judgment in a leasing statute confirms the point by contrast: section 47-15.1-04 says a consumer rental purchase agreement 'may not contain' a confession of judgment, a negotiable instrument, a wage assignment or a waiver by the consumer of claims or defences, 'and, such included provision is not enforceable'. That chapter is rent-to-own of GOODS, not realty -- section 47-15.1-01(4)(d) expressly excludes a bailment of personal property incidental to a lease of real property -- so it does not govern your lease. But it shows the legislature knows how to ban one expressly, and it never did so for residential leases, which is why 9-08-05 has to carry the weight. Practical instruction: do not include a confession of judgment, a cognovit, a warrant of attorney, a term authorising anyone to appear for the tenant, or a term under which the tenant consents in advance to entry of judgment for possession or for rent. If you inherited a lease with one, do not act on it; file the eviction and get a judgment. ONE COURT RULE, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: chapter 28-10 reads '[Superseded by North Dakota Rules of Civil Procedure, Rule 68]', and N.D.R.Civ.P. 68(c) still allows 'A judgment by confession ... without action, either for money due or to become due'. It needs a separate 'written statement ... signed by the defendant, and verified by oath', stating the amount and 'the concise facts underlying the debt', which a court must find sufficient before the clerk enters judgment. It reaches money only, never possession, and it is not a lease clause. Whether a court rule is a law 'specifically permit[ting]' a confession under 9-08-05, and whether a sworn statement taken from a residential tenant at signing would survive 9-08-05 and the unconscionability rule in 47-16-13.3, only case law could settle. The cautious course is the one above: no confession term in the lease, and no Rule 68(c) statement taken from a tenant at signing.

title: North Dakota habitability: the short list of what you owe, and the long list of machinery that does not exist
bodyText:
North Dakota's habitability law is short. It is one section of duties, one self-help remedy, one unconscionability check and one fee provision - and almost none of the machinery other states bolt on to it exists here. This row is the inventory, so you can stop looking for the parts that are not there and concentrate on the few that are.

WHAT NORTH DAKOTA DOES HAVE

Section 47-16-13.1(1) is the duty list. A landlord of a residential dwelling unit shall: (a) comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; (b) make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition; (c) keep all common areas clean and safe; (d) maintain in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, 'supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord'; (e) provide and maintain receptacles for ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste and arrange for their removal; and (f) supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat.

Three things inside that section a landlord should know. Subsection (1)(f) carries three exceptions, so the heat and hot water duty does not apply if the building 'is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose', or if the unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control supplied by a direct public utility connection, or if the water or heat is unavailable due to supply failure by a public utility. Subsection (2) allows 'a reasonable time' to remedy a noncompliance with subdivisions (b) through (f) - note that subdivision (a), the code duty, is not in that grace. And subsection (3) provides that where the subdivision (a) code duty is greater than any other duty in the subsection, the landlord's duty is determined by reference to subdivision (a) - so an applicable building or housing code requirement becomes the controlling standard through the lease statute.

Section 47-16-13 is repair-and-deduct, and North Dakota's version is unusually strong for the tenant. If within a reasonable time after notice from the lessee of dilapidations which the lessor ought to repair the lessor neglects to do so, the lessee may repair and deduct the expense from the rent, or recover it in any other lawful manner, or vacate - and on vacating 'shall be discharged from further payment of rent or performance of other conditions'. Section 47-16-07.2 requires a signed statement describing the condition of the facilities at the time of entering the rental agreement, which 'constitute[s] prima facie proof of the condition of the facilities and the premises at the beginning of the rental agreement'. Section 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable rental agreement or provision, and separately review an unconscionable settlement waiving a right under sections 47-16-13.1 to 47-16-13.6. Section 47-16-13.6 makes those rights 'enforceable by action' and lets the court award reasonable attorney's fees TO THE PREVAILING PARTY - which cuts both ways and favours a landlord who successfully defends a weak habitability claim.

WHAT NORTH DAKOTA DOES NOT HAVE

No severity threshold. The words 'material breach', 'material noncompliance' and 'substantial breach' appear nowhere in North Dakota landlord-tenant law. 'Materially affecting' appears only twice, in section 47-16-13.1(1)(a) and in the mirror-image tenant duty in section 47-16-13.2(1), and in both places it qualifies which CODE REQUIREMENTS are in scope - not how bad a defect must be. So there is no threshold a defect has to clear before section 47-16-13 is engaged, and you cannot answer a repair demand by saying the problem is too minor to count.

No habitability presumption, in either direction. Nothing presumes the unit was habitable at move-in and nothing presumes it was not. The section 47-16-07.2 condition statement does the work a presumption would, which is exactly why you should complete it carefully and keep it.

No required habitability statement. There is no prescribed habitability disclosure, warranty text or form of words to put in the lease - and the opposite temptation is the real risk: a clause purporting to narrow or define down the section 47-16-13.1 duties runs into section 47-16-13.3 and, through the violation-of-law limb of section 9-08-02 with section 9-08-01(2), into unlawfulness.

No rent escrow and no rent into court. There is no procedure for a tenant to deposit rent with a court or into an escrow account pending repair, no court-held repair fund, and consequently no escrow exemption and no exemption notice. The only escrow provisions in North Dakota property law are the delivery of a grant in escrow (sections 47-09-08 and 47-09-09), closing agents' escrow accounts (chapter 47-34) and mortgage escrow accounts (chapter 47-10.2) - none has anything to do with rent. Counterclaims in an eviction are barred except as a setoff, so habitability does not become a vehicle for a rent-withholding standoff.

No cap and no threshold on repair-and-deduct. Section 47-16-13 carries no dollar cap, no percentage-of-rent limit, no cost ceiling, and no minimum cost the tenant must reach before vacating. It also prescribes no form of notice - the statute says only 'notice from the lessee' - and no fixed period, only 'a reasonable time'. Treat any notice as starting the clock.

No temperature figure. Section 47-16-13.1(1)(f) says 'reasonable heat' and 'reasonable amounts of hot water'. There is no degree figure anywhere in the statutes, no seasonal date range, and no water-heater setting. If a building code applies, section 47-16-13.1(3) will make the code figure the controlling standard - The State Building Code consists of the international building, residential, mechanical and fuel gas codes, and the plumbing code is the 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code (N.D.C.C. § 54-21.3-03(1); N.D. Admin. Code § 62-03.1-01-01). No state statute or rule sets a heat or water-heater figure, but any figure in those model codes or a local code controls, so check the code your city enforces.

No ability to move the core duties in a multi-unit building. Section 47-16-13.1(4) lets the landlord and tenant OF A SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant perform the duties in subdivisions (e) and (f) plus specified repairs, maintenance, alterations and remodeling. Section 47-16-13.1(5), for 'any dwelling unit other than a single-family residence', reaches ONLY 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling' and never mentions (e) or (f). So in a duplex or an apartment building the duties to provide waste receptacles and arrange removal and to supply running water, hot water and heat CANNOT be shifted to the tenant by any agreement at all. Even the narrower shift that subsection (5) allows requires good faith, a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration, work not necessary to cure a subdivision (e) failure, and no diminution of your obligations to other tenants. And subsection (6) bars treating performance of the separate agreement as a condition of the lease - its text says 'subsection 4' while subsection 5 is the one describing a separate writing, so apply the bar to both.

No essential-services or utility-interruption statute. North Dakota has none at all. Section 47-16-13.6 is not one - it is headed 'Enforcement of sections 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6' and does only what is described above. There is no unlawful-cutoff provision, no penalty for interrupting service and no statutory damages for it.

No pest or bed-bug statute, no carpet rule, no window-guard, radiator-cover, pool, water-heater-temperature, balcony-inspection, sprinkler, asbestos, lead, well-testing, drywall or recycling duty in the statutes (no building code may require sprinklers in a house or a two-unit building, § 54-21.3-03(4), and the state asbestos and lead rules bind you only when you renovate or abate, N.D. Admin. Code chs. 33.1-15-13 and 33.1-15-24), and no landlord-held repair-contact requirement outside a mobile home park. No retaliation bar: 'retaliat-' occurs three times in the whole statutes scope and North Dakota has no general landlord-retaliation statute.

ONE DUTY THAT IS NOT IN CHAPTER 47-16, AND IT MATTERS. North Dakota does impose a smoke-alarm duty. 'All residential rental property' must be equipped with smoke detection systems or other approved alarm systems, installed and maintained to the state fire marshal's standards (N.D.C.C. § 23-13-15(1)). In a single-family rental the tenant maintains and inspects the system. In other dwellings you install it and ensure it works 'upon the occupancy of each new tenant', and the tenant maintains it during the tenancy. On a deaf tenant's written request you must provide a visual alarm, unless you rent no more than one building of four or fewer units (§ 23-13-15(2)). Willfully failing to install a system is a class B misdemeanor (§ 23-13-15(4)). An earlier version of a row in this library said the Century Code imposes no alarm duty; that was wrong.

IF IT IS A MOBILE HOME PARK, read section 47-10-28 as well - it is a separate and stricter regime with its own utility code, its own complaint-acknowledgment deadline and a civil penalty of not less than two thousand five hundred dollars.

What to do. Complete and keep the section 47-16-07.2 condition statement. Respond to any repair notice promptly in writing and fix within a reasonable time, because there is no severity threshold to hide behind and repair-and-deduct is uncapped. Do not try to shift waste, water, hot water or heat to a tenant in anything but a single-family house, and in a single-family house do it in a separate signed writing with real consideration. Do not write a habitability definition or disclaimer into the lease. Check the building code your city enforces, because its figures control. And install smoke alarms and check them at every new tenancy (§ 23-13-15).

title: What North Dakota renting law simply does not have - the inventory outside habitability
bodyText:
North Dakota is a thin-statute state for renting, and a landlord who comes to it from Colorado, Minnesota or almost anywhere on either coast will keep reaching for machinery that is not here. This row is the inventory of the significant absences outside habitability, so you stop looking. Everything on it is scoped to the statutes that could be read; the companion rows on habitability absences and on what the pass could not read cover the rest.

THE THREE STRUCTURAL ABSENCES THAT EXPLAIN MOST OF THE OTHERS

1. North Dakota has not adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. There is no URLTA framework, which is why there is no act-wide definitions section, no act-wide remedies section, no act-wide non-waivable-rights section, and no student-housing or employee-housing carve-out - because there is no act to carve anything out of.

2. There is no landlord-tenant non-waiver statute anywhere in North Dakota. No provision says that a tenant's rights may not be waived, and the security deposit section carries no non-waiver clause of its own, unlike most states'. The single anti-contracting-out phrase in the whole of chapter 47-16 is in section 47-16-26, on double letting: one who rents part of a room for a dwelling 'is entitled to the whole of the room, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary' - and if a landlord lets a room to more than one family, every tenant in the building under the same landlord 'is relieved from all obligation to pay rent to the landlord while such double letting of any room continues'. What stands in the place of a non-waiver statute is section 47-16-13.3 (unconscionability) and chapter 9-08, especially section 9-08-03 (contractual penalties are void), section 9-08-04 (damages fixed in advance are void to that extent unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix) and section 9-08-05 (a clause restricting enforcement of rights by the usual legal proceedings, or shortening the time to enforce them, is void except as specifically permitted by the laws of this state).

3. There is no list of prohibited lease provisions. Neither chapter 47-16 nor chapter 47-32 contains one, and there is no exculpation ban in either. The word 'exculpatory' appears nowhere in North Dakota law - the state's phrase is 'exempting ... from responsibility', in section 9-08-02. So the limits on what you may put in a lease come from chapter 9-08 and section 47-16-13.3, not from an enumerated list you can check against.

NO GENERAL RETALIATION BAR - BUT TWO TARGETED ONES, AND THEY ARE EASY TO MISS

There is no general landlord-retaliation statute in North Dakota. A landlord may end a month-to-month tenancy without cause and without giving a reason, and a tenant has no statutory retaliation defence to it. But do not read that as a licence, because two targeted bars exist and the second is invisible to the word 'retaliation':

- Section 47-16-17.1(10): a person may not refuse to rent, refuse to negotiate for the rental of, 'or in any other manner make unavailable or deny a dwelling to an individual, or otherwise retaliate in the rental of a dwelling solely because a tenant or applicant or a household member of the tenant or applicant exercised the right to terminate a lease under this section' - that is the domestic-violence early-termination right. Section 47-16-17.1(11) backs it with statutory damages of one thousand dollars plus actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, costs and disbursements.
- Section 14-02.5-45(2), in the fair housing chapter: 'It is a discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with any individual in the exercise or enjoyment of, or on account of the individual having exercised or enjoyed, or on account of the individual having aided or encouraged any other individual in the exercise or enjoyment of, any right granted or protected by this chapter.' Section 14-02.5-45(1) makes intimidation or interference by force or threat of force a class A misdemeanor. That is an anti-retaliation provision in everything but name, and it reaches any fair-housing right.

Note also that section 14-02.4-18 is headed 'Retaliation prohibited' - but it sits in the Human Rights Act, and all three of that chapter's housing sections were repealed in 1999 and 2001 while keeping their headings. Fair housing in North Dakota is chapter 14-02.5, not chapter 14-02.4. Do not cite the Human Rights Act for a housing duty.

MONEY AND FEES - ALMOST ENTIRELY UNREGULATED

No application-fee or screening-fee rule of any kind: no cap, no refund right, no disclosure duty. No holding-deposit rule, so pre-lease money from an applicant is unregulated as to amount, receipt and return. No fee-transparency or fee-schedule requirement. No duty to abate a fee when an amenity closes. No late-fee cap for a conventional rental - the ten per cent monthly and five dollar daily caps in section 47-10-28(11) are mobile-home-park only. No collection-fee authority and no notice-service-fee authority. No deposit cost schedule, no tenant right to pay a deposit in instalments, no last-month's-rent rule, no non-refundable deposit (the word 'nonrefundable' appears nowhere in North Dakota landlord-tenant law, so no notice can make a deposit non-refundable), no duty to disclose how a deposit amount is set, and no expedited deposit-return route. No fee-in-lieu-of-deposit regime. No general rent-increase notice statute - the only one in the Code is section 47-10-28(7)'s ninety days for a park tenant, so any claim that 'North Dakota requires N days' notice of a rent increase' is the park rule quoted out of its chapter; for an ordinary tenancy the mechanism is section 47-16-07 (changing the terms of a month-to-month) with section 47-16-15(3)'s twenty-five days for the tenant to terminate in response. No utility allowance and no cap on one outside a park. No submetering or ratio-billing disclosure - 'submeter', 'master-metered' and 'ratio utility billing' return zero. No conservation charge. No holdover-rate cap. No duty or right to report rent to a credit bureau.

What does bind you on money: section 47-16-07.1 (the deposit cap of one month's rent with a closed two-item exception list, the separate pet deposit at the greater of $2,500 or two months' rent with a service-animal carve-out, the federally insured interest-bearing account, the thirty-day itemisation, and treble damages for a deposit withheld without reasonable justification), section 47-16-20.1 (no fee for accepting cash, a cheque or a money order), section 47-16-20 (rent is payable in arrears absent contract or usage), and chapter 9-08.

SCREENING, PRIVACY AND RECORDS

No tenant-screening statute: no criteria, no adverse-action notice, no limits on what you may consider. The one statutory screening lever sits oddly in the deposit section - section 47-16-07.1(1)(a) and (b) let you take up to two months' security from an applicant convicted of a felony 'as an incentive to rent' or from one with a judgment for violating a previous rental agreement. No employee-screening mandate and no key-control policy at any portfolio size. No smart-access or keyless-entry law: 'keyless' and 'mobile credential' appear nowhere, nothing regulates entry-data retention and nothing guarantees a physical-key alternative. No tenant right of access to records except in a mobile home park, where section 47-10-28(1)(f) gives a lease copy within ten business days of a written request - and that is the only tenant right of access to records in the entire Century Code. One provision runs hard the other way and you must not breach it: section 47-16-17.1(4) bars disclosing domestic-violence documentation at all - it 'may not be entered into any shared database or provided to any person' save as evidence in an eviction, in a claim for unpaid rent or damages, 'or as otherwise required by law' - with no consent exception, so a consent-to-disclose clause is unlawful, not merely empty.

DISCLOSURES - THE REQUIRED SET IS VERY SHORT

What you must give a tenant is: the section 47-16-07.2 signed condition statement; the section 47-16-07.1(3) deposit itemisation and thirty-day notice; the section 47-16-15(4) stated-and-initialled notice requirement if your lease demands more than one month's notice from the tenant; the section 47-16-06.1 automatic-renewal notice not less than thirty days before the lease's expiration date if you want to enforce an automatic renewal clause; and, in a park only, section 47-10-28(9)'s lease-and-rights summary with section 47-10-28(1)(g)-(h)'s owner and manager details. That is the whole list.

There is no truth-in-renting act, no required handbook, no tenant-rights statement, no rights-and-responsibilities guide outside a park, no plain-language mandate, and no duty to translate a lease or provide an interpreter. And there is no required disclosure to a tenant about: sex offenders, a death or crime on the premises, methamphetamine contamination, a military air installation or noise zone, flood risk, a property-tax change, a certificate of occupancy, a condominium or cooperative conversion, a pending foreclosure, homeowners-association obligations, shoreline access, an ordnance site, demolition, a shared meter, defective drywall, a California-style Proposition 65 warning, single-family occupancy, or a special district. Several of those duties exist in North Dakota - but owed by a SELLER to a BUYER, not by a landlord to a tenant: section 47-10-02.1(2)'s seller disclosure form and section 47-10-02.3's fifteen association items are the siblings that prove the negative.

TERMINATION AND EVICTION

No good-cause requirement and no notice of cause - a month-to-month may be ended without a reason. No cold-weather restriction on a termination notice or an eviction, which is worth saying plainly in a state with North Dakota's winters: there is no winter moratorium. No expedited criminal-eviction track and no third-party petition route. No possession bond or bond-to-stay. No tenant right to redeem after judgment. No opt-in lockout, and no statute permitting self-help lockout by agreement. No tenant opportunity to purchase on a sale. No age-, health- or infirmity-based early termination for a tenant - the contrast with section 47-16-17.1's domestic-violence right is deliberate. No environmental-event termination beyond sections 47-16-14(4) and 47-16-17(2)'s destruction rules. No shutdown or emergency rent protection, and in a park sections 47-10-28(13) and (14) cut the other way by preserving occupancy while providing that the tenant shall continue paying rent.

A vocabulary warning that trips up imported forms: 'notice to vacate', 'notice to quit' and 'notice to remove' occur ZERO times in North Dakota law. Section 47-17-01 says the landlord gives notice 'to remove from the premises' within not less than one month; section 47-32-02 calls its three-day notice a 'notice of intention to evict', and requires it only for grounds 4, 5, 6 and 8 of section 47-32-01 - so grounds 1, 2, 3 AND 7 need no notice of intention to evict at all, which makes the disturbance ground at section 47-32-01(7) the fastest route against a disruptive tenant and grounds 1 to 3 the squatter route.

TENANT RIGHTS THAT DO NOT EXIST HERE

No tenant right to organise, meet or canvass. No canvasser, candidate or petition right of access to a rental building. No religious or cultural display right. No right to summon emergency assistance without penalty. No tenant solar right. No right to a window air conditioner. No tenant electric-vehicle-charging right - section 47-04.1-16 gives a condominium UNIT OWNER one and is the sibling that proves a tenant has none. No veterans' rental incentive or preference. No defence to nonpayment based on a late benefit or voucher payment. No pet-eviction fact sheet. And two that run against the tenant: sections 47-16-07.5 and 47-16-07.6 penalise a TENANT who misrepresents an assistance animal, and there is no landlord-facing penalty for wrongly refusing one; and there is no landlord right to enter to care for an animal.

INSURANCE, LIABILITY AND VEHICLES

No statute requires a landlord to carry liability insurance or to name anyone on a policy, and nothing regulates requiring renters' insurance, capping it or limiting what the lease may demand - so a renters-insurance requirement is lawful and wholly contractual. And a gap that is NOT in your favour: there is no statutory authority for a landlord to tow a vehicle, so the lease is your only authority.

TWO THINGS THE LIBRARY SHOULD NOT TELL YOU ARE ABSENT, BECAUSE THEY ARE NOT

North Dakota DOES have a state servicemember relief act. Section 37-01-43, the North Dakota military civil relief act, as amended in 2025, gives an individual called or ordered to active service for thirty consecutive days or longer 'all of the protections afforded to persons in the military service of the United States under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act ... in effect on December 31, 2024'. It is a state analogue, so a servicemember tenant has state-law protections and not only federal ones; its trigger is thirty consecutive days stated in the state's own words; and it is a frozen-standard incorporation, so later federal amendments do not flow through and the state right can diverge over time. And North Dakota DOES have rent-control preemption: section 47-16-02.1 bars a political subdivision from any ordinance with the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged, with a carve-out for property the subdivision holds in fee.

What to do. Do not import a clause that assumes a non-waiver statute, a prohibited-terms list, a retaliation bar or an escrow procedure - in North Dakota those clauses are empty, and a waiver clause invites the tenant to believe they gave something up. Test every money term against sections 9-08-03 and 9-08-04 and every dispute-resolution term against section 9-08-05, since those are the real limits. Measure fees by actual cost rather than a round number. And use North Dakota's own words in your notices.

title: North Dakota Rules Outside the Landlord-Tenant Chapters
bodyText:
Read this row before relying on any statement in this library that North Dakota 'has no' rule about something. North Dakota's renting law is not all in one place. Chapter 47-16 is the landlord-tenant chapter and chapter 47-32 is the eviction chapter, but duties that bind a North Dakota landlord also sit in the health, fire, building-code, utility, lien, nuisance, criminal and civil-procedure titles. This row records what those other titles say.

THE READING RULE THAT MATTERS MOST: A HEADING IS NOT A LAW, AND A REPEALED SECTION KEEPS ITS HEADING. At least eighty-five sections are repealed but still carry their old headings, in the official chapter PDFs and in the Legislative Council's index, with nothing in the body but 'Repealed by S.L. ...'. Section 47-16-24 still reads 'Lessee must give written notice before removal of property from premises' and has no content whatever. Section 47-16-12, the old lessor repair duty, was repealed in 1977. All three housing sections of chapter 14-02.4 were repealed in 1999 and 2001 while keeping their headings, which is why fair housing lives in chapter 14-02.5 instead. So a section heading, an index line or a search hit on a section number proves that the NUMBER exists - not that the section has any text, and not that it is in force. Read the body of a section, every time, before you act on it.

1. Section 23-13-15, 'Smoke detection systems for residential rental property - Penalty'. North Dakota does impose an alarm duty. 'All residential rental property' (other than lodging establishments covered by section 23-09-02.1) 'must be equipped with smoke detection systems or other approved alarm systems', installed and maintained to the fire protection standards in the state fire marshal's rules. In a single-family rental the tenant maintains and inspects the system. In other dwellings you install it and ensure it works 'upon the occupancy of each new tenant', and the tenant maintains it during the tenancy. On a deaf tenant's written request you must provide a visual alarm, unless you rent no more than one building of four or fewer units. Willfully failing to install a system is a class B misdemeanor (N.D.C.C. § 23-13-15). Never rely on an alarm-duty absence.

2. Chapter 54-21.3, the State Building Code. It consists of the international building, residential, mechanical and fuel gas codes, adopted by rule, and leaves out the State Plumbing Code, the electrical standards and the State Fire Code (N.D.C.C. §§ 54-21.3-03(1), 54-21.3-04(1)). It applies where a city, township or county elects to enforce it, and they may amend it (§ 54-21.3-03(6)). It may not require fire sprinklers in a single-family dwelling or a building of no more than two dwelling units (§ 54-21.3-03(4)). This changes answers: section 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes you comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and section 47-16-13.1(3) measures your duty by the code where it asks more. The model codes' own text is published by their private author, not the state. So every statement in this library that North Dakota sets no figure for heat, hot-water temperature, window guards, pool fencing or radiator covers is scoped to the statutes and state rules. Check your local code and comply.

3. Section 32-03-29, 'Damages for forcible exclusion from realty'. 'For forcibly ejecting or excluding a person from the possession of real property, the measure of damages is three times such a sum as would compensate for the detriment caused to the person by the act complained of.' That is the treble-damages source for a self-help lockout. Its neighbours set the holdover measures. A tenant who gave notice of intention to leave and fails to give up the premises owes 'double the rent' (§ 32-03-27). A tenant who willfully holds over after the term ends, after notice of intention to evict and a demand for possession, owes 'double the yearly value of the property for the time of withholding', plus compensation for the harm caused (§ 32-03-28).

4 and 5. Sections 19-24.1-33 ('Limitations') and 19-24.1-34 ('Acts not prohibited - Acts not required'), in the medical-marijuana chapter. Section 19-24.1-34(1)(c) says the chapter does not require 'A landlord to allow production or processing on rental property', and (1)(b) does not require a person in lawful possession of property to let a guest or visitor possess or consume marijuana there. Section 19-24.1-33 does not authorize smoking or vaping where the smoke or vapor would be inhaled by a minor who is not the patient, or any activity prohibited by the sections of chapter 23-12 it lists. Nothing in the chapter bars a landlord from refusing or limiting a patient's use, so a lease smoking ban may cover marijuana. The only other 'landlord' in the chapter is section 19-24.1-37(3), letting the department confirm a cardholder's status to a third party 'such as a landlord' on the cardholder's written request. One trap: the 2025 session-law volume also prints, in full and with section numbers, an initiated cannabis measure the voters REJECTED, under 'INITIATED MEASURES DISAPPROVED'. Its sections are numbered 19-24.2- and they are NOT law.

6. Sections 23-09-01 ('Definitions') and 23-09-08 ('Bolts or locks to be supplied on doors of sleeping rooms'). Section 23-09-08 requires bolts or locks on sleeping-room doors 'in any lodging establishment', operable from within and impossible to open from outside while locked, with a class B misdemeanor for the proprietor. A 'lodging establishment' is a place 'held out to the public as a place where sleeping accommodations are furnished to transient guests for a charge', excluding single structures with five or fewer guest rooms and ten or fewer occupants (§ 23-09-01(9)). An ordinary residential tenancy is not furnished to transient guests, so this lock mandate does not reach it. A large short-term rental may be a lodging establishment.

SQUATTERS AND UNAUTHORISED OCCUPANTS. Section 12.1-22-03 was amended and reenacted as a whole section by a 2025 Act. North Dakota now has a squatter-specific criminal provision. Subsection (2): 'An individual who unlawfully detains, occupies, or trespasses upon a residential dwelling is guilty of a class C felony for the first offense and a class B felony for a second or subsequent offense if the second or subsequent offense occurred at the same residential dwelling as the first offense.' Subsection (1) makes it a class C felony to enter or remain in a dwelling or in highly secured premises knowing you are not licensed or privileged to do so.
