Subsection (3) covers entering or remaining in a building, occupied structure or storage structure, or in any place enclosed by a fence or otherwise enclosed so as manifestly to exclude intruders - 'unless the individual is a licensed hunter or angler who is lawfully hunting or fishing' - and defines 'fence' as a permanent structure on nonurban private property maintained and capable of containing livestock. Subsection (4) makes it a class B misdemeanor to enter or remain where notice against trespass is given 'by actual communication to the actor by the owner or an individual authorized by the owner or by posting in a manner reasonably likely to come to the attention of intruders', and requires the name of the person posting to appear on each sign in legible characters; substantial compliance plus notice clear from the circumstances is enough, and a second offence within two years is a class A misdemeanor. Subsection (5) gives a peace officer a noncriminal citation route with a two hundred fifty dollar fine per violation and a bond-by-mail procedure. And the companion amendment broadened the definition: 'Dwelling' now 'means real property or residential property, including a building, structure, or part of a building or structure, used or intended to be used as a home or residence'. Alongside that, grounds 1, 2 and 3 of section 47-32-01 need no notice of intention to evict at all, which is North Dakota's civil squatter route.

A RENT RECEIPT DUTY - yes, on request. 'A debtor has a right to require from the debtor's creditor a written receipt for any property delivered in performance of the debtor's obligation' (N.D.C.C. § 9-12-22). A tenant paying rent is a debtor performing an obligation, so if a tenant asks for a written receipt, for cash or any other payment, you must give one. Section 57-21-05, 'Receipts a defense in action for rent', is narrower than its heading: it covers rent a county treasurer collects under a court order for unpaid property taxes. The safe practice is to give a written receipt for every cash payment and keep a copy.

LANDLORD REGISTRATION AS A PRECONDITION TO A POSSESSION JUDGMENT. Chapter 47-32 contains no registration, licensing or certification precondition to an eviction or a possession judgment: section 47-32-01 lists the grounds, section 47-32-02 the three-day notice of intention to evict (required only for grounds 4, 5, 6 and 8), and section 47-32-04 what an eviction may be joined with. But business-registration statutes outside chapter 47-32 can stop you suing. An out-of-state limited liability company or corporation that owns income-producing real property here is transacting business and may not maintain an action until it has a certificate of authority (N.D.C.C. §§ 10-32.1-82(2), 10-32.1-84(1), 10-19.1-142(1) and 10-19.1-143(3); see "North Dakota does not make you name an in-state agent in the lease, but an out-of-state entity must register before it can sue"). A partnership renting under a fictitious name may not maintain an action on contracts made in that name until it files a fictitious name certificate, though once it files it may sue on earlier contracts too (N.D.C.C. §§ 45-11-01(2) and 45-11-04). Anyone else renting under a trade name must register it with the secretary of state before doing business under it; that chapter states no bar on suing (N.D.C.C. § 47-25-02). There is no state landlord registration scheme at all - with one exception, which is a real one: a mobile home park needs an annual licence under section 23-10-03, and section 47-10-28(13) lets the district court SUSPEND that licence for a violation, with all park tenants allowed to remain during the suspension and no rule changes, rent increases or terminations without cause while it runs; section 47-32-01.1 makes a section 47-10-28 violation a defence to the eviction. Whether any North Dakota municipality has a rental-registration or rental-licensing ordinance conditioning a possession action: check your city's ordinances before filing.

What to do. Treat every statement that North Dakota 'has no' rule about something as covering only the state statutes and rules cited for it; city and county ordinances, utility tariffs and court decisions can still add rules. If your question is about alarms, locks, building-code figures, zoning or anything a city regulates, check your local code too. And when anyone cites you a North Dakota section, read the body of that section - not its heading.

title: North Dakota has no condominium-conversion notice, no tenant right of first refusal, and nothing a lease must carry as its first clause
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has no condominium conversion statute. Nothing requires an owner who converts a rental building to condominiums to give sitting tenants notice, ninety days or otherwise, to offer them a right of first refusal, to relocate them, or to put a conversion statement in the lease - let alone as the first clause or in capitals. A lease clause reciting a conversion notice right is reciting a rule that does not exist, and because it is printed the tenant may be able to enforce it against you as a contract term.

North Dakota's condominium chapter, N.D.C.C. ch. 47-04.1, has sixteen sections and none of them mentions a tenant. The conversion mechanism is purely a recording act: under 47-04.1-02, when the sole owner or all the owners, or the sole lessee or all the lessees, wish to submit a parcel to a condominium project, "a declaration to that effect shall be executed and acknowledged" and recorded with the county recorder. That is the whole procedure. Section 47-04.1-10 handles withdrawal of property from a project the same way. There is no tenant-notice step anywhere in the chapter, no preemption clause addressing local conversion moratoria or tenant rights beyond the act - so the question whether the condominium act preempts local tenant protections has no answer in the act itself - and no prohibition on converting rental housing to hotel or other transient use or demolishing it for that purpose. The only "right of first refusal" anywhere in these statutes is in N.D.C.C. 47-33-01, which defines it for the purpose of regulating private transfer fee obligations between sellers and buyers.

Mobile home parks are the exception and they are the real answer for a park operator. N.D.C.C. 47-10-28 imposes a change-of-ownership regime on "a person that owns or purchases an existing mobile home park": written notice to each tenant of the change of ownership within five business days after it becomes effective, including the contact information required by subdivision c (subsection 1(d)); the name, address and telephone number of the legal entity that owns the park (1)(g); the telephone number of any existing property manager or designated site agent (1)(h); a designated telephone number manned on weekdays from eight to five and an operational emergency number manned at all times (1)(c)); and a copy of the existing lease terms with any modifications on a tenant's written request within ten business days (1)(f). Subsection 2 forbids requiring a tenant who owns their home to sell or transfer it to the park owner. Subsection 7 forbids a purchaser from increasing the monthly rent for six months if the rent was increased within the sixty days before the purchase, and requires ninety days' notice of any rent increase in a month-to-month arrangement. Subsection 3 requires thirty days' advance written notice of a rule change and then gives a tenant whose home does not comply three months to remedy or vacate before eviction, extendable if a professional relocator certifies the home cannot be moved in time. A violation of any of it carries a civil penalty of not less than two thousand five hundred dollars under subsection 12, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, and under N.D.C.C. 47-32-01.1 is a defence to the eviction.

What to do: outside a mobile home park, do not print a conversion notice clause and do not promise a right of first refusal unless you actually mean to give one as a negotiated term. If you are selling or buying a park, work through 47-10-28(1) as a five-business-day checklist and calendar the six-month rent freeze and the ninety-day increase notice - the penalty floor makes this the most expensive paperwork in North Dakota landlord-tenant law. And note that whether a city may impose its own conversion moratorium or tenant protection is a question of municipal law: N.D.C.C. 47-16-02.1 does bar a political subdivision from controlling the amount of rent charged.

title: No defective-drywall disclosure exists in North Dakota - the word drywall is not in the Century Code
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota implies no warranty about wallboard, and no statute requires a landlord or a lease to say anything about defective, corrosive or so-called Chinese drywall. There is no state remediation standard, no state registry, no rider and no tenant termination remedy tied to it. The word "drywall" does not appear anywhere in the North Dakota Century Code - not in title 47, not in the 2025-26 session laws, and not in the Legislative Council master index of every section name in the code. "Wallboard" does not appear either.

Two things fill the space instead. First, the landlord's general condition duties: N.D.C.C. 47-16-13.1(1)(b) requires the landlord to "make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition", and 47-16-13.1(1)(a) requires compliance with "applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety", which 47-16-13.1(3) makes controlling where it is the greater duty. Sulfide-emitting wallboard that corrodes wiring and gas lines is a fitness-and-habitability problem on that wording, whether or not any statute names it. If the landlord does not repair after notice, 47-16-13 gives the tenant repair-and-deduct with no dollar cap, recovery "in any other lawful manner", or the right to vacate and be discharged from further rent. Second, the caveat that changes this answer: the State Building Code is ch. 54-21.3 and is not readable in this research, so a code-level material standard would bind the landlord through 47-16-13.1(1)(a) without appearing in the lease statutes at all.

What to do: do not print a defective-drywall disclosure as a North Dakota requirement, and do not print a waiver of one - a waiver of a rule North Dakota does not have is empty, not protective, and it suggests to the tenant that something was given up. If you know of suspect wallboard, record it in the 47-16-07.2 condition-of-premises statement, which is the one document North Dakota does require to accompany a rental agreement, and remediate it as a habitability repair.

title: Why a Pre-Set Cleaning and Damage Price List Backfires Here
bodyText: Default rule in North Dakota: no statute authorises a pre-set cost schedule, for carpet cleaning or anything else, and the deposit statute is written in the language of actual cost. You may apply the deposit on termination to damages from deterioration or injury caused by the tenant's pet or the negligence of the tenant or the tenant's guest, to any unpaid rent, and to the costs of cleaning or other repairs which were the tenant's responsibility and which are necessary to return the unit to its original state when the tenant took possession, reasonable wear and tear excepted (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(3)). 'The costs of' means what it cost. Whatever you do not return must be itemised, and the itemisation and the amount due must be delivered or mailed to the tenant at the last address furnished to you, with written notice, within thirty days after termination of the lease and delivery of possession. A price list makes that worse rather than easier, for three reasons. Penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (§ 9-08-03). A contract that fixes the amount of damages in advance is void to that extent unless it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage (§ 9-08-04) - and a cleaning invoice or a carpet quote is neither impracticable nor extremely difficult, which is precisely why the exception does not rescue a cleaning schedule. And a figure above your real cost is security deposit money withheld without reasonable justification, which carries treble damages (§ 47-16-07.1(4)). What to do instead: complete the § 47-16-07.2 statement describing the condition of the facilities at move-in and have both of you sign it, because that statement is prima facie proof of the condition the unit started in and it is the document that makes a later charge stick. Then charge the actual documented cost, keep the invoice, and itemise. If you want tenants to know roughly what cleaning runs, say so in a move-out letter as an estimate - not as an agreed sum in the lease, which is the form § 9-08-04 strikes down.

title: No Tenant Right to Pay the Deposit in Instalments
bodyText: Default rule in North Dakota: there is none, in either direction. No statute gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in instalments, and no statute stops you from agreeing to it. North Dakota regulates the size of the deposit, not when it arrives: a lessor may not demand or receive security, however denominated, in excess of one month's rent, with the two narrow exceptions for an applicant convicted of a felony and an applicant with a judgment for violating a previous rental agreement (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1)), and a pet security deposit is capped separately at the greater of $2,500 or two months' rent (§ 47-16-07.1(2)). Nothing in the section speaks to the date the money is due. So you may ask for the whole deposit before move-in, and you may also offer an instalment arrangement as a letting concession without any statutory conditions attaching to it. Four things to get right if you do offer one. Put the schedule and the unpaid balance in the written lease: violating a material term of a written lease agreement is its own eviction ground on three days' written notice of intention to evict (§§ 47-32-01(8), 47-32-02), and an instalment promise you never wrote down is not a material term of anything. Do not add a charge for the instalment itself where the tenant pays by cash, cheque or money order - you may not charge a tenant a fee to accept any of those for rent or any other payment required under the lease (§ 47-16-20.1). Do not set a flat sum payable on a missed instalment: penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void (§ 9-08-03) and damages fixed in advance are void unless the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (§ 9-08-04). And remember each instalment is deposit money the moment you receive it, so it goes straight into the federally insured interest-bearing account held for the tenant's benefit (§ 47-16-07.1(1)) rather than into your operating account until the balance is complete.

title: Last Month's Rent Is Security If You Hold It Like Security
bodyText:
Default rule in North Dakota: there is no last-month's-rent rule. Nothing bars you from applying the deposit to the final month's rent, nothing bars you from collecting rent in advance, and no statute says prepaid rent is or is not a deposit.

Two provisions decide the question anyway. First, the deposit may be applied on termination to 'any unpaid rent' (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(3)(b)), so if the tenant leaves the last month unpaid you may take it out of the deposit - but you must still itemise what you kept and deliver or mail the itemisation with written notice to the tenant's last address furnished to you within thirty days after termination of the lease and delivery of possession.

Second, and this is the trap: the cap is on 'security, however denominated' (§ 47-16-07.1(1)). A sum you collect at the start, label 'last month's rent', hold to the end and return if the tenant performs is security whatever you call it, and it counts against the one-month-rent ceiling. So one month's rent as a deposit plus a month labelled 'last month's rent' is two months of security, which you may take only from an applicant convicted of a felony as an incentive to rent to them, or from an applicant with a judgment against them for violating a previous rental agreement (§ 47-16-07.1(1)(a)-(b)). A term that collects more than the statute permits is a provision contrary to an express provision of law and therefore unlawful (§ 9-08-01(1)). Rent of lodgings is payable monthly at the end of each month where there is no contract to the contrary (§ 47-16-20), so you may contract for rent in advance - what you may not do is use the rent label to carry security past the ceiling.

What to do: pick one. Either take a security deposit within the cap and apply it to unpaid rent at the end under subsection 3(b), or genuinely require the first and final months' rent in advance as rent, credit each to its own named month in the lease, and do not treat either as returnable security.

title: No Duty to Name a Repair Contact — Unless You Run a Mobile Home Park
bodyText:
For an ordinary house or apartment tenancy, North Dakota requires nothing here. There is no statute making you designate a repairer, a maintenance contact, a managing agent, an emergency number or an address for repair requests, and no statute requiring any of that to be disclosed to the tenant or recited in the lease. The duty in N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1) is simply that "a landlord of a residential dwelling unit shall" do the listed things; it does not say through whom. Correspondingly, the tenant's self-help remedies under § 47-16-13 turn on "notice from the lessee of dilapidations which the lessor ought to repair" — notice to you, by any means — so there is no statutory address or agent that notice has to reach.

Mobile home parks are the exception, and the requirements are detailed. Under § 47-10-28(1), a person who owns or purchases an existing mobile home park must: obtain an annual license under § 23-10-03; designate an official local office, operational by the fifth business day after a change of ownership, unless the park has fewer than twenty-six lots; have a designated telephone number manned on weekdays between eight a.m. and five p.m.; have an operational emergency contact number manned at all times; designate at least one individual for the property who has the authority to make decisions on behalf of, and to perform or direct the performance of, the duties imposed on the owner; and provide each tenant with that individual's contact information. The owner must also give each tenant the name, address and telephone number of the legal entity that owns the park, and the telephone number of any existing property manager or designated site agent. Breach of any provision of that section exposes you to a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and not more than the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, and the park's license can be suspended by the district court with a daily penalty while it remains suspended. That section was amended by S.L. 2025, ch. 238 (S.B. 2385), effective August 1, 2025.

What to do for an ordinary tenancy: name a repair contact anyway, in the lease or in a move-in letter — a person, a telephone number, an email address and an after-hours number. Nothing compels it, but everything about your exposure rewards it. Because § 47-16-13 and § 47-16-13.1(2) both measure you against "a reasonable time after notice," a single published channel is how you find out early and how you later prove when you were told. The risk of having no channel is that notice reaches a handyman, a neighbour or an unread voicemail, and the clock runs anyway.

One thing to avoid: do not write a clause requiring the tenant to use a contractor you designate as a condition of the repair-and-deduct remedy. Section 47-16-13 lets the tenant "repair the premises and deduct the expense of such repair from the rent" without naming a contractor, obtaining your approval, or satisfying any other precondition, and a lease term adding one purports to narrow a statutory remedy. It would be open to unconscionability review under § 47-16-13.3(1)(a). Designate a contact so the tenant calls you first; do not try to make your contractor a gatekeeper.

title: Taking In People Displaced by a Disaster: Only Your Lease Decides
bodyText:
The default rule first: North Dakota law sets no limit on how many people may live in a rental and gives a tenant no statutory right to house anyone. The only occupancy cap that exists is the one your lease sets, plus any local ordinance or health-and-safety standard - the state's fair housing chapter expressly leaves 'a reasonable local or state restriction on the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling' and health-and-safety restrictions untouched (N.D.C.C. 14-02.5-12(1)).

So there is no North Dakota rule either way about a tenant taking in friends or relatives displaced by a fire, a flood or a declared disaster. No statute allows it over your lease's occupancy limit, suspends an occupancy limit during an emergency, adds rent for extra occupants, or makes you accept a displaced guest. Equally, no statute lets you treat the extra people as a lease breach unless your lease makes them one.

What the statutes do give you, once someone is on the premises, is this. The tenant must require other people on the premises with the tenant's consent to behave in a way that does not disturb the neighbours' peaceful enjoyment (47-16-13.2(7)), and you may evict where 'a lessee or a person on the premises with the lessee's consent acts in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment of the premises' (47-32-01(7)). An eviction on that ground needs no notice of intention to evict before filing (47-32-02 requires the three-day notice only for subsections 4, 5, 6 and 8 of 47-32-01). Note that a judgment resting in whole or in part on a disturbance of the peace also strips the tenant of the hardship stay that 47-32-04 otherwise allows.

Do this: set the occupancy limit and the guest-stay limit in the lease in plain numbers, say whether a longer stay needs your written consent and whether it adds rent, and decide in advance whether you will grant a short written exception after a disaster. Nothing obliges you to, and nothing stops you. Do not put a term in the lease that says the tenant waives a statutory right to house displaced persons - North Dakota has no such right, so the waiver is empty and it suggests to the tenant that they gave something up.

title: After a Disaster: When the Tenancy Ends and Whether Rent Keeps Running
bodyText:
The default rule first. North Dakota settles damage to a rental by two general lease provisions, not by a disaster statute. A leasing of real property terminates by destruction of the property leased (N.D.C.C. 47-16-14(4)) - automatically, and with no fault exception, so even a total loss the tenant caused ends the tenancy and leaves you a damages claim rather than a continuing lease. Short of destruction, the tenant may terminate where the greater part of the property, or the part that was the material inducement to take it, perishes from any cause other than the tenant's own ordinary negligence (47-16-17(2)), or where you do not meet your obligations within a reasonable time after request (47-16-17(1)). The tenant may also give you notice of dilapidations you ought to repair and then repair and deduct, recover the cost in any other lawful manner, or vacate and be discharged from further rent and all other lease conditions (47-16-13).

Now the answer. A declared natural disaster changes nothing by itself. North Dakota has no disaster or declared-emergency provision for a tenancy anywhere in its landlord-tenant statutes: no automatic termination, no extended notice period, no eviction moratorium, and - this is the one landlords most often assume - no rent abatement while the unit is unusable. Rent keeps running under the lease until the tenancy actually ends by one of the routes above. The only proportioning rule is 47-16-21: when a leasing is terminated before the time originally agreed upon, the tenant pays the due proportion for the use actually made of the property, unless that use is 'merely nominal and of no benefit to the tenant' - which can reduce the final bill to nothing where the tenant got no real use after the event. In a mobile home park the rule runs the other way again: tenants keep occupancy through a licence suspension, and during a pending action under 47-10-28 'the tenant shall continue paying rent' (47-10-28(13) and (14)).

One point is not settled, and here is the cautious course. North Dakota's emergency-services chapter, 37-17.1, says nothing about rent, leases or eviction. A local mandatory evacuation order may be declared only by the county's or city's principal executive officer and lasts no more than seven days without the governing board's consent (37-17.1-10(1)). In a declared disaster the governor may 'Direct and compel the evacuation' of an area, 'Control ingress and egress ... and the occupancy of premises therein', and commandeer private property subject to compensation (37-17.1-05(6)(d), (e), (g)). So an executive order could reach occupancy, but the statute itself does not suspend rent or possession; whether an evacuation does so by law only case law could settle. Read any order that applies to your property, and otherwise treat rent as continuing to accrue but do not treat a tenant who is out under an evacuation order as a holdover or a defaulter: do not serve a notice of intention to evict or file while the order is in force, document the dates, and settle the rent for that period by written agreement. Then do this generally: decide in the lease what happens on partial damage - whether rent is reduced or suspended, on what evidence, and whether you may offer another unit - because no North Dakota statute decides any of it for you, and put your insurance and your tenant's renter-insurance requirement in writing.

title: North Dakota has no drug-free housing addendum -- what it gives you instead
bodyText:
THE DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota does NOT require a drug-free or crime-free housing addendum, does not authorise one by statute, does not prescribe any wording for one, and does not give one any special effect. The words 'drug-free' and 'crime-free' do not appear anywhere in North Dakota's landlord-tenant statutes, and there is no statutory addendum of any kind for a residential lease. So if you use one, it is an ORDINARY LEASE TERM that stands or falls on general contract law -- not a statutory instrument.

AND A WAIVER WARNING, WHICH IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE ANSWER. Because North Dakota implies no drug-free term into a lease, an addendum in which the tenant 'waives' or 'gives up' anything in exchange for a drug-free promise is waiving a rule North Dakota does not have. That waiver is EMPTY, not lawful -- and printing it invites the tenant to believe they surrendered something they never had, which helps nobody and can cut against you.

WHAT NORTH DAKOTA ACTUALLY GIVES YOU. Four things, and together they do most of the work an addendum is meant to do.
1. N.D.C.C. s 47-32-01(8): an eviction is maintainable when 'The lessee violates a material term of the written lease agreement between the lessor and lessee.' A drug term in your WRITTEN lease is therefore evictable -- which is why an addendum is OPTIONAL but not pointless. The criminal-activity row covers this: North Dakota implies no crime-free term, deliberately unlike Colorado, so the term has to be in the written lease to exist at all. s 47-32-02 requires three days' written notice of intention to evict for a subsection-8 case.
2. s 14-02.5-02(4) -- the fair-housing permission: 'This section does not prohibit discrimination against an individual because the individual has been CONVICTED under federal law or the law of any state of the ILLEGAL MANUFACTURE OR DISTRIBUTION of a controlled substance.' Read it narrowly, because it is narrow: it needs a CONVICTION, and it reaches manufacture or distribution only. It does NOT cover possession, use, addiction, an arrest, a charge, or a conviction for anything else. Screening beyond those limits gets no shelter from this subsection.
3. The companion limit in the same chapter: a disability under North Dakota's fair-housing act excludes 'current illegal use or addiction to any drug or illegal or federally controlled substance' -- so current illegal use is not a protected disability, while a record of addiction in recovery may well be. Do not draft an addendum that treats the two the same.
4. s 12.1-32-08(1), as amended in 2025: when sentencing a person guilty of criminal activities causing pecuniary damages the court 'shall order that the defendant make restitution', and 'Restitution MUST include payment to the owner of real property that is contaminated by the defendant in the manufacturing of methamphetamine for the cost of removing the contamination and returning the property to the property's condition before contamination and to any other person that has incurred costs in decontaminating the property.' That is MANDATORY restitution to you as owner -- a far better remedy than any addendum clause, and it does not depend on your lease saying anything. Keep your decontamination invoices.

WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. (1) If you want a drug term, put it in the body of the written lease as a material term rather than in a separate 'addendum' -- North Dakota gives an addendum no special status, and s 47-32-01(8) keys on 'the written lease agreement'. Keep it in the prohibited-acts section with your other material terms. (2) Keep the term about CONDUCT ON THE PREMISES, not about a tenant's status, history or associations -- status-based terms run into s 14-02.5-02(2) (terms, conditions or privileges of rental) and get no help from subsection 4 unless there is a conviction for manufacture or distribution. (3) Do NOT attach a fixed fine or 'drug violation fee': s 9-08-03 makes 'Penalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance thereof' VOID, flatly, and s 9-08-04 voids damages fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. Charge actual cost. (4) Do not promise a 'drug-free building' to your tenants -- North Dakota imposes no such duty on you, and the promise creates one you then have to keep. (5) In a MOBILE HOME PARK, s 47-10-28 governs rule changes: thirty days' notice, and for non-sanitation rules three months to remedy or vacate before you may begin an eviction, with a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 (s 47-10-28(12)) and a defence to the eviction (s 47-32-01.1).

ONE LIMIT ON THIS ANSWER: MEDICAL MARIJUANA. Chapter 19-24.1 says three things that matter. s 19-24.1-34(1)(c): the chapter 'does not require ... A landlord to allow production or processing on rental property'. s 19-24.1-33(3) keeps the smoking ban of s 23-12-10, which covers 'any common areas in apartment buildings' (s 23-12-09(11)). But s 19-24.1-32(1) says a registered patient is not subject to 'the denial of any right or privilege' for use under the chapter, and nothing in the chapter says a landlord may ban a patient's use inside the unit. Whether a lease ban on that use is such a 'denial' is a question only case law could settle. Cautious course: ban growing and processing, keep a no-smoking rule that applies to every substance and every tenant, and do not ban or penalise a registered patient's non-smoked medical use in the unit.

title: What a Domestic Violence Victim Must Give You -- and What You May Not Ask For
bodyText: Default rule: North Dakota's domestic violence early-termination right is conditioned on a notice, not on a documentation package. Section 47-16-17.1(2) requires the tenant to give you advance written notice stating three things and only three: that the tenant fears imminent domestic violence "from a person named in a court order, an order prohibiting contact, or a civil protection order under chapter 14-07.7, or other record filed with a court"; that the tenant needs to terminate the tenancy; and the specific date the tenancy will terminate. The notice must be delivered by mail, by facsimile or in person before the tenancy terminates (section 47-16-17.1(3)). That is the whole list. The statute does not require the tenant to attach the order, to obtain a letter from a domestic violence advocate, a shelter, a counsellor, a healthcare provider, a social worker or a police officer, to swear an affidavit, or to use any form; and it does not create a qualified-third-party verification route, so there is no third party you may insist on. Note the one real limit the words do impose: the person feared must be named in a court order, an order prohibiting contact, a civil protection order under chapter 14-07.7, or another record filed with a court -- an advocate's letter standing alone is not one of those, and neither is a police report that was never filed with a court. Chapter 14-07.7, created by House Bill 1489, 2025 Session Laws chapter 145, effective January 1, 2026, is where those orders now come from: a disorderly conduct restraining order, a domestic violence protection order or a sexual assault restraining order, petitioned for with no filing fee and served with no service fee to the petitioner. Section 47-16-17.1(2)(a) was amended by the same act to name it. Your confidentiality duty is strict and expensive: under section 47-16-17.1(4) you may not disclose information the tenant gives you documenting domestic violence, it may not go into any shared database or to any person, and it may be used only as evidence in an eviction proceeding, in a claim for unpaid rent or damages arising out of the tenancy, or as otherwise required by law. Section 47-16-17.1(10) bars refusing to rent to, or retaliating against, anyone who exercised this right, and section 47-16-17.1(11) lets a court award statutory damages of one thousand dollars plus actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, costs and disbursements. What to do: accept a notice that says the three things, note the termination date, and do not build a document checklist -- a lease or a form demanding an advocate letter, a police report or a sworn statement adds a condition the statute does not have and is exposed under section 47-16-13.3. Cautious course on the one thing the statute does not say: if the tenant does not offer a copy of the order, you may ask for one but you may not make the termination conditional on getting it; keep whatever you receive out of your screening file, your software and any shared database, and limit who in your organisation can see it.

title: Reselling electricity or gas to tenants in North Dakota: no disclosure statute, and the utility rules bar it unless the tariff allows
bodyText:
Default rule: nothing in the North Dakota Century Code requires a landlord who meters and resells electricity or gas to tenants to make any disclosure, and nothing in it authorises it either. The word "submeter" does not appear anywhere in the North Dakota Century Code -- not in a single section and not in a single section heading in the Legislative Council master index. There is no prescribed disclosure form, no notice, no rate ceiling and no registration for a landlord who resells a metered utility.

The answer, with one real exception. If you rent mobile home lots, you are not in the unregulated space: N.D.C.C. sec. 47-10-28(8) lets a park owner buy utility service for a tenant and either fold it into rent or bill it as a separate charge based on actual usage, but it bars charging more than the actual cost per unit the owner paid the provider plus a reasonable administrative fee capped at three dollars, bars charging a utility fee at all unless every mobile home has an individual meter, and requires the owner to give the tenant access to the meter readings for that lot. Breaching any of it exposes you to a civil penalty of at least $2,500 under sec. 47-10-28(12) and gives the tenant a complete defence to an eviction under sec. 47-32-01.1.

The utility rules answer the question the statutes leave open. Title 49 defines a public utility only by the business it is in, such as electric utilities 'engaged in the generation and distribution of light, heat, or power' (N.D.C.C. §§ 49-01-01(3), 49-02-01(4)-(5)). But the Public Service Commission's service rules speak to the customer directly. Electricity a public utility supplies 'shall not be resold or submetered by a customer unless the rate schedule under which the customer receives service specifically so provides' (N.D. Admin. Code § 69-09-02-15). Gas 'shall not be resold or caused to be resold by any customer' unless the customer is in the gas distribution business with a commission-approved contract and a certificate of public convenience and necessity (§ 69-09-01-25). A city-owned utility is outside the commission's rate and service orders (N.D.C.C. § 49-02-01.1(1)), so its own terms govern.

What to do: do not submeter or resell electricity unless your provider's rate schedule expressly allows it, and do not resell gas at all. Read the provider's tariff, or ask it, before you install submeters. The safe routes are a separate account and meter in each tenant's name, or utilities included in the rent, which the commission's rules recognise. Whether an allocation by formula without meters counts as resale is not addressed by the rules; treat it as resale and ask the provider first. If a tariff does allow submetering, bill at no more than your actual cost per unit, put the method in the lease, and give the tenant the readings and the provider invoice on request.

title: No statutory right to call for help in North Dakota -- so never write a clause that chills it
bodyText:
THE DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota has NO statute protecting a tenant's right to call the police or emergency services, and NO statute making such a right non-waivable. There is nothing in chapter 47-16, chapter 47-32 or chapter 47-10 on the subject. There is also no nuisance-call or excessive-call ordinance-penalty statute of the kind other states have had to legislate against, and -- importantly -- NO GENERAL LANDLORD RETALIATION STATUTE either. So North Dakota neither grants the right nor penalises you for burdening it.

THAT IS NOT PERMISSION. READ THE NEXT THREE PARAGRAPHS BEFORE YOU DRAFT ANYTHING.

FIRST, A WAIVER OF THIS RIGHT IS EMPTY, NOT LAWFUL -- AND WORSE THAN USELESS. Because North Dakota confers no statutory right to call for help, a clause in which the tenant 'waives' or 'agrees not to exercise' such a right surrenders nothing. It gains you nothing enforceable. What it DOES do is tell a tenant, in writing, that they have given up the ability to call for help -- which is the single most damaging sentence a residential lease can contain. If a tenant does not call because of your clause and is harmed, you have created a factual record that your lease discouraged it. Do not write it.

SECOND, A 'NO EXCESSIVE CALLS' OR 'CALLS ARE A NUISANCE' TERM IS A TRAP, AND THE TRAP IS s 9-08-02. A clause penalising a tenant for calling emergency services, or charging a fee per call, runs into two provisions at once. s 9-08-03: 'Penalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance thereof are void' -- flat and unqualified, so a per-call fee is void. And s 9-08-02: a contract whose object is 'directly or indirectly, the exempting of anyone from responsibility for that person's own fraud or wilful injury to the person or property of another, or violation of law, whether wilful or negligent', is 'against the policy of the law', which s 9-08-01(2) makes unlawful. A term discouraging calls for help to the premises points straight at that: if a landlord's own habitability failure under s 47-16-13.1 is what the tenant would be calling about, a clause suppressing the call is a term tending to exempt the landlord from responsibility for a violation of law. See the exculpatory-clauses and unconscionability rows; the point here is simply that this is the worst place in a lease to test s 9-08-02.

THIRD, WHERE THE CALLER IS A VICTIM, THERE ARE REAL STATUTES AND REAL MONEY. North Dakota protects the victim rather than the caller, which comes to much the same thing in practice:
- s 47-16-17.1 lets a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, or who fears imminent domestic violence, terminate the lease 'WITHOUT PENALTY OR LIABILITY' on written notice and payment of the month's rent plus one month's rent. s 47-16-17.1(10) bars refusing to rent, refusing to negotiate, making unavailable, denying a dwelling 'or otherwise retaliat[ing] in the rental of a dwelling' because the right was exercised. s 47-16-17.1(11): statutory damages of ONE THOUSAND DOLLARS plus actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, costs and disbursements.
- s 47-16-17.1(4) is the one to be most careful about: you 'may not disclose information provided to the landlord by a tenant documenting domestic violence', and it 'may not be entered into any shared database or provided to any person', except as evidence in an eviction, in a claim for unpaid rent or damages, 'or as otherwise required by law'. THAT IS A CLOSED LIST WITH NO CONSENT EXCEPTION -- so a clause asking the tenant to consent to disclosure is UNLAWFUL, not merely empty.
- s 14-02.5-02(3): an applicant for or tenant of housing that is part of a STATE HOUSING PROGRAM 'may not be denied admission to, denied assistance under, terminated from participating in, or EVICTED FROM HOUSING ON THE BASIS THAT the applicant or tenant is or has been a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking', if otherwise qualified.
- s 14-02.5-45(2): 'It is a discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with any individual in the exercise or enjoyment of ... any right granted or protected by this chapter' -- including the individual who 'aided or encouraged any other individual' in exercising it. s 14-02.5-45(3) makes the force-or-threat version a CLASS A MISDEMEANOR.
- Chapter 14-07.7, in force since 1 January 2026, lets an individual who is or has been a victim of disorderly conduct, domestic violence or sexual assault petition for a civil protection order that can prohibit the restrained individual from 'Entering or remaining on premises' (s 14-07.7-01(1)(a)(2)). A disorderly conduct restraining order or a sexual assault restraining order may grant relief for up to two years (s 14-07.7-05(3), s 14-07.7-09(3)). A domestic violence protection order has no such cap and runs to the expiration date the order sets (s 14-07.7-03(3)).

WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. (1) Write nothing at all about calling police or emergency services. Silence is the correct drafting choice: North Dakota gives you no term worth having and the downside is severe. (2) Delete any 'excessive calls', 'nuisance calls', 'police call fee' or 'crime-free' call-counting language inherited from another state's form -- it is void under s 9-08-03 as a penalty and dangerous under s 9-08-02. (3) If disturbance at the premises is the real problem, use the route North Dakota actually gives you: s 47-16-13.2(7) obliges the tenant to conduct themselves, and to require other persons on the premises with the tenant's consent to conduct themselves, so as not to disturb neighbours' peaceful enjoyment; and s 47-32-01(7) makes a disturbance by 'a lessee or a person on the premises with the lessee's consent' an eviction ground in its own right -- with NO three-day notice required, because s 47-32-02 lists only subsections 4, 5, 6 and 8. Proceed on the conduct, never on the call. (4) Never treat a tenant's call for help as the disturbance. Where the tenant is the victim, s 47-16-17.1(10), s 14-02.5-02(3) and s 14-02.5-45(2) are live and carry statutory damages, fee-shifting and, in one case, criminal liability. (5) In a MOBILE HOME PARK you must 'Have an operational emergency contact number manned at all times' (s 47-10-28(1)(c)(2)) and acknowledge tenant complaints within two business days (s 47-10-28(1)(e)), with a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 (s 47-10-28(12)) and a defence to the eviction (s 47-32-01.1) if you do not.

title: If the Property Is Taken for Public Use: Put a Condemnation Clause in the Lease
bodyText:
The default rule first, and in North Dakota it is thin. The Constitution requires that private property not be taken or damaged for public use without just compensation 'first made to, or paid into court for the owner', with compensation ascertained by a jury unless waived, and it excludes economic-development benefits from 'public use' (N.D. Const. art. I, 16). It speaks of the owner. It says nothing about a tenant, a leasehold, or whether rent stops.

The landlord-tenant statutes say nothing either. 'Eminent domain' appears once in all of title 47 of the Century Code, in the environmental-covenants chapter (47-37-08(1)(e)), and the words 'condemnation' and 'just compensation' do not appear in title 47 at all. There is no provision ending or shrinking the tenant's rent when the leased property is taken, and no provision letting a court cancel the lease in a condemnation case. Two related points. First, 'condemnation' in the Century Code means eminent domain only - it is not the word North Dakota uses for a building condemned as unfit, so searching for 'condemned premises' finds nothing. Second, your general covenant of quiet possession (47-16-08) binds you against 'all persons lawfully claiming the same', which is a title covenant; a public taking is not a claim to your title, so do not assume it answers this.

The eminent domain chapter, 32-15, does not answer it either. It never says whether a taking ends a lease or stops rent. What it does say: anyone "in occupation of, or having or claiming an interest in" the property may appear and defend (32-15-20), and the jury must value "each and every separate estate or interest therein" (32-15-22(1)). So a tenant's leasehold can be valued apart from your interest, and only the lease decides how the two of you share. Separately, chapter 54-01.1 (Relocation Assistance) has the displacing agency pay a displaced residential tenant's moving expenses (54-01.1-03) and a replacement-housing payment of up to $5,250 if the tenant occupied the unit for at least ninety days (54-01.1-05). Those are the tenant's claims against the agency, not part of your award.

So here is the cautious course. Do not rely on North Dakota law to sort this out, because no North Dakota statute does. Put a condemnation clause in the lease: say that if all or a material part of the premises is taken by eminent domain or conveyed under threat of it, the lease ends on the date the condemnor takes possession or title, whichever is earlier; that rent is prorated and paid to that date and any prepaid rent and the security deposit are returned; that on a partial taking rent is reduced in the proportion the taken part bears to the whole, or either party may end the lease; and that the award belongs to the landlord except for any part separately awarded to the tenant for the tenant's trade fixtures, moving costs or relocation benefits. Keep the tenant's own claim carved out rather than assigned to you - an assignment is the part most likely to be attacked, and a term restricting a party from enforcing its rights by the usual legal proceedings is void (9-08-05). Tell the tenant in the lease where to send notices, because a tenant who receives notice of a proceeding to recover the property must inform you immediately and deliver the notice to you, and is liable to you for damages from any failure to do so (47-16-25). And note that a fixture the tenant installed for trade, manufacture, ornament or domestic use may be removed by the tenant at any time during the term if it can be done without injury to the premises (47-06-04), which is worth settling before a condemnor takes possession.

title: North Dakota requires no staff background checks — but its off-duty-conduct rule limits what you can act on
bodyText:
The default rule: North Dakota does not require you to screen the people you hire to work in rental housing. No provision in the North Dakota statutes requires a background check, a criminal history record check or fingerprinting for an apartment manager, caretaker, maintenance worker or contractor, at any portfolio size — and nothing requires one before you hand someone a key. North Dakota imposes no key-control duty at any portfolio size and no employee-screening mandate for rental housing. See the key-control-policy row for the key half.

So screening your staff is a choice, and because it is a choice, employment discrimination law is the only thing shaping how you do it. Four North Dakota rules matter.
1. The protected list for employment is not the same as the one for housing. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.4-03(1) makes it a discriminatory practice to refuse to hire, to discharge, or to accord adverse or unequal treatment 'with respect to application, hiring, training, apprenticeship, tenure, promotion, upgrading, compensation, layoff, or a term, privilege, or condition of employment' because of 'race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, physical or mental disability, status with respect to marriage or public assistance, or participation in lawful activity off the employer's premises during nonworking hours which is not in direct conflict with the essential business-related interests of the employer'. That last limb is distinctively North Dakota and it is the one a background check can trip over: lawful off-duty conduct that a check turns up — what someone posts, drinks, belongs to or does at the weekend — is a protected characteristic unless it is in direct conflict with your essential business interests. A criminal conviction is not protected and you may screen for it; lawful off-duty behaviour generally is.
2. Medical questions come only after a conditional offer, and the answers live in a separate file. § 14-02.4-10(3): 'After a conditional offer of employment, it is not a discriminatory practice' to require a physical examination to determine capability to perform the essential functions of the job with or without reasonable accommodations, or to investigate medical history for the same purpose — but only 'if every entering employee in the same job category is subjected to the examination' or investigation. And § 14-02.4-10(4): medical history 'must be collected and maintained separate from nonmedical information and must be kept confidential'. So if your screening vendor returns medical information in the same report as the criminal and credit results, you have a problem to fix before you file it.
3. Tests are allowed, with a condition. § 14-02.4-09 lets an employer 'give and ... act upon the results of any professionally developed ability test', provided the test, its administration or the action on the results is not designed, intended or used to discriminate on the protected grounds — including that off-duty-lawful-activity ground. 'Professionally developed' is the operative qualifier; an improvised personality quiz is not within it.
4. Security clearances are safe. § 14-02.4-07 makes it not a discriminatory practice to refuse to hire or to discharge where occupancy of the position, or access to the premises where the duties are performed, is subject to a national-security clearance requirement the individual has not met.

What to do. Decide in advance which roles get checked and what disqualifies, write it down, and apply it the same way to everyone in the same job category — that single discipline is what §§ 14-02.4-09 and 14-02.4-10(3) both reward. Ask criminal and reference questions before any offer if you want, but keep medical and disability questions until after a conditional offer, and keep the medical answers in a separate, confidential file. Do not reject someone for lawful off-duty activity unless you can say why it directly conflicts with the essential business interests of a landlord. Train anyone who holds keys: because North Dakota gives you no key-control duty, the only limits on what your staff may do inside a tenant's home are § 47-16-07.3 and your own instructions — your employee entering without notice is your breach, not theirs. And bear in mind the retaliation rule: § 14-02.4-18 makes it a discriminatory practice to retaliate against someone who opposed a discriminatory practice or who in good faith complained, testified or assisted in a proceeding.

Exposure, so you can size it. § 14-02.4-20: the department or the court may enjoin the practice, grant equitable relief and award back pay 'limited to no more than two years from the date a minimally sufficient complaint was filed', reduced by interim earnings or amounts earnable with reasonable diligence; 'Neither the department nor an administrative hearing officer may order compensatory or punitive damages under this chapter'; the court may award the prevailing party a reasonable attorney's fee; and if the court finds the complaint false and not made in good faith it 'shall order the complainant to pay court costs and reasonable attorney's fees' — a provision that protects an employer facing a bad-faith claim. Note the contrast with housing, where § 14-02.5-32 reaches civil penalties of up to $55,000; the employment chapter is the milder of the two.

One mobile home park point: § 47-10-28(1)(c)(3) requires the park to 'Designate at least one individual for the property who has the authority to make decisions on behalf of and perform, or direct the performance of, duties imposed on the owner', (c)(4) to give tenants that individual's contact information, and (1)(h) to provide the telephone number of any existing property manager or designated site agent. That is a duty to NAME a person, not to vet one — but if you do not have such a person, the omission carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and is a defence to an eviction under § 47-32-01.1.

title: North Dakota has no energy-data release statute: a lease clause will not make the utility hand you a tenant's usage data
bodyText:
Default rule: North Dakota has no statute about tenant energy-usage data. Nothing authorises a lease clause by which the tenant consents to release of usage data to the owner; nothing requires a utility to release it on the tenant's authorisation; and nothing requires benchmarking of a building's energy use. There is no North Dakota law here in either direction.

What that means in practice, and it is the opposite of reassuring. Because no statute gives a tenant's authorisation legal effect against the provider, a release clause in your lease does not oblige the utility to give you anything. The provider will apply its own customer-privacy policy and its own tariff, and will almost always require its own signed authorisation form from the account holder, naming the account and a period. A lease clause is at best evidence that the tenant agreed to co-operate; it is not a key to the data.

Where you do have a right to meter information. Two places, neither of them a data-release statute. If you rent mobile home lots and you bill the utility, N.D.C.C. sec. 47-10-28(8) requires you to give the TENANT access to the records of meter readings taken at that tenant's lot -- a duty running the other way, from you to the tenant. And if you hold the account yourself, the data is already yours, because you are the customer; that is the simplest route to building-level consumption figures and it needs no consent from anyone.

What to do. Do not put an energy-data release in the lease and treat it as done. If you need a tenant's usage data -- for benchmarking, for a green certification, for an efficiency project or to verify a submetered bill -- do three things. Ask the provider what form it requires and use that form, signed by the account holder, for a stated account and a stated period. Ask the tenant for it as a separate request, not buried in the lease, so the consent is informed and revocable and so you are not relying on a term the tenant may never have read. And where you can, get what you need without tenant data at all: hold the master account, or read your own submeters, and work from building-level figures. If you do ask a tenant to sign a release, limit it to consumption quantities and billing periods for the premises, do not ask for payment history or personal information you have no use for, and say in writing what you will use it for.

title: If an LLC or corporation owns the property, confirm who may appear in the eviction
bodyText:
Start with the default rule: no North Dakota statute names who may stand up in court for a landlord that is a corporation, an LLC or a partnership, but one statute comes close. The eviction chapter touches representation exactly once, and narrowly — N.D.C.C. § 47-32-03 lets executors and administrators bring eviction actions "in the district courts in the same manner as their testators and intestates". There is no companion sentence for a business entity. N.D.C.C. § 47-32-02 assumes an attorney may act (an affidavit of "the plaintiff or the plaintiff's attorney") but never requires one.

The statute that comes close is N.D.C.C. § 27-11-01: "Except as otherwise provided by state law or supreme court rule, a person may not ... commence, conduct, or defend in any court of record of this state, any action or proceeding in which the person is not a party concerned" without admission to the bar and an annual licence. A violation is a class A misdemeanor. When an LLC or corporation owns the property, the entity is the party; on the natural reading its officer, member or property manager is not "a party concerned", so filing and arguing the eviction would be practising law. The statute leaves room for "supreme court rule", and § 27-02-07 lets the supreme court "make all necessary rules for the restraint of persons unlawfully engaging in the practice of the law". Small claims court is the one place the statutes relax this: under § 27-08.1-03 "the plaintiff and the defendant may appear without counsel" - but small claims handles money claims, not evictions. The eviction chapter itself touches representation only for estates (§ 47-32-03).

What to do. Do not assume an officer, member or property manager can file and argue the eviction. An appearance by someone not entitled to make it can cost you the action and not merely a continuance, and § 27-11-01 makes it a crime. For a money claim of $15,000 or less in small claims court, § 27-08.1-03 lets the parties appear without counsel. The cautious and cheap course, and the one to take whenever there is any doubt, is to have a licensed North Dakota attorney file for the entity. If the owner is an estate rather than a company, § 47-32-03 is your authority and you should cite it. Nothing here is a term for the lease to carry — it is a filing decision, so there is no clause for it.

title: Mold, Contamination and Other Environmental Events: No Statutory Exit Either Way
bodyText:
The default rule first. A North Dakota lease ends early only on the grounds the statutes or the lease itself give. A leasing terminates by destruction of the property leased (N.D.C.C. 47-16-14(4)); the tenant may terminate where the greater part, or the part that was the material inducement, perishes from any cause other than the tenant's ordinary negligence (47-16-17(2)), or where you do not meet your obligations within a reasonable time after request (47-16-17(1)); and the tenant may give notice of dilapidations you ought to repair and then repair and deduct, recover the cost in any other lawful manner, or vacate and be discharged from further rent and all other lease conditions (47-16-13). As the landlord, your only statutory early-termination grounds are that the tenant uses the property contrary to the agreement, or does not make repairs the tenant is bound to make within a reasonable time after request (47-16-16).

Now the answer. North Dakota has no environmental-event termination right, for either side. There is no mold statute, no asbestos or lead provision for rentals, no methamphetamine-contamination provision, and no radon duty owed to a tenant. The radon and property-condition disclosure sections people point to - 47-10-02.1, 47-10-02.2 and 47-10-02.3 - run from a seller to a buyer of real property, not from a landlord to a tenant, and 47-10-02.1 expressly exempts transfers by a mortgagor in default to a mortgagee and transfers pursuant to a foreclosure sale. Chapter 47-37, the Uniform Environmental Covenants Act, is about recorded covenants on land and says nothing about a lease. So contamination that stops short of destroying the property does not end the lease by itself, and you have no statutory right to end it in order to remediate.

Do this. If you want the option to end a tenancy so a unit can be remediated, the lease has to give it to you - North Dakota recognises a lease-reserved right of re-entry and sets the procedure for it (three days' previous written notice of intention to re-enter under 47-17-04, or an action for possession without that notice under 47-17-05), so draft the trigger narrowly: a written order or determination by a public authority, or a written determination by a qualified professional, that the unit cannot safely be occupied during remediation. Three limits to respect. First, it cannot be used to escape your own duties: you must keep the premises fit and habitable and comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (47-16-13.1(1)(a) and (b)), and a contract exempting anyone from responsibility for a violation of law, whether wilful or negligent, is against the policy of the law (9-08-02), so a clause that lets you terminate over a condition you caused or failed to repair will not hold. Second, do not attach a fixed sum: penalties imposed by contract are void (9-08-03) and damages fixed in advance are void to that extent unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (9-08-04). Third, the whole term is subject to unconscionability review (47-16-13.3). Also note that your absence of a statutory right is matched by the tenant's: a tenant who wants out over mold must use 47-16-13 or 47-16-17, so handling a complaint promptly is what keeps the tenancy intact.

title: No Tenant Right to EV Charging -- the Condominium Statute Does Not Reach Rentals
bodyText:
Start with the default rule: North Dakota gives a tenant no right of any kind to install or use an electric vehicle charging station at a rental property. No statute requires you to allow one, to supply one, to act on a request within any deadline, or to give a reason for saying no. A lease term that prohibits or conditions EV charging is an ordinary lease term, and it binds.

North Dakota does have one EV charging statute, and it is the sibling that proves the point. N.D.C.C. § 47-04.1-16 sits in the Condominium Ownership Act. It voids any covenant, restriction or condition in a deed, contract or security instrument, and any association bylaw, that effectively prohibits or unreasonably restricts the installation or use of a charging station within an OWNER's unit or in a designated parking space -- a deeded space, a space in the owner's limited common area, or a space designated for use by a particular owner. It gives an OWNER sixty days: if the condominium's administrative body does not deny the application in writing within sixty days of receipt, the application is deemed approved (unless the delay is a reasonable request for more information). Every actor in the section is a unit owner or a condominium association. The words landlord, tenant, lessor, lessee and lease do not appear in it, and nothing in chapter 47-16 picks it up. It is not a landlord-tenant provision and it does not give your tenant anything.

So the lease does all the work here. Decide the question in writing rather than in a conversation at move-in. If you are prohibiting charging, say so in terms that cover the ways it actually happens -- a cord run from the unit's own outlet, an extension cord across a walkway, and use of a shared-area or garage outlet -- because a bare ban on "installing a charging station" does not reach any of those. If you are allowing it, set the conditions in the lease (see the EV charging installation clause in this library). Two North Dakota wrinkles: if you own a condominium unit and rent it out, § 47-04.1-16 gives the right against the association to YOU as the unit owner, not to your tenant, so you are the one who would have to apply; and if you sit on the association's administrative body, § 47-04.1-16(8) makes a willful violation of the section a liability for actual damages plus a civil penalty of up to $1,000 payable to the applicant.

title: Shared-Area EV Charging Is Your Amenity, Not a Tenant Right
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota gives a tenant no right to install, use, or be allocated an electric vehicle charging station in a parking lot, garage, carport, or any other shared area of a rental property, and no statute requires a landlord to create one, to reserve a space for one, or to let a tenant run a cord across a shared area. Access to shared-area charging is whatever your lease and house rules say it is.

The only North Dakota statute on shared-area charging is a condominium provision and it does not reach rentals. N.D.C.C. § 47-04.1-16(4) lets a unit OWNER install in a limited common area, and obliges the association to approve if the owner agrees in writing to the association's architectural standards, to use a licensed contractor, to provide a certificate of insurance within fourteen days naming the association as an additional insured and to renew it yearly, to pay installation and electricity costs, and to comply with reasonable regulations on number, size, location and placement. Subsection (5) lets the association authorise a common-area installation under a licence agreement where the owner's own space will not work; (6) lets the association install a common-area station for all members and set terms of use; (7) lets it create a new parking space to make an installation possible; and (4)(f) lets it deny an installation on bona fide safety requirements consistent with an applicable building code or recognised safety standard. Every one of those powers and duties runs between a unit owner and a condominium association. None of it binds a landlord or helps a tenant.

What to do. If you install a charger in a shared area, it is your amenity and your liability: § 47-16-13.1(1)(c) requires you to keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition, (1)(d) to maintain in good and safe working order the electrical facilities you supply, and (1)(a) with (3) makes applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety binding and controlling where they demand more. You cannot shift that to tenants in the lease: in any dwelling other than a single-family residence, § 47-16-13.1(5) allows a tenant to take on specified repairs or maintenance only in a SEPARATE writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration, and § 47-16-13.1(6) bars treating performance of that separate agreement as a condition of the lease. So charge for charging if you like -- recover your actual cost (see the EV charger installation clause) -- and put allocation, hours, idle-time and etiquette in the house rules, but keep the maintenance duty where the statute puts it. If you do not want tenant charging in shared areas, say so expressly and include cords run from a unit and use of shared outlets, because a ban on "installing a charging station" does not reach either.

title: No Ban on Eviction Penalty Clauses, and No Prohibited-Terms List
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute banning a lease clause that charges the tenant for an eviction, and no list of prohibited residential lease provisions at all. Three general limits do the work instead. A penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance is void outright (N.D.C.C. § 9-08-03). A sum fixed in advance as damages is void unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (§ 9-08-04). And an eviction action may be joined only with a claim for rents and profits accrued or for damages arising by reason of the tenant's possession (§ 47-32-04), so a contractual eviction charge is not something you can add to the eviction itself - you would be suing for it separately, against those two sections. A court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision (§ 47-16-13.3).

title: How a North Dakota Eviction Actually Runs, Start to Finish
bodyText: The default rule is that possession in North Dakota is recovered only by an action of eviction in the proper district court. There is no administrative route, no justice-court route (the old eviction chapter, ch. 33-06, is repealed) and no self-help. Here is the whole statutory shape. First, grounds: section 47-32-01 lists eight, and only four of them need notice. For holdover or rent unpaid three days after it is due, for possession held after a judicial sale or a cancelled contract for deed, for wrongful possession after a partition judgment or court-ordered sale, and for violation of a material term of the WRITTEN lease, you must give three days' written notice of intention to evict before you can file. For the other four -- entry by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth; turning the occupant out by force, threats or menacing conduct; holding by force or threats of violence; and a tenant or a person there with the tenant's consent acting in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment -- no notice is required at all. Second, that notice is a notice of INTENTION TO EVICT, not a pay-or-quit notice: North Dakota gives the tenant no statutory right to cure, and no right to pay rent into court or into escrow to stop the case. Third, service: the summons must set an appearance not fewer than three nor more than fifteen days out; personal service in the county must be at least three days before that date, any other mode at least seven days before; and if the person cannot be found in the county and service has been tried at least once between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m., you may post the summons on the door of the residential unit after filing an affidavit and mailing a copy to the last known address. Fourth, scope: the eviction cannot be joined with any other action except for rents and profits accrued or damages arising from the defendant's possession, and the tenant can interpose no counterclaim except as a setoff against that demand. Fifth, judgment: if you win, the court SHALL enter judgment for immediate restitution -- but on the tenant's showing of substantial hardship to them or their family the court may stay the special execution for up to five days, and that stay is unavailable where the judgment rests in whole or in part on a disturbance of the peace. What North Dakota does NOT have: for-cause protection after twelve months' tenancy; any rent-escrow or pay-into-court mechanism; a bad-faith fee award against a landlord; a rule that only the legislature may change eviction procedure; a bar on courts requiring a particular notice or pleading form; a bar on eviction servers filming service, with or without statutory damages; a federal-shutdown continuance for federal employee or contractor tenants; and any cap on wage attachment for a residential-lease judgment. TWO TIMING POINTS. Writ timing: N.D.R.Civ.P. 62(a) stays 'execution on a judgment and proceedings to enforce it' for 30 days after notice of entry 'unless the court orders otherwise', while section 47-32-04 calls for judgment for 'immediate restitution'. Rule 81(a) excludes a special statutory proceeding from the rules only 'to the extent they are inconsistent', and whether an eviction judgment escapes the 30-day stay only case law could settle. So ask the court, in your proposed judgment, to order the writ to issue immediately, and do not schedule a turnover until the clerk has issued it; the sheriff then delivers possession under the execution (sections 28-21-03 and 28-21-06). Counting days: section 1-02-15 excludes the first day and includes the last 'unless the last is a holiday', and every Sunday is a holiday (section 1-03-01); Rule 6(a) also skips a last day falling on a Saturday. Count calendar days from the day after service, and if the last day is a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, treat the next business day as the last.

title: Do Not Rely on Serving Eviction Papers on Someone the Lease Names Instead of the Tenant
bodyText: The default rule is that North Dakota prescribes who gets handed the papers, and you should not count on the lease changing it. Section 47-32-02 says the three days' written notice of intention to evict 'must be given to the lessee, subtenant, or party in possession', and may be served and returned as a summons is, or, if that party cannot be found, by the sheriff or a process server posting it conspicuously on the premises. For the summons itself, if the person cannot be found in the county and service has been attempted at least once between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m., you may post it on the door of the residential unit after filing an affidavit and mailing a copy to the last known address. The one neighbouring statute that lets you hand papers to somebody else is section 47-17-02, for terminating an estate at will: that notice may be delivered 'to the tenant or to some person of discretion residing on the premises', and if neither can be found with reasonable diligence, by affixing it to a conspicuous part of the premises. Note what that is and is not -- a person of discretion who actually lives there, not a person the lease nominated. No North Dakota statute authorises a lease to name an agent to accept eviction papers, and nothing in the statutes makes papers for a participant in any address-confidentiality programme go to the secretary of state, because North Dakota has no such programme in its statutes. So do not put a service-agent designation in your lease and do not rely on one if a lease you inherited has one. Where section 47-32-02 does not say how to serve, the North Dakota Rules of Civil Procedure fill the gap; they give way to the eviction statute only where the two conflict (N.D.R.Civ.P. 4(m), 81(a)). Rule 4(d)(2)(A) lets you serve an individual personally, by leaving a copy at the tenant's dwelling with 'a person of suitable age and discretion who resides there', by signed-receipt mail delivered to the tenant, or by delivering it to 'the individual's agent authorized by appointment or by law to receive service of process'. So a tenant can appoint an agent for service. Whether a clause you drafted into your own lease counts as the tenant's appointment, and whether it reaches the notice of intention to evict, is a question only the courts could settle. The cautious course is to serve the tenant, subtenant or party in possession exactly as section 47-32-02 and Rule 4 direct, use posting as the statute's own fallback, and treat any lease-named agent as an extra courtesy copy rather than as service.

title: Why "Landlord Is Not Liable" Does Less Than You Think - and the 30-Day Release Trap
bodyText: North Dakota has no exculpation rule inside its landlord-tenant chapter, which is why it is easy to assume a broad non-liability clause works here. The rule is in the contracts title instead, and it is enumerated, not a judge-made doctrine. A provision whose object is, directly or indirectly, to exempt anyone from responsibility for their own fraud, for willful injury to another person or their property, or for violation of law - whether the violation is willful or negligent - is against the policy of the law (N.D.C.C. § 9-08-02), and a provision contrary to the policy of express law is unlawful even though it is not expressly prohibited (§ 9-08-01(2)). Read the two together, because § 9-08-02 by itself never uses the word void. Know what that does and does not reach. It does not strike out an exemption from ordinary carelessness as such - its three targets are fraud, willful injury, and violation of law. But your habitability duties are statutory (§ 47-16-13.1), so a loss that traces to your failure to keep the premises fit is a violation of law, and a clause disclaiming that is inside § 9-08-02 even when the failure was merely negligent. A flat "Landlord is not liable for any loss" sentence therefore protects you least exactly where you most want it to. The same section is what limits a hold-harmless or indemnity clause: making the tenant cover a loss caused by your own statutory violation is the same thing as exempting yourself from it. A tenant indemnity for the tenant's own conduct is a different matter and is not affected. Two more limits sit beside it. A clause that restricts a party from enforcing its rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or shortens the time to do so, is void unless a North Dakota statute specifically permits it (§ 9-08-05). And § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision and makes a settlement waiving a habitability right reviewable on its own terms. Then there is the trap most landlords walk into after something has already gone wrong. If a tenant is injured, a release you obtain quickly is voidable: a settlement of a personal-injury claim is voidable if made within thirty days after the injury, or while the injured person is under disability from the injury and within six months of it (§ 9-08-08), and the injured person can undo it by written notice within six months - or simply by suing, which avoids the settlement outright (§ 9-08-09). Money already paid is not a bar to the action; it becomes an offset. So the fast signature is worth nothing and the slow one is worth something. What to do instead of drafting around it: carry liability insurance rather than relying on a disclaimer, keep any tenant indemnity confined to the tenant's own acts and omissions, fix habitability complaints rather than disclaiming them, and after an injury refer it to your insurer and let the statutory periods run before asking anyone to sign anything.

title: There Is No Separate Fast-Track Eviction for Crime -- But One Ordinary Ground Needs No Notice
bodyText:
The default rule is that North Dakota has one eviction action and one only, under chapter 47-32, and it has no expedited, summary or emergency track for drug activity, violence, firearms, gang activity or any other criminal conduct. Nothing in the statutes makes criminal activity an eviction ground in its own right.

What North Dakota gives you instead is ground 7 of section 47-32-01 -- a lessee, or a person on the premises with the lessee's consent, acting in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment -- and the real advantage of that ground is procedural: section 47-32-02 attaches the three days' written notice of intention to evict only to grounds 4, 5, 6 and 8, so ground 7 needs no notice at all. You can file the same day. Ground 7 also has a second edge: section 47-32-04's five-day hardship stay is unavailable where the eviction judgment rests in whole or in part on a disturbance of the peace, so a ground-7 judgment is not delayed the way a nonpayment judgment can be.

Grounds 1, 2 and 3 likewise need no notice and reach a person who entered by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth, or who turns the occupant out or holds possession by force or threats of violence.
