The one route that reaches criminal conduct as such is ground 8, violation of a material term of the WRITTEN lease -- and that only works if your written lease actually contains a crime-free or criminal-activity term, which is why North Dakota is a state where that clause is worth having (see the criminal-activity topic, where it is an optional clause for exactly this reason). Ground 8 does carry the three-day notice.

Practical upshot: for conduct that disturbs the other tenants, use ground 7 and file at once. For criminal conduct that does not disturb anyone, you need a written lease term and a three-day notice.

title: Thirty Days Is the Only Deadline - and No Fee to Beat It
bodyText: Default rule in North Dakota: one deadline, no shortcuts, no fee. Whatever you do not return must be itemised, and the itemisation together with the amount due must be delivered or mailed to the tenant at the last address furnished to you, with written notice, within thirty days after termination of the lease and delivery of possession by the tenant (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(3)). There is no expedited disposition the tenant can ask for, no shorter period triggered by a written request, no reduced deadline where you make no claim against the deposit, and no statutory fee for returning the money early. You may of course return it sooner, and doing so is usually the better commercial answer - the whole thirty days is a ceiling on your time, not an entitlement to use it. What you must not do is charge for it. The deposit and accrued interest may be applied on termination only towards damages from deterioration or injury caused by the tenant's pet or the negligence of the tenant or the tenant's guest, any unpaid rent, and the costs of cleaning or other repairs that were the tenant's responsibility and were necessary to return the unit to its original state, reasonable wear and tear excepted (§ 47-16-07.1(3)(a)-(c)); the only other deduction North Dakota allows is storage and moving expenses for abandoned property in excess of the sale proceeds (§ 47-16-30.1). An expedited-return or administration fee is not on that list, so taking it out of the deposit is security deposit money withheld without reasonable justification and exposes you to treble damages (§ 47-16-07.1(4)). One real exception to the trigger, not to the deadline: where a tenant terminates under the domestic-violence section, the clock starts on the first day of the month after that tenant vacates if they were the only tenant, or on expiry of the lease if other tenants remain bound (§ 47-16-17.1(8)).

title: No Duty to Tell You the Tenant Will Be Away
bodyText: North Dakota imposes no duty on a tenant to notify you of an extended absence, and sets no number of days after which an absence must be reported. The statute runs the other way: you may enter the dwelling unit at any time if you reasonably believe the tenant has abandoned the premises (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.3(1)), so your protection is a right of entry on a reasonable belief rather than a report from the tenant. Nothing stops you from asking for notice of a long absence in the lease, and in a North Dakota winter there is a real reason to: an unoccupied dwelling with the heat turned down is how pipes freeze, and your duty to supply reasonable heat (§ 47-16-13.1(1)(f)) does not depend on whether anyone is home. Treat such a clause as a contract term you chose, not a statutory duty you are restating.

title: Family Child Care in Rentals
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota has no statute requiring a landlord to allow a tenant to operate a family child care home, and no statute setting conditions - insurance, liability waivers, numbers - on which a landlord must allow one. The contrast inside North Dakota's own law is the telling part: the Century Code contains § 50-11-11, headed "Agency foster home for adults - Zoning", so the legislature DID give a zoning protection to one kind of residential care facility, and gave no equivalent to family child care. That section makes an agency foster home for adults 'a permitted use in a single-family or equivalent least-density residential zone'. Nothing in ch. 50-11.1, the Early Childhood Services chapter, is addressed to a landlord.

SO THE LEASE DECIDES, AND IT HAS TO SAY SO. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-11: "When real property is leased for a particular purpose, the lessee must not use it for any other purpose. If the lessee violates the lease in this respect, the lessor may hold the lessee responsible for the safety of the property during such use in all events or may treat the contract as rescinded thereby." The restriction bites only where the lease stated the purpose. And N.D.C.C. § 47-32-01(8) makes an eviction maintainable only where "[t]he lessee violates a material term of the written lease agreement between the lessor and lessee", with § 47-32-02 requiring "three days' written notice of intention to evict" for that ground. A handshake refusal is unenforceable; a written purpose term with a consent mechanism is not.

THE FAIR-HOUSING LINE, AND DO NOT BLUR IT. Refusing to allow a child-care BUSINESS is not the same thing as refusing to rent to a family with children, and the second is unlawful in North Dakota. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-02(1) and (2) bar refusing to rent, and discriminating in "the terms, conditions, or privileges of ... rental of a dwelling or in providing services or facilities in connection with a ... rental", because of (among other grounds) age and FAMILIAL STATUS - which § 14-02.5-01(9) defines as "one or more minors being domiciled with a parent or another person having legal custody of the minor or minors; or the designee of the parent or other person having such custody with the written permission of the parent or other person", extending to a person who is pregnant or securing legal custody. Section 14-02.5-03 extends the same bar to advertising. That is why the lease clause includes the sentence disclaiming any restriction on the occupancy of the tenant's own children; without it the clause reads as a children ban. Section 14-02.5-06(3)(b) separately requires a reasonable accommodation "in rules, policies, practices, or services" for a person with a disability, which can reach a care arrangement.

TWO PRACTICAL POINTS. First, your own position: § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) obliges you to comply with "applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety" and § 47-16-13.1(3) makes that duty controlling where it is greater than any other subdivision's, so if licensed child care pulls the premises into a different code occupancy class or triggers a fire requirement, the compliance problem lands on you. Keep consent in your own hands and get the licensing requirements in writing first. Second, do not overreach in the clause: § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce a lease provision that "was unconscionable when made", enforce the remainder without it, or limit its application - so an indemnity or insurance figure out of all proportion to the risk is the wrong place to economise on drafting care.

WHAT LICENSING DOES AND DOES NOT ASK OF YOU. Chapter 50-11.1 does not require the property owner's consent to a licence, self-declaration or registration. The department inspects the premises and licenses only on a showing that they 'are in fit and sanitary condition, are properly equipped to provide for the health and safety for all children, and are maintained according to rules adopted by the department' (§ 50-11.1-04(1)(a)); it may let a local governmental unit do the inspection (§ 50-11.1-08(3)). The department's child care rules put those premises standards on the provider, not the landlord (N.D. Admin. Code chs. 75-03-08, 75-03-09). Zoning is a city matter. Before consenting, ask the tenant for the department's written licensing requirements for the premises and check the zoning with the city in writing. Before refusing, make sure you are refusing the business and not the children.

title: North Dakota Has No Fee-in-Lieu Programme - Do Not Run One
bodyText: Default rule in North Dakota: there is no fee-in-lieu-of-deposit statute, and that is a reason to avoid the product rather than a licence to sell it. No North Dakota statute authorises a monthly fee, an insurance-backed deposit alternative or a damage waiver in place of a security deposit; none sets the disclosures, the offer-to-all duty, the right to switch back to a deposit, or the notice before a damage claim goes to a credit bureau or a collector that other states attach to these programmes; and no state agency has been told to write regulations for one. The problem is what the deposit section does say. A lessor who requires money as a security deposit, however denominated, shall deposit the money in a federally insured interest-bearing savings or checking account for the benefit of the tenant, and the deposit and any interest on it must be paid to the tenant on termination (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1)); and a lessor may not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's rent (same subsection). Those four words - 'however denominated' - exist to stop money being taken out of the deposit rules by renaming it. So a fee you require instead of a deposit, keep, and do not put in an account for the tenant is a candidate for being treated as a security deposit you failed to hold and failed to return, with treble damages for money withheld without reasonable justification (§ 47-16-07.1(4)). CAUTION, UNSETTLED: whether 'however denominated' reaches a genuine third-party product is not settled by the words alone, and only a court could settle it, so take the cautious course. Charge a security deposit within the cap and hold it the way the statute says. If you offer any alternative at all, make it a real insurance policy the tenant buys from an insurer and pays the insurer directly, take no part of the premium yourself, keep it voluntary with a deposit always available instead, and never deduct a fee or premium from deposit money - the deposit may be applied only to pet or negligence damage, unpaid rent, and cleaning or repairs that were the tenant's responsibility (§ 47-16-07.1(3)). Separately, a programme described to tenants in a way that is deceptive or unconscionable is an unlawful practice the attorney general can act on (§ 51-15-02).

title: No All-In Pricing or Fee Disclosure Law, but Do Not Charge an Unlisted Fee
bodyText:
Default rule: North Dakota has no rental fee-transparency law. There is no all-in or total-price advertising rule, no requirement that rent appear as one figure including every mandatory fee, no first-page fee disclosure, no verbatim statutory sentence to reproduce, no junk-fee or honest-pricing statute, no auto-renewal regulation reaching residential leases, and no general landlord-fee prohibition sitting outside the landlord-tenant title of the kind Colorado keeps in title 6. There is also no subsidy-format exemption, because there is no rule to be exempted from.

What North Dakota does have is one targeted ban -- no fee for accepting cash, a check or a money order (section 47-16-20.1) -- plus the general contract rules in sections 9-08-01, 9-08-03 and 9-08-04, and the case-by-case unconscionability power in section 47-16-13.3, under which a court may refuse to enforce a rental-agreement provision that was unconscionable when made.

One point only a court could settle: whether the consumer fraud law reaches a residential lease. It bars deceptive or unconscionable practices 'in connection with the sale or advertisement of any merchandise', and 'merchandise' includes real estate and services (N.D.C.C. §§ 51-15-01(3), 51-15-02). A 'sale' is defined as a sale, offer or attempt to sell, which a lease may not be. But an 'advertisement' includes any attempt to induce a person to 'acquire any title or interest in any merchandise' (§ 51-15-01(1)), which a rental listing arguably is. Assume your rental advertising is covered.

The cautious course is the same either way: write every mandatory fee into the lease with the amount or its calculation method, show the monthly total of rent plus every fee the tenant cannot avoid somewhere in the lease even though nothing makes you, advertise a figure you can actually honour, and never collect a charge that does not appear in the signed lease or a signed amendment. Treat a fee you never disclosed as uncollectible rather than as a bargain you can enforce.

title: Charging for a Service You Do Not Actually Provide
bodyText:
Default rule: North Dakota has no statute saying you may not charge a fee for a service you do not provide, and no statute requiring you to abate a fee when an amenity closes or a service stops. That absence is not permission, and three provisions do the work instead.

First, if the "service" is one section 47-16-13.1 already makes your job -- repairs and habitability, common areas clean and safe, the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems and appliances in good and safe working order, waste receptacles and removal, running water, hot water and reasonable heat -- then it is not a service you may sell the tenant at all. You may shift subdivisions (e) and (f) only to the tenant of a single-family residence, in writing and in good faith, together with specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling (section 47-16-13.1(4)); for any other dwelling unit the tenant may take on specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling only in a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration, not where the work is needed to cure a waste-removal failure, and not in a way that diminishes your duties to other tenants (section 47-16-13.1(5)); and you may not make the tenant's performance of that separate agreement a condition of the lease (section 47-16-13.1(6)).

Second, a fixed monthly fee for an amenity the tenant cannot use is exposed under section 9-08-01, which makes a provision unlawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law or to the policy of express law, and under section 47-16-13.3, under which a court may refuse to enforce a rental-agreement provision that was unconscionable when made, enforce the rest without it, or limit its application.

Third, you may not charge a fee simply to accept cash, a check or a money order (section 47-16-20.1) -- the clearest North Dakota statement that a fee has to buy the tenant something.

What to do: tie every service fee in the lease to a service you actually deliver, say in the lease what happens to the fee if the service stops, stop billing a fee the day the amenity closes, and never bill separately for anything section 47-16-13.1 already obliges you to supply.

title: No statutory sprinkler or retrofit duty for North Dakota rentals - and no code may require one in a house or duplex
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a residential landlord to install fire sprinklers, to retrofit an existing building with them, to maintain them to a stated standard, or to have them inspected on any schedule. There is no retrofit deadline, no square-footage or storey threshold, no exemption schedule and no penalty, because there is no statutory duty to exempt anyone from. "Sprinkler", "standpipe", "fire suppression", "fire protection system" and "retrofit" all return nothing in any North Dakota statute chapter searched.

But the duty you actually owe does not depend on a sprinkler statute, and two routes reach you. First, the code route, and this is the one that changes the answer: 47-16-13.1(1)(a) requires the landlord to "comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and 47-16-13.1(3) provides that where that duty is greater than any other duty in the subsection, "the landlord's duty shall be determined by reference to" it. So a sprinkler requirement that lives in the State Building Code is a binding lease obligation, enforceable by the tenant, without any sprinkler statute at all. Two state rules frame that route. The State Building Code, and any building code a city, township or county adopts, 'may not include a requirement that fire sprinklers be installed in a single family dwelling or a residential building that contains no more than two dwelling units' (54-21.3-03(4)). So a house or a duplex can never be made to have sprinklers by a building code. For three or more units, the State Fire Code is the 2018 International Fire Code with North Dakota's amendments (N.D. Admin. Code § 10-07-01-04), and none of those amendments adds a sprinkler retrofit. The fire code applies to existing buildings, but a condition lawful when it was adopted may continue unless the state fire marshal finds it 'a distinct hazard to life or property' (§ 10-07-01-02(2)). The model codes' own text is published by the International Code Council, not the state, so for a building of three or more units check the code your city enforces. Second, the maintenance route: 47-16-13.1(1)(d) requires you to "maintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord". A sprinkler system you supplied is such a facility, so if you have one you must keep it working whether or not any statute made you install it. And 47-16-13.1(1)(b) requires all repairs necessary to keep the premises "in a fit and habitable condition".

Where "sprinkler" actually appears in North Dakota law, it is not about rentals. The Legislative Council master index names exactly one sprinkler section in the whole Century Code: 18-12-17, "Sprinklers", and it sits in ch. 18-12, the Fire Prevention Code for School Buildings - a chapter whose neighbours are 18-12-12 interior finish, 18-12-13 fire extinguishers, 18-12-16 fire alarm systems, 18-12-18 heating plant rooms and 18-12-24 change of occupancy. School buildings, not dwellings. The fire provisions aimed at places people sleep are in ch. 23-09 (Food and Lodging Establishments and Assisted Living Facilities): 23-09-02.1 smoke detection devices or other approved alarm systems, 23-09-03 exiting requirements, 23-09-04 and 23-09-05 fire escapes in hotels and lodginghouses, 23-09-06 chemical fire extinguishers and standpipes, 23-09-07 elevator fire protection, 23-09-12 certificate of inspection and its posting, and 23-09-20 requirements of a fireproof hotel. Chapter 23-09 names no sprinkler section, though 23-09-06 says 'Standpipe and sprinkler systems must be installed as required by the state building code and state fire code' - and it governs lodging establishments, not ordinary residential rentals. Two of the sections listed, 23-09-04 and 23-09-12, have been repealed.

The enforcement machinery that does exist is in ch. 18-01, the State Fire Marshal Department chapter: 18-01-04 (rules for prevention of fires to be issued), 18-01-14 (abatement of fire hazards), 18-01-15 (abatement of conditions dangerous to persons - order - failure to comply - penalty), 18-01-16 (order of abatement - to whom directed - contents - how served - service by publication), 18-01-17 and 18-01-18 (appeals), 18-01-19 to 18-01-26 (court proceedings and judgment) and 18-01-27 (costs and the lien for them). So North Dakota's answer to a dangerous fire condition is a fire marshal's abatement order against the property, enforceable in district court with a cost lien - a regulatory route, not a lease term and not a disclosure. Chapter 18-01 was read whole: 18-01-15 lets the fire marshal order 'the immediate removal or correction' of any condition that is 'a danger or a menace to the safety of life and limb of the occupants', and failing to comply is a class B misdemeanor; 18-01-27 makes enforcement costs a lien on the premises.

What to do: do not tell a tenant North Dakota has no fire-protection requirements - check the locally enforced building code and the municipal fire ordinance, because that is where a sprinkler or retrofit duty will be if there is one. Do not try to shift sprinkler maintenance to the tenant. In a single-family residence 47-16-13.1(4) lets the parties agree in writing and in good faith that the tenant perform specified repairs and maintenance tasks plus the duties in subdivisions e and f; in anything else, 47-16-13.1(5) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" and only with good faith, a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration, work that is not needed to cure a subdivision e failure, and no diminution of your obligations to other tenants - and 47-16-13.1(6) bars you from making performance of the separate agreement a condition of the lease. Life-safety equipment serving a whole building is a poor candidate for that in any event. If a system is out of service, repair it promptly: under 47-16-13 a tenant who gives notice of a dilapidation you neglect may repair and deduct the expense from rent with no cap, recover it in any other lawful manner, or vacate and be discharged from further rent.

title: Firearm rules in a North Dakota lease: yours to set, but leave lawful guns locked in parked cars alone
bodyText:
THE DEFAULT RULE FIRST. Nothing in North Dakota's landlord-tenant law says a word about firearms. Chapters 47-16 (residential leases), 47-32 (eviction) and 47-10 do not contain the words 'firearm', 'weapon', 'handgun' or 'ammunition' anywhere. There is no statute protecting a tenant's firearm possession in a rental, no statute voiding a lease firearm restriction, and no statute requiring you to permit firearms. So as far as the landlord-tenant statutes go, a firearm rule in your lease is an ordinary lease term.

THE CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHT DOES NOT BIND YOU -- AND THIS IS THE POINT MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG. N.D. Const. art. I, s 1 is strong: individuals have the inalienable right 'to keep and bear arms for the defense of their person, family, property, and the state, and for lawful hunting, recreational, and other lawful purposes, WHICH SHALL NOT BE INFRINGED.' But a state constitutional right restrains GOVERNMENT. A private landlord writing a private lease is not the state, so art. I, s 1 does not make your firearm rule unenforceable. Expect a tenant to quote it at you; it is not an answer to a lease term. (If you are a HOUSING AUTHORITY or other public landlord, this reasoning does not help you and you need separate advice -- that is exactly the case where state action is present.)

THE PREEMPTION YOU WILL BE TOLD ABOUT AIMS AT CITIES, NOT AT YOU. North Dakota's firearm preemption is s 62.1-01-03, whose heading is 'Limitation on authority of political subdivision regarding firearms - Civil action'. A preemption aimed at a POLITICAL SUBDIVISION says nothing whatever about a private lease -- it stops a city passing a gun ordinance; it does not stop you writing a rule. North Dakota's own drafting proves the distinction. s 47-16-02.1 ('Rent controls - Prohibited') reads: 'A POLITICAL SUBDIVISION may not enact, maintain, or enforce an ordinance or resolution that would have the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged...'. That is what a North Dakota preemption looks like -- addressed to the subdivision, and silent about private parties. Section 62.1-01-03 does follow that pattern: it forbids a political subdivision to enact a firearm ordinance 'more restrictive than state law', and its civil action lies only 'against a political subdivision'. It does not reach your lease.

THE PARKING-LOT STATUTE, AND THE ONE DOUBT. Section 62.1-02-13 says 'A public or private employer may not' prohibit 'any customer, employee, or invitee from possessing any legally owned firearm, if the firearm is lawfully possessed and locked inside or locked to a private motor vehicle in a parking lot'. Nor may the employer ask about or search a vehicle for a firearm (only an on-duty officer may search), or expel a customer or invitee for exercising the right to keep and bear arms. A person aggrieved may sue, and the court must award costs and attorney's fees to the prevailing party (s 62.1-02-13(5)). The doubt: the statute speaks of an 'employer' and its 'customer, employee, or invitee', not of a landlord and tenant. If your rental business employs anyone, a tenant or guest in your parking lot may well be its customer or invitee, and only a court could say. So assume it applies: do not forbid lawfully owned firearms locked in or to private vehicles in your parking areas, and do not ask about or search tenants' vehicles for firearms.

WHAT I COULD READ, AND IT DOES NOT REACH YOU. s 62.1-02-05 ('Possession of a firearm or dangerous weapon at a public gathering - Penalty - Application'), as amended in 2025, bars possession at (a) a school or school-sponsored event on school property, (b) 'A church or other place of worship', and (c) 'A publicly owned or operated building'. PRIVATE RENTAL PROPERTY IS NOT ON THAT LIST, and the list is closed. So the public-gathering prohibition neither restricts your tenants nor supports a lease rule.

WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. (1) If you want a firearm rule, write it as a rule about CONDUCT AND STORAGE in the common areas you control -- no discharge, no brandishing, no display, secure storage -- rather than a flat ban on lawful possession inside the dwelling. A conduct rule is easier to defend and easier to enforce. (2) Put it in the WRITTEN lease: s 47-32-01(8) makes only 'a material term of the written lease agreement' an eviction ground, so a rule kept out of the lease has no teeth. (3) Do NOT attach a fixed fine: s 9-08-03 makes 'Penalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance thereof' void, flatly. (4) Do not carve out, or single out, any protected class in a firearm rule -- s 14-02.5-02(2) bars discrimination 'in the terms, conditions, or privileges of ... rental' on the listed grounds, and a facially neutral rule applied selectively is the usual way landlords get into trouble here. (5) Keep any firearm rule out of the parking lot: under s 62.1-02-13 a firearm lawfully locked in or to a private vehicle is the one thing to leave alone, and the same goes doubly for a tenant who is also your employee. (6) In a MOBILE HOME PARK, any new or changed firearm rule is a rule modification under s 47-10-28: thirty days' advance written notice, and for a rule not addressing sanitation and safety, three months for the tenant to remedy or vacate before you may start an eviction -- with a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 under s 47-10-28(12) and a defence to the eviction under s 47-32-01.1.

title: North Dakota requires no flood or floodplain disclosure to a tenant - floodplain status is a local ordinance matter
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a landlord, or a residential lease, to tell a tenant that the property lies in a floodplain, a floodway, a flood fringe or a special flood hazard area, and none gives a tenant a termination right or a rent remedy because of flood risk or a past flood. There is no state model form, no signed rider, no point-size requirement and no penalty - because there is no duty. The one place in the whole Century Code where "floodplain" sits next to a notice duty is N.D.C.C. 11-33.2-12.1, "Contents of plat - Location and elevation of lakes, rivers, or streams - Notification of floodplain", and that is a duty on whoever files a subdivision plat, not on a landlord. Treat it as the sibling that proves the negative, not as a landlord obligation.

What North Dakota does instead is delegate. 61-16.2-04 has the department delineate floodplains and floodways; 61-16.2-05 provides for floodplain management ordinances, and 11-11-71 (counties), 40-05-27 (cities) and 58-06-11 (townships) each carry an identically named "Floodplain management ordinances - Requirements - Limitations - Definitions - Enforcement" section; 61-16.2-06 to 61-16.2-08 set permissible and prohibited uses in the floodway and flood fringe; 61-16.2-13 addresses flood insurance; and 61-16.2-15, new in 2025, has the department keep a publicly accessible electronic repository of local floodplain ordinances and certifications - which tells you whether your city, county or township regulates floodplains, not whether your property lies in one. So flood regulation in North Dakota is a mapping-and-zoning regime enforced by the city, county or township Those sections were read: none imposes a notice or disclosure duty on a landlord or mentions a lease or tenant. A city that undertakes floodplain management must enact an ordinance covering all persons and property in its zoning jurisdiction (40-05-27(2)), and the plat rule in 11-33.2-12.1 is a duty on a subdivider to mark the hundred-year flood elevation. A local ordinance may impose a notice duty that state law does not.

What to do: do not print a flood disclosure as a North Dakota requirement and do not build a tenant termination remedy on one. If the property has flooded or sits in a mapped floodplain, say so voluntarily - it costs nothing, and the condition-of-premises statement required by 47-16-07.2 is the natural place for a past-flood note. Then check the municipal or county floodplain ordinance, because that is where any real notice duty would live. Remember the two general rules that do bite: 47-16-13.1(1)(b) requires the landlord to keep the premises "in a fit and habitable condition", and under 47-16-14(4) the leasing terminates outright "by the destruction of the property leased", with 47-16-17(2) letting the tenant terminate when the greater part of the property "perishes from any cause other than the ordinary negligence of the lessee". A flood that destroys the dwelling ends the lease by operation of law; you do not need a flood clause to get there.

title: Foreclosure and Your Tenants: What North Dakota Statutes Actually Say
bodyText:
The default rule first. North Dakota has no tenant-protection-at-foreclosure statute. The word 'foreclosure' does not appear anywhere in chapter 47-16 (leases), chapter 47-17 (termination of estates) or chapter 47-32 (eviction). What the Century Code does supply is four general rules.

First, a buyer steps into your shoes: a person to whom the property is transferred or devised with rent reserved, or to whom the rent is transferred, is entitled to the same remedies for recovering rent, for breach of the lease, and for waste or forfeiture as you had (N.D.C.C. 47-16-28). Second, the tenant owes you a reporting duty, not the other way round: a tenant who receives notice of any proceeding to recover the property or its possession must inform you immediately and deliver the notice to you, and is liable to you for all damages you may sustain by reason of any failure to do so where the notice was in writing; and the tenant's attornment to a stranger is void unless you consented or a court of competent jurisdiction so adjudged (47-16-25). Third, there is an eviction ground for the post-sale occupant: an eviction lies where 'a party continues in possession after a sale of the real property under mortgage, execution, order, or any judicial process and after the expiration of the time fixed by law for redemption, or after the execution and delivery of a deed', or after cancellation of a contract for deed (47-32-01(5)) - and note that it says 'a party', not 'the mortgagor', so on its words it can reach a tenant in possession. That ground requires three days' written notice of intention to evict before proceedings are instituted (47-32-02). Fourth, an eviction cannot be joined with other actions except for rents and profits accrued or damages from the defendant's possession; on a judgment for the plaintiff the court orders immediate restitution, but on a showing that immediate restitution would work a substantial hardship on the defendant or the defendant's family - except where the judgment rests in whole or in part on a disturbance of the peace - the court may stay the special execution for a reasonable period not exceeding five days (47-32-04). A tenant subject to an eviction order for nonpayment or damage who has resolved the claims may move to seal the records seven years after the eviction order has been satisfied, if not evicted from another property in those seven years (47-32-05).

There is one genuinely new piece and it protects a residential tenant. The 2025 legislature enacted the Uniform Commercial Real Estate Receivership Act as chapter 32-10.1 (S.L. 2025, ch. 325). Where a receiver is appointed over mortgaged real property, a lease is an 'executory contract' the receiver may normally ask the court to adopt or reject, and rejection counts as a breach effective immediately before the appointment (32-10.1-16(2) and (5)). But a receiver may NOT reject an unexpired lease under which the owner is the landlord if the tenant occupies the leased premises as the tenant's primary residence (32-10.1-16(8)(a)), nor where the receiver was appointed at the request of anyone other than a mortgagee, nor where a mortgagee asked for the receiver and the lease is senior to the mortgage, or the tenant has a non-disturbance agreement, or the mortgagee consented to the lease or failed to object in time, or the lease was commercially reasonable when made and the tenant did not know it breached the mortgage (32-10.1-16(8)(b) and (c)). Two practical consequences for you. Once a tenant has notice of a receiver's appointment, the tenant must pay the rent to the receiver and cannot discharge it by paying you (32-10.1-10(1) and (2)). And the chapter does not reach a receivership over property improved by one to four dwelling units unless one of four conditions applies - one of which is that the owner collects or has the right to collect rents from someone who is not an affiliate (32-10.1-03(2)(d)), so an ordinary small rental property generally is covered.

What chapter 32-19 (foreclosure of real estate mortgages) says, read whole. The redemption period for ordinary residential property is sixty days after the sheriff's sale (32-19-18), and during it "the debtor or owner of the premises is entitled to the possession, rents, use, and benefit of the real property sold" (32-19-06), so you keep collecting rent until then. The sheriff's deed then vests "all the right, title, and interest of the mortgagor ... at the time the mortgage was executed" and bars all persons claiming under the parties "subsequent to the commencement of the action" (32-19-09). The judgment binds every defendant and anyone claiming through one (32-19-39), and a holder of an unrecorded conveyance need not be joined at all (32-19-40). Read together, a lease made after the mortgage is likely cut off by the sale once the redemption period ends, while a lease that predates the mortgage likely survives. No section says so about tenants in terms, and whether an unjoined tenant in possession is bound is a question only a court could settle. So here is the cautious course. Assume a tenant's lease may NOT survive the sale and plan around it: tell the tenant in writing as soon as a foreclosure action is served, remind the tenant of the 47-16-25 duty to deliver any notice they receive, keep collecting rent in the ordinary way until a receiver or a purchaser with a deed directs otherwise in writing, and do not purport to end the tenancy early just because a foreclosure has started - none of your statutory grounds (47-16-16) is a foreclosure. If you are the buyer at the sale, do not lock anyone out: use 47-32-01(5) with the 47-32-02 three days' written notice of intention to evict, and remember that North Dakota has no statute authorising self-help eviction. Finally, North Dakota has no equity-skimming statute that this library can find, so a tenant of a buyer who collects rents without paying the mortgage has no special North Dakota claim; the tenant's remedies are the ordinary ones in 47-16-13 and 47-16-13.6.

title: No Duty to Tell a North Dakota Tenant About a Foreclosure - and the Duty That Runs the Other Way
bodyText:
The default rule first: North Dakota requires no foreclosure disclosure to a tenant. There is no statute obliging an owner who has been served with a foreclosure complaint, or who is in default on the mortgage, to tell a prospective tenant before signing, to tell existing tenants, to name a foreclosure contact, or to state the time, date and place of a sale. If your library forms carry a foreclosure-notice paragraph, it comes from another state's statute, not North Dakota's.

North Dakota's property disclosure statutes do not fill the gap, because they run from a seller to a buyer and not from a landlord to a tenant. Section 47-10-02.1 applies to a transaction for the sale, exchange or purchase of a residential dwelling of no more than four units and requires the seller to give a prospective BUYER a written disclosure of material facts; it expressly does not apply to a transfer by a mortgagor in default to a mortgagee, to a transfer pursuant to a foreclosure sale, or to a transfer by a mortgagee or deed-of-trust beneficiary who acquired by foreclosure, by a deed in lieu of foreclosure, or by a collateral assignment of beneficial interest (47-10-02.1(7)(c) to (e)). Section 47-10-02.2 is a prior-radon-test disclosure to a buyer, and 47-10-02.3 is a homeowners'-association and condominium disclosure to a buyer. None mentions a tenant.

The statutory notice duty in this area actually runs toward you. A tenant who receives notice of any proceeding to recover the property occupied by the tenant, or its possession, must inform you immediately and deliver the notice to you, and is liable to you for all damages you may sustain by reason of any failure to do so where the notice was in writing; and the tenant's attornment to a stranger is void unless you consented or a court of competent jurisdiction so adjudged (47-16-25). That is the provision worth putting to work.

Do this. Reproduce or summarise 47-16-25 in the lease and give the tenant a named person and address to send such notices to, so the duty is real and the tenant knows where to send a foreclosure summons, a receiver's notice or a sheriff's notice. Decide separately whether to disclose a pending foreclosure voluntarily: nothing requires it, but a tenant who signs a twelve-month lease weeks before a sheriff's sale has a misrepresentation argument that no disclosure statute is needed to make, and a contract whose object is to exempt you from responsibility for your own fraud is against the policy of the law (9-08-02), which means a lease term disclaiming that risk will not save you. Do not write a term saying the tenant waives a right to foreclosure notice: North Dakota gives none, so the waiver is empty and it tells the tenant they gave something up.

title: Citizenship is irrelevant to a town rental, but a lease of agricultural land is a restricted interest
bodyText:
Default rule first, and North Dakota states it expressly. N.D.C.C. § 47-01-11 provides: "Except as provided in chapter 47-10.1, any person, whether citizen or alien, may take, hold, and dispose of property, real or personal, within this state." So for an ordinary house or apartment, citizenship is irrelevant — there is no general alien land law in North Dakota, and nothing in chapter 47-16 or chapter 47-32 touches the subject. You do not need to ask a residential applicant about citizenship or immigration status, and asking creates fair-housing exposure under § 14-02.5-02 (national origin is a protected class) without buying you anything.

The exception is real, though, and it catches leases — which is the part most landlords miss. Chapter 47-10.1 restricts interests in AGRICULTURAL LAND, and § 47-10.1-01(5) says in terms: "'Interest in agricultural land' includes any leasehold interest." There is no carve-out for short leases. A one-year farmhouse lease is inside the chapter if the land is agricultural land. "Agricultural land" means land capable of use in producing crops, livestock, poultry, milk or horticultural products, but § 47-10.1-01(1) excludes "any land zoned by a local governmental unit for a use other than, and nonconforming with, agricultural use" — so a city rental zoned residential is outside, and a rural dwelling on farm ground may well be inside.

Inside the chapter, the restrictions are strict and the conditions are cumulative:
• § 47-10.1-02(1): an individual who is not a US citizen, not a Canadian citizen and not a permanent resident alien may not acquire, directly or indirectly, any interest in agricultural land unless ALL FIVE of (a) to (e) are satisfied — treaty-investor status, residing in this state at least ten months of every year, actively participating in the operation, a holding not exceeding six hundred forty acres, AND a holding that "includes a dairy operation". They are joined by "and", so four out of five is a violation.
• § 47-10.1-02(2): a person who does qualify must notify the agriculture commissioner of any land acquisition within thirty days, and must annually give the commissioner every address at which they resided in the previous year and the dates. Because a leasehold is an "interest", that reporting duty reaches a qualifying alien TENANT of agricultural land.
• § 47-10.1-02(4): a partnership, limited partnership, limited liability company, trustee or other business entity may not take any interest in agricultural land unless the ultimate beneficial interest is held by US citizens or permanent resident aliens. This is the limb most likely to bite a foreign-owned entity tenant.
• § 47-10.1-02(8): since June 30, 2023 a foreign government may not hold a "foreign governmental interest in agricultural land" — but note the asymmetry, because § 47-10.1-01(4) defines that term to "not include a leasehold interest". The foreign-government ban therefore does NOT reach a lease, while the individual and entity restrictions in (1) and (4) do.
• § 47-10.1-02(5) to (7) and (9) carve out devise and inheritance, security for debt and lien enforcement (with three years to dispose), industrial sites (with conditions), treaty rights and certain railroads, and a state-controlled enterprise using up to one hundred sixty acres for agricultural research or development.

A violating leasehold is NOT void, and that matters. § 47-10.1-04 gives enforcement to the attorney general, who sues in the district court where the land lies, records a notice of pendency, and on a finding obtains an order; the holder then has "a period of one year from the date of the order to divest itself of the lands", the one-year period "is deemed a covenant running with the title", and land not divested "shall be sold at public sale in the manner prescribed by law for the foreclosure of a real estate mortgage by action". The section ends: "No title to land shall be invalid or subject to forfeiture by reason of the alienage of any former owner or person having a former interest therein." A violation is also a class A misdemeanour under § 47-10.1-06. And there is no recording or instrument-naming requirement of the Alaska kind: § 47-10.1-03, "Recording", was repealed by S.L. 2005, ch. 388, § 1.

What to do. (1) For city and town residential rentals, do nothing — § 47-01-11 is your answer and citizenship questions are a fair-housing risk, not a precaution. (2) Before leasing a dwelling that sits on farm or ranch ground, check the zoning first: if the land is not zoned for a nonconforming non-agricultural use, treat chapter 47-10.1 as engaged and get advice, because the lease itself is the interest the chapter regulates. (3) If your tenant is a foreign-owned entity — staff housing for an employer is the common case — § 47-10.1-02(4) is the limb to check, and it turns on ultimate beneficial ownership, not on where the entity is registered. (4) Do not write a citizenship representation into a residential lease; for an agricultural tenancy, raise an eligibility representation with counsel rather than drafting one from this entry. (5) Remember the remedy is divestment and a misdemeanour, not a void lease — so do not assume a non-compliant tenancy simply evaporates and leaves you free to re-let.

title: Relief Against Forfeiture of a Lease: Nothing in the Landlord-Tenant Statutes, but a General Statute Allows It
bodyText: The default rule in North Dakota's landlord-tenant statutes is that a lease ends when the statute says it ends and there is no second chance written into those statutes. Nothing in chapter 47-16, chapter 47-17 or chapter 47-32 lets a residential tenant ask a court to relieve them against a forfeiture of the lease, reinstate a terminated term, or buy back a tenancy after breach. The forfeiture machinery that does exist in chapter 47-16 is for oil, gas and mineral leases -- sections 47-16-36, 47-16-37 and 47-16-41, which are about getting a terminated or forfeited lease released of record and include a statutory notice form and a $100 damages figure. Those have nothing to do with a dwelling. What North Dakota gives a landlord instead is termination and re-entry: section 47-16-16 lets the lessor terminate and reclaim before the end of the term when the lessee uses the property contrary to the agreement or fails to make repairs the lessee is bound to make; section 47-16-11 lets the lessor treat the contract as rescinded where the property is used for a purpose other than the one leased; and sections 47-17-04 and 47-17-05 govern a reserved right of re-entry, which may be exercised on three days' previous written notice of intention to re-enter, or enforced by action without that notice. BUT A GENERAL STATUTE OUTSIDE THOSE CHAPTERS DOES ALLOW IT. N.D.C.C. 32-01-12, "Conditions of relief from forfeiture": "Whenever by the terms of an obligation a party thereto incurs a forfeiture, or a loss in the nature of a forfeiture, by reason of the party's failure to comply with its provisions, the party may be relieved therefrom upon making full compensation to the other party, except in case of a grossly negligent, willful, or fraudulent breach of duty." And N.D.C.C. 9-01-15: "A condition involving a forfeiture must be interpreted strictly against the party for whose benefit it is created." A lease is an obligation, so on their words a tenant who pays everything owed may ask a court to relieve them of a lease forfeiture, unless the breach was grossly negligent, willful or fraudulent. How far courts apply 32-01-12 to a residential eviction is a question only case law could settle. The cautious course is to assume a court WILL relieve against a bare forfeiture and so not to rely on a lease forfeiture clause as self-executing: terminate on the statutory ground, serve the notice chapter 47-32 requires, and get a judgment of restitution, rather than declaring the lease forfeited and acting on your own declaration.

title: Renting a Furnished Unit
bodyText:
North Dakota's default rule leaves furniture out of almost every landlord-tenant statute, and that cuts against the landlord. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(d) runs only to "facilities and appliances", so there is no statutory duty to maintain furniture and no statutory standard for its condition. N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-09 and 47-16-10 oblige the lessee to use ordinary care and to repair deteriorations - but both speak of "real property", not of a landlord's sofa. And N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(3)(a) lets a deposit be applied to "deteriorations or injuries to the real property or dwelling" - again not to the landlord's furniture. The one route in is § 47-16-07.1(3)(c), which reaches "[t]he costs of cleaning or other repairs which were the responsibility of the lessee". That responsibility has to come from the lease.

What the landlord should actually do: write the list out item by item, with condition noted, and have it signed on the same day as the § 47-16-07.2 statement of condition - without that record there is nothing to measure a deposit deduction against. Do not overreach at the end of the tenancy: § 47-16-07.1(4) makes a lessor "liable for treble damages for any security deposit money withheld without reasonable justification", and a furniture claim with no signed inventory behind it is exactly the kind that fails. Do not write a clause taking title to Tenant's own furnishings - under § 47-06-04 a tenant may remove anything affixed "for the purpose of trade, manufacture, ornament, or domestic use" at any time during the term where removal causes no injury and the thing has not become an integral part of the premises.

title: Your Termination Notice Does Not Have to Give a Reason in North Dakota
bodyText: The default rule is that North Dakota requires no good cause to end a residential tenancy and requires no statement of cause in the notice that ends it. For a month-to-month tenancy, section 47-16-15(2) lets either party terminate with at least one calendar month's written notice at any time, and says nothing about a reason. For an estate at will, section 47-17-01 lets the landlord give notice to remove within a period of not less than one month, and section 47-17-02 prescribes the form exhaustively: it 'must be in writing and must be served by delivering the same to the tenant or to some person of discretion residing on the premises', or by affixing it to a conspicuous part of the premises if neither can be found with reasonable diligence. Writing and service -- no reason, no grounds, no recital of facts. Even the three days' written notice of intention to evict under section 47-32-02 carries no content requirement: the statute says when it must be given and how it may be served, and nothing about what it must say. North Dakota has two notice-content mandates in the whole of its landlord-tenant law and neither is a reason. Section 47-16-15(4) requires a lease that makes the tenant give more than one month's notice to state that requirement and give the tenant space to initial next to it. Section 47-10-28(10) requires a notice of intent to evict a mobile home park tenant to include clear, boldfaced language saying: 'You do not have to vacate immediately. You have the right to remain until a court issues an eviction order.' The only place 'without cause' appears in North Dakota landlord-tenant law is section 47-10-28(13) and (14), which forbid a park owner terminating a tenant's lease without cause while its licence is suspended or an action under that section is pending. PRACTICAL ADVICE THAT CUTS THE OTHER WAY: because no statute requires a reason, giving one is a choice, and a stated reason is something a tenant can argue about. State the statutory ground when you are evicting on a ground that needs a three-day notice, because the court needs to see which of the eight grounds you are on. Do not volunteer reasons in an ordinary month-to-month termination.

title: Fines Caused by a Tenant
bodyText: The lease clause on fines caused by the tenant lets you recover the amount actually imposed and paid. The cautious course: do not rely on that clause in place of a negligence claim, and do not deduct any such amount from the security deposit.

title: Guests and Occupants
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota gives a tenant's guest no statutory rights at all. There is no right of access for a guest or a supplier, no provision for buildings of three or more households, no non-waivability rule and no bar on a guest fee. In the whole of chapters 47-16, 47-17, 47-10, 47-32 and 14-02.5, the word "guest" appears exactly once, and it appears against the tenant: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(3)(a) lets a lessor apply the security deposit to "[a]ny damages the lessor has suffered by reason of deteriorations or injuries to the real property or dwelling by the lessee's pet or through the negligence of the lessee or the lessee's guest." "Visitor", "invitee" and "supplier" appear in none of those chapters.

TWO THINGS ALREADY IMPLIED, SO THE LEASE CLAUSE DOES NOT REPEAT THEM. First, the tenant already owes you guest control: § 47-16-13.2(7) requires a tenant to "[c]onduct oneself and require other persons on the premises with the tenant's consent to conduct themselves in a manner that will not disturb the tenant's neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises." Second, and this is the strongest tool in the chapter, § 47-32-01(7) makes an eviction maintainable where "[a] lessee or a person on the premises with the lessee's consent acts in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment of the premises" - and § 47-32-02 requires the three-day written notice of intention to evict only "[i]n all cases arising under subsections 4, 5, 6, and 8 of section 47-32-01". Ground 7 is not on that list, so a disturbance eviction needs NO pre-suit notice. Note North Dakota's vocabulary: both sections say "person on the premises with the lessee's consent", never "guest".

WHAT THE LEASE STILL HAS TO CARRY. Two things the statutes do not supply: the line between a guest and an occupant, and responsibility for a guest's conduct and damage that is not negligent.

WHY THE "WHETHER OR NOT NEGLIGENT" WORDS MATTER. Without them your deposit claim for guest damage is confined to § 47-16-07.1(3)(a), which reaches only damage "through the negligence of the lessee or the lessee's guest". Non-negligent guest damage gets in only through § 47-16-07.1(3)(c) - "[t]he costs of cleaning or other repairs which were the responsibility of the lessee" - and only the lease can make it the tenant's responsibility. The same goes for § 47-16-09 and § 47-16-10, which bind "[t]he lessee of real property" to ordinary care and to repairing deteriorations "occasioned by the lessee's ordinary negligence", not a guest's. Do not overreach the other way either: § 47-16-07.1(4) makes a lessor "liable for treble damages for any security deposit money withheld without reasonable justification", and § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce a lease provision that "was unconscionable when made".

THE FAIR-HOUSING LINES ON GUESTS. A guest policy is one of the easiest places to create a discrimination claim. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-02(1) bars discrimination in the sale or rental of a dwelling on any of the nine grounds it lists, and § 14-02.5-06(1) extends the DISABILITY ground beyond the renter to "an individual residing in or intending to reside in that dwelling after it is sold, rented, or made available" and to "any individual associated with the buyer or renter", and § 14-02.5-02(2) bars discrimination in "the terms, conditions, or privileges of ... rental of a dwelling or in providing services or facilities in connection with a ... rental" because of race, colour, religion, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin, or status with respect to marriage or public assistance. Section 14-02.5-06(3)(b) makes refusing "a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices, or services" discrimination, which is why a live-in aide must be carved out of any guest limit. And § 14-02.5-45(2) provides that "[i]t is a discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with any individual in the exercise or enjoyment of ... any right granted or protected by this chapter", while § 14-02.5-45(1) with (3) makes intimidating or interfering with an individual by force or threat of force, on a protected ground and because of their occupying or negotiating for a dwelling, a CLASS A MISDEMEANOR. So: apply the guest limit by the clock, to every household alike, and never by who the guest appears to be. One North Dakota permission to note rather than rely on: § 14-02.5-02(5) provides that "[n]othing in this chapter prevents a person from refusing to rent a dwelling to two unrelated individuals of opposite gender who are not married to each other" - that is a refusal-to-rent permission, not a licence to police a tenant's visitors.

ONE MORE TRAP, AND IT IS SEVERE. Do not solve an overcrowding problem by letting part of the premises to someone else. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-26 entitles a tenant of part of a room to the whole room "notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary", and relieves every tenant in the building under the same landlord of all obligation to pay rent while the double letting continues.

title: There Is No "Material Breach" Threshold on Your Habitability Duties
bodyText:
The default rule in most states is that a tenant must show the defect was material or substantial before any habitability remedy opens up. North Dakota has no such threshold, and you should not assume one protects you.

N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1) lists six duties, and only the first one carries a materiality word: you must comply with building and housing codes "materially affecting health and safety" (subdivision a). That phrase narrows which codes that one duty reaches — it is not a grading standard for your other duties. Subdivision b, the core duty to "make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition," has no materiality qualifier at all. Neither does the tenant's self-help trigger in § 47-16-13, which opens on "notice from the lessee of dilapidations which the lessor ought to repair" — the word is dilapidations, with no requirement that they be serious, major or substantial.

What does limit your exposure is different, and it is about time and reasonableness rather than severity. Under § 47-16-13.1(2) you are allowed "a reasonable time" to remedy noncompliance with subdivisions b through f — note that subdivision a, code compliance, is deliberately left out of that grace. Section 47-16-13(1) likewise only opens the tenant's remedies if you neglect to repair "within a reasonable time after notice." The heat and hot-water duty in subdivision f is itself stated in terms of "reasonable amounts of hot water" and "reasonable heat." And under § 47-16-13.1(3), if a building or housing code imposes a greater duty than any other subdivision, your duty is measured by the code, not by the lesser statutory wording.

What to do: treat every reported defect you "ought to repair" as actionable and respond within a reasonable time, rather than triaging on whether it looks material. Do not write a lease term that makes a habitability remedy conditional on the defect being material, substantial or health-threatening. Such a term is not supported by any North Dakota statute, it is reviewable for unconscionability under § 47-16-13.1's companion section § 47-16-13.3(1)(a), and to the extent it exempts you from the consequences of breaching a statutory duty it runs into § 9-08-02 with § 9-08-01(2), which make a contract exempting anyone from responsibility for a violation of law contrary to the policy of express law.

title: Which Habitability Duties You Can Move to the Tenant, and Which You Cannot
bodyText:
The default rule is that N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1) imposes all six habitability duties on you by statute, in every residential tenancy, whether or not the lease mentions them. They are modifiable only through the two narrow routes in § 47-16-13.1(4) to (6), and which route you get depends entirely on the kind of property.

For a single-family residence: you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant performs your subdivision (e) duty (waste receptacles and arranging removal) and your subdivision (f) duty (running water, reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, and reasonable heat), and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodelling. The only condition is that the transaction is entered into in good faith (§ 47-16-13.1(4)).

For any other dwelling unit, the route is much narrower, and this is where landlords go wrong. The tenant may agree to perform only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" (§ 47-16-13.1(5)). Subdivisions (e) and (f) are simply not on that list, so in a multi-unit building you cannot move the waste-removal duty or the water, hot-water and heat duty to the tenant at all. On top of that, all three of these conditions must hold: the agreement is in good faith and is set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration; the work is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subdivision (e); and the agreement does not diminish or affect your obligation to other tenants in the premises. "Separate writing" means separate — a section inside the lease will not do, and nor will consideration that is really just the tenancy itself, because the statute demands adequate consideration for this agreement specifically.

There is also a no-leverage rule: you may not treat performance of the separate agreement as a condition to any obligation or performance of any rental agreement (§ 47-16-13.1(6)). So you cannot make signing or performing a maintenance agreement a precondition of granting, renewing or continuing the tenancy. Subsection (6) cross-refers to "the separate agreement described in subsection 4" although it is subsection (5) that describes a separate writing, so the subsection it was aimed at is genuinely unclear. CAUTIOUS COURSE: treat the no-condition rule as applying to both routes — never make the tenant's performance of any maintenance agreement, single-family or otherwise, a condition of the lease.

On the specific question of waiving the water or hot-water duty where the premises have no well or utility water: you do not need a waiver, and you cannot get one in a multi-unit building. Subdivision (f) carries its own three built-in exceptions and they operate by force of the statute, not by agreement — the duty does not apply if the building is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose, or if the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection, or if the water or heat is unavailable due to supply failure by a public utility.

What to do: never put a habitability-duty shift in the lease body for anything other than a single-family residence. Use a separate signed document with its own stated consideration, keep it to specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodelling, and keep waste removal and the water-and-heat duty on yourself. Any such agreement remains reviewable for unconscionability under § 47-16-13.3, and a settlement in which the tenant gives up a claim under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 is expressly reviewable too.

title: No Presumption That the Unit Was Habitable, and None That It Was Not
bodyText:
Some states give one side a head start by statute: the unit is presumed habitable unless the tenant proves otherwise, or a code violation is prima facie evidence that it was not. North Dakota has neither. There is no statutory presumption, no prima facie rule, no conclusive-evidence provision and no burden-shifting device anywhere in its landlord-tenant law on the condition of a dwelling.

What that means in practice is that habitability in North Dakota is proved the ordinary way, on the evidence, by whichever party is asserting something. If a tenant claims you failed to keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition under N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(b), they have to establish it; nothing in the statute presumes it from a complaint, an inspection report or a code citation. Equally, nothing presumes the unit was fine because the tenant moved in, signed a lease, paid rent for months, or signed a move-in checklist. A clean move-in inspection is useful evidence and nothing more.

Two features of the chapter are sometimes mistaken for presumptions and are not. Section 47-16-13.1(3) says that if a building or housing code imposes a greater duty than another subdivision of subsection 1 does, your duty is measured by the code — that raises the standard, it does not presume a breach. And § 47-16-13.3(2) provides that where unconscionability is put in issue, the parties "shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present evidence as to the setting, purpose, and effect" of the rental agreement or settlement — that is a guarantee of an evidentiary hearing, the opposite of a presumption.

What to do: build the record, because nothing will be assumed in your favour. Do a dated, signed move-in condition report with photographs, log every repair request with the date you received it and the date you responded, keep contractor invoices and dates, and document each inspection. Since § 47-16-13(1) and § 47-16-13.1(2) both turn on whether you acted within a reasonable time after notice, your dated response log is usually the most valuable document you own. Do not write a lease term declaring that the unit "is presumed habitable" or that the tenant's signature is conclusive evidence of good condition: North Dakota gives no statutory support for it, § 47-16-13.3(1)(a) lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision, and § 9-08-05 makes void any contract stipulation restricting a party from enforcing their rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals.

title: Your Lease Does Not Have to Promise a Habitable Unit (and Should Not Try to Narrow the Duty)
bodyText:
In some states the lease itself must carry a habitability promise — Maryland, for instance, requires the lease to state that the landlord will deliver the unit fit for habitation. North Dakota imposes no such requirement. In fact North Dakota prescribes no lease content at all for a residential tenancy: chapter 47-16 contains no provision telling you what a lease must say, must contain or must disclose.

The reason the omission does not hurt the tenant is that N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1) does the work without the lease. It says a landlord of a residential dwelling unit "shall" comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition; keep common areas clean and safe; maintain in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances supplied or required to be supplied; provide and maintain waste receptacles and arrange removal; and supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat, subject to that subdivision's own exceptions. Those duties attach to the tenancy by force of the statute, whether your lease repeats them, contradicts them or says nothing.

ONE EXCEPTION, and it is a disclosure duty rather than lease content. If you own or have purchased a mobile home park, § 47-10-28(9) requires you to provide each tenant with "a summary outlining the tenant's lease and the rights and obligations of the tenant and mobile home park owner under state law" — so a mobile home park operator does have to hand over a written summary of the statutory rights, habitability duties included. That section was amended by S.L. 2025, ch. 238 (S.B. 2385), effective August 1, 2025, and § 47-10-28(12) backs it with a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and not more than the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs. Nothing comparable applies to an ordinary apartment or house tenancy.

So outside a mobile home park, adding a habitability statement to your lease is optional and changes nothing legally. The real risk runs the other way. A lease that paraphrases the duty narrowly — for example promising only to keep the unit "in the condition it was in at move-in," or to make repairs "as Landlord deems necessary" — does not shrink your statutory duty, but it does create a document that reads as if you believed it had. A court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision under § 47-16-13.3(1)(a), and to the extent a term exempts you from responsibility for breaching a statutory duty it collides with § 9-08-02 read with § 9-08-01(2). The only lawful way to move any of these duties onto the tenant is the narrow route in § 47-16-13.1(4) to (6), which for anything other than a single-family residence must be a separate signed writing with adequate consideration rather than a lease clause.

What to do: leave the statutory duties out of the lease, or state them accurately and in full if you prefer tenants to see them. Never state them partially. And keep your repair-request and response records, since § 47-16-13.1(2) gives you a reasonable time to remedy noncompliance with subdivisions (b) through (f) and your dated log is what proves you used it.

title: Habitability: What You Can Shift to the Tenant, and What You Cannot
bodyText: North Dakota has no provision making its habitability duties non-waivable, which puts it on the opposite side of the line from most states. Instead the statute says when a shift works. For a single-family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant performs your waste-receptacle duty and your running-water, hot-water and heat duty, and also specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodelling (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(4)). For any other dwelling unit the same agreement works only if it is in good faith, set out in a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration, does not cover work needed to cure a failure of the waste-receptacle duty, and does not diminish or affect what you owe other tenants (§ 47-16-13.1(5)). You may not treat the tenant's performance of such an agreement as a condition of any obligation under the rental agreement (§ 47-16-13.1(6)). And one duty never shifts: where your duty to comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety is greater than any other duty in the list, that duty governs (§ 47-16-13.1(3)). A court may also refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision, and a settlement in which a party waives a habitability right is itself reviewable for unconscionability (§ 47-16-13.3).

title: No Duty to Give Tenants the Health Rules -- but the Local Code Still Controls Your Habitability Duty
bodyText:
Default rule first: outside a mobile home park, no North Dakota statute requires a landlord to give a tenant a copy of the local health authority's rental regulations, on request or otherwise, and none requires a landlord to refer a tenant to the health authority or to print its contact details in the lease. If a tenant asks for the health regulations, you may hand them over as a courtesy, but you are not obliged to have them, hold them or produce them.

The health authority is real, though, and knowing its shape is worth more than a handout duty would be. North Dakota's old health districts chapter (ch. 23-14) is repealed; the regime is now PUBLIC HEALTH UNITS. Under § 23-35-02(1) 'all land in the state must be in a public health unit', and subsection (2) gives every unit core functions including environmental public health -- preventing environmental hazards by providing information and education 'to facility operators and managers and to community members', assuring the availability of environmental health services 'to prevent and respond to community and residential environmental hazards', and permitting and inspecting onsite wastewater treatment systems, with an in-person or virtual inspection within one business day of a request. Under § 23-35-08 each board of health may make rules 'regarding any nuisance, source of filth, and any cause of sickness which are necessary for public health and safety' (subsection 5), may make rules in a health district or county public health department and recommend ordinances to a city's governing body (7), may inquire into any nuisance, source of filth or cause of sickness (10), may conduct a search or seize material on private property under an administrative search warrant to ascertain the property's condition as it relates to public health and safety, except in an emergency (11), and may abate or remove any nuisance, source of filth or cause of sickness when necessary to protect the public health and safety (12). Those rules are subordinate to a conflicting local ordinance or civil service rule within the board's jurisdiction, or a tribal code, ordinance or policy.

Here is why that matters to your lease even without a handout duty: § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes you 'comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety', and § 47-16-13.1(3) provides that where that duty is greater than any other duty in the subsection, your duty 'shall be determined by reference to subdivision a'. So a local health or housing code requirement is imported into your landlord obligations and CONTROLS over the statute's own lower standards -- and § 47-16-13.6 makes those duties enforceable by action with attorney's fees to the prevailing party. A code you have never read can therefore be the measure of your habitability duty.

If you operate a mobile home park the picture is different and much stricter. § 47-10-28(1)(a) requires an annual licence under § 23-10-03; § 47-10-28(1)(e) requires you to acknowledge receipt of a tenant inquiry or complaint about the park, under § 23-10-10.1, within two business days; § 23-10-10.1 itself requires a procedure for emergencies and complaints that reaches someone with authority to act, 'posted conspicuously' in the park or given to the tenants in writing; § 23-10-10 requires you to 'post or distribute a digital or hard copy of the relevant rules and regulations to each tenant in the park', with the department supplying the material free; and § 47-10-28(12) backs every duty in that section with a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and not more than the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, while § 47-32-01.1 makes a violation a defence to an eviction. § 47-10-28(13) goes further: a district court may suspend the park licence for a violation, with a daily civil penalty equal to half the monthly rent roll divided by the days in the month, tenants allowed to remain throughout, and no rule changes, rent increases or no-cause terminations during the suspension.

Cautious course: do not tell a tenant that no health rule applies to your property. Find out which public health unit covers it, ask whether it has a rental, nuisance or onsite-wastewater rule, and comply -- because § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) and (3) make a local code requirement binding on you through the lease statute whether or not your lease mentions it. If the board finds a nuisance, § 23-35-09(1) lets it serve notice on 'the owner or occupant' to abate it within a time 'not exceeding thirty days', and if you do not, the cost is charged 'against the lot, piece, or parcel of land'.

title: Heat Is Your Duty, the Standard Is "Reasonable" With No Temperature, and You Can Only Shift It in a Single-Family Home
bodyText:
North Dakota makes heat your duty by statute and sets no thermostat number. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(f) requires a landlord of a residential dwelling unit to "supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat." The standard is reasonable heat — not sixty-eight degrees, not any figure. There is no statutory minimum temperature, no heating season, and no thermostat setting anywhere in North Dakota's landlord-tenant law. Separately, § 47-16-13.1(1)(d) requires you to maintain in good and safe working order and condition all heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply, so the furnace or boiler itself must work regardless of what the indoor temperature happens to be.

Subdivision (f) carries three exceptions and they are statutory, not matters of agreement. The duty does not apply if the building that includes the dwelling unit is not required by law to be equipped for that purpose; or if the dwelling unit is so constructed that heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the exclusive control of the tenant and supplied by a direct public utility connection; or if the water or heat is unavailable due to supply failure by a public utility. The second of those is the one that matters in practice: where the unit has its own heating installation under the tenant's exclusive control fed by a direct utility connection, the statute itself lifts the duty. That is North Dakota's version of the separately-metered-equipment idea, and note that it works by the construction of the building, not by anything you write in the lease.

On shifting the duty, the rule is strict and it turns entirely on property type. For a single-family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant performs your subdivision (f) duty — water, hot water and heat — along with your waste-receptacle duty and specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodelling, provided the transaction is entered into in good faith (§ 47-16-13.1(4)). For any other dwelling unit, you cannot shift it at all. Section 47-16-13.1(5) permits an agreement only that the tenant perform "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling," and subdivision (f) is simply not on that list, so in a duplex, a fourplex or an apartment building the heat duty stays with you no matter what the lease says and no matter what consideration is offered.

Two more mechanics. Under § 47-16-13.1(2) you are allowed a reasonable time to remedy noncompliance with subdivisions (b) through (f), so a heat failure is not an instant breach — but under § 47-16-13.1(3), if an applicable building or housing code imposes a greater duty than subdivision (f) does, your duty is measured by the code. That matters here: the statute sets no temperature, but a State Building Code or municipal housing code provision could, and § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) and (3) would make it binding on you. CAUTIOUS COURSE: check the building code and any housing code adopted by your city, and treat its figure as your floor. If no local figure applies, understand that "reasonable heat" in a North Dakota winter will be judged against habitability, not against your fuel bill.

If you fail, the tenant has real options without going to court: under § 47-16-13 they may repair and deduct the expense from rent, recover it in any other lawful manner, or vacate and be discharged from further rent and from the lease's other conditions; under § 47-16-17(1) they may terminate the lease outright; and under §§ 47-16-13.5 and 47-16-13.6 they may recover appropriate damages by action, with the court free to award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party.

What to do: service the heating plant before each heating season and keep the invoices; respond to a no-heat call the same day and log it; never put a heat-duty shift in a lease for anything but a single-family house, and even there use a signed writing made in good faith; and do not treat a tenant-controlled thermostat as transferring the duty unless the unit actually meets subdivision (f)'s exclusive-control-and-direct-utility-connection description.

title: North Dakota Gives an Association No Power Over Your Tenant
bodyText:
Default rule: North Dakota has almost no association-and-tenant law, and the little it has protects your tenant rather than empowering the association.
