There is no provision requiring or permitting an association to approve a lease, no cap on a per-applicant approval fee, no association-held lessee deposit, no power for an association to demand rent from your tenant when you fall behind on assessments and no corresponding immunity for the tenant, no limit on an association's rental restrictions or on when they bind an owner who bought before them, no limit on what tenant information or rental fees an association may demand, and no protection for a renter's home child care against the association.

The whole of North Dakota's association law is the Condominium Ownership of Real Property chapter, and it is addressed to owners: section 47-04.1-08 obliges "each unit owner" to comply strictly with the bylaws, the administrative rules and regulations and the covenants, conditions and restrictions, and section 47-04.1-11 makes a reasonable common-expense assessment a debt of the owner at the time it is made and a lien on the unit once recorded. Your tenant is not a unit owner.

There is one real North Dakota limit on the association, and it is worth knowing because it is the renter-neutrality rule most states lack: section 47-04.1-07(2) forbids the bylaws from containing provisions that base the assessment of common charges on whether the occupant of a unit is an owner, a tenant or another person, or that base the payment of losses, the division of profits, the disposition of hazard proceeds "or any other topic that is within the scope of the bylaws" on that distinction. An association may not charge you more, or pay you less, because you rent your unit out. Section 47-04.1-07(3) also requires all bylaws, rules and regulations to be reduced to writing and made available to every owner of any interest in the project, which is your route to the documents.

Two consequences follow, and they cut in opposite directions. In your favour: an association cannot go round you to your tenant. It has no statutory route to the rent, no statutory route to fine the tenant directly, and no statutory route to approve or refuse your lease -- whatever it has comes from the recorded declaration, which binds you as owner, not from statute.

Against you: your tenant owes the association nothing and owes you nothing in respect of its rules unless your lease says so. Section 47-04.1-08 will not do that work for you.

What to do: use the shared Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance clause, which North Dakota is tagged on, because in North Dakota that clause is the only thing making your tenant follow the association's rules; read the recorded declaration before you sign a lease, since any approval requirement, rental cap or tenant-information demand lives there and binds you personally as the owner even though it cannot reach your tenant; and if the declaration lets the association fine you for your tenant's conduct, pass that through by the lease and bill it rather than taking it from the security deposit, which section 47-16-07.1(3) does not permit it to be applied to.

title: Money Taken to Hold a Unit, Before There Is a Lease
bodyText: Default rule in North Dakota: there is no holding-deposit statute. Nothing regulates money taken from an applicant before a lease is signed - no cap, no receipt or disclosure duty, no deadline to return it, no rule on whether it must be credited to the security deposit or to the first month's rent, and no doubling remedy if you are the one who backs out. The exposure is in general contract law instead. Penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void (N.D.C.C. § 9-08-03). A contract that fixes the amount of damages in advance for a breach is void to that extent unless it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage (§ 9-08-04) - and what an applicant's withdrawal actually costs you is a few days' lost rent and a re-advertising bill, which is neither impracticable nor extremely difficult to work out. And any provision contrary to an express provision of law is unlawful (§ 9-08-01(1)). So a form that says the holding money is 'non-refundable' or 'forfeited' if the applicant does not sign is the weakest version of this arrangement, not the strongest. The second trap is the one that bites later: once a lease is signed and you keep that money, it becomes money required as a security deposit 'however denominated' under § 47-16-07.1(1), so it counts against the one-month-rent ceiling, it has to go into the federally insured interest-bearing account for the tenant's benefit, and on termination it can be applied only to pet or negligence damage, unpaid rent, and cleaning or repairs that were the tenant's responsibility (§ 47-16-07.1(3)). What to do: take the money under a short written receipt that says what it is for, says it will be credited in full to the security deposit or the first month's rent if a lease is signed, and says what you will actually retain if the applicant withdraws - your real, documented out-of-pocket cost, stated as a reimbursement of actual loss and not as a forfeiture or a fixed sum. Keep the amount small, keep the holding period short, and return the money promptly if you are the one who lets the unit to someone else.

title: No Cap on a Holdover Rate -- Which Is Exactly Why You Should Not State One
bodyText:
The default rule is that North Dakota sets no holdover rate and caps none. There is no statutory per diem, no percentage ceiling on a lease-set holdover charge, no 150-percent-of-per-diem limit, and no separate rule for HUD or other subsidised units.

But the absence of a cap is not permission to pick a number, and this is the whole point of the topic. Two general contract sections do the limiting instead. Section 9-08-03 says flatly that 'Penalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance thereof are void' -- unqualified, with no exception to argue about. Section 9-08-04 says a contract fixing the amount of damages in anticipation of a breach is 'to that extent void', except that the parties may agree on an amount presumed to be the damage sustained 'in cases in which it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage'.

Holdover damages are not impracticable or extremely difficult to fix -- the rental value of the unit is the most readily provable number in a residential tenancy -- so a stated daily or monthly holdover multiple in a North Dakota lease is exposed on both sections at once: void as a fixing under 9-08-04 and, if it looks punitive, void outright as a penalty under 9-08-03. A charge measured by what you actually lost is outside both. So claim actual damages and the reasonable rental value of the property for the period the tenant stays, and do not state a rate. That is what the North Dakota holdover clause in this library does, and deliberately.

Two further things to know: section 47-16-06 means that if you ACCEPT rent from a residential tenant who stays after the lease expires, the lease is presumed renewed as a month-to-month tenancy, so accepting a holdover payment can convert the holdover into a tenancy; and North Dakota has two statutory double-damages measures for a holdover, each with a narrow trigger, which the holdover topic covers separately -- a lease clause claiming only actual damages should not be drafted so as to look like a waiver of them.

title: Home-Based Businesses
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota has no home-business statute. So there is no statute making a home-based business a permitted use of a dwelling and none stopping a lease restricting it. But there is a statute that makes your restriction work, and it works only if the lease says what the premises are for. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-11 provides: "When real property is leased for a particular purpose, the lessee must not use it for any other purpose. If the lessee violates the lease in this respect, the lessor may hold the lessee responsible for the safety of the property during such use in all events or may treat the contract as rescinded thereby." Note two things. First, the duty bites only where the property was "leased for a particular purpose" - a lease silent on purpose has nothing to breach. Second, the remedy is unusually strong: strict responsibility for the safety of the property "in all events" during the unauthorised use, or rescission.

AND EVICTION NEEDS A WRITTEN MATERIAL TERM. N.D.C.C. § 47-32-01(8) makes an eviction maintainable where "[t]he lessee violates a material term of the written lease agreement between the lessor and lessee" - a written lease, and a material term. There is no eviction ground for using a dwelling commercially as such. So the purpose clause is not belt-and-braces; it is the eviction ground. Under § 47-32-02, a ground 8 eviction also requires "three days' written notice of intention to evict" before proceedings are instituted.

WHAT THE LANDLORD SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. Write the purpose down - "private residence only" - and keep the lease written, because § 47-32-01(8) gives you no eviction ground otherwise. Be specific about what you are banning, because a blanket ban on every occupation is both unenforceable in practice and exposed: § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce a lease provision that "was unconscionable when made", enforce the remainder without it, or limit its application. Remember that North Dakota law itself anticipates trade use of leased premises - § 47-06-04 gives a tenant the right to remove anything affixed "for the purpose of trade, manufacture, ornament, or domestic use" at any time during the term where removal causes no injury and the thing has not become an integral part - so a tenant's business equipment stays the tenant's, and a clause claiming it would fail. Where the business generates noise or traffic, you have a second route that needs no lease term at all: § 47-32-01(7) makes an eviction maintainable where "[a] lessee or a person on the premises with the lessee's consent acts in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment of the premises", and § 47-16-13.2(7) already obliges a tenant to conduct themselves, and to require others on the premises with their consent to conduct themselves, so as not to disturb the neighbours' peaceful enjoyment.

CAUTIOUS COURSE on zoning, which state law leaves to local ordinance. Whether a home business is lawful at the address is a zoning question, delegated in North Dakota to cities (ch. 40-47), counties (ch. 11-33) and townships (ch. 58-03). Those chapters let the local body regulate "the location and use of buildings, structures, and land for trade, industry, residence, or other purposes" (§ 40-47-01), and none of them mentions home occupations. Do not tell a tenant their business is permitted, and do not tell them it is forbidden; make the lease condition consent on zoning compliance and put the burden of checking on the tenant, as the lease clause does. Note separately that § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) obliges you to comply with "applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety" and § 47-16-13.1(3) makes that duty controlling where it is greater than any other - so if a tenant's business use pulls the building into a different code occupancy class, the resulting compliance problem is yours, not theirs. That is the strongest practical reason to keep the consent requirement in your hands.

title: A Tenant Has No Homestead Exemption to Waive
bodyText: North Dakota's homestead exemption protects an OWNER-occupant's equity from execution by creditors: it fixes an area and value, says how it is selected and conveyed, and when it is subject to execution (N.D.C.C. ch. 47-18). It protects an owner's equity: § 47-18-01 describes the homestead as the land on which the claimant resides and the dwelling house on it, valued 'over and above liens or encumbrances', and the rest of the chapter is about selling, conveying and encumbering it. Whether a residential leasehold can ever be a homestead the statute doesn't say, and only case law could settle it; on the ordinary reading a tenant has nothing to waive, so a lease clause in which the tenant waives the homestead exemption is at best empty. The one waiver provision in the chapter, § 47-18-05.1, requires notice for a waiver of the exemption in a conveyance or encumbrance of the homestead by its owner, which is a mortgage-and-deed question, not a lease one. Leaving the clause out is better than leaving it in: a waiver that does nothing still invites an argument about what else the tenant was asked to give up.

title: North Dakota has no immigration-status rule for residential tenants — but farmland leases are different
bodyText:
The default rule, and it runs in both directions: North Dakota says nothing about a residential tenant's immigration status. No provision in the North Dakota statutes prohibits a landlord from asking about immigration status or citizenship, and none makes it unlawful to rent to a person who is not lawfully present. There is no immigrant tenant protection act, no immigration-status inquiry ban, no immigration-status protection, and no verification or E-Verify duty for a landlord. North Dakota has not legislated on this at all.

Do not mistake that silence for either permission or prohibition, because two other bodies of law fill it.

First, North Dakota fair housing. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-02(1) and (2) protect 'national origin', and § 14-02.5-03 bars an advertisement indicating a preference or limitation on that ground. National origin is not the same thing as immigration status, but in practice they are hard to keep apart: an inquiry, a document demand or a policy that you apply only to applicants who sound or look foreign is national-origin discrimination whatever you call it, and a single-form policy applied to everyone identically is the only safe way to run any identity check. The penalties are not nominal — § 14-02.5-32 allows departmental civil penalties up to $11,000, $27,000 or $55,000 depending on history, on top of actual damages, fees and costs, and § 14-02.5-37 allows up to $50,000 for a first and $100,000 for a later violation in a pattern-or-practice case.

Second, federal law. Anti-harassment and discrimination rules and any obligation to report or verify status are federal questions, not North Dakota ones. Do not assume a federal duty to verify a tenant's status exists, and do not assume one does not — take advice. Nothing in North Dakota law requires it.

North Dakota does have one citizenship rule about property, and it is worth getting right because it cuts the opposite way from what people expect. § 47-01-11: 'Except as provided in chapter 47-10.1, any person, whether citizen or alien, may take, hold, and dispose of property, real or personal, within this state.' So a non-citizen may hold a leasehold in North Dakota as a matter of express statute. The exception matters only for farmland: § 47-10.1-02(1) says an individual 'who is not a citizen of the United States, a citizen of Canada, or a permanent resident alien of the United States may not acquire directly or indirectly any interest in agricultural land' unless a narrow set of conditions is met (treaty entry while actively investing substantial capital, residence in the state at least ten months a year, active participation in the operation, a holding not over 640 acres, and a dairy operation), subsection 4 extends the restriction to entities unless the ultimate beneficial interest is held by citizens or permanent resident aliens, and subsection 8 bars a foreign government from acquiring or holding agricultural land after June 30, 2023. 'Any interest' is broad enough to include a leasehold, and § 47-10.1-04 is the enforcement section with § 47-10.1-06 the penalty.

What to do. (1) For a residential tenancy, screen on ability to pay and tenancy history and leave status alone. If you need to confirm identity, use one form, one document list and one process for every applicant, and keep the record of having done so. (2) Do not put an immigration-status representation, a status-change termination right or a verification covenant in a residential lease. North Dakota gives you no such right, the clause would add nothing to your position, and it is close to an admission of a national-origin screen. (3) Never use status, or a threat to report it, as leverage over rent, repairs or a move-out. Besides the federal exposure, § 14-02.5-45 makes intimidation or interference by force or threat of force, because of national origin and because the person is renting or occupying a dwelling, a class A misdemeanour, and subsection 2 makes it a discriminatory practice to 'coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with any individual in the exercise or enjoyment of' a right the chapter grants. (4) If you lease FARMLAND, this is different: get the tenant's citizenship or permanent-resident status confirmed before you sign, because chapter 47-10.1 reaches 'any interest in agricultural land' and the penalty falls on the holding, not on the tenant's paperwork. (5) If an immigration authority contacts you about a tenant, treat it the way the law-enforcement-cooperation row describes: ask for the legal process, and give nothing voluntarily that you have not taken advice on.

title: Illness, Disability or a Move to Care: No Early-Exit Right in North Dakota
bodyText:
The default rule first: a fixed-term North Dakota lease runs to the end of its term (N.D.C.C. 47-16-14(1)), and a month-to-month tenancy ends on at least one calendar month's written notice from either side, with rent due to and including the termination date (47-16-15(2)). Nothing in that turns on the tenant's health.

North Dakota gives a tenant no early-termination right for infirmity. There is no physician's-certificate exit, no nursing-home or assisted-living exit, no age-based exit and no disability-based exit. The contrast is deliberate and worth seeing: the legislature did write an early-termination statute for one situation - domestic violence, at 47-16-17.1, where a tenant who gives advance written notice naming a court order, an order prohibiting contact, a civil protection order under chapter 14-07.7 or other record filed with a court pays the current month plus one month's rent and is released, subject to your duty to mitigate. There is no equivalent for illness or infirmity, and the absence of one next to a statute that exists is strong.

The one health-adjacent provision is 47-16-18, and it is narrower than it looks. Notice of the death or incapacity of a party terminates a lease of real property ONLY where the lease is 'terminable at the pleasure of one of the parties' - that is, an at-will or month-to-month tenancy - 'but in no other case is it terminable thereby'. So incapacity does not end a fixed-term lease. The same section adds a separate residential death rule: on the death of a residential tenant, and at the option of any surviving tenant or of the decedent's estate, the lease terminates on the last day of the month in the month following the death, unless the term expires sooner.

What that means in practice. A fixed-term tenant who must move into care stays liable for the rent, but not without limit: you must mitigate your damages (47-16-13.5, and 47-16-13.7 for a tenant evicted according to law), and if you re-let, the tenant pays the due proportion for the use actually made of the property, unless that use was 'merely nominal and of no benefit' (47-16-21). Do this: decide in advance whether to offer a medical or infirmity early-release term, and if you do, write it in the lease - a stated notice period, written evidence from a treating professional, and a release fee measured by your actual re-letting cost rather than a round number, because a contractual penalty is void (9-08-03) and damages fixed in advance are void to that extent unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (9-08-04). Do not write the release as a 'statutory right' and do not write a term saying the tenant waives one: North Dakota has none, so the waiver is empty and it invites the tenant to think they gave something up. Separately, a request to end a tenancy early because of a disability may be a request for a reasonable accommodation, and disability is a protected class in the rental of a dwelling under 14-02.5-02 - so handle it as an accommodation question rather than purely as a lease question.

title: No duty to disclose an outstanding inspection or condemnation order in North Dakota - and no state condemned-building statute
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant about an outstanding code-inspection report, notice of violation, correction order, abatement order, condemnation order or order to vacate affecting the property - not before signing, not during the tenancy, and not when one is issued. There is no disclosure form, no deadline, no tenant termination right keyed to such an order and no penalty.

Where North Dakota's condemnation power over unfit housing actually lives: 40-58-18, "Ordinances relating to repair, closing, and demolition of dwellings unfit for human habitation", in ch. 40-58 (the Urban Renewal Law). That is an enabling section - the state authorises municipalities to adopt ordinances, and the operative rules, the inspection, the order, the placard, the hearing and the consequences are all in the municipal code. It puts no disclosure duty on a landlord. It does make the public officer serve the complaint on "all parties in interest in the dwelling, including persons in possession", and post a copy of the complaint or order "in a conspicuous place on the premises affected". Note too that in the Century Code "condemnation" as a term of art means eminent domain: the condemnation sections in its master index are ch. 32-15 eminent domain, a highway or water-project taking, a diseased animal, a seized food item or a weighing device. There is no "condemned building" statute at state level at all. The state-level inspection-and-order machinery that does exist is the state fire marshal's: 18-01-14 abatement of fire hazards, 18-01-15 abatement of conditions dangerous to persons - order - failure to comply - penalty, 18-01-16 order of abatement - to whom directed - contents - how served - service by publication, 18-01-17 to 18-01-26 appeals and district court enforcement, and 18-01-27 costs and the lien for them. For a mobile home park there is also 23-10-12 (revocation or suspension of license), 23-10-13 (change in use or closure of a mobile home park) and ch. 23-10.1 (Mobile Home Park Receiver, 23-10.1-02 conditions for appointment of a receiver). For a lodging establishment there is 23-09-11 (inspection - reports), 23-09-18 (failure to comply with chapter - notice - how served) and 23-09-22 (license canceled). None of those sections requires a landlord to tell a tenant about an order; 18-01-20 has the fire marshal serve the court notice on the "lessee, tenant, occupant" among others.

What does bind you, and why no disclosure clause is needed to get there: 47-16-13.1(1)(a) requires you to "comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and 47-16-13.1(3) makes that duty controlling where it is the greater one. An outstanding code order is, by definition, evidence that you are not complying - so the order itself puts you in breach of a term the statute has already written into the lease. 47-16-13.1(1)(b) adds the duty to make all repairs necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable, and 47-16-13.1(2) allows a reasonable time to remedy a failure under subdivisions b to f (but notably not under subdivision a). The tenant's remedies under 47-16-13 - uncapped repair-and-deduct, recovery in any other lawful manner, or vacating and being discharged from further payment of rent - all turn on notice from the TENANT of a dilapidation, not on anything you disclose. 47-16-13.6 makes those rights enforceable by action with attorney's fees to the prevailing party, which cuts both ways. And 47-16-17(1) lets the tenant terminate when you do not, within a reasonable time after request, put the property into good condition or repair it. Important caveat, because it narrows every absence stated here: the State Building Code (ch. 54-21.3) is the international codes, adopted by rule and enforced locally under 54-21.3-05.

What to do: disclose an outstanding order voluntarily and in writing. Nothing compels it, but a tenant who discovers a live condemnation or vacate order after signing has strong arguments under 47-16-13, 47-16-13.1 and 47-16-17(1), and the 47-16-07.2 condition-of-premises statement - the one document North Dakota does require with a rental agreement - is prima facie proof of the condition at the start of the tenancy and the natural place to record it. Never ask a tenant to waive the right to be told: there is no state right to waive, so the waiver is empty and it invites the tenant to believe something was given up. Do not represent that the premises are free of orders unless you have checked with the municipality and the fire marshal. If an abatement order under 18-01-15 or 18-01-16 is served, note that 18-01-27 creates a lien for the costs of enforcement, so the cost of ignoring one runs against the property.

title: No statutory penalty for entering without notice in North Dakota — and why that is not a free pass
bodyText:
The default rule first: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.3 does tell you when you may enter, and it does say "A landlord shall not abuse the right of access or use it to harass or intimidate the tenant." What it does not do is attach any consequence. There is no civil penalty, no statutory damages figure, no multiple of rent, no fine and no criminal offence anywhere in the North Dakota statutes for entering a dwelling unit without notice, for entering outside reasonable hours, or for abusing the right of access. North Dakota also gives the tenant no statutory cause of action for it: § 47-16-13.6, the only enforcement section in the residential chapter, is limited by its own caption to §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 and does not reach the entry section at all.

Do not read that as a free pass, because the exposure is real and it is simply not quantified by statute. A tenant whose unit you entered unlawfully can sue you for trespass as a matter of common law; can rely on § 47-16-08, which binds you to secure the tenant's quiet possession for the term; can ask a court under § 47-16-13.3 to refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision, including the access provision you relied on; and can use the entry in front of a judge as the colour for everything else in the dispute, which in practice is where the cost lands. Nothing in § 47-16-07.3 caps what a court may award, precisely because nothing in it mentions a remedy.

What to do. Give the notice even when you think you do not have to, and make it the kind § 47-16-07.3 describes: state a time certain, deliver it personally, post it conspicuously in or about the unit, or use any method that actually reaches the tenant, and keep a dated copy. If the tenant does not object, consent is presumed and you are on the statute's own ground. Enter in reasonable hours, in a reasonable manner, and only for a purpose subsection 2 lists — inspection, necessary or agreed repairs or improvements, supplying necessary or agreed services, or showing the unit to the people subsection 2 names. Keep an entry log: date, time, who entered, purpose, the notice given, whether the tenant objected. Where you rely on subsection 1 instead — emergency, a reasonable belief the tenant has abandoned the premises, or a reasonable belief the tenant is in substantial violation of the lease — write down the facts behind the belief before you go in, because the statute protects a reasonable belief and the log is the only thing that will show it was one.

One North Dakota feature worth knowing: § 47-16-13.6 awards reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party, not to the tenant. That cuts both ways and it favours a landlord who defends a weak habitability claim — but it only applies to §§ 47-16-13.1 to 47-16-13.6, so it will not help you on an entry dispute either.

title: Jury-Trial Waiver in a Lease: Untested Here
bodyText: North Dakota's constitution says the right of trial by jury shall be secured to all and remain inviolate (N.D. Const. art. I, § 13), and elsewhere in the same article it contemplates that a jury may be waived. No North Dakota statute authorises a pre-dispute jury waiver in a contract, and none forbids one. Two general contract sections bear on it: a stipulation restricting a party from enforcing its rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or limiting the time to enforce them, is void unless a North Dakota statute specifically permits it (N.D.C.C. § 9-08-05), and an unconscionable lease provision may be refused enforcement (§ 47-16-13.3). Whether a jury waiver is a restriction on enforcing rights 'by the usual legal proceedings' has not been decided here. Treat a jury-waiver clause as untested in North Dakota rather than safe, and take advice before relying on one.

title: No Key-Control or Employee Screening Mandate for Rental Housing
bodyText: Default rule: North Dakota imposes no key-control duty on a landlord of any size. There is no requirement to keep a written key-control policy, no master-key handling rule, no record of keys issued, no unit-count threshold that triggers one, and no requirement to run a background check on an employee who holds keys to occupied units -- no Virginia-style 200-unit key-policy rule and no Nevada-style covered-premises duty. The only key-control statutes in the entire Century Code govern the state's own capitol complex: officials and employees are responsible for keys issued to them and must return them on leaving (sections 44-08-18 and 54-06-15, the latter providing for payment of a fee in lieu of return), and the construction superintendent controls the issuance and return of keys and electronic card access to the capitol buildings (section 54-21-17.1). None of those reaches rental housing. What that means in practice is that a key failure is judged against your general duties, not against a safe-harbour checklist. Section 47-16-08 binds you to secure the tenant's quiet possession, section 47-16-13.1(1)(c) requires you to keep all common areas in a clean and safe condition, and section 47-16-07.3 limits when you may use your own access -- only in an emergency, on a reasonable belief of abandonment or substantial lease violation, or during reasonable hours for an enumerated purpose after notice and consent that may not be unreasonably withheld -- and it expressly forbids abusing the right of access or using it to harass or intimidate the tenant. Because there is no statutory standard, a written policy is how you show you met the general one. What to do: keep a key log recording who holds each key and each master key and when it was issued and returned; limit master keys to named staff; collect keys the day employment ends; re-key a unit at turnover as a matter of practice rather than of law; screen anyone who will hold a master key; and keep the record of every entry you make under section 47-16-07.3.

title: No penalty for using an unlawful lease term in North Dakota -- but the term is still void
bodyText:
THE DEFAULT RULE FIRST. In states that have adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a landlord who KNOWINGLY uses a lease provision the statute prohibits is liable to the tenant for actual damages, and often more. NORTH DAKOTA HAS NO SUCH PENALTY. It has not adopted URLTA, chapters 47-16 and 47-32 contain NO list of prohibited lease provisions at all, and there is nothing in North Dakota law that penalises a landlord for putting an unenforceable term in a lease, however deliberately. Knowledge, intent and bad faith are all legally irrelevant to the question.

SO WHAT DOES HAPPEN? THE TERM IS SIMPLY VOID, AND THAT IS ALL. North Dakota's answer comes from general contract law in chapter 9-08, and the consequence is always the same shape -- the offending words have no effect, and the rest of the lease carries on:
- s 9-08-03: 'Penalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance thereof are void.' Flat and unqualified -- so a fixed fine for breaking a rule is void, and nothing more happens to you for having written it.
- s 9-08-04: a provision fixing damages in anticipation of a breach is void 'TO THAT EXTENT', except where it would be 'impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage'. Note 'to that extent' -- it voids the fixing, not the clause.
- s 9-08-05: a stipulation restricting a party from enforcing rights 'by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals', or limiting the time to do so, is 'void, except as otherwise specifically permitted by the laws of this state'.
- s 9-08-02: a term exempting anyone from responsibility for their own fraud, wilful injury or violation of law is 'against the policy of the law', which s 9-08-01(2) makes unlawful.
- s 47-16-13.3 (unconscionability) can strike a term, including a settlement waiving a right under ss 47-16-13.1 to 47-16-13.6.
NONE of these carries a penalty, a civil fine, statutory damages or a fee award against the landlord for having used the term. See the exculpatory-clauses and unconscionability rows for how each operates; this row's point is the absence of a sanction.

DO NOT MISTAKE THESE THREE PENALTIES FOR A KNOWING-USE PENALTY -- THEY ARE THE ONLY PENALTIES NORTH DAKOTA PUTS ON A LANDLORD, AND EACH IS TIED TO CONDUCT, NOT TO DRAFTING.
1. s 47-16-17.1(11): in an action for a violation of the domestic-violence termination section 'the court MAY award statutory damages of one thousand dollars', plus actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, costs and disbursements. This bites on DISCLOSING a tenant's domestic-violence documentation or retaliating against her for terminating -- and note that a clause purporting to obtain the tenant's CONSENT to disclosure is unlawful, not merely empty, because s 47-16-17.1(4)'s exceptions are a closed list with no consent exception.
2. s 47-10-28(12): a mobile home park owner who violates that section is liable for 'a civil penalty not less than two thousand five hundred dollars but not exceeding the greater of ten thousand dollars or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs' -- and under s 47-32-01.1 a violation is a DEFENCE to the eviction. s 47-10-28(13) adds licence suspension and a daily penalty measured by the park's rent roll. This is the heaviest landlord penalty in North Dakota law, and it is park-only.
3. s 47-16-07.1(4): treble damages on security deposits. It is the only treble-damages provision in chapter 47-16. The other treble measure that reaches a landlord is s 32-03-29: three times the detriment for forcibly ejecting or excluding a person from possession of real property, which is what a lockout or a forced move-out is.
And one more that is NOT about landlords at all but is often miscited: s 47-04.1-16(8) makes 'An administrative body governing a condominium which willfully violates this section ... liable for actual damages' and a civil penalty for an EV-charging denial. That is a condominium association, not a landlord. Do not cite it as a landlord penalty.

WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. (1) Do not take comfort from the absence of a penalty. A void term still loses you the case it was written to win, you still pay your own lawyer, and s 47-16-13.6 lets the court award reasonable attorney's fees to 'the prevailing party' in a habitability action -- which cuts both ways, and against you if you lose. (2) Do not rely on a severability clause to rescue a penalty term: s 9-08-03 voids the penalty outright, so there is nothing to save. Write charges as ACTUAL cost instead. (3) Because North Dakota publishes no list of prohibited lease provisions, you cannot check your lease against a statutory list -- the limits are in chapter 9-08 and s 47-16-13.3 and you have to apply them yourself. That is a reason to be more conservative in a North Dakota lease, not less. (4) The three penalties above are where your real exposure is: do not disclose domestic-violence documentation, do not mishandle a security deposit, and if you run a park, read s 47-10-28 whole.

title: What a Tenant Can Actually Do If You Breach: Four Routes, and Fees Cut Both Ways
bodyText:
North Dakota has not adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so there is no single remedies section. The tenant's routes are scattered across chapter 47-16, and three of the four need no court at all.

Route one, self-help under N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13. If within a reasonable time after notice from the tenant of dilapidations you ought to repair you neglect to do so, the tenant may repair the premises and deduct the expense of such repair from the rent, or recover that expense from you in any other lawful manner, or vacate the premises — and a tenant who vacates on that ground "shall be discharged from further payment of rent or performance of other conditions." No cap, no court, no pre-approval.

Route two, termination under § 47-16-17(1). The tenant may end the lease before the end of the term where you do not fulfil your obligations, if any, within a reasonable time after request, as to placing and securing the tenant in quiet possession, putting the property into a good condition, or repairing it.

Route three, damages under § 47-16-13.5. "Any party aggrieved under sections 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 may recover appropriate damages. However, the aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages." Two things follow. The measure is "appropriate damages" — actual loss, with no multiplier, no statutory sum and no penalty. And the mitigation duty is reciprocal: it binds the tenant as the aggrieved party, so a tenant who sits on a worsening problem rather than limiting the loss has their recovery cut back. Note also that this mitigation duty is scoped by its own first sentence to parties aggrieved under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6; North Dakota has no general statutory duty to mitigate outside that range and § 47-16-13.7 (an evicted tenant's liability for rent through the term, subject to your duty to mitigate).

Route four, an action under § 47-16-13.6. Any right or action provided by §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 "is enforceable by action and the court may award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party." Read that carefully, because it is the most useful sentence in the chapter for you: the fee award is discretionary ("may"), and it runs to the prevailing party, whoever that is. If a tenant brings a habitability claim and loses, you may be awarded your reasonable fees. That cuts in both directions and is worth saying out loud in settlement discussions.

Two more things shape your exposure. Section 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision, and expressly reaches a settlement in which a party waives or agrees to forego a claim or right under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 — so a signed release of habitability claims is reviewable rather than final. And if the lease is terminated, § 47-16-13.4 preserves your side: you have a claim for possession and for rent, and a separate claim for actual damages for breach.

If you operate a mobile home park the exposure is different in kind. Section 47-10-28(12) imposes a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and not more than the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, for violating any provision of that section, and § 47-10-28(13) lets the district court suspend the park's license with a daily penalty while suspended. Under § 47-10-28(14) the tenant may elect small claims court or district court for those damages.

What to do: respond to repair notices on a dated log, because every route above runs through "a reasonable time after notice" and your log is the only evidence of it. Do not rely on a signed release of habitability claims. And if you are defending a weak habitability claim, remember § 47-16-13.6 cuts both ways on fees.

title: North Dakota does not make you carry landlord liability insurance -- and your policy is not a substitute for the repair duties
bodyText: Default rule first: North Dakota imposes no insurance requirement on a residential landlord. No statute requires liability insurance, fire or hazard insurance, or any minimum coverage; there is no rental registration or licensing scheme that conditions letting on proof of insurance (the state has no landlord registration at all); there is no obligation to name the tenant or anyone else on your policy, to furnish a certificate of insurance, or to tell the tenant whether you carry insurance; and there is no statute making an uninsured landlord liable differently from an insured one. Even the one licensing regime that does exist for rentals -- the annual licence a mobile home park, recreational vehicle park or campground must obtain under N.D.C.C. Section 23-10-03 -- lists what the application must contain (local zoning approval, the proposed water supply and how water is assessed or metered, the proposed sewerage and garbage disposal method, and other information the department requires) and insurance is not among them. What to do: carry liability insurance anyway, and carry enough of it, because North Dakota gives you no statutory ceiling on your exposure and three things make the exposure real. Your habitability duties under Section 47-16-13.1 are statutory, so breaching them is a violation of law, and Section 9-08-02 makes any contract term exempting you from responsibility for your own violation of law -- 'whether willful or negligent' -- against the policy of the law; you cannot insure yourself by lease drafting. If you neglect a repair after notice, the tenant may repair and deduct the cost from the rent with no dollar cap, or vacate and be discharged from all further rent (Section 47-16-13). And Section 47-16-13.6 awards reasonable attorney's fees to the PREVAILING PARTY in an action to enforce Sections 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6, which cuts both ways but means a lost habitability claim costs you the tenant's lawyer as well as your own. Tell your insurer what you actually rent and how, keep the policy current, and do not let a lease clause stand in for coverage. Separately, your policy does not cover the tenant's own belongings -- say so in the lease and require renter's insurance if you want it.

title: You have no landlord's lien on a North Dakota tenant's belongings -- but there are two real exceptions
bodyText: Default rule first: North Dakota gives a residential landlord NO lien and no security interest in a tenant's personal property for unpaid rent, and no self-help seizure. There is no distress for rent -- the word 'distrain' appears in North Dakota law only for trespassing livestock and for the sheriff's collection of delinquent personal property taxes, never for a landlord. Do not put a landlord's-lien, 'security interest in tenant's property' or seizure-and-sale clause in a residential lease: it has no statutory foundation, you would be asserting a right the law does not give you, and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision (N.D.C.C. Section 47-16-13.3). To collect unpaid rent you sue, and you may join a money claim for rent with an eviction; to deal with belongings left behind, use the abandoned-property route, not a lien. Two exceptions matter. First, AGRICULTURE is genuinely different. Section 47-16-03 lets a farm lease reserve title in the lessor to crops in excess of the lessor's rental share until the lease conditions are met -- but the lease must be filed with the county recorder, and/or electronically in the central indexing system, BEFORE JULY FIRST of the year the crops are raised, and failure to file 'constitutes a waiver by the lessor of all rights reserved by that person over and above that person's rental share' as against any subsequent purchaser or encumbrancer of the tenant. Diary that July 1 deadline. Separately, the Uniform Commercial Code as North Dakota has it expressly recognises both categories: Article 9 'does not apply to a landlord's lien, other than an agricultural lien' (Section 41-09-09(4)(a)), while it DOES apply to an agricultural lien (Section 41-09-09(1)(b)), and an agricultural lien is defined to include an interest in farm products securing 'Rent on real property leased by a debtor in connection with the debtor's farming operation' created by statute in favour of a person that 'Leased real property to a debtor in connection with the debtor's farming operation' (Section 41-09-02(1)(e)). So any statutory farm-rent lien is an Article 9 agricultural lien and has to be perfected by filing like any other. And Section 35-05-01, which otherwise voids security interests in growing crops, exempts one 'created by contract to secure ... the rental ... of the land upon which the crops covered by the contract are to be grown' -- so a farm lease may take a crop security interest for the rent. Second, MOBILE HOME LOTS: Section 35-20-17 gives 'A landlord of a mobile home lot' a lien 'for accrued rents, storage, and removal relating to any mobile home left on the lot after the tenant has vacated the premises after an eviction or the expiration of the lease term'. It ranks behind a prior perfected security interest, and you may keep the home until paid. To bind a good-faith purchaser you must post a signed, dated notice of lien, with the contents the section lists, on the home's primary entrance. You may sell thirty days after mailing notice to the owner and secured parties of record, and must forward any surplus to the former owner (or treat it as abandoned property under chapter 47-30.2). Removing the posted notice without authority is a class B misdemeanor. What to do: for a residential dwelling, assume you have no lien and write none into the lease. For a farm lease, use the Section 47-16-03 reservation and file it before July first. For a mobile home lot, use Section 35-20-17 only for a home left after the tenant has vacated following an eviction or the end of the lease, and follow its posting, mailing and thirty-day steps exactly.

title: No state landlord registration, except that a mobile home park needs an annual licence and a local office
What You Can Claim When the Tenancy Ends Badly, and What You Must Claim Separately
bodyText: The default rule is that North Dakota splits your remedies in two, and the split is procedural as well as substantive. Section 47-16-13.4 is the whole of it in one sentence: 'If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord has a claim for possession and for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement.' So possession and rent travel together; actual damages for breach is a separate claim. That matters because section 47-32-04 will not let you bundle them: an eviction action 'cannot be brought in a district court in connection with any other action, except for rents and profits accrued or for damages arising by reason of the defendant's possession'. Rent that has already accrued and damage caused by the tenant staying can ride along with the eviction. Your claim for the cost of repairing what the tenant broke, or for re-letting costs, cannot -- that is a second lawsuit. The flip side is that the tenant cannot bundle either: 'No counterclaim can be interposed in such action, except as a setoff to a demand made for damages or for rents and profits.' On future rent, section 47-16-13.7 is clear and so is its limit: 'A lessee evicted according to law is liable for rent during the remainder of the term of the lease. However, this section does not relieve the landlord of the duty to mitigate damages.' Section 47-16-13.5 repeats the duty for any aggrieved party. North Dakota has NO acceleration statute -- nothing authorises you to declare the whole remaining rent immediately due -- and an acceleration clause in the lease is exposed to section 9-08-04, which voids a contract fixing damages in anticipation of breach except where actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, and to section 9-08-03, under which contractual penalties are void outright. Rent for the remainder of the term, less what you mitigate, is already what the statute gives you; an acceleration clause tries to take the mitigation discount away and that is what makes it vulnerable. You may also terminate before the end of the term under section 47-16-16 where the lessee uses the property contrary to the agreement or fails to make repairs the lessee is bound to make after a reasonable time following a request, and under section 47-16-11 you may treat the lease as rescinded where the property is used for a purpose other than the one leased. Where a money claim belongs. Chapter 47-32 sends the eviction to 'the proper district court'. A claim for money alone, up to fifteen thousand dollars, may instead go to small claims court (N.D.C.C. § 27-08.1-01(1)). If the tenant is an individual and the claim arose from the lease, it must be brought 'in the county where the real property is located unless the plaintiff and the defendant consent in writing to a proceeding in a different county' (§ 27-08.1-01(2)(e)), and the tenant cannot move it to their home county (subsection 3). Choosing small claims is irrevocable: if you discontinue, the dismissal is with prejudice unless the order says otherwise, and you give up any appeal (§ 27-08.1-04). The tenant may remove the case to district court, and if so the court 'shall award attorney's fees to a prevailing plaintiff'. A small claims judge may also dismiss a case too complex for that court without prejudice (§ 27-08.1-04.1). Above fifteen thousand dollars, or where you want an appeal, file in district court.

title: Late Fees: No Cap for an Apartment, a Hard Cap for a Mobile Home Park
bodyText:
Default rule: for an ordinary residential tenancy North Dakota sets no late-fee cap, no mandatory grace period and no limit on a daily late charge. One hard cap does exist, and it is easy to miss because it sits in the conveyancing chapter rather than in the landlord-tenant chapter: a mobile home park may not charge a monthly late fee of more than ten percent of the monthly rent, and on top of that may not charge a daily late fee of more than five dollars per day (section 47-10-28(11)). If you operate a mobile home park, that is your ceiling and it binds you whatever the lease says. For every other rental the limit is contract law, not a cap. Section 9-08-03 makes a penalty imposed by contract for nonperformance void outright, and section 9-08-04 makes an amount fixed in advance as the measure of damages void -- to that extent -- unless the actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. A late fee is therefore defensible in North Dakota as a pre-estimate of the real cost of a late payment, and indefensible as a punishment: the larger the flat figure and the less it resembles your actual carrying and collection cost, the more exposed it is. Section 47-14-05 points the same way from the other direction -- it allows a late-payment-penalty charge "only if the amount of the late charge or the method of calculation of the late charge has been agreed to by the parties" in the signed document. One more provision may matter: section 13-01-14 lets a creditor charge a late payment charge on "money due on account" of up to one and three-fourths percent per month, starting thirty days after the obligation is incurred, but it limits only the charge "allowed under this section", and whether it reaches rent the statute does not say. Cautious course, because the reach of these outside provisions is unsettled (see the notes): state the late fee and its calculation in the signed lease, keep it modest and tied to a real cost you can describe, give a short grace period, do not stack a daily charge on top of a percentage unless you are a mobile home park staying inside section 47-10-28(11), and never take a late fee out of the security deposit -- section 47-16-07.1(3) lets the deposit cover damage, unpaid rent and tenant-responsible cleaning or repairs, and nothing else, with treble damages under section 47-16-07.1(4) for withholding without reasonable justification.

The park caps apply per month and per day whatever the lease's late charge provision says, so an installment schedule must not be used to multiply them. A park that breaks them faces a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 (section 47-10-28(12)), and the violation is a defence to the eviction (section 47-32-01.1).

title: When police ask for a key: North Dakota gives you no right to let them in, and no duty to cooperate
bodyText:
The default rule: North Dakota imposes no duty on a landlord to cooperate with law enforcement, and gives you no right to let an officer into a tenant's home. No provision in the North Dakota statutes requires you to report a tenant's suspected criminal activity, to hand over tenant information to the police, to admit an officer to a leased unit, or to use a crime-free lease addendum; and none protects you if you do any of those things voluntarily. One general duty does bind you and your staff, as it binds anyone: a person who discovers a dead body or first learns of a death must immediately notify the coroner or a law enforcement officer of the known facts, and failing to is a class B misdemeanor; willfully disturbing a body you know died in a suspicious or unusual manner, or the clothing or articles on or near it, without the coroner's or an officer's authorization, is a class A misdemeanor (N.D.C.C. §§ 11-19.1-07(1) and 11-19.1-07.1). The duties to report child abuse or neglect and abuse of a vulnerable adult bind listed professionals and caregivers, not landlords as such, and anyone else may report (N.D.C.C. §§ 50-25.1-03 and 50-25.2-03). But anyone who finds images of sexual conduct by a child on a workplace computer, such as an office computer, must report it to the department of health and human services or its authorized agent, and a willful failure is a class B misdemeanor (N.D.C.C. §§ 50-25.1-03(3) and 50-25.1-13). There is no crime-free housing statute and no landlord-training or nuisance-abatement programme in the statutes. That means almost every decision here is yours, and the exposure is yours too.

Start from the entry statute, because it is the whole answer to the question officers ask most often. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.3 is the only authority you have to enter, and it is authority for YOU to enter, not for anyone you bring. Subsection 2 lets you enter during reasonable hours and in a reasonable manner for inspection, necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supplying necessary or agreed services, or exhibiting the unit to 'actual or potential purchasers, insurers, mortgagees, real estate agents, tenants, workmen, or contractors'. A peace officer is on none of those lists. Subsection 1 lets you enter at any time only in an emergency, on a reasonable belief that the tenant has abandoned the premises, or on a reasonable belief that the tenant is in substantial violation of the lease. None of that transfers to an officer, and your consent is not the tenant's consent.

So the rule to follow is simple and it is the cautious one: when an officer asks for a key, for a master key, or to be let in, ask what legal process they have. If they have a warrant or a court order, step back and let them execute it — you are not obstructing anything by declining to supply access they do not need you for. If they do not, say that you cannot consent on the tenant's behalf and that you will not enter for a purpose § 47-16-07.3 does not list. Do not open a door to let an officer look around. Do not accompany an officer into a unit to create a pretext of a repair inspection; that is using the right of access for a purpose the statute does not authorise, and § 47-16-07.3 says in terms that 'A landlord shall not abuse the right of access or use it to harass or intimidate the tenant.'

Information requests follow the same shape. Nothing in North Dakota law stops you telling an officer who lives in a unit — there is no general tenant-confidentiality statute here — but one category is absolutely off limits and it is the one most likely to come up. § 47-16-17.1(4): information a tenant gave you documenting domestic violence 'may not be entered into any shared database or provided to any person, but may be used as evidence in an eviction proceeding, in a claim for unpaid rent or damages arising out of the tenancy, or as otherwise required by law.' An officer asking is not 'required by law'; a subpoena, warrant or court order is. Get the process in writing before you hand that over, because § 47-16-17.1(11) lets a court award statutory damages of one thousand dollars plus actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, costs and disbursements. For everything else, the practical rule is to ask for the request in writing, give only what it asks for, keep a copy, and tell the tenant unless the process forbids it.

Where the law does bring officers into your tenancy, and it is worth knowing so you are not surprised. § 47-32-02 uses the sheriff or a process server to serve an eviction summons and, where the defendant cannot be found after an attempt between six and ten p.m., to post the summons on the door of the residential unit; it is also how the three-day written notice of intention to evict is served or posted conspicuously on the premises for § 47-32-01's subsections 4, 5, 6 and 8. § 14-07.7-19, new on January 1, 2026, lets a court order 'the sheriff or other appropriate law enforcement officer to accompany the petitioner and assist in placing the petitioner in possession of the dwelling or residence' under a protection order — so an officer may lawfully put one occupant into possession of your unit and exclude another, on a court order you were not party to. Comply, keep the paperwork, and do not treat the excluded person's belongings as abandoned without advice. And remember what you do NOT need an officer for: § 47-32-01's grounds 1 to 3 cover a party who entered by force, intimidation, fraud or stealth and detains the property, who turned out the possessor by force or threats, or who holds by force or menaces, and those grounds require no notice at all — they are North Dakota's route against a squatter, through the court rather than through self-help.

Three last things. Enforce behaviour through the lease and the eviction statute, not through the police: § 47-32-01(7) is a ground where a lessee or a person on the premises with the lessee's consent 'acts in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment of the premises', and (8) is a violation of a material term of the written lease — those are the levers. § 47-16-25 runs the other way and is easy to miss: a tenant who receives notice of any proceeding to recover the property must inform you immediately and deliver the notice, and is liable for damages you sustain from the omission if the notice was in writing. And § 14-02.5-02(4) is the one criminal-conduct permission North Dakota spells out: the fair housing section 'does not prohibit discrimination against an individual because the individual has been convicted ... of the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance' — manufacture or distribution, not possession, and a conviction, not an arrest or a police tip-off.

title: No lead-safe certificate exists in North Dakota - nothing has to be attached to the lease
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has no lead-safe certificate, no lead clearance or inspection certificate, and no statute requiring any certificate to be attached to a residential lease as an exhibit or at all. There is no state certifying authority for a dwelling's lead status, no form, no expiry period and no penalty, because there is no programme. A landlord who prints a "lead-safe certification" exhibit and calls it a North Dakota requirement is inventing one.

The lead picture in the North Dakota statutes, in full: the phrase "lead-based paint" appears only inside the name of one section - 23.1-06-05, "Licensing of asbestos and lead-based paint contractors and certification of asbestos and lead-based paint workers". That is a contractor-licensing and worker-certification provision in the air-quality chapter. It is the entire North Dakota lead statute. There is no state lead-poisoning-prevention chapter, no lead registry, no lead abatement order regime, no pre-1978 rental threshold, and no lease-related lead provision of any kind. The North Dakota statutes do not use the terms "lead-safe", "lead hazard" or "lead poisoning".

What North Dakota does have, and it is a duty on a contractor rather than on you: 23.1-06-05 licenses lead-based-paint contractors and certifies their workers. That certification runs to the person doing the work, not to the dwelling and not to the landlord - the same shape as 47-10-02.2 and 47-10-02.3, which are seller-to-buyer duties and not landlord duties. If you hire out paint work, hiring a licensed contractor is the compliance step; you will get the contractor's credential, not a certificate about the building. The Department of Environmental Quality runs that licensing by a rule that incorporates the federal lead-based paint activity standards (N.D. Admin. Code ch. 33.1-15-24). It reaches you only if you have lead-based paint abated, inspected or risk-assessed. Then the work must be done by a licensed firm and certified people, unless you do it yourself in a dwelling you own that no one outside your immediate family occupies. And the department must get ten days' notice before abatement in a residential dwelling begins (§§ 33.1-15-24-02, 33.1-15-24-03). The rule says 'nothing in this subpart requires that the owner or occupant undertake any particular lead-based paint activity', and it creates no certificate for the dwelling. The disclosure obligation you may be thinking of is federal; do not cite a North Dakota statute for it.

What to do: do not attach a lead-safe certificate as though North Dakota required one, and do not have the tenant sign an acknowledgment of a state certificate that does not exist. Satisfy the federal scheme on its own terms. If you have had paint testing or stabilization work done, record the condition in the 47-16-07.2 condition-of-premises statement, which is the one document North Dakota does require with a rental agreement, and keep the contractor's licence details in your file. Deteriorated paint is reachable anyway: 47-16-13.1(1)(b) requires the landlord to keep the premises "in a fit and habitable condition", and 47-16-13 gives the tenant uncapped repair-and-deduct, recovery in any other lawful manner, or the right to vacate if you do not repair after notice. One caveat that changes this answer: 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes the landlord comply with "applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety" and 47-16-13.1(3) makes that duty controlling where it is the greater one, and the State Building Code (ch. 54-21.3) and the state lead rule contain no lead certificate, so any such requirement could come only from a local code.

title: North Dakota adds no state lead notices, packets or forms on top of the federal scheme
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has no state lead notice. There is no state-prescribed lead disclosure form, no state pamphlet or information packet that must be delivered with a lease, no state acknowledgment of receipt, no registration or reporting of a rental unit's lead status, and no state penalty - because there is no state programme to notify anyone about. Unlike states that layer their own notices, certificates and packets on top of the federal disclosure, North Dakota has legislated nothing of its own.

The lead picture in the North Dakota statutes, in full: the phrase "lead-based paint" appears only inside the name of one section - 23.1-06-05, "Licensing of asbestos and lead-based paint contractors and certification of asbestos and lead-based paint workers". That is the entire North Dakota lead statute. The North Dakota statutes do not use the terms "lead-safe", "lead hazard" or "lead poisoning", and no section name in the whole Century Code pairs lead with a notice, a packet, a pamphlet or a certificate.

Federal law, not North Dakota law, is the source of the obligation you are thinking of. State the federal requirement as federal, cite no North Dakota statute for it, and describe the state position accurately: an absence. Nothing in the North Dakota statutes adopts, incorporates, supplements or enforces the federal lead scheme, and no North Dakota agency is given a role in it by statute. 23.1-06-05, has the department license lead-based paint contractors and certify workers "engaging in the abatement of lead-based paint", with standards following 40 C.F.R. part 745. Its rules, N.D. Admin. Code ch. 33.1-15-24, incorporate those federal abatement sections and require "Each owner or operator to which this chapter applies" to give the department written notice of intent to abate at least ten working days before abatement begins. Neither mentions a tenant, a lease or a notice packet.

What to do: deliver the federal disclosure and the federal pamphlet because federal law says so, and do not dress either up as a North Dakota requirement. Do not invent a "North Dakota lead notice" page, and do not ask the tenant to waive state lead rights - a waiver of a rule North Dakota does not have gives you nothing and tells the tenant they gave something up. If you hire lead-based paint abatement in pre-1978 housing, use a licensed firm and make sure the department gets its ten-working-day notice. Keep deteriorated paint inside the ordinary habitability route: 47-16-13.1(1)(b) requires you to keep the premises "in a fit and habitable condition" and 47-16-13 gives the tenant uncapped repair-and-deduct, recovery in any other lawful manner, or the right to vacate and stop paying rent if you do not repair after notice.

title: North Dakota Requires One Thing in the Lease Itself -- the Initialled Notice Requirement
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota does not tell you what to put in a residential lease. There is no mandatory lease form, no required headings or order, no font or type-size rule, no required signature block, no plain-language requirement, no translation requirement, and no statute voiding a lease for leaving something out. Chapter 47-16 also operates on unwritten tenancies throughout -- § 47-16-05 provides that a lease of real property other than lodgings, in places where there is no usage on the subject, 'is presumed to be for one year from its commencement, unless otherwise expressed in the lease', and §§ 47-16-06, 47-16-07 and 47-16-15 all work on tenancies with no stated term. Whether a longer lease must be in writing turns on the statute of frauds, ch. 9-06, which this review could not read.

There is exactly ONE thing North Dakota requires the lease document itself to contain. Under § 47-16-15(4), 'any agreement that requires a lessee to give notice that exceeds one month from the end of a month to terminate a lease of real property for residential purposes must state the notice requirement and provide space for the lessee to initial next to the notice requirement' -- and if the tenant does not initial it at the time of executing the lease, 'the lessee may terminate the lease on the last day of a month with at least one calendar month's notice'. That is a self-executing sanction: the term is not void, it simply does not bind, and you fall back to one month. If your lease asks for sixty days' notice, the initial line is the whole ballgame.

Two more requirements attach to the transaction rather than to the lease text, and both are easy to satisfy as exhibits. § 47-16-07.2 requires you to provide the tenant a statement describing the condition of the facilities in and about the premises to be rented AT THE TIME of entering the rental agreement, 'agreed to and signed by the landlord and tenant', and makes it prima facie proof of the condition of the facilities and premises at the beginning of the rental agreement -- it is your best evidence at move-out, so sign it with the lease rather than later. § 47-16-07.1(3) then requires an itemisation of any part of the security deposit you keep, delivered or mailed to the tenant's last furnished address with a written notice stating any amount still due or the refund due, within thirty days after termination of the lease and delivery of possession; § 47-16-07.1(4) makes a lessor liable for TREBLE DAMAGES for deposit money withheld without reasonable justification. In a mobile home park, add § 47-10-28(9)'s summary outlining the tenant's lease and the rights and obligations of both parties under state law, and § 47-10-28(1)(g)-(h)'s name, address and telephone number of the owning legal entity and the telephone number of any property manager or site agent -- all backed by § 47-10-28(12)'s civil penalty of not less than $2,500.

Beyond that the constraints on lease content are about what you may NOT say, not what you must. § 47-16-02 caps the term -- ten years for agricultural land, ninety-nine years for a city lot. § 9-08-01 makes a provision unlawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law, contrary to the policy of express law though not expressly prohibited, or otherwise contrary to good morals; § 9-08-02 puts a term exempting anyone from responsibility for their own fraud, willful injury or violation of law against the policy of the law; § 9-08-03 makes contractual penalties for nonperformance void outright; § 9-08-04 voids damages fixed in anticipation of a breach 'to that extent' unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix; and § 9-08-05 voids a stipulation restricting a party from enforcing its rights by the usual legal proceedings or limiting the time to do so, except as specifically permitted by law. § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable rental agreement provision. And § 47-16-13.1(5)-(6) means that in anything other than a single-family residence you cannot shift maintenance duties to the tenant in the lease at all -- it takes a separate writing signed by both parties and supported by adequate consideration, and performance of it may not be made a condition of the lease.

What to do: build the lease around the one statutory content rule and the two documents. Put the longer-than-one-month notice requirement in its own clause with an initial line; sign the condition statement at lease signing and keep a copy; and diary the thirty-day deposit itemisation. For the full inventory of what North Dakota makes you DISCLOSE -- as opposed to what the lease must contain -- see the required-disclosures row.

title: You may record a lease but never have to, except a farm lease reserving crop title
bodyText:
Default rule first: recording is permitted, not required. N.D.C.C. § 47-19-01 provides that "[a]ny instrument affecting the title to or possession of real property may be recorded as provided in this chapter" — "may", and note that it reaches possession and not only title. No North Dakota statute requires a residential lease to be recorded, and no statute makes an unrecorded residential lease invalid, unenforceable or void between you and your tenant. On the contrary, § 47-19-46 says expressly that "[a]n unrecorded instrument is valid as between the parties thereto and those who have notice thereof." There is no memorandum-of-lease statute, no short-form-lease statute, no Torrens or land-title registration system and no land registry separate from the county recorder — none of those phrases appears anywhere in the North Dakota statutes. (For the avoidance of doubt, § 11-18-01.1 simply renamed the old "register of deeds" the recorder.)

What recording does buy is notice, and that is where it can change a right. § 47-19-19: "The record of any instrument shall be notice of the contents of the instrument, as it appears of record, as to all persons." Against that, § 47-19-41 provides that "[a]n unrecorded conveyance of real estate is void as against any subsequent purchaser in good faith, and for a valuable consideration" of the same real estate, or as against an attachment or judgment against the owner of record recorded before the conveyance. And § 47-19-42 defines "conveyance", for § 47-19-41, to "include every instrument in writing by which any estate or interest in real property is created, aliened, mortgaged, or encumbered, or by which the title to any real property may be affected, except a will or power of attorney." A written lease creates a right of possession in land, so on the natural reading it is such an instrument (§ 47-19-43 itself speaks of an assignee of a "lease, or other conditional estate") and an unrecorded lease is at risk against a later good-faith purchaser who does not have notice of it. Take the cautious course: a tenant in possession is often obvious, and § 47-19-46 protects a lease against anyone who "ha[s] notice thereof", but do not rely on that for a lease you cannot afford to lose. If a lease has real value to you — a long term, a below-market rent, an option, a build-out — record it, or get the buyer to acknowledge the tenancy in writing on a sale.

If you do record, § 47-19-03 sets the price of admission: unless the instrument is in one of the classes in § 47-19-02 or § 47-19-40, its execution must be established by acknowledgment before an authorised officer — and "before an instrument may be recorded, the document and any acknowledgment must be executed with an original signature." So a lease you want recorded has to be notarised and wet-signed. An ordinary unnotarised lease simply is not recordable.

One kind of lease North Dakota does require to be filed, and it is not residential. § 47-16-03: when a lease of a FARM reserves title in the lessor to any part of the crops above the lessor's rental share until the lease conditions are met, the lease "must be filed in the office of the recorder in the county in which the land described therein is located if notice by a real estate recording is sought, and must be filed electronically in the central indexing system if recording in the central notice system is sought, prior to July first in the year in which the crops are raised" to make the reservation effective against subsequent purchasers or encumbrancers. Subsection 2 states the sanction: failing to file "constitutes a waiver by the lessor of all rights reserved" above the rental share, as against any subsequent purchaser or encumbrancer of the lessee. Subsection 3 lets the lessor file an electronic statement through the secretary of state's system with the same effect, and subsection 4 sets the fees by reference to § 11-18-05 and § 41-09-96. Note that the sanction is loss of the crop-title reservation, not invalidity of the lease. Separately, § 47-16-40 gives recording a special effect for oil, gas and mineral leases: the record imparts notice of the lease's validity "for the definite term therein expressed, but no longer", and an owner relying on a contingency extension must record an affidavit before the definite term expires.

What to do. (1) Do not record ordinary month-to-month or one-year residential leases; it costs money, it needs notarisation, and it publishes your tenant's rent. (2) Do consider recording, or taking a recorded memorandum signed and acknowledged by both parties, for a long or valuable lease, and raise it with counsel — there is no statutory short-form in North Dakota, so what you record would be a document of your own design. (3) If you are buying tenanted property, search the records and ask for the leases; § 47-19-46 means notice binds you, so "I did not know" is only as good as your diligence. (4) If you lease farm ground and reserve crop title, calendar July 1 — § 47-16-03 is a hard date and the penalty is losing the reservation. (5) Nothing here goes in the lease as a clause; recording is something you do with the lease, not a term inside it.

title: The ten-year and ninety-nine-year caps are maximum terms only, not a list of banned lease clauses
bodyText:
North Dakota's lease-term limit is one short section, and the most important thing about it is how little it does. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-02, "Limitations on leases", reads in full: "No lease or grant of agricultural land reserving any rent or service of any kind for a longer period than ten years shall be valid. No lease or grant of any city lot reserving any rent or service of any kind for a longer period than ninety-nine years shall be valid."

That is a MAXIMUM-TERM CAP and nothing else. It is not a list of prohibited lease terms, it does not ban any clause, and it says nothing about what a lease may contain. If you have seen it cited for the proposition that North Dakota regulates lease content, that citation is wrong: chapter 47-16 and chapter 47-32 contain no prohibited-provisions list and no exculpation ban at all — the real limits on what a lease may say are in title 9, principally § 9-08-03 (contractual penalties void), § 9-08-04 (damages fixed in advance void to that extent unless actual damage is impracticable or extremely difficult to fix) and § 9-08-05 (no term restricting a party from enforcing rights by the usual legal proceedings or shortening the time to do so), plus § 47-16-13.3 on unconscionability.

For practical purposes: a one-year or two-year apartment or house lease is nowhere near either cap, and no residential landlord is likely ever to meet one. The ten-year limit bites only on agricultural land and the ninety-nine-year limit only on a "city lot" — and neither phrase is defined anywhere in chapter 47-16, so a rural dwelling that is neither farm ground nor a city lot may not be covered by either sentence at all. Do not assume a cap applies, and do not assume one does not, without advice on a genuinely long lease. Beware a nearby false friend too: § 47-05-02.1(2) also caps an interest at ninety-nine years, but it governs easements, servitudes and nonappurtenant restrictions on the use of real property — not leases — and it is a different rule with different exceptions.

On the execution formalities the topic asks about, North Dakota is permissive and the answer is clear:
• No seal. § 47-10-05 provides that "[t]he absence of the seal of any grantor or grantor's agent from any grant of an estate made in real property shall not invalidate or in any manner impair the same." There is no District-of-Columbia-style seal requirement.
• A writing, signed by the right person, for anything over a year. § 47-10-01 requires an estate in real property, other than an estate at will or a term not exceeding one year, to be transferred "by an instrument in writing, subscribed by the party disposing of the same or by the party's agent thereunto authorized by writing." So the owner signs, or an agent whose authority is itself in writing. That is the only power-of-attorney-like requirement, and it is triggered by using an agent, not by the length of the term.
• Acknowledgment is about recording, not validity. § 47-10-05's first sentence requires proof by a subscribing witness only "to entitle the same to be recorded", and § 47-19-03 requires an acknowledgment and an original signature before any instrument may be recorded. An unnotarised long lease can still be a good lease.
