The spousal-consent question is the one real trap, and it is a homestead rule rather than a lease rule. § 47-18-05, "Homestead - How conveyed": "The homestead of a married person, without regard to the value thereof, cannot be conveyed or encumbered unless the instrument by which it is conveyed or encumbered is executed and acknowledged by both the husband and wife." Note "and acknowledged" — both signatures AND notarisation. Whether leasing counts as conveying or encumbering a homestead is not answered by any statute, and only a court could settle it; it cuts both ways: § 47-18-01 defines the homestead as the land and dwelling "in which the homestead claimant resides", which argues that a property let out entirely is not a homestead at all, while a long lease of the family home, or the letting of part of a home the owner still lives in, looks much more like an encumbrance. Take the cautious course: where a married owner leases a home they live in or have lived in, have BOTH spouses sign and have the signatures acknowledged, and get advice before granting a long lease over it. The cost is a notary; the risk the other way is an invalid instrument.

What to do. (1) Set residential terms normally; the caps are irrelevant to ordinary lettings. (2) Never cite § 47-16-02 for anything other than maximum term. (3) For any lease over a year, make sure the signer is the owner or holds written authority. (4) For a married owner's homestead, get both spouses to sign and acknowledge. (5) For a genuinely long lease — ground lease, farm lease over ten years, anything approaching ninety-nine — take advice, because what "agricultural land" and "city lot" mean here, and whether an over-long lease fails entirely or only as to the excess, are not settled by the section's words. (6) None of this is a lease clause; it is a validity rule that operates whatever the lease says.

title: Charging and Treating Month-to-Month Tenants Differently Is Allowed in North Dakota
bodyText:
The default rule first: North Dakota does not require parity between lease types. No statute bars terms more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant or the reverse, and none caps the difference in rent between them. You may charge a month-to-month premium, offer a fixed-term discount, or apply different fees, deposits within the 47-16-07.1 limits, or rules to the two groups. Note also that no local government can interfere: a political subdivision may not enact, maintain or enforce an ordinance or resolution having the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged for leasing private residential or commercial property (47-16-02.1).

What North Dakota does instead is attach different DEFAULT RULES to the two lease types, and those you cannot simply drop. A lease of real property other than lodgings is presumed to be for one year unless otherwise expressed (47-16-05), and the renting of lodgings for an unspecified term is presumed to be for the period the parties adopt for estimating the rent, monthly in the absence of agreement (47-16-19). In a month-to-month tenancy you may change the terms of the lease to take effect at the expiration of the month on at least thirty days' written notice before the expiration of the month, and the notice itself creates those terms as part of the lease if the tenant holds over (47-16-07) - a power you do not have over a fixed term. Either party may end a month-to-month tenancy on at least one calendar month's written notice at any time, with rent due to and including the termination date, unless the parties have agreed in writing to a longer notice period or a different notice time (47-16-15(2)); a tenant who receives a 47-16-07 change of terms may terminate at the end of the month on at least twenty-five days' notice (47-16-15(3)); and where a lease has converted to month-to-month under 47-16-06 or 47-16-06.1, either party may terminate on the last day of a month with at least one calendar month's notice (47-16-15(5)).

The one near-parity rule is about notice, and it is the trap. If you require the LESSEE to give notice exceeding one month from the end of a month to terminate a residential lease, the lease must state the notice requirement AND provide space for the lessee to initial next to it. If the lessee has not initialled it at the time of executing the lease, the lessee may terminate on the last day of a month with at least one calendar month's notice (47-16-15(4)) - so an uninitialled sixty-day clause simply collapses to thirty-plus days. Separately, an automatic renewal clause in a residential lease of a specified term of two months or more is unenforceable unless you gave written notice of the renewal provision, personally or by first-class mail, at least thirty days before the current lease expires; without it the lease expires and converts to month-to-month (47-16-06.1). For a mobile home park there is an express differential notice rule: any month-to-month tenancy agreement must give at least ninety days' notice before a rent increase takes effect, and a purchaser of an existing park may not increase the monthly rent for six months if it was raised within the sixty days before the purchase (47-10-28(7)).

Do this. Price and term the two products however you like, but make the notice architecture explicit: state the notice each side must give, and if the tenant's notice exceeds one month from the end of a month, lay it out with an initial line and get it initialled at signing. Apply your differences by lease type and not by who the tenant is: age, familial status, disability, sex, race, colour, religion, national origin and status with respect to marriage or public assistance are protected classes in the rental of a dwelling (14-02.5-02), so a month-to-month-only rule that in practice falls on one of those groups is exposed even though no parity statute exists. And remember that any term remains open to unconscionability review (47-16-13.3) and that a fixed fee has to survive 9-08-03 and 9-08-04.

title: No minimum print size for a North Dakota lease - and the only two sizes that change your duties
bodyText:
'Size' can mean two things here and North Dakota answers both the same way - no, with two small exceptions. The default is that North Dakota imposes no formatting rules on a residential lease and applies one rule set to every landlord whatever their size.

PRINTED TYPE SIZE. There is no minimum type size, typeface, font or boldface requirement for a residential lease in North Dakota, and no evidentiary sanction of the New York kind - nothing makes a small-print lease inadmissible or unenforceable. This is not because the legislature has never thought about type size: it has, repeatedly, just never for a residential lease. A consumer rental purchase agreement - rent-to-own of goods - needs a boldface ten-point notice above the signature line and disclosures in at least eight-point type (sections 47-15.1-02 and 47-15.1-03). A notice of private transfer fee obligation needs a fourteen-point boldfaced title (section 47-33-05). A wind easement or wind energy lease - a lease of real property - must be delivered with a cover page in at least sixteen-point type carrying a prescribed 'Special message to property owners' (section 17-04-06). A mobile-home-park eviction notice needs 'clear, boldfaced language' in prescribed words (section 47-10-28(10)). If you record a lease, the recorder will reject a page that is not legible and, unless it is a government form, needs a font at least ten point Calibri (section 11-18-05(1)(a)(2)). So the tools exist and the legislature knows how to use them. It has simply not pointed any of them at a residential lease.

The one formatting rule that does bind your residential lease is not about size at all - it is about placement and initialling. Under section 47-16-15(4), if your lease requires the tenant to give more than one month's notice from the end of a month to terminate, the lease 'must state the notice requirement and provide space for the lessee to initial next to the notice requirement', and if the tenant has not initialled it when the lease was signed, the tenant may terminate on the last day of a month with one calendar month's notice. That is a real sanction - your longer notice period simply does not work - so set that one out separately with an initial line beside it.

BUILDING SIZE AND PORTFOLIO SIZE. See the row on portfolio thresholds: there is no small-landlord exemption anywhere in North Dakota, and the fair-housing carve-outs at sections 14-02.5-09 and 14-02.5-11 are much narrower than they look. This row adds only the two places where size genuinely changes something:

1. Single-family versus everything else, in the habitability duties. Section 47-16-13.1(4) lets the landlord and tenant OF A SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant will perform the landlord's duties under subdivisions (e) and (f) of subsection 1 - waste receptacles and removal, and running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat - plus specified repairs, maintenance, alterations and remodeling. Section 47-16-13.1(5), for 'any dwelling unit other than a single-family residence', reaches only 'specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling' and does not mention (e) or (f) at all. So in a duplex or an apartment building the duties to supply water, hot water and heat and to deal with waste CANNOT be shifted to the tenant by any agreement, and even the narrower shift that is allowed needs good faith, a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration, work that is not needed to cure a subdivision (e) failure, and no diminution of the landlord's obligations to other tenants. One dwelling versus two is the sharpest size line in North Dakota landlord-tenant law.

2. Twenty-six lots, in a mobile home park. Section 47-10-28(1)(b) requires a person who owns or purchases an existing mobile home park to 'Designate an official local office, except if the mobile home park contains fewer than twenty-six lots, which must be operational on the fifth business day after the change of ownership'. That is the only express small-operator exemption of its kind in the chapter - and note how narrow it is. Everything else in section 47-10-28(1) applies to a park of any size: the annual licence, the manned weekday telephone number, the around-the-clock emergency contact, the named decision-maker, written notice of a change of ownership within five business days, a two-business-day acknowledgment of a complaint, a copy of the lease within ten business days of a written request, and the owning entity's and manager's details.

What to do. Print your lease in a size a tenant can comfortably read even though nothing makes you - a court asked to enforce an unusual term in tiny print has section 47-16-13.3 (unconscionability) available to it, and legibility is cheap insurance. Give section 47-16-15(4)'s notice requirement its own line with an initial space. And do not assume you are a small landlord for any purpose: in North Dakota the only two thresholds that change anything are one dwelling versus more than one, and twenty-six park lots.

title: How Long You Have to Sue for Unpaid Rent -- and Why You Cannot Shorten It by Lease
bodyText: The one thing that is settled, and it is the thing that matters for drafting, is that you cannot shorten the period by lease. Section 9-08-05 is categorical: 'Every stipulation or condition in a contract by which any party thereto is restricted from enforcing that party's rights under the contract by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals or which limits the time within which that party thus may enforce that party's rights is void, except as otherwise specifically permitted by the laws of this state.' A lease clause saying the tenant must sue within six months, or must give notice of a claim within thirty days as a condition of suing, is void unless some North Dakota statute specifically permits it -- and no statute in the landlord-tenant chapters does. Note that 9-08-05 is symmetrical: it voids a shortening against you as well as against the tenant, so do not write one in the belief it only binds the tenant. The companion sections point the same way. Section 9-08-03 voids contractual penalties for nonperformance outright, and section 9-08-04 voids a provision fixing damages in anticipation of a breach except where actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. THE PERIODS. North Dakota's limitation periods are in chapter 28-01. Section 28-01-16(1) gives six years for 'An action upon a contract, obligation, or liability, express or implied'. Section 28-01-15(2) gives ten years for 'An action upon a contract contained in any conveyance or mortgage of or instrument affecting the title to real property'. Whether a lease is such an instrument only case law could settle, so the cautious course is to sue within six years of each missed payment and never rely on ten. Section 28-01-36 says an acknowledgment or new promise extends the period only if it is 'contained in some writing signed by the party to be charged', but 'does not alter the effect of any payment' -- whether a partial payment restarts the clock is again case law, so assume it does not. One rule helps you: under section 28-01-32, if a tenant 'departs from and resides out of this state' for a year or more, that absence is not counted -- unless North Dakota courts had jurisdiction over the tenant meanwhile. Diary the arrears and do not let them sit.

title: Pre-Agreed Damage Figures Are Void Here, With One Narrow Exception
bodyText:
Default rule in North Dakota: a figure the lease fixes in advance for a breach is void. The phrase 'liquidated damages' appears nowhere in North Dakota's statutes, which is exactly why this gets missed - the rule is written in different words. 'Penalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance thereof are void' (N.D.C.C. § 9-08-03), full stop, no exception. And 'every contract by which the amount of damages to be paid, or other compensation to be made, for a breach of an obligation is determined in anticipation thereof is to that extent void, except that the parties may agree therein upon an amount presumed to be the damage sustained by a breach in cases in which it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage' (§ 9-08-04).

Read the exception carefully, because it is narrower than it looks. It does not ask whether your figure was reasonable, or whether the tenant agreed, or whether you called it an estimate rather than a penalty. It asks whether fixing the ACTUAL damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult - a question about the nature of the loss, not about the drafting. Lost rent has a number. A cleaning invoice has a number. A carpet quote has a number. Re-letting costs have receipts. So the charges landlords most want to fix in advance - an early-termination fee, a re-letting or administration fee, a flat holdover charge, a set carpet-replacement sum, a fixed late fee, a charge for a missed deposit instalment - are the ones least likely to fit the exception.

You do not need them, because North Dakota already gives you the remedies. If the lease is terminated you have a claim for possession and for rent and a separate claim for actual damages (§ 47-16-13.4); a tenant evicted according to law remains liable for rent for the remainder of the term (§ 47-16-13.7); and in both cases you must mitigate (§§ 47-16-13.5, 47-16-13.7). Note too that the deposit may be applied only to pet or negligence damage, unpaid rent, and cleaning or repairs that were the tenant's responsibility (§ 47-16-07.1(3)) - deducting a liquidated sum that is not one of those is withholding without reasonable justification and carries treble damages (§ 47-16-07.1(4)).

What to do: charge what it cost, keep the invoices and the re-letting record, and claim actual damages. Where the legislature wanted a flat figure in a tenancy it set one itself - a tenant ending a lease under the domestic-violence section owes the month plus an amount equal to one month's rent (§ 47-16-17.1(5)) - which is a reminder that you do not get to legislate your own.

title: North Dakota Has No Opt-In Lockout for Unpaid Rent, and the Lease Cannot Create One
bodyText: The default rule is that possession in North Dakota changes hands by court judgment and special execution, and by nothing else. A handful of states let a landlord and tenant opt in by lease to a self-help lockout for delinquent rent, usually with advance notice and a promise of key access within twenty-four hours. North Dakota has nothing of the kind. There is no lockout statute, no lock-change statute, no key-access rule and no self-help provision anywhere in the statutes -- the words lock, locks, key and keys do not appear in a single North Dakota landlord-tenant section. Because there is no statutory permission, a lease term purporting to let you lock a delinquent tenant out is not a lawful opt-in; it is an agreement to do something the law does not allow, and section 47-32-01 turns it against you: subsection 2 makes an eviction action maintainable against a party who, after peaceably entering, 'turns out by force, threats, or menacing conduct the party in possession', and subsection 3 against a party who 'by force or by menaces and threats of violence' holds possession. Those are grounds the person you locked out can sue on, and they require no notice before filing. Section 47-17-03 is equally blunt about timing: after the notice to terminate an estate at will has been served and the period in it has expired, 'but not before', may the landlord re-enter or proceed to recover possession. So: never change the locks, never bar access, and do not accept a lease you inherited that says you may. Separately, there is a money exposure for forcible exclusion in the general damages chapter, which the self-help-eviction topic already covers.

title: North Dakota has no meter conservation charge -- and no notice duty or rent deduction to go with one
bodyText:
Default rule: North Dakota has no energy-efficiency or meter conservation charge of any kind. There is no statute authorising a landlord to add a conservation charge to a tenant's utility bill, none requiring you to notify each new tenant that such a charge applies, and none giving a tenant a rent deduction if you fail to give that notice. The phrase "conservation charge" appears nowhere in the North Dakota Century Code; the word "conservation" appears in it only in connection with soil and water conservation districts, water and wildlife conservation projects, coal reclamation and state appropriations.

The submetered-water question other states answer, and North Dakota does not. North Dakota has no counterpart to the Kansas scheme. There is no statute exempting a landlord who furnishes water from utility regulation on condition that it charges only the city or district rate; no statute barring a surcharge for the meter itself; and no statute requiring you to give the tenant a monthly statement showing both meter readings. For an ordinary North Dakota tenancy none of those three rules exists in either direction -- you are not required to do them and you are not protected by having done them.

The one place North Dakota does regulate this, and it is the closest thing to the Kansas rule. If you rent mobile home lots, N.D.C.C. sec. 47-10-28(8) answers all three questions and answers them against the charge. The owner "may not charge a tenant more than the actual cost per unit amount paid by the landlord to the utility service provider, except for a reasonable administrative fee that may not exceed three dollars" -- so a conservation surcharge above actual cost is barred, and the three-dollar administrative fee is the only add-on allowed. A park "may not charge a fee for a utility without an individual meter for each mobile home", so there is no charging for the meter where there is no meter. And the owner "shall provide the tenant access to the records of meter readings taken at the mobile home lot of the tenant", which is North Dakota's version of the meter-reading statement, framed as a right of access rather than a monthly mailing. A violation draws a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 under sec. 47-10-28(12) and bars the eviction under sec. 47-32-01.1.

What limits a conservation charge even outside a park. Because no statute authorises it, a conservation charge is simply a contract term, and a flat one is exposed: sec. 9-08-03 makes contractual penalties void outright and sec. 9-08-04 voids an amount of damages fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. A charge measured by the actual cost you incurred sits outside both; a round monthly figure labelled a conservation charge does not, and it is also material to unconscionability under sec. 47-16-13.3.

What to do. Do not add a line item called a conservation charge, an efficiency charge or a meter charge. If you want the tenant to bear a utility cost, bear it the way the utilities clause does: pass through your actual cost per unit with the method stated in the lease, keep any administrative charge separate, small and disclosed, and give the tenant the meter reading and the provider invoice on request. If the property is a mobile home park, the administrative charge must be three dollars or less and you must give meter-reading access.

title: North Dakota has no meth-lab disclosure, reporting duty or habitation ban - what it gives a landlord instead is restitution
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a landlord, or a lease, to disclose that a dwelling was used to manufacture methamphetamine or is contaminated by it. There is also no duty to report a known or suspected lab to the police within twenty-four hours or at all, no habitation ban or posted-notice regime, no state decontamination standard or clearance test, no contamination determination procedure and no civil penalty - none of the machinery that other states build around this topic exists here. "Methamphetamine", "clandestine" and "drug lab" appear in no statute chapter searched, and no section anywhere in the Century Code is named about meth or drug-lab contamination.

What North Dakota does give you is a remedy, not a duty. N.D.C.C. 12.1-32-08(1) provides that when a court sentences a person for criminal activities that caused pecuniary damages, "Restitution must include payment to the owner of real property that is contaminated by the defendant in the manufacturing of methamphetamine for the cost of removing the contamination and returning the property to the property's condition before contamination and to any other person that has incurred costs in decontaminating the property." That is a landlord's recovery right against the convicted tenant or occupant, and it is mandatory on the court. It was amended and reenacted by S.L. 2025, ch. 120 (H.B. 1417). Note what it is not: it is not a disclosure duty, it does not run to a future tenant, and it is triggered by a conviction rather than by any notice you give or receive. The other rental-side provision is a screening permission: 14-02.5-02(4) says the fair-housing section "does not prohibit discrimination against an individual because the individual has been convicted under federal law or the law of any state of the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance."

What to do: do not print a meth disclosure or a meth waiver as a North Dakota requirement. If you learn a unit was used as a lab, treat it as a habitability problem on the statute's own wording - 47-16-13.1(1)(b) requires you to "make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition" - and decontaminate before reletting, because a tenant who gives notice and is not repaired has uncapped repair-and-deduct, recovery "in any other lawful manner", or the right to vacate and stop paying rent under 47-16-13. Disclose voluntarily and in writing to the next tenant; there is no state form, so use the 47-16-07.2 condition-of-premises statement. Document the cost of decontamination carefully so you can claim it as restitution under 12.1-32-08(1), and if a prosecution is pending, give the prosecutor your itemised costs within the window 12.1-32-08(2) sets for a victim's claim. Two related rules. The nuisance chapters (ch. 42-01, ch. 42-02) set no meth rule, but 42-02-06 lets you end the lease "by giving three days' notice thereof in writing to the tenant" when the premises are closed or adjudged a nuisance. And 19-03.1-24(1)(e) makes it a class C felony knowingly to keep a dwelling "used for keeping or selling" controlled substances. Municipal ordinances and the N.D. Administrative Code were outside the search.

title: North Dakota created military impact zones in 2025 and attached no disclosure duty to them
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota requires no lease disclosure about a military installation. There is no noise-zone disclosure, no accident-potential-zone disclosure, no military-impact-district disclosure, no avigation-easement disclosure, and no thirty-day termination right for a tenant who learns the property is near a base. A lease that promises one is inventing it.

This is worth stating carefully because North Dakota did legislate in this area in 2025 and still created no disclosure. S.L. 2025, ch. 345 (S.B. 2398) enacted a new chapter of title 37; it is three short provisions. It defines "encroachment" as an action that interferes with or negatively impacts military base testing, training and other operations and overall military readiness, including noise pollution, land development and competition for airspace. It defines a military impact zone as a geographic zone extending from the perimeter of each military base in the state that requests assistance, with the outer boundary set by a compatible use study. And it lets the agriculture commissioner create military compatibility committees, composed of the commissioner, county, township and city representatives and, voluntarily, each installation commander, whose job is to give guidance to local governments and to establish a uniform process under N.D.C.C. chs. 11-33, 40-47 and 40-48 and section 58-03-12 for coordinating zoning, land use, construction, energy development and telecommunications. Every duty in the chapter belongs to the agriculture commissioner, the committees and the political subdivisions. Not one word is addressed to an owner, a landlord or a tenant, and the chapter creates no disclosure of any kind.

What to do: do not put a military-zone disclosure or a related termination right in the lease - there is no statute to anchor either, and a termination right you print becomes a contract right the tenant can enforce against you even though no law required it. Two practical caveats. First, because the 2025 chapter works through local zoning, the city or county the property sits in may have adopted something. Second, federal law is separate: if the property is in a federally designated noise or accident potential zone, or if a federal programme or a lender requires a notice, that obligation does not come from North Dakota statute. If you rent near a base and want to manage expectations, describe the aircraft noise factually in the listing and the lease as a disclosure you are choosing to make, not as one the state requires - and do not attach a termination right to it.

title: Renting to someone under 18: get an adult to sign, because the capacity rule is not in the lease law
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota's landlord-tenant and eviction chapters say nothing at all about minors as tenants. Chapter 47-16 mentions a minor exactly three times, all in § 47-16-17.1 (termination for domestic abuse), and every one of them is about "the tenant's minor children" — minors as members of the household, never as the person who signed. Chapter 47-32, the eviction chapter, does not use the words minor, infant, guardian or age of majority anywhere. So there is no North Dakota statute saying who may be named as an eviction defendant, no minor-tenant filing bar, and no special procedure for evicting a tenant under the age of majority.

That does not mean a lease signed by a 17-year-old is safe. North Dakota's capacity rules are in N.D.C.C. ch. 14-10 (Minors). Minors are "persons under eighteen years of age" (§ 14-10-01). § 14-10-09 says "A person under the age of eighteen may not make a contract relating to real property or any interest therein". A residential lease is a contract relating to real property, so on the statute's words a minor cannot make one. § 14-10-12 says a minor "cannot disaffirm a contract, otherwise valid, to pay the reasonable value of things necessary for the minor's support" when not under the care of a parent or guardian able to provide. Whether that lets you recover the reasonable value of housing from a minor who could not make the lease is a question only case law could settle. Assume the lease is not enforceable against the minor.

On a minor as a party: § 14-10-04 lets a minor sue only through "a guardian ad litem", and § 28-26-20 makes the guardian answer for costs adjudged against an "infant" plaintiff. For a defendant, N.D.R.Civ.P. 17(b)(1) lets a minor's general guardian defend for the minor, and Rule 17(b)(2) says "The court must appoint a guardian ad litem, or issue another appropriate order, to protect a minor or incompetent person who is self-represented in an action."

What to do. (1) Do not rent to anyone under the age of majority on the minor's signature alone. Get an adult of full age to sign as a guarantor or co-tenant, in writing, in the lease itself — that is the one piece of paper that actually protects you, and it is the subject of the guaranty clause in this library. (2) Ask for proof of age before signing rather than after a dispute; § 14-10-00.1 presumes that the date of birth on a government birth certificate, ID, passport or similar document is the legal date of birth, and § 14-10-02 makes everyone "eighteen years of age and over" an adult. (3) If you must evict a tenant who is or may be under the age of majority, raise it with counsel before filing and expect a guardian or guardian ad litem under N.D.R.Civ.P. 17(b) — serving and taking judgment against a minor without a representative is the kind of defect that unwinds a judgment later. (4) Do not add a minor-tenant clause to the lease; no North Dakota statute requires one and there is no statutory rule for a clause to carry.

title: Can a tenant's unpaid water or garbage bill become a lien on your North Dakota property? No statute says so -- but ask your city, because its ordinances decide
bodyText:
Default rule: the section headings of the North Dakota Century Code show liens for taxes, for special assessments, for construction, repairs, crops, hospitals, innkeepers, storage, aircraft, child support and a landlord's own mobile home lien -- and not one lien on the property served for unpaid water, sewer, garbage or other utility SERVICE charges. There is also no North Dakota statute of the kind other states have that exempts a non-occupying owner from a tenant's unpaid bill on filing an affidavit or a lease with the utility, and none putting a tenant's garbage fees on the owner's property tax bill. So there is no affidavit to file and no proviso to rely on.

Why you should still ask locally. The city and county chapters do not change that answer. Sec. 40-01-25 and sec. 11-10-32, despite the caption "Prohibition - Connection of utility services", only bar a city or county from impeding an energy connection "based on fuel source"; they say nothing about old balances. Sec. 40-22-16 lets a city pay for a sewer or water improvement partly from service charges; it makes no unpaid bill a lien. Sec. 40-24-01 makes a special assessment "a lien upon the property upon which the assessment is levied". And a home rule city may "establish charges for any city or other services" and levy "special assessments for benefits conferred" (sec. 40-05.1-06). What your city's charter or ordinances do with a delinquent account is local, and no statute answers it.

Both readings. On the first, there is no utility service lien in North Dakota: a municipal utility collects a service charge as a contract debt from its customer, and only a special assessment for a capital improvement -- a sewer main, a water main -- becomes a lien, which is a charge on the owner for the owner's own improvement and not for a tenant's unpaid bill. On the second, a home rule city may provide by ordinance that delinquent water, sewer or garbage service charges are certified and collected as a special assessment, which sec. 40-24-01 would arguably then make a lien attaching on approval of the assessment list -- in which case a tenant's unpaid bill can reach your property regardless of what the lease says, because the lien arises from the ordinance and not from the lease.

The cautious course, and it is cheap. Assume your property is exposed and manage it rather than rely on a statutory exemption that may not exist. First, call the city or county utility that serves the property and ask one question: if the tenant's account goes delinquent, do you certify it against the property? The answer is local, it is free, and it governs. Second, if the answer is yes, keep the service in your own name and bill the tenant as additional rent under the utilities clause -- then you control the account and you learn of a problem from your own bill. Third, if the tenant holds the account, have the tenant authorise the provider to copy you on shutoff and past-due notices, and check the account periodically. Fourth, do not rely on a lease clause or an affidavit to defeat a lien: no North Dakota statute gives either of them that effect, and a lien created by ordinance is not something your tenant can waive for you.

One thing you should not confuse with this. Sec. 35-20-17 is a landlord's mobile home lien -- a lien you may get against a tenant's mobile home, not a lien a municipality gets against your land.

title: There Is No Such Thing as a Non-Refundable Deposit Here
bodyText: Default rule in North Dakota: a security deposit is refundable, and no notice makes it otherwise. The word 'nonrefundable' appears nowhere in North Dakota's landlord-tenant law, so there is no statute permitting a non-refundable deposit, no prescribed wording, no bold-type or capital-letters requirement, and no disclosure that would validate one. The reason is the deposit section itself: a lessor who requires money as a security deposit, however denominated, must put it in a federally insured interest-bearing savings or checking account for the tenant's benefit, and 'the security deposit and any interest accruing on the deposit must be paid to the lessee upon termination of a lease' (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1)). The only money you keep is what you properly apply to pet or negligence damage, unpaid rent, or cleaning and repairs that were the tenant's responsibility and were needed to return the unit to its original state, reasonable wear and tear excepted, all of which must be itemised and notified within thirty days (§ 47-16-07.1(3)). Keeping any of it on the strength of a 'non-refundable' label is security deposit money withheld without reasonable justification, and that carries treble damages (§ 47-16-07.1(4)). A fee is different from a deposit only if it really is different. A genuine charge that buys the tenant something - permission to keep an animal, a parking stall, a service - and is earned when paid rather than held against the tenant's performance is not a deposit and is not caught by the section. But the four words 'however denominated' mean the label does not decide it: money you hold back against possible damage or unpaid rent is security whatever the lease calls it, and it counts against the one-month-rent ceiling. What to do: do not use the word 'non-refundable' next to the word 'deposit' anywhere in a North Dakota lease. If you charge an earned fee, name what it buys, charge it as rent or as a separate consideration, do not call it a deposit, and do not hold it against damage.

title: No Separate Signed Notice Will Make a Deposit Non-Refundable
bodyText: Default rule in North Dakota: the deposit and any interest on it must be paid to the tenant when the lease ends, less only what you properly apply and itemise (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1), (3)). There is no separate-notice route around that. No statute requires - or permits - a non-refundable deposit to be set out in a separate written notice, a separate signed document, an addendum, boldface type, capital letters or a line for the tenant's initials, and no such formality will make an otherwise unlawful retention lawful. This matters because North Dakota does use both of those devices elsewhere, so their absence here is a choice rather than an oversight. A tenant of anything other than a single-family residence may take on specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodelling only if the agreement is in good faith and 'set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration', and you may not make performance of that separate agreement a condition of the lease (§ 47-16-13.1(5), (6)). And an agreement requiring the tenant to give more than one month's notice to end the tenancy 'must state the notice requirement and provide space for the lessee to initial next to the notice requirement', failing which the tenant may terminate on one month's notice anyway (§ 47-16-15(4)). The legislature knew how to demand a separate signed writing and knew how to demand initials; it attached neither to the deposit. What to do: do not draft a non-refundable deposit addendum, a deposit waiver, or an initialled acknowledgement that part of the deposit will be kept. Charge a deposit inside the cap, hold it in the federally insured interest-bearing account for the tenant's benefit, and justify every deduction by itemisation within thirty days - the only paper that protects you is the § 47-16-07.2 move-in condition statement, signed by both of you, which is prima facie proof of the condition the unit started in.

title: North Dakota does not make you name an in-state agent in the lease, but an out-of-state entity must register before it can sue
bodyText:
Default rule first, and it is a short one: North Dakota's lease law does not require you to name anybody in the lease. There is no landlord-identification disclosure, no in-state agent requirement, and no rule that a nonresident owner must appoint anyone before renting or before suing. The only thing North Dakota requires to accompany a rental agreement is unrelated: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.2 obliges the landlord to give the tenant "a statement describing the condition of the facilities in and about the premises to be rented at the time of entering a rental agreement", signed by both, which is "prima facie proof of the condition of the facilities and the premises at the beginning of the rental agreement." That is a condition report, not an identification of the owner or an agent. Two batteries found no registered, resident, statutory or designated agent duty anywhere in the whole of title 47, and no rent-withholding provision there either.

There is also no surety hurdle for a nonresident owner who has to sue. N.D.C.C. § 28-26-25, "Nonresident must furnish surety", was repealed by S.L. 1983, ch. 364, § 1. Be aware of a loose end, though: § 28-26-28 still says that a plaintiff who becomes a nonresident after commencing an action "shall give surety for costs in the same manner as is required of a nonresident in commencing an action" — a cross-reference back to the section that was repealed. Do not read § 28-26-28 as reviving a requirement to post surety when you file; read the repeal.

But none of that means a nonresident or out-of-state owner has nothing to do, because the duties that do exist sit outside the lease law:
• If the owner is an out-of-state LLC or corporation, title 10 governs. Owning "income-producing real property" here counts as transacting business (§ 10-32.1-82(2) for an LLC, § 10-19.1-143(3) for a corporation). An entity transacting business without a certificate of authority "may not maintain an action or proceeding in this state" (§ 10-32.1-84(1); § 10-19.1-142(1)), so it cannot bring an eviction until it registers, and it faces a civil penalty of up to $5,000. Its leases stay valid (§ 10-32.1-84(2)). Once authorized, it must "continuously maintain a registered agent" in North Dakota (§§ 10-32.1-78 and 10-19.1-138). An entity that transacts business here without a certificate is treated as having appointed the secretary of state as its agent for service of process, so a tenant can sue it by serving the secretary of state (§§ 10-32.1-84(4) and 10-19.1-142(3)). And any owner, individual or entity, who has an interest in property in North Dakota can be sued here on a claim arising from it, wherever the owner lives (N.D.R.Civ.P. 4(b)(2)(E)).
• North Dakota does not withhold income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. Chapter 57-38's withholding rules cover wages, lottery winnings and oil and gas royalties, not rent; nonresidents are taxed on income from property they own here (§ 57-38-03). But if the owner is a passthrough entity (an LLC, partnership or S corporation), it must withhold at the top rate on income distributed to each nonresident member, unless an exception applies (§ 57-38-31.1(3)).

What to do. (1) Put the landlord's or manager's name and a current North Dakota notice address in the lease anyway, using {{landlord_notice_name}} and {{landlord_notice_address}}, or {{owner_agent_name}} and {{owner_agent_address}} if an agent handles the tenancy. No statute makes you, but § 47-16-25 requires the tenant to inform you "immediately" of any proceeding against the property and § 47-16-13 lets the tenant repair and deduct after "notice from the lessee" — both of which work against you if the tenant has nowhere to send anything. (2) If you own through an out-of-state entity, get its certificate of authority from the North Dakota Secretary of State and keep a registered agent before you need to file an eviction. (3) If the owner is a passthrough entity with nonresident members, ask a North Dakota accountant about § 57-38-31.1 withholding before the first distribution, not after. (4) Do not draft the lease as though North Dakota had an in-state-agent-or-no-suit rule for the tenant's benefit; the title 10 bar is a rule about the entity's standing to sue, not a lease term, and promising the tenant a protection the law does not give is a promise you can be held to. ONE EXCEPTION, AND IT IS A BIG ONE: a mobile home park. Section 47-10-28 imposes exactly the duties this row says North Dakota does not have, but only on a park. A park with twenty-six or more lots must maintain an official local office (subsection 1(b)); a park must name a person authorised to make decisions (subsection 1(c)(3)); and a park must disclose the name, address and telephone number of the entity that owns it, together with the manager's telephone number (subsections 1(g) and (h)). Violating section 47-10-28 carries a civil penalty of not less than two thousand five hundred dollars (subsection 12) and is a defence to an eviction (section 47-32-01.1). So if you operate a park, read section 47-10-28 and treat this row's general answer as inapplicable to you.

title: No Rule on Charging the Tenant for Serving a Notice
bodyText: No North Dakota statute authorises or forbids a lease charge for serving a notice of intention to evict or for filing an eviction action. That silence is not permission. A flat charge is exposed as a contractual penalty, void under N.D.C.C. § 9-08-03, or as damages fixed in advance, void under § 9-08-04 unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. And § 47-32-04 lets an eviction be joined only with a claim for rents and profits accrued or damages arising by reason of the tenant's possession, so the charge cannot ride along with the eviction. If you want to recover what service actually cost you, charge the actual cost and keep the receipt rather than a stated figure.

title: No Waivable Notice to Quit
bodyText: North Dakota has no notice to quit to waive. Its eviction chapter requires three days' written notice of intention to evict, and only for four of the eight grounds - holding over or failing to pay rent for three days after it is due, possession after a judicial sale or a cancelled contract for deed, possession after a partition judgment, and violating a material term of the written lease (N.D.C.C. §§ 47-32-01, 47-32-02). Nothing lets the tenant waive that notice, and nothing says it is non-waivable either; a lease clause purporting to waive it would be asking a court to let you skip a statutory precondition to filing, which is not a bargain the chapter contemplates. What the lease can change runs the other way: a tenant's termination notice may be made longer than one calendar month by written agreement, and then only binds the tenant if the tenant initials the requirement (§ 47-16-15(2), (4)).

title: The Only Extra Wording North Dakota Makes You Put in a Notice to Evict
bodyText: The default rule is that North Dakota imposes no content requirements on a notice ending a residential tenancy. The phrases 'notice to vacate' and 'notice to quit' do not appear in the North Dakota statutes at all; what the statutes have are a notice to remove under section 47-17-01 and a notice of intention to evict under section 47-32-02, and neither section tells you what the notice must say. Section 47-17-02, which is actually captioned 'Form', requires only that the notice be in writing and be served by delivery to the tenant or to some person of discretion residing on the premises, or by affixing it to a conspicuous part of the premises if neither can be found with reasonable diligence. Section 47-32-02 requires only three days' written notice before proceedings may be instituted, served and returned as a summons is or, if the party cannot be found, by the sheriff or a process server posting it conspicuously on the premises. No required language, no required recital, no required statement of cause, no required advice about the tenant's rights -- with ONE exception, and it is mandatory. MOBILE HOME PARKS: under section 47-10-28(10), 'A notice of intent to evict a tenant from a mobile home park under section 47-32-02 must include clear, boldfaced language stating: "You do not have to vacate immediately. You have the right to remain until a court issues an eviction order."' That is a verbatim requirement in boldface, and a park owner who leaves it out has violated section 47-10-28 -- which, under section 47-32-01.1, is a defence the tenant may raise, and the court 'may not order an eviction' if it finds the violation. In a park, omitting that sentence can cost you the eviction. The other park duty worth reading alongside it is section 47-10-28(3): before you can even start an eviction for failure to comply with MODIFIED park rules, you must have given thirty days' advance written notice of the modification, then written notice of the failure to comply, then three months to remedy or vacate -- extendable if the tenant produces a signed statement from a professional mover that the home cannot be relocated in that time. Two further points for ordinary residential lettings. The one notice-content mandate outside parks runs against the LANDLORD'S lease drafting, not the notice: section 47-16-15(4) says an agreement requiring the tenant to give more than one month's notice must state the requirement and provide space for the tenant to initial next to it, and if it is not initialled at signing the tenant may terminate on the last day of a month with one calendar month's notice. And North Dakota has NO rule forbidding you to carry out alterations, renovations or demolition that make a unit uninhabitable while a notice ending the tenancy is pending -- but your habitability duties under section 47-16-13.1 keep running until the tenancy actually ends, so that absence is not a licence to make the place unlivable.

title: Nuisance in North Dakota: your in-lease route is the eviction ground, but title 42 can reach your building
bodyText:
THE DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota's landlord-tenant chapters contain NO nuisance provision. The word 'nuisance' does not appear in chapter 47-16 (residential leases), in chapter 47-32 (eviction) or in chapter 47-10. There is no nuisance-receivership statute you can be subjected to under those chapters, no drug-nuisance rent-escrow procedure, no statute requiring your lease to summarise a criminal statute, and no provision making you a necessary defendant in someone else's abatement case. So none of the mechanics other states put under this heading is part of North Dakota's landlord-tenant law.

WHAT YOU DO HAVE, AND IT IS ENOUGH FOR MOST CASES. Two sections, in nearly identical words, carry North Dakota's whole in-chapter answer to a disruptive tenant.
- N.D.C.C. s 47-16-13.2(7) is a duty the statute puts on every residential tenant: the tenant shall 'Conduct oneself and require other persons on the premises with the tenant's consent to conduct themselves in a manner that will not disturb the tenant's neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises.'
- N.D.C.C. s 47-32-01(7) is the matching eviction ground: an eviction is maintainable when 'A lessee or a person on the premises with the lessee's consent acts in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment of the premises.'
TWO PRACTICAL POINTS THAT FOLLOW. First, subsection 7 is a GROUND IN ITS OWN RIGHT -- you do not have to prove a lease breach to use it. Second, and this is the one landlords get wrong: s 47-32-02 requires the three days' written notice of intention to evict ONLY 'in all cases arising under subsections 4, 5, 6, and 8 of section 47-32-01'. Subsection 7 is NOT on that list, so a disturbance eviction under s 47-32-01(7) needs NO pre-suit notice. Serving one anyway costs you nothing and strengthens the record, but the statute does not require it.

NOTE THE WORDING, BECAUSE IT IS BROADER THAN 'GUEST'. Neither section uses the word 'guest' or 'visitor'. Both reach 'a person on the premises with the lessee's [or tenant's] consent' -- which takes in an unauthorised occupant, a partner, a relative, a contractor the tenant let in, and anyone else there by the tenant's leave. Draft your house rules in the statute's words, not in 'guest' language, or you will write a narrower rule than the law gives you. Note too that North Dakota's phrase is 'PEACEFUL enjoyment'. 'Quiet enjoyment' appears in North Dakota statute only as a conveyancing covenant (s 47-04-26, s 41-09-107) and is not the landlord-tenant standard.

A SEPARATE ROUTE YOUR DISTURBED TENANT CAN USE. Chapter 14-07.7, in force since January 1, 2026, lets an individual who is or has been a victim of 'disorderly conduct' petition for a disorderly conduct restraining order (s 14-07.7-02, s 14-07.7-05). 'Disorderly conduct' means 'intrusive or unwanted acts, words, or gestures intended to adversely affect the safety, security, or privacy of another individual', excluding constitutionally protected activity (s 14-07.7-01(3)). An order may prohibit the restrained individual from 'Entering or remaining on premises' (s 14-07.7-01(1)(a)(2)) and may last up to two years (s 14-07.7-05(3)). THE PETITION IS THE VICTIM'S, NOT YOURS -- you cannot bring it for a neighbour -- but pointing a complaining tenant to it is often faster than an eviction and does not put you in the middle.

ONE EXPOSURE THAT IS YOURS, NOT THE TENANT'S. s 47-16-26 ('Double letting of room prohibited'): if you rent a room as a dwelling for more than one family, the first tenant of any part of it is entitled to the whole room 'notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary', and EVERY TENANT IN THE BUILDING under the same landlord 'is relieved from all obligation to pay rent to the landlord while such double letting of any room continues.' That is a building-wide rent holiday triggered by your own letting practice -- the one nuisance-shaped penalty in these chapters that falls on the landlord.

WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. (1) Put a disturbance rule in the written lease in the statute's own words -- 'Tenant and any person on the premises with Tenant's consent' -- so that you can proceed under s 47-32-01(8) (material breach of the written lease, which DOES need three days' notice) as well as under s 47-32-01(7) (no notice). Having both routes is worth the paragraph. (2) Keep dated complaint records from the OTHER tenants: subsection 7 is measured by what 'unreasonably disturbs other tenants', so other tenants' evidence is the case. (3) Do not promise in the lease to abate a nuisance, close a unit, or terminate another tenant's lease on request -- North Dakota imposes no such duty on you and a promise creates one. (4) In a MOBILE HOME PARK, check s 47-10-28 before acting: it requires thirty days' notice of any rule modification and, for modifications other than sanitation and safety ones, three months to remedy or vacate before you may begin an eviction, with a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 under s 47-10-28(12) and a defence to the eviction under s 47-32-01.1.

AND WHERE TITLE 42 CAN STILL REACH YOU. North Dakota's general nuisance law is title 42, read whole. Three sections matter to a landlord. First, s 42-01-01.2: 'An owner or lessee, or both, of a house or building that is used in a manner that habitually disturbs the peace, comfort, or decency of the immediate neighborhood is guilty of maintaining a public nuisance' - and while 'A lessee is not guilty of an offense under this section unless the lessee is the cause of the nuisance', the section gives the OWNER no such shelter. Second, s 42-02-01 lets the attorney general, the state health officer, the state's attorney 'or any citizen of the county' sue to abate and enjoin a nuisance, and on judgment s 42-02-04 has the place closed 'against use by anyone' for one year, with fees against the defendants (s 42-02-09). Third, s 42-02-06: when leased premises are closed under an injunction or adjudged a nuisance, you may 'terminate the lease by giving three days' notice thereof in writing to the tenant', and get the premises back if you prove you were 'without fault' and had not 'knowingly nor negligently permitted' the nuisance. So a neighbour or a prosecutor CAN reach your building. Act on repeated disturbance complaints promptly and keep the record, because it is your proof that you did not permit it.

title: No ordnance or demolition disclosure in North Dakota, and the only meter rule is a mobile home park prohibition, not a disclosure
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota requires no lease disclosure that the property was formerly used for ordnance or munitions, that it sits in a former ordnance or explosives area, that demolition of the building is planned or pending, or that the unit is served by a shared or master meter. The ordnance and demolition limbs of this topic are simply absent: the words ordnance, munitions and unexploded return nothing anywhere in the North Dakota statutes, the session laws or the constitution.

The meter limb needs more care, because North Dakota does regulate meters - in one place, in different words, and as a prohibition rather than a disclosure. N.D.C.C. 47-10-28(8) applies to mobile home parks only. It lets a park owner buy utility services including water and sewer on a tenant's behalf and either fold the cost into rent or bill it as a separate charge based on actual usage; it forbids charging more than the actual cost per unit paid to the provider, except a reasonable administrative fee that "may not exceed three dollars"; it provides that "a mobile home park may not charge a fee for a utility without an individual meter for each mobile home"; and it requires the owner to "provide the tenant access to the records of meter readings taken at the mobile home lot of the tenant". So in a park the answer to a shared meter is not disclosure, it is that you may not charge a utility fee at all without an individual meter per home - ratio billing is banned. The access-to-readings duty is a real duty, but it is a duty to let the tenant see records on request, not a duty to state anything up front. None of 47-10-28 applies outside a mobile home park, and a violation of any part of it carries a civil penalty of not less than two thousand five hundred dollars under subsection 12, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, and is a defence to the eviction under N.D.C.C. 47-32-01.1.

What to do: do not print an ordnance, demolition or shared-meter disclosure as a statutory requirement, because none exists. If you operate a mobile home park, the compliance work is not a disclosure at all - install an individual meter for each home before you charge any utility fee, keep the administrative fee at or under three dollars, bill no more than actual cost per unit, and keep the lot meter readings where you can produce them when a tenant asks. Outside a park, if the unit really is on a shared meter and the tenant is paying for it, say so plainly in the lease anyway: no statute requires it, but an unexplained utility charge is the kind of thing a tenant disputes, and the library's utilities rows deal with how to allocate it.

title: Shared Facilities and Amenities
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota has no amenity statute. A tenant's right to use a shared facility comes from the lease and nowhere else: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-27 says a tenant for years or at will may occupy the buildings, take the annual products of the soil, work open mines and harvest growing crops, and then that "[t]he tenant has no rights to the property other than such as are given the tenant by the agreement or instrument by which the tenant's tenancy is acquired or by the provisions of this section." That cuts both ways. Say nothing and the tenant has no right to the laundry room - but you also have no rules, no right to charge and, in a fixed-term lease, no clean way to close it.

AND SUPPLY CREATES A DUTY. The moment you supply a facility, N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(d) requires you to "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord" - North Dakota names elevators expressly. And § 47-16-13.1(1)(c) requires you to "[k]eep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition." Neither duty can be drafted away.

WHAT THE LANDLORD SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. Write the list; do not rely on the advertisement. Charge for a facility in the rent rather than by a separate fee unless you have a reason, because North Dakota has no statute authorising rental fees and a fixed sum has to live with § 9-08-03 ("[p]enalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance thereof are void") and § 9-08-04 (damages fixed in advance void to that extent unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix). Be careful about withdrawing or restricting a facility selectively: § 14-02.5-02(2) makes it unlawful to "discriminate against an individual in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling or in providing services or facilities in connection with a sale or rental of a dwelling" because of race, colour, religion, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin, or status with respect to marriage or public assistance - and age and familial status are protected classes in North Dakota, so an adults-only gym or a no-children laundry rule is the classic trap. Section 14-02.5-06(3)(b) adds that refusing "a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices, or services" needed to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling is itself discrimination, so your facility rules must bend where an accommodation is reasonable.

IN A MOBILE HOME PARK, DIFFERENT RULES ENTIRELY. N.D.C.C. § 47-10-28(3) requires at least thirty days' advance written notice of any modification to park rules or regulations, and then - for rules other than the sanitation and safety rules in subsection 4 and the tongue-hitch rules in subsection 5 - written notice of non-compliance and three months to remedy or vacate before any eviction action, extendable if a mover certifies the home cannot be relocated in time. Subsection 6 keeps the old rules in force until the modified ones take effect. Subsection 9 requires the owner to give each tenant "a summary outlining the tenant's lease and the rights and obligations of the tenant and mobile home park owner under state law". Subsection 12 carries a civil penalty of "not less than two thousand five hundred dollars but not exceeding the greater of ten thousand dollars or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs", and § 47-32-01.1 makes a violation of § 47-10-28 a defence to the eviction. Do not use the thirty-day rule-change sentence in the lease clause in a park without the three-month cure period.

IF YOU BOUGHT THE UNIT TO RENT IT OUT. Where the property is subject to a homeowners' association or a condominium project, N.D.C.C. § 47-10-02.3(2) obliges the seller to disclose in writing, by a mutually agreed date or within ten days of executing the agreement, both "(m) Notice of any homeowners' association or condominium project restrictions related to the leasing of a unit" and "(n) A list of homeowners' association or condominium project amenities". Get those two documents before you buy and read them against the facility list you intend to promise a tenant.

title: Changing Parking Rules
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota has no statute requiring parking or towing rules to be delivered before the lease is signed, no prescribed heading or type size for them, no limit on the vehicle information a landlord may demand, and no rule that a parking permit run with the lease term. "Parking rules" and "parking regulations" appear in North Dakota law only as traffic-law headings for public streets - §§ 39-10-50 and 39-13-03 - not for private rental property. What North Dakota does have is a tight limit on CHANGING rules once a tenancy has begun, and it is easy to miss.

THE ONLY STATUTORY WAY TO CHANGE TERMS, AND IT IS MONTH-TO-MONTH ONLY. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07 provides that "[i]n all leases of land or tenements, or of any interest therein, from month to month, the landlord may change the terms of the lease to take effect at the expiration of the month upon giving notice in writing at least thirty days before the expiration of the month", and that the notice, when served, "shall operate and be effectual to create and establish as a part of the lease the terms, rent, and conditions specified in the notice, if the tenant shall continue to hold the premises after the expiration of the month." Service may be "in any reasonable manner which actually informs the tenant". There is no equivalent provision for a fixed-term lease. So in a twelve-month lease you cannot impose a new parking rule on a sitting tenant unless the lease itself reserved the power - which is exactly why the lease clause exists.

WHAT THE LANDLORD SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. Put the rules in the lease, not on a laundry-room wall - posting alone makes nothing part of the lease. Keep a dated receipt for the rules. Do not make the change power unlimited: § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce a lease provision that "was unconscionable when made", enforce the remainder without it, or limit its application, and a clause letting the landlord rewrite material terms at will is the obvious target. Do not put a fixed money penalty in the rules: § 9-08-03 says "[p]enalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance thereof are void" and § 9-08-04 voids an amount of damages fixed in advance "to that extent" unless "it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage" - charge the actual towing or snow-removal cost you incur, evidenced by the invoice. And do not tow on your own authority; see the guidance on charging separately for parking, because North Dakota's abandoned-vehicle chapter is ch. 23.1-15 and § 47-16-30.1 permits disposing of property left on the premises without legal process only where it has "a total estimated value of not more than two thousand five hundred dollars" and only twenty-eight or more days after notice.

A MOBILE HOME PARK IS GOVERNED DIFFERENTLY AND MUCH MORE STRICTLY. Under N.D.C.C. § 47-10-28(3) a park owner "shall provide a tenant advance written notice of any modifications to park rules or regulations at least thirty days before the date the modifications take effect", and then - for rules other than the sanitation and safety rules in subsection 4 and the tongue-hitch or housing-finance modifications in subsection 5 - must give a tenant whose home fails to comply written notice of the failure and "three months to remedy the failure or vacate the premises before initiating an action for eviction", with the old rules governing in the meantime, and with the three months extended if the tenant supplies a signed document from a person in the business of relocating mobile homes declaring the home cannot be relocated in time. Subsection 6 keeps the rules in effect on the notice date in force until the modified rules take effect. Subsections 4 and 5 still require thirty days' advance written notice. Subsection 9 requires the owner to give each tenant "a summary outlining the tenant's lease and the rights and obligations of the tenant and mobile home park owner under state law". Subsection 12 carries a civil penalty of "not less than two thousand five hundred dollars but not exceeding the greater of ten thousand dollars or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs", and § 47-32-01.1 makes a violation of § 47-10-28 a defence to the eviction - so in a park, getting the notice wrong loses you the eviction. Do not use the thirty-day sentence in the lease clause in a park without the three-month cure period.

title: North Dakota Has No URLTA, So No Act-Wide List of Non-Waivable Rights
bodyText: North Dakota has not adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. There is no Part 5, no enumerated list of rights a lease may not waive, and no provision voiding a lease term that waives a right under the landlord-tenant chapter. What North Dakota has instead is narrower and scattered: a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision, and may do the same with a settlement in which a party waives or agrees to forego a right under the habitability sections (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.3); the double-letting rule applies notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary (§ 47-16-26); a tenant's notice period longer than one calendar month binds the tenant only if initialled (§ 47-16-15(4)); and the general contract chapter voids penalties, damages fixed in advance, exemptions from liability for one's own fraud, willful injury or violation of law, and restrictions on enforcing rights (§§ 9-08-02 to 9-08-05). Read a North Dakota lease against those, not against a Part 5 that does not exist.

title: No State Pet-and-Eviction Fact Sheet to Give Tenants
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has no state fact sheet about pets and eviction, and no duty to give a tenant one. There is no publication to hand over, no trigger based on your knowing the tenant has a dog or a cat, no attachment requirement, and no penalty for not doing it -- because the document does not exist. If a form has been handed to you as a "required North Dakota pet notice", it is not a state-required document.

North Dakota requires a landlord to hand over very little, and the complete statutory list does not include anything about pets: a signed statement describing the condition of the facilities in and about the premises, agreed to and signed by both parties at the time of entering the rental agreement (§ 47-16-07.2); an itemisation of any part of the security deposit not returned, with a written notice, within thirty days after termination and delivery of possession (§ 47-16-07.1(3)); and, if the lease requires the tenant to give more than one month's notice to terminate, that requirement stated in the agreement with space for the tenant to initial next to it (§ 47-16-15(4)). The only required SUMMARY of a tenant's rights in North Dakota is a mobile home park rule: § 47-10-28(9) obliges a park owner to give each tenant a summary outlining the tenant's lease and the rights and obligations of the tenant and the park owner under state law, and § 47-10-28(1)(g)-(h) requires the owning entity's name, address and telephone number and the telephone number of any property manager or site agent. A park owner who leaves that summary out faces § 47-10-28(12)'s civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and not more than the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs. If you operate a park, that summary is the place a pet rule should be described -- there is no separate pet handout.

What to do: do not promise a tenant a state pet fact sheet, and do not import another state's form. Put your pet rules, the pet deposit, and the consequences of an unauthorised animal in the lease and the house rules, where North Dakota leaves them, and remember two statutory limits when you draft: a service animal or companion animal required by a tenant with a disability as a reasonable accommodation is outside the pet deposit entirely (§ 47-16-07.1(2)), and keeping an unauthorised pet is a breach of the lease to be handled under chapter 47-32's eviction grounds like any other breach -- there is no pet-specific eviction procedure and no pet-specific notice.

title: Pet Money Is Deposit Money -- Separate Cap, Interest Account, 30-Day Itemisation, Treble Damages
bodyText:
North Dakota answers this one in the security deposit section, and the structure is what matters. § 47-16-07.1(1) caps ordinary security: a lessor 'may not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's rent', with exactly two exceptions -- up to two months' rent from an applicant convicted of a felony offence, as an incentive to rent to them (subdivision a), and up to two months' rent from an applicant against whom a judgment has been entered for violating the terms of a previous rental agreement (subdivision b). A pet deposit is NOT one of those two exceptions. It is authorised by its own subsection: § 47-16-07.1(2) says a lessor 'may charge a lessee a pet security deposit for keeping an animal that is not a service animal or companion animal required by a tenant with a disability as a reasonable accommodation under fair housing laws', and that it 'may not exceed the greater of two thousand five hundred dollars or an amount equivalent to two months' rent'. Subsection (2) is a separate grant with its own ceiling, so the pet security deposit is charged in addition to the one month of ordinary security rather than inside it -- read the other way, subsection (2)'s $2,500-or-two-months ceiling could never be reached and would do nothing.

Three consequences a landlord has to get right. First, a pet deposit is DEPOSIT MONEY. Subsection (1) applies to money required as security 'however denominated', so the pet deposit goes into a federally insured interest-bearing savings or checking account for the benefit of the tenant, and the deposit with any interest must be paid to the tenant on termination except as the statute allows it to be applied. No interest is owed if the occupancy was shorter than nine months. Second, you may apply it only to what subsection (3) lists: damage from deteriorations or injuries to the property caused by the lessee's PET or through the lessee's or a guest's negligence; unpaid rent; and the costs of cleaning or other repairs that were the tenant's responsibility and are necessary to return the unit to its original state, reasonable wear and tear excepted. Whatever you keep must be itemised, and the itemisation with the amount due must be delivered or mailed to the tenant's last furnished address with a written notice within thirty days after termination of the lease and delivery of possession. Third, the sanction is severe: § 47-16-07.1(4) makes a lessor 'liable for treble damages for any security deposit money withheld without reasonable justification'. It is the only treble damages in North Dakota's landlord-tenant chapter. The other treble measure that reaches a landlord is § 32-03-29, for forcibly ejecting or excluding a person from possession.

What North Dakota does not regulate is the rest of the pet money. There is no statute on pet rent, no statute on a non-refundable pet fee, and no statutory definition of 'security deposit' to argue about. Be careful here rather than creative: money you take up front and keep is still 'security, however denominated' if it functions as security, so a 'non-refundable pet fee' invites the argument that it is deposit money that had to be banked, itemised and returned -- with treble damages attached. The safe structure is a pet security deposit under subsection (2), banked and itemised, plus monthly pet rent charged as rent if you want recurring revenue. Keep both out of the lease for a qualifying assistance animal: subsection (2) excludes a service animal or companion animal required as a reasonable accommodation, and § 47-16-07.5 limits what documentation you may ask for.

title: North Dakota has no plain-language statute for leases - but its consumer act reaches real estate, and whether it reaches a lease is unsettled
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has no plain-language statute. The phrase "plain language" appears nowhere in the North Dakota statutes, and there is no readability test, no required statement of consumer restrictions listing the rights a tenant waives, no Attorney General preapproval procedure for lease forms, and no dollar threshold above which a lease escapes such a regime. Nothing prescribes a type size, a sentence length or a reading level for a residential lease.

North Dakota does have the components - it has simply never aimed them at leases. N.D.C.C. 47-15.1-03 requires a consumer rental purchase agreement to carry, immediately above or adjacent to the consumer's signature, "a clear, conspicuous, printed or typewritten notice, in boldface, ten-point type" reading "NOTICE TO CONSUMER - READ BEFORE SIGNING / DO NOT SIGN THIS BEFORE YOU READ THE ENTIRE AGREEMENT ... / DO NOT SIGN THIS IF IT CONTAINS ANY BLANK SPACES. / YOU ARE ENTITLED TO AN EXACT COPY OF ANY AGREEMENT YOU SIGN.", with all other disclosures made clearly and conspicuously in at least eight-point type. That chapter is rent-to-own of goods, and it excludes a residential lease twice over: 47-15.1-01(4) reaches only an agreement under which the consumer may become the owner of the property, and subdivision (4)(d) expressly excludes "a lease or a bailment of personal property incidental to the lease of real property and which contains no provision for the consumer to have an option to purchase", while (4)(f) excludes a hiring under chapter 47-15. More recently, S.L. 2025, ch. 143 (H.B. 1447) created N.D.C.C. 13-09.1-51, which requires a virtual-currency kiosk operator to "disclose in a clear, conspicuous, and easily readable manner in the chosen language of the customer" all relevant terms and conditions, to receive acknowledgment of receipt via confirmation of consent, and to post a prescribed bold warning. So in 2025 the legislature wrote a readability duty, a customer's-language duty, an acknowledgment duty and prescribed warning text - for crypto kiosks, not for leases. Treat all of these as siblings that prove the negative, not as landlord duties.

One point is genuinely unsettled, and only a court could settle it. North Dakota's consumer protection chapter is N.D.C.C. ch. 51-15. Section 51-15-01(3) defines "merchandise" to mean "any objects, wares, goods, commodities, intangibles, real estate, charitable contributions, or services" - real estate is in the definition. Section 51-15-01(5) defines "sale" as "any charitable solicitation or any sale, offer for sale, or attempt to sell any merchandise for any consideration". Section 51-15-02 then declares unlawful any deceptive act or practice, fraud, false pretense, false promise or misrepresentation "with the intent that others rely thereon in connection with the sale or advertisement of any merchandise", and separately any act or practice in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise "which is unconscionable or which causes or is likely to cause substantial injury to a person which is not reasonably avoidable by the injured person and not outweighed by countervailing benefits". Whether letting residential property is a "sale" of "merchandise" within those definitions - so that an unconscionable lease term or a misdescribed fee is an unlawful practice exposed to Attorney General enforcement - is not resolved by the text.

The cautious course, and what to do: write the lease in plain English and do not rely on the absence of a plain-language statute. Specifically - describe every fee accurately and where the tenant will see it before signing, do not advertise a rent that omits a mandatory charge, do not bury a waiver in a wall of text, and do not print a clause that misstates North Dakota law in your favour. Each of those is cheap to do and each is the conduct that 51-15-02 would reach if it does apply to leases. Two independent North Dakota rules point the same way regardless of how 51-15 comes out: N.D.C.C. 47-16-13.3 makes an unconscionable lease, or an unconscionable settlement waiving a right under sections 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6, unenforceable; and N.D.C.C. 9-08-05 voids any stipulation restricting a party from enforcing their rights by the usual legal proceedings or limiting the time to do so. Do not add a statement of consumer restrictions or a plain-language certification to the lease - no statute requires one, and a certification that the lease is plainly written is a representation you can be held to.

title: Canvassers, petitions and yard signs: North Dakota is silent, so make your rule content-neutral
bodyText:
The default rule: North Dakota gives nobody a right of political access to your rental property, and gives you no statutory power to prohibit it either. No provision in the North Dakota statutes requires a landlord to admit a candidate, a canvasser, a petition circulator or a tenant organiser to a building or its common areas; none protects a tenant's political activity in or about a dwelling; none protects a political sign in a window or on a balcony; and there is no tenant-organising or tenant-union access right anywhere in the statutes. On this subject North Dakota is simply silent, and your own rules and lease govern.

The constitutional provisions do not change that, and it is worth being precise about why. The North Dakota Constitution, article I, § 5, says 'The citizens have a right, in a peaceable manner, to assemble together for the common good, and to apply to those invested with the powers of government for the redress of grievances, or for other proper purposes, by petition, address or remonstrance.'
