Article III, which creates the initiative, referendum and recall, requires only that 'The petition shall be circulated only by electors' who swear that the signers signed in their presence — it says nothing about where circulation may happen. Those are rights against the state. Neither gives a circulator or a candidate a right to walk into private rental housing, and nothing in the statutes converts them into one.

One important exception you may be inside without realising it. If your landlord is a public body, the analysis is different, because the constraint runs against government. § 47-16-07.1(6) confirms that public landlords exist in North Dakota — the security deposit section 'applies to the state and to political subdivisions of the state that lease real property or dwellings' — and the entry section's own closing words preserve 'the right of a political subdivision to manage and control residential property in which the political subdivision has a [financial] interest'. If you manage housing for a city, a county or a housing authority, do not apply a blanket no-politics rule without advice; a private owner is in a materially better position here than a public one.

So here is what actually governs, and the useful point is that your tools are ordinary ones.
• You control the common areas, and you owe a duty over them: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(c) requires you to 'Keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition.'
• Your tenant's rights are closed and defined: § 47-16-27 lists what a tenant may do and adds that 'The tenant has no rights to the property other than such as are given the tenant by the agreement or instrument by which the tenant's tenancy is acquired or by the provisions of this section.' A canvasser's access, if any, comes through the tenant who invited them.
• Disruption, not politics, is the thing you can act on: § 47-16-13.2(7) requires the tenant to conduct themselves, and to require persons on the premises with their consent to conduct themselves, so as not to disturb neighbours' peaceful enjoyment; § 47-32-01(7) makes that an eviction ground against the lessee, with no notice of intention to evict required. (8) makes violation of a material written lease term one, and § 47-32-02 requires three days' written notice of intention to evict for that ground.
• You cannot use entry as a tool here: § 47-16-07.3's purposes are closed, and the section says 'A landlord shall not abuse the right of access or use it to harass or intimidate the tenant.' Entering to take down a poster is not on the list.

What to do. (1) Write a content-neutral solicitation and common-area rule — no door-to-door solicitation by non-residents, no leafletting of doors, no unattended literature in the lobby, meeting rooms by booking — and apply it to a charity, a church, a political campaign and a window cleaner identically. A rule that reaches only political callers is the one that creates a problem; a rule about solicitation generally is the one that holds. (2) Let tenants invite whoever they like into their own units and do not police who knocks on a door at a tenant's invitation. (3) Decide your signage rule once, write it in the lease or the rules, and keep it about size, placement, fixing method and damage rather than content — which keeps it inside your legitimate interest in the building and outside any argument about viewpoint. (4) Do not threaten non-renewal or eviction over a tenant's political activity: North Dakota has no statutory retaliation bar in the residential chapter to stop you, but the step is indefensible if the real reason surfaces, and in a mobile home park § 47-10-28's machinery will make it slow and expensive anyway. (5) If a tenant organises other tenants about the condition of the building, treat it as a habitability conversation under § 47-16-13.1 and answer it, rather than as a political one to be shut down.

Mobile home parks, where this comes up most. § 47-10-28 contains no political-access rule, but it makes a new or changed park rule hard to deploy quickly: subsection 3 requires thirty days' advance written notice of any modification to park rules or regulations, and then, for a tenant who owns a home that does not comply, written notice of the failure and three months to remedy or vacate before an eviction can be started — extendable where a professional relocator certifies in a signed document that the home cannot be moved in that time. During the three months the pre-change rules govern. Subsections 4 and 5 keep the same thirty days for sanitation and safety rules and for tongue-hitch or similar modifications. A violation of § 47-10-28 carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and up to the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, and is a defence to the eviction under § 47-32-01.1. So a park rule invented in reaction to a canvasser cannot be enforced against a homeowner-tenant for months.

title: North Dakota has no pool statute - your duty is the common-area duty, and you cannot waive it
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. A North Dakota landlord's duties are the closed list in N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1). The one that reaches a pool is subdivision (1)(c): "Keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition." A pool, deck, gate and pump room at a rental property are common areas, so the clean-and-safe duty applies to them - and it applies whatever the lease says, because § 47-16-13.6 makes the §§ 47-16-13.1 to 47-16-13.6 rights "enforceable by action" with fees to "the prevailing party".

THE ANSWER. There is no provision in the North Dakota statutes imposing a pool barrier, fence, enclosure, cover, gate, self-latching-gate, depth-marking, lifeguard, water-quality or pool-safety-notice duty on a residential landlord, and none requiring a pool safety notice at lease signing. The phrases "swimming pool", "wading pool", "hot tub", "lifeguard", "natatorium", "water recreation", "pool barrier", "pool enclosure" and "pool fence" appear nowhere in the North Dakota Century Code, and neither does "drown", "self-latching" or "self-closing". The only fencing chapters in title 47 are agricultural - ch. 47-26 and ch. 47-27 ("Closing Fence Gates"), about farm premises. So no North Dakota STATUTE regulates apartment pools. But a health rule does, as the next paragraph explains.

WHERE A DUTY DOES COME FROM: RULES, NOT STATUTES. Three routes. First, and this one applies to an apartment or park pool now: N.D. Admin. Code ch. 33-29-01 (Pool Facilities) covers a "semipublic" pool, meaning a pool or spa "on the premises of, or part of, a motel, mobile home park, apartment, condominium" or similar place where use is included in the rent (§ 33-29-01-01(8)). It requires a free chlorine residual of at least one milligram per liter "at all times" (§ 33-29-01-07), water clear enough to see the deep-end main drain (§ 33-29-01-06), a bacteria limit (§ 33-29-01-04), and daily records of pH, disinfectant residual and temperature kept for three years (§ 33-29-01-08). A stricter local ordinance controls (§ 33-29-01-12). It sets no fence, gate or barrier rule. Second, § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes the landlord "[c]omply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and § 47-16-13.1(3) makes that duty controlling wherever it is greater than any other subdivision's - so a code or an adopted standard is imported into the lease statute and becomes binding and controlling. The State Building Code (ch. 54-21.3; N.D. Admin. Code ch. 108-01-01) is the international building and residential codes, applied where a city, township or county "elect[s] to adopt and enforce building codes", and its appendix chapters apply only "if specifically adopted" - so whether a barrier standard reaches your pool depends on your local code. Third, if the property is a mobile home park, a recreational vehicle park or a campground, it is licensed annually under ch. 23-10 and the licence is conditioned on compliance with "any rules adopted by the department" of health and human services - § 23-10-06 as amended by S.L. 2025, ch. 238 (S.B. 2385) - and the department's inspection power sits in § 23-10-04. The department's park rules (N.D. Admin. Code chs. 33-33-01 and 33-33-02) say nothing about pools.

CAUTIOUS COURSE, which is the real content of this row. Treat the pool as if a code applies. Fence and gate it to the standard in the building code adopted in your city, keep the gate self-closing and self-latching, keep depth markings and a shepherd's crook and ring buoy, keep a dated inspection log, and keep the daily chemistry records § 33-29-01-08 requires for three years. If the property is a park, RV park or campground, ask the department of health and human services in writing what its rules require of a pool at a licensed park before opening it - a licence suspension under § 23-10-12 is a far worse outcome than closing the pool. If you cannot meet a standard, close the pool and lock it rather than open it with a notice.

THE CLAUSE TO AVOID. Do not write "swim at your own risk" as a waiver of your own liability. N.D.C.C. § 9-08-02 makes contracts whose object is "the exempting of anyone from responsibility for that person's own fraud or willful injury to the person or property of another, or violation of law, whether willful or negligent" against the policy of the law, and § 9-08-01 is what turns that into unlawfulness, including a provision "[c]ontrary to the policy of express law, though not expressly prohibited". A breach of the § 47-16-13.1(1)(c) common-area duty is a violation of law, so a negligent failure to keep the pool safe sits inside § 9-08-02's third limb and the exemption is not enforceable. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease provision, or an unconscionable settlement in which a party "waives or agrees to forego a claim or right under sections 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6". Posting house rules is fine and is worth doing - hours, no glass, no unaccompanied children under {{pool_minimum_age}}, no more than {{pool_guest_limit}} guests per unit - and the clause that makes pool access a privilege you grant rather than a right the tenant has is in the other-landlord-facilities row. Rules and records are your defence. A waiver is not.

title: No Tenant Right to a Window Air Conditioner, and No Disclosure If You Ban Them
bodyText:
A few states now give tenants an affirmative right to install a portable or window cooling device and require a lease that restricts window units to say so. Washington is the clearest example. North Dakota has neither side of that: no tenant right to install a portable or window cooling device, and no requirement that your lease disclose or justify a restriction on them.

Start with what North Dakota does not require of you. Cooling is not a habitability duty here. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(f) lists running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat — cooling is not in it. So you are under no obligation to air-condition a dwelling in North Dakota, however hot the summer. But read § 47-16-13.1(1)(d) before you relax: you must maintain in good and safe working order and condition all "electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord." The trigger is supply. If you supply air-conditioning — central, a through-wall unit, or a window unit you provided — you must keep it in good and safe working order, and a lease sentence disclaiming that duty will not help you, because a lease sentence is not how that duty moves. In anything other than a single-family residence, § 47-16-13.1(5) lets a tenant take on specified repairs or maintenance tasks only by a separate writing signed by the parties, made in good faith and supported by adequate consideration.

Now the tenant's side. Because North Dakota grants no installation right, you may restrict or prohibit tenant-installed window and portable units — but only by saying so in the lease or the rules, because nothing in the statute prohibits a tenant from installing one. If your lease is silent, your position rests on the general provisions, and they are thinner than landlords expect: § 47-16-13.2(6) stops a tenant from deliberately or negligently damaging the premises, § 47-16-13.2(5) requires reasonable use of the facilities and appliances, and § 47-16-10 makes the tenant repair deteriorations caused by their own ordinary negligence. Those reach a unit that falls out, leaks or overloads a circuit. They do not reach a competently installed window unit you simply did not want.

There is also a removal right you should know about, because it decides who owns the unit. Under N.D.C.C. § 47-06-04 a tenant may remove from the premises, at any time during the continuance of the term, anything affixed for the purpose of trade, manufacture, ornament or domestic use, if the removal can be effected without injury to the premises, unless the thing has become an integral part of the premises by the manner in which it is affixed. A window air conditioner is domestic use and is normally removable without injury, so it stays the tenant's to take. Note the timing words: that right runs during the term. The same section's opening rule is that where a person affixes their property to another's land without an agreement permitting removal, the thing affixed belongs to the owner of the land unless the owner chooses to require its removal — so a unit abandoned in place after the term may become yours, or you may require the tenant to take it out.

What to do: decide your policy and write it down, because silence favours the tenant on installation and favours argument on everything else. If you allow window units, say so and set conditions you can actually justify — proper brackets or a support, no damage to the frame, a drip arrangement, removal at the end of the term, and restoration of any damage, which § 47-16-10 already backs. If you prohibit them, say that plainly and offer an alternative such as floor-standing units, since a flat ban with nothing else may push a tenant toward an unsafe self-installed fix. State separately and explicitly whether you supply any cooling equipment and, if so, which, because that sentence is what determines your § 47-16-13.1(1)(d) maintenance exposure. Do not claim in the lease that North Dakota law gives the tenant a right to install a cooling device, or that it requires you to disclose a restriction — neither is true, and printing it creates expectations the statute does not support.

title: No Tenant Solar Right, and No Statute Voiding Solar Restrictions
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota gives a tenant no right to install or use a solar device at a rental property -- not a roof array, not a balcony or window panel, not a plug-in "balcony solar" unit, and not a battery. There is no notice-and-reasonable-restrictions procedure, no deadline for a landlord to respond, no landlord-of-more-than-four-units rule, and no future commencement date. A lease term prohibiting or conditioning a tenant solar installation is an ordinary lease term and it binds.

There is also no North Dakota statute voiding instrument restrictions on solar energy systems. That matters because North Dakota has twice made exactly that choice elsewhere: in the Condominium Ownership Act it voids deed covenants and association bylaws that prohibit or unreasonably restrict an electric vehicle charging station (§ 47-04.1-16(2)) and it bars a declaration, bylaw or other rule from prohibiting the display of political signs (§ 47-04.1-14). It has not done so for solar, in the condominium chapter or anywhere else, so a covenant, a declaration, a set of house rules or a lease term restricting solar equipment stands on ordinary contract and property principles.

What North Dakota does have is narrow and runs the other way. §§ 47-05-01.1 and 47-05-01.2 recognise a SOLAR EASEMENT: an easement for the exposure of a solar energy device to the direct rays of the sun must be created in writing and recorded like any other easement, and the instrument must state the vertical and horizontal angles in degrees, the terms on which it is granted or terminated, and any compensation provisions. A solar easement is a voluntary grant of an interest in land by the owner of the burdened property; it is not a right a tenant can create over the landlord's land or over a neighbour's, and it does nothing about restrictions on the equipment itself. For contrast, North Dakota wrote a whole chapter of property rights for wind -- ch. 17-04, wind option agreements, wind easements, limits on severance and lease termination -- and nothing equivalent for solar.

Two further default rules decide most disputes. Under § 47-06-04 a tenant may remove something affixed for trade, manufacture, ornament or domestic use only during the term, only if removal can be done without injury to the premises, and not if it has become an integral part of the premises by the manner in which it is affixed -- a panel left behind at the end of the term belongs to you, and a roof-mounted or hard-wired array may not be removable at all. And § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) with (3) makes applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety binding and controlling on you, while (1)(d) puts the electrical facilities you supply in your hands -- so a tenant's unapproved plug-in panel backfeeding your circuits is your code exposure, not just theirs.

What to do: require prior written approval for any solar or battery equipment, inside or out, including a plug-in device that uses the unit's own outlet, and make approval conditional on licensed installation, permits, insurance, and removal and restoration at the end of the term. The Public Service Commission's small power production rules, N.D. Admin. Code ch. 69-09-07, give a qualifying facility of "one hundred kilowatts or less" net energy billing and make it pay the interconnection costs the commission assesses; they say nothing about tenants or landlords, and nothing read exempts a tenant device from them. So before approving anything that feeds power back into the building's wiring, require written evidence of the electric utility's consent and of permitting. And a tenant battery has its own rule: N.D. Admin. Code § 24.1-06-01-40(4) says rooms, basements and attached garages "in which an energy storage system is installed must be protected by smoke alarms" powered from the premise wiring and interconnected.

title: There is no small-landlord exemption in North Dakota, and the fair-housing three-house carve-out is narrower than it looks
bodyText:
Default rule first, and it is the headline: North Dakota's landlord-tenant chapter has NO small-landlord exemption and no portfolio tiering at all. Chapter 47-16 contains not one numeric threshold and not one exemption provision. Whether you own one duplex or four hundred units, you owe the same habitability duties under § 47-16-13.1, the same security deposit rules under § 47-16-07.1 with the same treble-damages exposure in subsection (4), the same condition statement under § 47-16-07.2, the same notice rules under §§ 47-16-07, 47-16-15 and 47-16-06.1, and the same repair-and-deduct exposure under § 47-16-13. Do not import a small-landlord carve-out from another state's act; North Dakota has not adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and has no landlord-tenant non-waiver statute either.

What North Dakota does tier is by PROPERTY TYPE, not by how much you own. § 47-16-13.1(4) lets the landlord and tenant of a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant perform the landlord's duties in subdivisions (e) and (f) of subsection 1 — waste receptacles and removal, and running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat — plus specified repairs, maintenance, alterations and remodelling. § 47-16-13.1(5), for "any dwelling unit other than a single-family residence", reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" and does NOT mention (e) or (f) at all, and it requires good faith plus "a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration", that the work is not needed to cure a subdivision (e) failure, and that the agreement not diminish the landlord's obligation to other tenants. So in a multi-unit building the heat, hot water, water and refuse duties cannot be shifted to the tenant by any agreement. That turns on the building, not the portfolio.

The real portfolio thresholds in North Dakota are in the fair housing chapter, and they are the trap this topic exists to catch. § 14-02.5-09(1) exempts §§ 14-02.5-02 through 14-02.5-08 for "the sale or rental of a single-family house sold or rented by the owner", but ONLY if every limb is satisfied, and they are cumulative:
• the owner does not own more than three single-family houses at any one time, and holds no interest in, nor has reserved on their behalf, title to or any right to any part of the proceeds from the sale or rental of more than three single-family houses at any one time;
• "[i]n addition, the house must be sold or rented without the use of the sales or rental facilities or services of a licensed real estate broker, agent, or realtor, or of a person in the business of selling or renting dwellings, or of an employee or agent of any such broker, agent, realtor, or person; or the publication, posting, or mailing of a notice, statement, or advertisement prohibited by section 14-02.5-03" — read this as "without either", because the "or" follows "without". Using a letting agent forfeits the exemption, and so does a discriminatory advertisement; and
• the exemption "applies only to one sale or rental in a twenty-four-month period, if the owner was not the most recent resident of the house at the time of the sale or rental."
And watch the definition that sits underneath it. For this subsection a person is "in the business of selling or renting dwellings" if ANY of three things is true — three or more transactions as principal in the preceding twelve months; two or more as agent in the preceding twelve months, other than selling their own residence; OR being "the owner of any dwelling designed or intended for occupancy by, or occupied by, five or more families." Those limbs are alternatives, so owning a single five-plex makes you a person in the business, and the three-house exemption is gone even though you own one building.

Two other thresholds worth knowing:
• § 14-02.5-09(2) is the owner-occupied exemption: § 14-02.5-02 and §§ 14-02.5-04 through 14-02.5-08 do not apply to the rental of rooms or units in a dwelling "occupied by or intended to be occupied by not more than four families living independently of each other, if the owner maintains and occupies one of the living quarters as the owner's residence." Read the list of exempted sections carefully: § 14-02.5-03, the advertising and publication prohibition, is deliberately NOT in it. An owner-occupied fourplex is still bound by the advertising rule.
• § 47-10-28(1)(b) requires a mobile home park owner to designate an official local office "except if the mobile home park contains fewer than twenty-six lots". That carve-out excuses the office and nothing else — every other duty in § 47-10-28(1) applies to a park of any size.

What to do. (1) Stop looking for a small-landlord exemption from chapter 47-16; there is none, and assuming otherwise is the most expensive mistake on this page. (2) Before you rely on the § 14-02.5-09(1) three-house exemption, check all of it: the count, no agent, no prohibited advertisement, and the one-rental-in-twenty-four-months limit. If you use a property manager — and most owners reading this do — you are outside it. (3) Count families, not buildings: one five-plex puts you "in the business". (4) If you own an owner-occupied fourplex, you may rely on § 14-02.5-09(2) for the rental decisions but never for your advertising. (5) Treat these exemptions as the narrow things they are and comply anyway; the cost of compliance is far below the cost of a § 14-02.5-39 civil action or a department charge.

title: No Possession Bond: Nobody Posts Security to Win or Keep Possession in North Dakota
bodyText: The default rule is that a North Dakota eviction is decided on the merits at a hearing set three to fifteen days after the summons issues, and no bond or security changes who holds the property in the meantime. Some states have a possession bond -- a landlord posts security and gets possession quickly unless the tenant posts a counter-bond, sometimes coupled with a confessed judgment at the end of the term. North Dakota has no such procedure. There is no possession bond, no forthcoming bond, no undertaking a landlord posts to accelerate turnover, and no bond a tenant posts to stay in place. The only thing that can delay turnover is section 47-32-04's hardship stay of the special execution, up to five days, and that is granted on a showing of substantial hardship, not on money -- the tenant posts nothing for it, and it is unavailable where the judgment rests in whole or in part on a disturbance of the peace. Do not write a bond or security-for-possession term into your lease: there is no statute for it to operate under, section 9-08-05 voids any stipulation that restricts a party from enforcing rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals except as specifically permitted by the laws of this state, and a lease term conditioning a tenant's defence of the case on posting money is squarely the kind of restriction that section is aimed at. Budget for the hearing, not for a bond.

title: No duty to test a private well or give a North Dakota tenant the results - but you must still supply running water
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a landlord to test a private well serving a rental dwelling, to test it on any schedule, to test for any particular contaminant, or to give a tenant a copy of the results. There is no state well-water disclosure, no required sampling interval, no certified-laboratory requirement for a private well and no tenant remedy keyed to water quality. "Private well", "well water", "potable", "nitrate", "coliform" and "cistern" return nothing in any statute chapter searched.

What North Dakota does impose is a supply duty, not a quality duty. 47-16-13.1(1)(f) requires the landlord to "supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat", subject to three exceptions: the building is not required by law to be equipped for the purpose, the heat or hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection, or the water or heat is unavailable because of a public utility supply failure. None of those exceptions fits a private well that the landlord controls, so running water from a well is squarely the landlord's obligation. And the duty cannot be shifted in a multi-unit building: 47-16-13.1(4) lets the landlord and tenant of a single-family residence agree in writing in good faith that the tenant perform the duties in subdivisions e and f, but 47-16-13.1(5), which governs "any dwelling unit other than a single-family residence", reaches only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling and does not mention subdivision f at all. Water quality is reachable through 47-16-13.1(1)(b) as well - repairs necessary to keep the premises "in a fit and habitable condition" - and if you do not act after notice, 47-16-13 gives the tenant uncapped repair-and-deduct, recovery in any other lawful manner, or the right to vacate and stop paying rent.

The state well statutes point at the driller, not at you: 23.1-01-16, "Standards for well drilling and installation of water well pumps, pitless units, and monitoring wells - Reports required", and 61-03-27, "Requirements for firms engaged in water well work, installation of water well pumps and pitless units, monitoring well work". The Safe Drinking Water Act is ch. 61-28.1 and it is a public-water-system regime - approval of water systems (61-28.1-04), variances (61-28.1-05), onsite inspection (61-28.1-06), certification of laboratories (61-28.1-07) - not a private-well regime. But watch its threshold: a 'public water system' is any system piping water for human consumption that 'has at least fifteen service connections or regularly serves at least twenty-five individuals', and whoever owns or operates one is a 'supplier of water' (61-28.1-02(5), (6)). A well serving a large apartment complex or a mobile home park can cross that line, and then the Act and the department's rules apply to you. The one drinking-water standard aimed at an accommodation provider is 23-09-10, in the Food and Lodging Establishments chapter, which does not cover ordinary residential rentals. Those sections were read: 23.1-01-16 makes well construction and pump installation comply with the Department of Environmental Quality's rules, and none of these chapters mentions a landlord, lease or tenant.

What to do: if the dwelling is on a private well, test it voluntarily before each tenancy and keep the results - a nitrate or coliform problem is a habitability failure under 47-16-13.1(1)(b) whether or not a statute names it, and the tenant's remedy for an unrepaired dilapidation is uncapped. Give the tenant the results; nothing requires it and nothing forbids it, and it is far cheaper than a repair-and-deduct dispute. Do not promise state-standard compliance you cannot verify, and do not shift well testing or treatment to a tenant in a multi-unit building, because 47-16-13.1(5) does not allow the water duty to move. The Department of Environmental Quality's well-construction and public-water-system rules, and municipal ordinances and county health regulations: check them if your well serves fifteen or more connections or twenty-five or more people.

title: Move-In Repair Promises: No Required Form, But an Open-Ended Promise Is a Termination Right
bodyText:
The default rule in some states is regulatory: Wisconsin, for example, requires a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve the unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date, and to be given before the lease is signed. North Dakota has no equivalent. There is no statute requiring a repair promise to be written, no required completion date, no timing rule about when the promise must be made, and no disclosure form.

But do not read that as freedom, because North Dakota attaches a serious consequence to a promise you do not keep. Under N.D.C.C. § 47-16-17(1) the tenant may terminate the lease before the end of the term when the lessor "does not fulfill the lessor's obligations, if any, within a reasonable time after request, as to placing and securing the lessee in the quiet possession of the property leased, or putting it into a good condition, or repairing it." Read the three words that matter: "obligations, if any." That provision does not create the obligation — your promise does. So a casual assurance that you will put the unit into good condition becomes an obligation whose breach lets the tenant walk away from the whole term, and because you never fixed a date, the only yardstick is "a reasonable time after request," which a court decides after the fact.

Separately, and whether or not you promised anything, § 47-16-13 lets a tenant who has given you notice of dilapidations you ought to repair, and waited a reasonable time, repair the premises and deduct the expense from rent, recover the expense from you in any other lawful manner, or vacate and be discharged from further payment of rent and from performing the lease's other conditions. A broken move-in promise and a neglected repair therefore run on two separate tracks, and both are open to the tenant without going to court first.

What to do: write down every repair, cleaning, painting or improvement you have agreed to do, each with a specific completion date, and have both parties sign it. North Dakota does not make you do this, but it is the only way to convert an open-ended "reasonable time" into a date you control, and it is your evidence that you performed. Add a sentence stating that no promises to clean, repair, decorate or improve have been made other than those listed. Then actually calendar the dates — an unperformed written promise is worse than none, because it proves both the obligation and the deadline. Avoid blanket language like "Landlord will put the unit in good condition," which imports § 47-16-17(1)'s termination right with no boundary at all.

title: North Dakota has no Proposition-65-style chemical warning for rentals - do not copy California's sign
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has nothing resembling California's Proposition 65. There is no list of chemicals "known to the state to cause cancer" or reproductive harm, no agency charged with maintaining one, no duty to warn a tenant or a visitor about chemical exposure, no posted-sign requirement at a residential rental, no safe-harbour warning text and no private right of action or bounty provision. The phrase "known to the state to cause" appears nowhere in the North Dakota Century Code. "Carcinogen" appears in no North Dakota statute chapter; in the 2025 session laws it appears only in a reference to the federal EPA's carcinogenicity classification for pesticides. The North Dakota statutes do not use the term "reproductive harm" at all.

This matters because the Proposition 65 sign is one of the most-copied pieces of lease boilerplate in the country, and in North Dakota it is pure decoration with a downside. Printing it suggests to the tenant that a state chemical-warning regime exists, invites argument that you admitted a known hazard you then failed to abate, and sits oddly beside the duties you really do have under 47-16-13.1(1)(a) to (d). A waiver of Proposition 65 rights is worse than useless: a waiver of a rule North Dakota does not have is empty, and it tells the tenant they gave something up.

Where North Dakota does use conspicuous-warning language, it is about something else entirely, and each instance is worth knowing so you do not mistake one for a chemical warning: 47-16-07.3 lets a landlord's notice of intent to enter be given "by posting the notice in a conspicuous place in or about the dwelling unit"; 47-17-02 lets a notice to remove from the premises be served "by affixing it on a conspicuous part of the premises"; 47-32-02 allows the eviction notice to be posted conspicuously; ch. 47-15.1 requires clear and conspicuous boldfaced ten-point disclosures in a consumer rental-purchase agreement, which is a goods transaction and not a lease of real property; and 47-18-05.1 requires the homestead-exemption waiver notice in a mortgage to be "printed in a conspicuous manner". All of those are service and contract-form rules. None is a health or chemical warning.

What to do: delete any Proposition 65 or chemical-exposure warning from a North Dakota lease. If there is a real known hazard in the unit, deal with it as a repair under 47-16-13.1(1)(b) and record the condition in the 47-16-07.2 condition-of-premises statement, and disclose it in plain words because it is the right thing to do, not because a statute compels it. This is an absence in the North Dakota statutes. Occupational chemical-hazard rules exist federally for workplaces, which a rental property is not.

title: No North Dakota statement of the property-tax portion of rent, and the tax disclosures it has are a seller's
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota requires no statement to a tenant of how much of the rent is attributable to property taxes or special assessments - not annually, not each July, not on a rent change, and not in the lease. There is no tax-component-of-rent statement, no tax-increase pass-through notice, and no renter's property tax statement duty on a landlord in the North Dakota statutes.

The trap here is the same one that catches the other disclosure topics. North Dakota's property-related tax and assessment disclosures run from a seller to a buyer. N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.3, headed "Required disclosures - Seller to provide" and created in 2025, makes the seller of a property subject to a homeowners' association or condominium project disclose in writing, by a mutually agreed date or within ten days of executing the agreement to sell, "the amount of the periodic common expense assessment, maintenance fees, or other charges and any unpaid common expenses or special assessments currently due and payable from the seller" and "the amount of approved special assessments". That is a seller's duty to a prospective buyer, and the sibling radon provision at 47-10-02.2(1)(a) defines a buyer as a person acquiring or acquiring the right to acquire title. A tenant is not a buyer. Do not read 47-10-02.3 as a landlord duty. N.D.C.C. 47-04.1-13 likewise just levies real property taxes and special assessments on each condominium unit separately; it says nothing about telling anyone.

Two related points you may be looking for. North Dakota bans local rent control: N.D.C.C. 47-16-02.1 says a political subdivision "may not enact, maintain, or enforce an ordinance or resolution that would have the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged for leasing private residential or commercial property". So there is no rent regulation whose tax component a statute would make you itemise. And if you want to pass a tax increase through mid-tenancy, the mechanism is not a disclosure, it is N.D.C.C. 47-16-07: in a month-to-month tenancy you may change the terms effective at the end of the month on at least thirty days' written notice, and in a park N.D.C.C. 47-10-28(7) requires ninety days' notice before any rent increase takes effect in a month-to-month arrangement.

What to do: do not print a property-tax-portion-of-rent statement as a statutory requirement. If you want the right to pass through a tax or assessment increase during a fixed term, that must be a negotiated term of the lease and the library's rent and escalation rows govern how to write it - and remember that a fixed-sum charge for a future event runs into N.D.C.C. 9-08-04, which voids an amount of damages determined in anticipation of a breach except where actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. Charge the actual increase, documented, rather than a round number.

title: North Dakota requires no recycling notice to tenants -- but it does make you provide waste receptacles and arrange removal, and that duty is hard to shift
bodyText:
Default rule: North Dakota imposes no duty on a landlord to tell tenants where or how to recycle. There is no counterpart to the Oregon provision, no required notice, no required recycling container, and no statute making recycling a tenant obligation. The word "recycling" appears in the Century Code only in connection with medical equipment reuse by state agencies, onsite wastewater recycling, oilfield special-waste recycling facilities, municipal waste-reduction public education materials, and renewable and recycled energy credits -- never in a landlord-tenant context.

The duty North Dakota does impose, and it is the one to get right. Under N.D.C.C. sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(e) a landlord of a residential dwelling unit must "[p]rovide and maintain appropriate receptacles and conveniences for the removal of ashes, garbage, rubbish, and other waste incidental to the occupancy of the dwelling unit and arrange for their removal." That is both halves: the receptacles AND the arranging of collection. It is implied into every residential lease and you do not need to print it.

Shifting it to the tenant is harder than most landlords assume. Sec. 47-16-13.1(4) lets the landlord and tenant of a SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE agree in writing, entered into in good faith, that the tenant perform the duties in subdivisions (e) and (f) -- so for a single-family house you can put the bins and the hauler contract on the tenant. For anything else you cannot. Sec. 47-16-13.1(5), which governs "any dwelling unit other than a single-family residence", reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" and does not list subdivision (e) at all; it then adds that even a permitted agreement must be in a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration, must not cover work needed to cure a subdivision (e) failure, and must not diminish your obligation to other tenants. And sec. 47-16-13.1(6) forbids making the tenant's performance of that separate agreement a condition of any obligation under the rental agreement. So in a duplex or an apartment building, waste receptacles and removal stay yours.

What the tenant does owe. Sec. 47-16-13.2(3) requires the tenant to "[p]eriodically remove all ashes, garbage, rubbish, and other waste from the tenant's dwelling unit, and dispose of them in a clean and safe manner" -- the tenant takes the rubbish out, you provide somewhere for it to go and have it collected. If you fail: sec. 47-16-13(1) lets the tenant arrange removal and deduct the cost from rent, or recover it, or vacate and be discharged from further rent, with damages under sec. 47-16-13.5 and attorney's fees under sec. 47-16-13.6.

Mobile home parks. Sec. 47-10-28(3) requires thirty days' advance written notice of any change to park rules, and then -- for an ordinary rule change -- written notice of non-compliance plus three months to remedy or vacate before you may start an eviction. A new recycling or waste-sorting rule falls under that, so you cannot impose one and evict on it quickly. Sec. 47-10-28(4) gives a shorter path for rules addressing sanitation and safety concerns: thirty days' advance written notice. A violation draws a civil penalty of at least $2,500 under sec. 47-10-28(12) and bars the eviction under sec. 47-32-01.1.

What to do. Do not print a recycling notice as though North Dakota required one. If your municipality runs a recycling programme, tell tenants about it in the move-in packet or the house rules as a convenience, not as a statutory disclosure -- local ordinances vary and the duty, if any, is the city's rule and not state law. Make sure you are actually meeting sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(e): adequate bins, in a serviceable condition, with a collection arrangement in place. If you want a tenant to handle waste removal, do it only in a single-family house and only in a good-faith written agreement, and check your municipality's rules first.

title: A North Dakota Tenant Has No Right to Pay Up and Stay -- But Watch What Accepting Rent Does
bodyText: The default rule is that once an eviction ground exists in North Dakota, paying does not undo it. There is no statutory redemption, no reinstatement right and no deadline -- forty-eight hours before the execution or any other -- by which a tenant can pay the arrears and keep the tenancy. The three days' written notice of intention to evict under section 47-32-02 is a notice of intention, not an invitation to cure, and section 47-32-01(4) makes the action maintainable once rent is unpaid for three days after it is due. Nothing obliges you to accept a late payment, from the tenant or from a charity or a government agency on the tenant's behalf, and no statute dictates how a payment may be tendered. The word redemption does appear in section 47-32-01(5), but read it carefully: it is about possession held after a judicial sale and after 'the expiration of the time fixed by law for redemption' -- mortgage and execution-sale redemption, which belongs to the owner, not the tenant. HERE IS THE TRAP, and it is the whole practical point of this topic. North Dakota regulates nothing about partial rent, has no mandated reservation-of-rights wording for a receipt, and gives you no safe-harbour language -- but section 47-16-06 says that if a residential lessee remains in possession after the lease expires and the lessor accepts rent, the parties are PRESUMED to have renewed the lease as a month-to-month tenancy. So accepting money after the term has ended can hand the tenant a fresh tenancy even though it cannot redeem a defaulted one. If you take a payment while an eviction is pending or contemplated, take it in writing, state what it is applied to and state that you do not waive the eviction. North Dakota will not supply that wording for you, so the lease and the receipt have to.

title: No religious or cultural display right in North Dakota -- and the fair-housing limit that still binds you
bodyText:
THE DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota gives a residential tenant NO statutory right to display a religious or cultural object on, at or in the dwelling, and it places NO statutory limit on a landlord's rule about one. There is no mezuzah statute, no religious-object statute, no cultural-display statute, and nothing resembling any of them in North Dakota's landlord-tenant law. In North Dakota's statutes, the only provision using the vocabulary of this topic -- religious display, religious object, religious symbol, cultural display, cultural symbol, mezuzah, crucifix, wreath, doorpost, doorframe -- is N.D.C.C. s 15.1-06-17.1 'Religious objects or documents - Display', which is a PUBLIC SCHOOL statute in the education title. It has nothing to do with rentals.

AND THE WAIVER WARNING THAT GOES WITH THAT. Because North Dakota gives the tenant no display right, a clause in which the tenant 'waives any right to display religious or cultural items' is waiving a right North Dakota does not confer. That waiver is EMPTY, not lawful -- and printing it tells your tenant they gave up something they never had, which reads badly, invites a dispute about religion that you do not want, and achieves nothing a plain rule would not.

SO YOU ARE FREE TO SET A DISPLAY RULE -- SUBJECT TO ONE REAL LIMIT, WHICH IS FAIR HOUSING. s 14-02.5-02(2): 'A person may not discriminate against an individual in the TERMS, CONDITIONS, OR PRIVILEGES of sale or rental of a dwelling or in providing services or facilities in connection with a sale or rental of a dwelling because of race, color, RELIGION, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin, or status with respect to marriage or public assistance.' A lease term IS a term or condition of rental. So:
- A rule that singles out religious items -- 'no religious objects on doors' -- is a condition of rental drawn on the ground of religion, and it is the clearest way to lose a fair-housing complaint on this topic.
- A NEUTRAL rule applied neutrally is on far safer ground: 'no items affixed to the exterior of the entry door' applied to a wreath, a flag, a sports pennant and a mezuzah alike is a rule about doors, not about religion.
- Applying a neutral rule SELECTIVELY is the trap. Permitting Christmas wreaths every December while refusing a mezuzah is religion-based in operation whatever the rule says on paper, and that is how these cases are actually proved.
s 14-02.5-45(2) adds that 'It is a discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with any individual in the exercise or enjoyment of ... any right granted or protected by this chapter', and s 14-02.5-45(1) makes intimidation by force or threat of force because of religion a CLASS A MISDEMEANOR. Do not let a display dispute escalate.
Note which chapter to cite. North Dakota's fair-housing law is CHAPTER 14-02.5, not the Human Rights Act in chapter 14-02.4 -- all three of chapter 14-02.4's housing sections were repealed while keeping their headings, so citing them for a housing duty is a known error.

THE CONSTITUTION WILL BE QUOTED AT YOU, AND IT DOES NOT APPLY. N.D. Const. art. I, s 3: 'The free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession and worship, without discrimination or preference shall be forever guaranteed in this state.' That restrains GOVERNMENT. A private landlord's lease is not state action, so art. I, s 3 does not void your display rule. (A HOUSING AUTHORITY or other public landlord is in a different position and needs separate advice.) What DOES bind you is s 14-02.5-02(2) above -- a statute, not the constitution.

TWO MORE SECTIONS THAT ACTUALLY BEAR ON THIS. s 47-06-04 gives a North Dakota tenant a statutory right to REMOVE anything the tenant affixed 'for the purpose of trade, manufacture, ORNAMENT, or domestic use' at any time during the term, if it can be done without injury to the premises and it has not become an integral part of them. That cuts in your favour on this topic: a tenant's affixed ornament remains the tenant's to take, which is a reason to let it stay up and a reason your rule should require restoration rather than forbid attachment outright. And s 47-16-27 ('Right of tenant') ends: 'The tenant has no rights to the property other than such as are given the tenant by the agreement or instrument by which the tenant's tenancy is acquired or by the provisions of this section.' In North Dakota the lease is the measure of the tenant's rights in the premises -- which is the statutory reason your display rule works, and the reason it has to be IN the lease.

WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. (1) Write a NEUTRAL display rule about surfaces and methods -- what may be attached, where, and how -- and never about subject matter, faith or culture. (2) Put it in the WRITTEN lease: s 47-32-01(8) makes only 'a material term of the written lease agreement' an eviction ground. (3) Apply it the same way to every tenant, every time, and keep a record of how you applied it. (4) Expect to grant an accommodation on request where refusing would single out a faith, and grant it in writing. (5) Do not print a waiver of a religious display right -- there is nothing to waive. (6) Do not attach a fixed fine: s 9-08-03 makes contractual penalties void, flatly; charge actual restoration cost instead. (7) In a MOBILE HOME PARK, a new or changed display rule is a rule modification under s 47-10-28 -- thirty days' advance written notice, and three months to remedy or vacate before eviction for a rule not addressing sanitation and safety, with a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 under s 47-10-28(12).

title: No City Can Cap Your Rent
bodyText: North Dakota forbids a political subdivision to enact, maintain or enforce an ordinance or resolution that would have the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged for leasing private residential or commercial property (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-02.1). The ban is on the effect, not the label, so a measure that caps increases or ties rent to a formula is reached whatever it is called. One carve-out: the section does not impair a political subdivision's right to manage and control residential property in which it holds a fee title interest - so a city may set rents in housing it owns. There is no state rent cap either, and no limit on how much or how often you may raise the rent; what you do have to observe is the notice rule for changing the terms of a month-to-month tenancy.

title: The Two Situations Where North Dakota Stops You Collecting Rent - and a Third If Your Property Taxes Go Unpaid
bodyText: The default rule in North Dakota is that rent stays due. There is no licensing or registration condition on collecting residential rent, no rule that a defective notice bars a rent demand, and nothing that stops you suing for rent after an eviction -- section 47-16-13.7 says the opposite, that a lessee evicted according to law is liable for rent during the remainder of the term, subject to your duty to mitigate. But there are two real bars, and the first is easy to walk into. One: double letting. Under section 47-16-26, someone who rents part of a room for a dwelling is entitled to the whole room notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, the first person you rented any part of it to is entitled to possession of the whole room for the term agreed, and -- this is the sting -- 'Every tenant in the building under the same landlord is relieved from all obligation to pay rent to the landlord while such double letting of any room continues.' Not just the tenants in that room. Every tenant in the building. Two: domestic-violence termination. Under section 47-16-17.1 a tenant who terminates for domestic violence owes rent for the full month of termination plus an additional amount equal to one month's rent, subject to your duty to mitigate, and is then 'relieved of any other contractual obligation for payment of rent or any other charges for the remaining term of the lease'. That relief is conditional: subsection 7 requires the extra month to be paid on or before termination for it to apply, and subsection 6 preserves liability for rent already delinquent before termination. For mobile home parks there is a related but different exposure: a violation of section 47-10-28 is a defence to the EVICTION under section 47-32-01.1, and the court may not order eviction if it finds one -- but that is a bar on possession, not on rent, and section 47-10-28(14) expressly requires a park tenant who has commenced an action to keep paying rent. Three: unpaid property taxes. If taxes or special assessments on a rent-producing property have been delinquent for more than twelve months, the county treasurer may petition the district court, and must if the county commissioners direct, for an order that the rents be paid to the treasurer (N.D.C.C. § 57-21-01). The petition is served on you and the tenant (§ 57-21-02). After a hearing the court may order the tenant to pay all rent due or to become due to the treasurer, who applies it to the taxes, penalties, interest and costs; the court may let you keep up to half (§ 57-21-03). A tenant under such an order must pay the treasurer, on pain of contempt (§ 57-21-04). The treasurer gives the tenant a receipt, and 'the payment thereof and the receipt therefor constitutes a complete defense to a suit by any person for such rent' (§ 57-21-05). So rent paid under the order is gone from you. Keep your property taxes current; if an order is made, credit every receipted payment rather than suing the tenant for it.

title: Raising the rent in North Dakota: the thirty-day change-of-terms notice, and the ninety-day rule that is mobile-home-park only
bodyText:
Default rule: rent is a term of the lease, so in North Dakota you raise it the way you change any other term -- there is no separate rent-increase notice statute for conventional rentals. In a tenancy from month to month you may change the terms of the lease, rent included, to take effect at the expiration of the month by giving written notice at least thirty days before the end of that month, served in any reasonable manner that actually informs the tenant; if the tenant holds the premises past month end, the rent stated in the notice becomes part of the lease (N.D.C.C. Section 47-16-07). A tenant who receives that notice may instead end the tenancy at the same month end on at least twenty-five days' notice (Section 47-16-15(3)), so build a vacancy into your plan.

What North Dakota does not give you: no statutory notice period for raising rent during a fixed term, so a mid-term increase is available only if the lease itself carries an escalation term; no nonrenewal-notice duty separate from the ordinary one-calendar-month termination notice; and no price-gouging, emergency-pricing or rent-freeze statute reaching dwelling-unit rent during or after a declared emergency.

The one express rent-increase rule in the North Dakota statutes is a mobile-home-park rule, and it is widely misquoted as general law -- do not apply it to an apartment. In a park, a month-to-month tenancy agreement must provide the tenant a minimum of ninety days' notice before any rent increase is effective, and a person who purchases an existing park may not increase the monthly rental obligation for six months if the rent was increased within the sixty days before the purchase closed (Section 47-10-28(7)); a violation carries a civil penalty of not less than two thousand five hundred dollars (Section 47-10-28(12)) and is a defence to an eviction (Section 47-32-01.1).

What to do: for a conventional rental, serve a dated written change-of-terms notice at least thirty days before the end of a month and keep proof of service; for a park, serve ninety days and check the purchase freeze first. Do not look for a local cap -- Section 47-16-02.1 forbids a political subdivision from enacting anything with the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged.

title: Eviction Counterclaims Are Barred Except as a Setoff, and No Rent Goes Into Court
bodyText:
In many states an eviction defendant who wants to raise a habitability counterclaim must first pay the disputed rent into a court registry, and a long adjournment or a jury demand can trigger the same requirement. North Dakota has no rent-into-court mechanism of any kind, and it does not need one, because it restricts the counterclaim itself.

N.D.C.C. § 47-32-04 does two things. First, an eviction action "cannot be brought in a district court in connection with any other action, except for rents and profits accrued or for damages arising by reason of the defendant's possession." Second, and this is the part that matters here: "No counterclaim can be interposed in such action, except as a setoff to a demand made for damages or for rents and profits." So a tenant cannot turn your eviction into a habitability trial. If you sue only for possession, there is no demand for damages or rents for a counterclaim to set off against, and the tenant's habitability complaints have no place in the action at all. If you do join a claim for accrued rents and profits or for damages arising from the possession, you open the door — but only to the extent of a setoff against that demand, not to an affirmative recovery.

That is a strategic choice you make when you file. Joining your money claim to the eviction is convenient, but it is also what lets the tenant raise the condition of the premises as a setoff. Keeping the eviction to possession alone and suing separately for the money keeps the two apart, at the cost of a second proceeding.

Nothing requires the tenant to deposit or pay rent anywhere in order to defend. There is no court registry for rent, no escrow, no bond, and no deposit condition attached to a jury demand, a continuance or an adjournment. If the court rules for you it must enter judgment for immediate restitution of the premises, though on the tenant's showing that immediate restitution would work a substantial hardship on them or their family the court may stay the special execution for a reasonable period not exceeding five days — unless the eviction judgment rests in whole or in part on a disturbance of the peace, in which case no stay is available.

There is one keep-paying rule in North Dakota and it is not a court deposit. For mobile home parks, § 47-10-28(14) provides that if an action between a landlord and tenant under that section is commenced, "the tenant shall continue paying rent and comply with all park rules and regulations in effect at the time the action was commenced." The rent continues to come to you, not to a court. That subsection also bars you, while the action is pending, from modifying park rules, modifying the tenant's rental arrangement, increasing the rent, or terminating the lease without cause.

What to do: decide before you file whether to join your money claim, because that decision controls whether habitability can be raised at all. Do not draft a lease clause requiring the tenant to deposit rent with the court or a third party as a condition of defending or counterclaiming — North Dakota provides no such procedure, and § 9-08-05 makes void any stipulation restricting a party from enforcing their rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals.

title: Rent Receipts: Give One When the Tenant Asks (N.D.C.C. § 9-12-22)
bodyText: North Dakota's landlord-tenant chapter says nothing about rent receipts, and the only receipt duty elsewhere in the property title belongs to the consumer rental-purchase chapter, which governs rent-to-own of personal property and not a dwelling lease. But the general contract chapter on extinguishing an obligation does: "A debtor has a right to require from the debtor's creditor a written receipt for any property delivered in performance of the debtor's obligation" (N.D.C.C. § 9-12-22). Paying rent is performance of the tenant's obligation, so if a tenant asks for a written receipt for a rent payment, give one. The right arises on the tenant's demand; the statute does not make you issue receipts unasked. There is no anti-waiver provision attached to it. North Dakota's general rule is that a party may waive the benefit of a code provision "unless such waiver would be against public policy" (§ 1-02-28), so a lease clause by which the tenant gives up receipts is not void on its face. Whether such a waiver offends public policy only a court could settle. It is not worth having either way: a receipt costs you nothing and is the only record either side can produce for a cash payment.

title: Rent reporting in North Dakota: no state rule either way, so the duties you must meet are federal
bodyText:
The default rule: North Dakota has no rent-reporting law in either direction. No provision in the North Dakota statutes requires a landlord of any size to offer positive rent reporting, or to carry an election or signature block in the lease for the tenant to opt in; none forbids a landlord from reporting rent payments to a credit bureau; none requires you to notify the tenant in writing before you report late or unpaid rent; and there is no state rent-reporting programme at all, so there is nothing a tenant could be required to join and nothing to protect them from being required to join. Several states have each of those rules. North Dakota has none of them.

What that means in practice is that the rules you must actually follow are federal. The duties of a furnisher of information to a consumer reporting agency — accuracy, investigating a dispute, and marking an account as disputed — come from the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, not from North Dakota law. Take them seriously and get advice before you start reporting, because the federal duties attach the moment you become a furnisher and they do not switch off because the state is silent.

Three North Dakota points that do bear on this.
1. Considering a credit history is expressly protected. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.4-17 makes it a discriminatory practice to deny credit or impose different credit terms on the protected grounds, 'except as permitted or required by the Equal Credit Opportunity Act [15 U.S.C. 1691]', and then says the section 'does not prohibit a party to a credit transaction from considering the credit history of a person or from taking reasonable action thereon'. So looking at credit is safe ground in North Dakota, whatever you decide about reporting.
2. Old evictions may lawfully vanish, which is a reason to keep your own records rather than rely on a bureau's. § 47-32-05, new on August 1, 2025, lets a person evicted for nonpayment of rent or damage who has resolved all those claims move to seal the court records seven years after the order was satisfied, if not evicted elsewhere during those seven years; and lets a tenant evicted because of a domestic violence incident move to seal on the assailant's conviction or on a disorderly conduct restraining order, sexual assault restraining order or domestic violence protection order.
3. You cannot charge for the payment method, which is where a reporting programme usually hides a fee. § 47-16-20.1, new on August 1, 2025, prohibits a fee for accepting cash, a check or a money order. And a flat 'credit reporting fee' or a fixed charge for a missed report is a contractual penalty: § 9-08-03 makes 'Penalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance' void outright, and § 9-08-04 voids a sum fixed in anticipation of a breach unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix.

What to do if you want to report. Decide whether you are reporting positive payments, negative ones, or both, and say so plainly in writing to the tenant before the first report — not because a North Dakota statute requires the notice, but because the federal accuracy and dispute duties are much easier to meet when the tenant knew and had a channel to object, and because an undisclosed negative report is the kind of thing § 51-15-02 reaches when it declares unlawful an act or practice that 'is unconscionable or which causes or is likely to cause substantial injury to a person which is not reasonably avoidable by the injured person'. Keep your own ledger and the deposit itemisation you already owe under § 47-16-07.1(3) — that, not a bureau file, is what you will produce if the report is challenged. Never report an amount that is in dispute without marking it as disputed. And do not promise the tenant a credit benefit you cannot deliver; the bureaus, not you, decide what they accept.

Mobile home parks: § 47-10-28 says nothing about credit reporting, but it does cap a park's monthly late fee at ten per cent of monthly rent and its daily late fee at five dollars under subsection 11, and a violation of the section carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and is a defence to an eviction under § 47-32-01.1. If your reporting programme is tied to late-fee accounting, that cap is the figure to build it on.

title: Is there a tax on residential rent in North Dakota, and may you add it to the rent?
bodyText: Default rule: rent in North Dakota is quoted, billed and collected as rent. Nothing in the landlord-tenant law adds a tax line to residential rent, and nothing in it tells you what to do about one, so the lease is where any tax charge has to come from. Ordinary residential rent is not taxed. The state sales tax reaches 'the leasing or renting of a hotel or motel room or other accommodations' at five percent (N.D.C.C. § 57-39.2-02.1(1)(e)). But it exempts accommodations 'occupied by the same person or persons for residential housing for periods of thirty or more consecutive days', and the same for a rented manufactured home (§ 57-39.2-04(22)). City and county lodging taxes, of up to two percent plus up to one percent more, reach only lettings 'for periods of fewer than thirty consecutive calendar days or one month' (§§ 40-57.3-01, 40-57.3-01.1, 11-09.2-01, 11-09.2-02). A home-rule city or county's own sales and use taxes must follow the state's taxable and exempt status, and an ordinance enacted after August 1, 2017 may not allow any tax its home-rule statute does not name (§§ 40-05.1-06(5), 11-09.1-05(5)). So a city cannot invent a tax on apartment rent. The risk case is the short stay: a nightly, weekly or under-thirty-day letting is taxable accommodation, and you are the 'retailer' who must collect and remit the tax (§ 57-39.2-01(22)). Ask the Office of State Tax Commissioner about permits before you let short-term. North Dakota has no statute banning a pass-through of a tax or putting the burden of proving one on you. If you do collect a tax, state it in the lease as a separate charge, name the tax and the authority imposing it, show it separately on every receipt and statement, and stop charging it the day the tax ends -- North Dakota gives you no statutory right to keep collecting a repealed tax and gives the tenant no statutory remedy either, so your lease and your records are the only thing standing between you and a dispute. Do not write the lease so the tenant owes 'rent plus any tax' open-endedly; state the tax by name or leave it out.

title: No statewide rental inspection law in North Dakota — and the lease cannot consent for the tenant
bodyText:
The default rule: there is no statewide rental inspection or rental licensing programme in the North Dakota statutes. No provision in the North Dakota statutes requires a residential rental dwelling to be inspected, licensed or certified before occupancy, and none creates a housing inspector, a rental registry or a certificate of occupancy for rental housing. Where rental inspection exists in North Dakota it is a municipal creation.

Two statutes still bind you. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes you 'Comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety' — that is how a city housing code becomes your lease obligation, enforceable by the tenant, without the code saying a word about leases. And § 47-16-13.2(1) makes the tenant 'Comply with all obligations primarily imposed upon tenants by applicable provisions of building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety' — so if your city's code puts an access or cooperation duty on the occupant, the tenant already owes it and your lease does not need to say so.

Now the question this topic really asks: can the lease itself authorise a housing inspector to enter, so the tenant must give access without separately consenting? Treat the answer as no, and plan around it. § 47-16-07.3 governs your entry, not an inspector's. Subsection 2 lets you enter 'for the purpose of inspecting the premises' during reasonable hours, in a reasonable manner, after notice identifying a time certain and with consent that is presumed if the tenant does not object. Its separate list of people you may bring in — 'actual or potential purchasers, insurers, mortgagees, real estate agents, tenants, workmen, or contractors' — is for exhibiting the unit and does not include a government inspector. More to the point, a public inspector's authority to enter an occupied home comes from the inspection law and from the occupant's own consent or a warrant; it is not something a private lease can hand over on the tenant's behalf. The statute that lets a city build such a programme says the same: under § 40-58-18(6)(c) a city's unfit-dwelling ordinance may let its officer 'enter any premises for the purpose of making examinations' with 'the least possible inconvenience to the persons in possession', and 'obtain an order for this purpose from a court' if entry is denied; § 40-58-18(10) lets a city set minimum standards for the use and occupancy of dwellings.

The cautious course. (1) Schedule the inspection with the tenant and give your own § 47-16-07.3 notice of a time certain for your own entry, in writing, keeping a copy. (2) Put a cooperation duty in the lease, not a consent waiver: the tenant will permit access for an inspection required by law and will not obstruct it. That is an enforceable lease covenant and, if breached, is the kind of thing that can amount to a substantial violation of the lease. (3) If the tenant refuses, do not force entry — tell the inspecting authority and let it use its own powers. (4) Never tell the tenant that signing the lease was their consent to a government inspection; in North Dakota that is not a right you can show a statute for, and asserting it invites the tenant to believe they gave up something they did not.

If the unit is a mobile home or in a park, there is more law and it is stricter. § 47-10-28(1)(a) requires the park owner to 'Obtain an annual license under section 23-10-03'. § 23-10-03(1) bars operating a park 'without first obtaining a license from the department', and under § 23-10-04 'The department must have access to and may inspect mobile home parks ... at reasonable times', on a complaint, a violation or a routine schedule. § 23-10-02.1 lets the department accept local inspection instead. So your park is licensed and inspectable, and note that a violation of § 47-10-28 itself carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and is a defence to an eviction under § 47-32-01.1.

title: Requiring renter's insurance in North Dakota: no statute helps you, and no statute stops you
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has no renter's-insurance law at all. So there is no statute requiring a tenant to carry insurance, none permitting it, none limiting the coverage or deductible you may require; no statutory advisory you must give stating that your policy will not cover the tenant's belongings; no flood-and-insurance notice before signing; and -- this is the important one -- no statute authorising you to buy a policy for a tenant who fails to provide proof and bill it on, and no statutory administrative fee for doing so.

Several states give landlords exactly that force-placement power with a capped admin fee. North Dakota does not, so you have only what the lease says, and three North Dakota rules shape what the lease may safely say.

First, charge actual cost and nothing more: penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (N.D.C.C. Section 9-08-03), and an advance fixing of damages is void unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (Section 9-08-04), so a round 'administrative fee' for placing coverage is the shape that gets struck while a pass-through of the premium you actually paid, with the invoice shown, is not.

Second, an unpaid insurance charge is not recoverable from the security deposit unless your lease makes it rent: the deposit may be applied only to damage from the tenant's pet or the negligence of the tenant or a guest, to any unpaid rent, and to cleaning and repairs that were the tenant's responsibility (Section 47-16-07.1(3)) -- and withholding deposit money without reasonable justification exposes you to treble damages (Section 47-16-07.1(4)).

Third, insurance is not a substitute for your own duties: a term exempting you from responsibility for your own violation of law, willful or negligent, is against the policy of the law (Section 9-08-02), so requiring the tenant's policy to cover conditions you are obliged to fix will not transfer that liability, and a court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision (Section 47-16-13.3).

What to do: use the library's tenant's-property-insurance clause, which already applies in North Dakota -- it states that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, sets a liability minimum, and lets you ask for evidence of coverage. Give the tenant a real deadline to produce the certificate, say in the lease that a lapse is a breach, and if you want the right to place coverage, say so expressly and limit the charge to the premium you actually pay, with no markup and no flat fee. Apply the requirement to every tenant the same way, since terms and conditions of a rental are covered by the fair housing law, and do not require liability insurance for an assistance animal.

title: No Dollar Cap on Repair-and-Deduct, and No Cost Threshold for the Tenant to Walk
bodyText:
In many states the tenant's self-help repair remedy comes with a ceiling — a flat dollar cap, or one month's rent, or a share of the annual rent — and a tenant can only terminate over a repair if the cost or the damage crosses some threshold. North Dakota has no ceiling and no threshold anywhere in its landlord-tenant law. That is the single most important thing to understand about repair exposure here.

N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13 says that if, within a reasonable time after notice from the tenant of dilapidations you ought to repair, you neglect to do so, the tenant may: repair the premises and deduct the expense of such repair from the rent; recover it in any other lawful manner from you; or vacate the premises, in which case the tenant "shall be discharged from further payment of rent or performance of other conditions." Notice what is absent. There is no dollar limit on "the expense of such repair." There is no requirement that the expense be reasonable in amount, no cap tied to rent, no requirement that the tenant get estimates or use a licensed contractor, no notice to you before the work, and no court approval. And the vacate option carries no cost threshold at all — the tenant does not have to show the repair was expensive, major, or uneconomic to fix. A neglected repair of any size, after notice and a reasonable time, can discharge the tenant from the rest of the term.

There is a second termination route with no cost threshold either. Under § 47-16-17(1) the tenant may terminate before the end of the term when you do not fulfil your obligations within a reasonable time after request as to putting the property into a good condition or repairing it. Section 47-16-17(2) adds the casualty route, and its test is about magnitude of loss rather than cost of repair: the tenant may terminate when the greater part of the property, or the part that was the material inducement to lease, perishes from any cause other than the tenant's ordinary negligence. Under § 47-16-14(4) the leasing terminates outright on destruction of the property.

The absence runs in your direction too, and this is where landlords are often surprised: North Dakota gives you no right to terminate instead of repairing because the repair is uneconomic. There is no provision letting you end a tenancy on the ground that the cost of putting the unit right exceeds its value, the rent, or any other figure. Your statutory exits are the ones in §§ 47-16-14 and 47-16-17, plus the eviction grounds in ch. 47-32 — none of which is cost-based.

What to do: fix things promptly, because the cheapest version of this risk is the repair itself. Once the tenant's reasonable time runs out you lose control of both the contractor and the price, and you may lose the rest of the term. Keep a dated repair log so "a reasonable time" is measured against your actual response, not the tenant's recollection. Do not write a lease term capping what a tenant may spend and deduct, or requiring your pre-approval or your chosen contractor as a condition of deducting: that limits a statutory remedy the legislature left uncapped, it is open to unconscionability review under § 47-16-13.3(1)(a), and a fixed-sum cap would separately have to survive § 9-08-03, under which penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void, and § 9-08-04, which voids damages fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix.

title: There Is No Rent Escrow in North Dakota, So No Exemption and No Exemption Notice
bodyText:
In rent-escrow states the machinery works like this: a tenant with a repair complaint pays rent into a court-held escrow account instead of to the landlord, the court supervises the repairs and releases the money, and certain landlords can claim an exemption from the whole scheme — usually by giving the tenant a prescribed notice that says so. North Dakota has none of this. There is no rent escrow, no court registry for rent, no court-supervised repair fund, no exemption from a scheme that does not exist, and therefore no exemption notice to give. Do not put one in your lease or your move-in packet: a notice claiming exemption from a non-existent remedy tells the tenant that such a remedy exists and that you were worried about it.

What North Dakota has instead is faster and operates entirely outside court. Under N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13, once the tenant has given you notice of dilapidations you ought to repair and a reasonable time has passed without your repairing them, the tenant may repair the premises and deduct the expense from rent, recover that expense from you in any other lawful manner, or vacate and be discharged from further payment of rent and from performing the lease's other conditions. None of those three requires a filing, a deposit, a hearing or a judge's permission.
