The practical consequence is the reverse of escrow: in an escrow state the disputed rent is preserved for you under court control, whereas in North Dakota the tenant simply spends it on the repair and hands you the invoice, or stops paying altogether by vacating.

The related point about litigation is worth knowing because landlords often expect a deposit requirement there too, and there is none. Section 47-32-04 provides that an eviction action cannot be brought in connection with any other action except for rents and profits accrued or damages arising by reason of the defendant's possession, and that no counterclaim can be interposed in such an action except as a setoff to a demand made for damages or for rents and profits. Nothing in it requires the tenant to pay or deposit rent anywhere in order to defend or to raise that setoff.

What to do: treat repairs as a cash-flow problem with no safety net. Respond to every notice promptly and document the date, because the only thing standing between you and an uncontrolled deduction is your own reasonable-time response. Keep the ability to pay for urgent repairs yourself, since you cannot force the dispute into an escrow process that would freeze the money. And do not draft around escrow — no exemption notice, no clause requiring the tenant to deposit disputed rent with a third party or a court, which would in any event run into § 9-08-05, voiding a contract stipulation that restricts a party from enforcing their rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals.

title: Repair Notice: Any Notice Starts the Clock, and the Clock Is "A Reasonable Time"
bodyText:
The default rule in many states is a statutory notice procedure: written notice, then a fixed number of days before the tenant's remedies open. North Dakota has the trigger but neither of the formalities. It fixes no number of days, and it does not require the tenant's notice to be in writing.

N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13 opens the tenant's remedies "if within a reasonable time after notice from the lessee of dilapidations which the lessor ought to repair the lessor neglects to do so." Read what that does and does not say. The notice must come from the lessee and must be of dilapidations you ought to repair — but the statute says "notice," not "written notice," and it says "a reasonable time," not thirty days or fourteen days or any other figure. Section 47-16-17(1) uses a different word again, allowing the tenant to terminate where you do not fulfil your obligations "within a reasonable time after request." And § 47-16-13.1(2) allows you "a reasonable time" to remedy noncompliance with subdivisions (b) through (f) of your habitability duties — pointedly not subdivision (a), code compliance, which gets no such grace.

So you have no statutory right to receive a written repair request, which means there is nothing for lease language to waive. You may certainly ask for written requests, and you should, because a dated written log is how you prove you responded within a reasonable time. What you should not assume is that a written-request clause converts § 47-16-13's statutory trigger into a writing requirement. The statute conditions the tenant's remedies on "notice from the lessee," and whether a lease term can add a condition the statute omits is unsettled in North Dakota; any such term is also open to review for unconscionability under § 47-16-13.3(1)(a). CAUTIOUS COURSE: treat any notice of a repairable condition as starting your reasonable time, however it reaches you — a phone call, a text, a message to your manager, or your own observation during an inspection. Respond and document; do not sit on an oral complaint waiting for a form.

If you operate a mobile home park there is one hard deadline, and it is short. Section 47-10-28(1)(e) requires you to acknowledge receipt of a tenant's inquiry or complaint about the park within two business days of receiving it. That is an acknowledgment duty, not a repair deadline, and breach exposes you to the § 47-10-28(12) civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and not more than the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs.

What to do: log every repair request on the day it arrives with the date, who reported it, how, and what you did; ask for written requests but accept and act on any notice; and never let a written-notice clause become the reason you delayed.

title: The complete list of what a North Dakota landlord must give or tell a tenant - and it is short
bodyText:
This row is the inventory. It is the single place to look for what North Dakota actually makes a residential landlord hand over or state, and the truth-in-renting, rights-responsibilities-guide and tenant-rights-statement rows all point here rather than repeating it.

Default rule first: North Dakota has not adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, has no landlord-tenant non-waiver statute, and has no omnibus required-disclosures section. There is no state-published pamphlet, guide, summary or tenant-rights statement that a landlord of ordinary rental housing must deliver, no signed acknowledgment that a statute conditions anything on, and no state form that must be the first page of a lease. Nothing in the North Dakota statutes prescribes a type size, a font, or a placement for anything in a residential lease.

What a North Dakota landlord of ordinary rental housing must give or state:
1. A condition statement, at signing. N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.2: "A landlord shall provide the tenant with a statement describing the condition of the facilities in and about the premises to be rented at the time of entering a rental agreement. The statement shall be agreed to and signed by the landlord and tenant." It is prima facie proof of the condition of the premises at the beginning of the agreement - which is as much your protection as the tenant's. This is the only document North Dakota makes every residential landlord hand over.
2. A stated notice requirement, with an initial line, if you want more than one month's notice from the tenant. N.D.C.C. 47-16-15(4): any agreement requiring a lessee to give notice exceeding one month from the end of a month must state the notice requirement and provide space for the lessee to initial next to it; if it is not initialled at signing, the tenant may terminate on the last day of a month with one calendar month's notice. This one genuinely has to be in the lease to work - the library has a lease clause stating the notice requirement with a space for the tenant's initials.
3. Thirty days' written notice of an automatic renewal provision, if you want to enforce one. N.D.C.C. 47-16-06.1: in a residential lease of a specified term of two months or more, the lessor may not enforce an automatic renewal clause unless the lessor notified the lessee in writing, delivered personally or by first-class mail, of the automatic renewal provision not less than thirty days before the current lease expires; without that notice the lease expires and converts to month to month.
4. Thirty days' written notice to change terms month to month. N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.
5. A deposit itemisation and written notice within thirty days after termination and delivery of possession, stating any amount still due or the refund due. N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.1(3) - and note subsection 4, treble damages for any deposit withheld without reasonable justification.
6. Notice of intent to enter at a time certain before entering. N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.3, which may be given by personal service, by posting in a conspicuous place in or about the dwelling unit for a reasonable period, or by any other method resulting in actual notice.
7. Termination and eviction notices. N.D.C.C. 47-17-01 and 47-17-02 for notice to remove from the premises, and 47-32-02 for the three-day notice of intention to evict, which is required only for grounds 4, 5, 6 and 8 of 47-32-01.

Mobile home parks carry a second, stricter layer. N.D.C.C. 47-10-28 adds, for a person that owns or purchases an existing park: the decision-maker's contact information (1)(c)(4)); written notice of a change of ownership within five business days (1)(d)); acknowledgment of a tenant inquiry or complaint within two business days (1)(e)); a copy of the existing lease terms and modifications within ten business days of a written request (1)(f)); the name, address and telephone number of the legal entity that owns the park (1)(g)); the telephone number of any existing property manager or designated site agent (1)(h)); thirty days' advance written notice of rule changes (subsections 3, 4 and 5); ninety days' notice of a rent increase in a month-to-month arrangement (subsection 7); access to the records of meter readings taken at the tenant's lot (subsection 8); a summary outlining the tenant's lease and the rights and obligations of the tenant and the park owner under state law (subsection 9); and, in a notice of intent to evict, clear boldfaced language stating verbatim "You do not have to vacate immediately. You have the right to remain until a court issues an eviction order." (subsection 10). A violation carries a civil penalty of not less than two thousand five hundred dollars under subsection 12, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, and is a defence to the eviction under N.D.C.C. 47-32-01.1.

The seller duties that are not yours. N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.1 ("Property disclosure - Requirements - Exceptions"), 47-10-02.2 (radon, with its prescribed capitalised warning) and 47-10-02.3 ("Required disclosures - Seller to provide", the association and condominium documents) all bind a seller and run to a buyer, and 47-10-02.2(1)(a) defines a buyer as a person acquiring or acquiring the right to acquire title. A tenant is not a buyer. The same is true of 47-33-04 (private transfer fee obligations, seller to purchaser) and 47-34-03 (closing agent to seller). Do not import any of them into a lease. The one qualification: if you grant the tenant an option to buy, the transaction may become a sale and these duties may then apply to you - get that reviewed before you sign.

What to do: build the lease pack around items 1 to 3, because those are the ones that fail if the paperwork is wrong - a condition statement signed by both parties, the initialled notice requirement if you want longer notice, and a calendared thirty-day automatic-renewal notice. Federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing is a separate federal duty and the library has its own row for it. Finally, this list is drawn from the statutes, and a local rental-licensing ordinance is the most likely place for a further disclosure.

title: No state rights-and-responsibilities guide in North Dakota - except in a mobile home park, where a summary is required and its contents are not specified
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota publishes no landlord-tenant rights and responsibilities guide that a landlord of ordinary rental housing must deliver before signing or at renewal, and requires no signed acknowledgment of one. There is no Delaware-style summary duty, no state agency charged with producing a guide, and no consequence attached to not giving one, because there is nothing to give. This is one of four topics that ask the same question at different scales. The full inventory of what a North Dakota landlord must give or tell a tenant is in the required-disclosures row ("The complete list of what a North Dakota landlord must give or tell a tenant - and it is short"); read that row rather than rebuilding the list. 

Mobile home parks are the real exception, and if you operate one this is a live duty with teeth. N.D.C.C. 47-10-28(9) says in full: "A mobile home park owner shall provide a tenant with a summary outlining the tenant's lease and the rights and obligations of the tenant and mobile home park owner under state law." That is North Dakota's only statutory rights-and-responsibilities summary duty, and the Legislative Council master index confirms it is the only tenant-rights provision in the entire Century Code. It is mandatory - "shall provide" - and a violation of any provision of 47-10-28 carries a civil penalty of not less than two thousand five hundred dollars and not more than the greater of ten thousand dollars or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, under subsection 12, and is a defence to the eviction under N.D.C.C. 47-32-01.1.

The difficulty is that the statute stops there. It does not say what the summary must contain, how long it must be, when it must be given, whether it must be in writing, whether a tenant must acknowledge it, or whether any agency publishes a form. No North Dakota statute or rule supplies any of that: chapter 23-10, which licenses parks, and the department's mobile home park rules (N.D. Admin. Code ch. 33-33-01) are silent on it, and no 2025 act added it. A park owner therefore cannot read the statute and know what satisfies it.

The cautious course, and what to do: treat subsection 9 as requiring a written document delivered at or before lease signing and again when the lease changes, and keep proof of delivery - a dated acknowledgment signed by the tenant, even though no statute requires one, because the penalty floor makes evidence of compliance worth more than the paperwork costs. Make the summary cover, at a minimum, the tenant's own lease terms and the rights and obligations in N.D.C.C. 47-10-28 itself - the designated and emergency telephone numbers and the decision-maker's contact details under subsection 1(c), the owning entity's name, address and telephone number under 1(g) and the manager's number under 1(h), the two-business-day complaint acknowledgment under 1(e), the right to a copy of the lease terms within ten business days of a written request under 1(f), the thirty-day rule-change notice and three-month remedy period under subsection 3, the ban on being made to sell the home to the park owner under subsection 2, the six-month rent freeze after a purchase and ninety days' notice of a rent increase under subsection 7, the utility rules and access to lot meter readings under subsection 8, the late fee caps under subsection 11, and the eviction protections in N.D.C.C. ch. 47-32 including the boldfaced notice language subsection 10 requires. Do not try to discharge the duty by printing a clause in the lease: the statute requires a summary of the lease and of state law, which a clause inside that same lease does not provide, and a court could readily hold that printing it in the document it is supposed to summarise is no summary at all. Chapter 23-10 adds one related duty: you must conspicuously post or distribute to each tenant a copy of the department's relevant rules and regulations, which the department provides free (N.D.C.C. § 23-10-10). That is a separate document from the subsection 9 summary.

title: No Duty to Disclose a Code Variance -- and the Underlying Code Duty Survives It
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a health- or sanitary-code variance to be given to tenants, attached to the rental agreement, posted, or even mentioned to an applicant, and no statute gives a tenant a right to object to one or to be told it has expired. There is no variance disclosure duty here of any kind.

North Dakota does have variance machinery, in two places this review could read. The newest is onsite wastewater: the new chapter to title 23.1 created by S.B. 2267, S.L. 2025, ch. 248 (effective 1 August 2025) gives the department of environmental quality EXCLUSIVE authority to adopt rules on licensing, permitting and inspection of onsite wastewater treatment systems -- commonly, septic systems serving a dwelling -- and voids a county or city ordinance, including one adopted under a home rule charter, that conflicts with those rules. In that chapter (now codified as ch. 23.1-07.1) the department 'may prescribe by rule a process for obtaining variances for existing nonconforming or nonfunctional onsite wastewater treatment systems', and the process 'shall consider the: a. Environmental impact; b. Impact to public health; c. Cost of compliance; and d. Least restrictive means'. A political subdivision's denial, modification or revocation of an install permit may be appealed to the department by petition for review filed within ten days of notice. Nothing in it says a word about telling the tenant. The other place is zoning: a municipal, county or township board of adjustment grants zoning variances -- those chapters (40-47, 11-33 and 58-03) require only that the board 'state the grounds upon which any request for a zoning amendment or variance is approved or disapproved' and keep written findings; they say nothing about tenants, and a zoning variance is about land use, not sanitation.

What should worry a landlord is not the missing disclosure but the operative effect of the code itself. § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes you comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and § 47-16-13.1(3) makes that duty CONTROLLING where it is greater than any other duty in the subsection. So a code requirement is imported into your landlord obligations through the lease statute, enforceable by action under § 47-16-13.6 with attorney's fees to the prevailing party, and if the code gives the enforcing authority power to relieve you of a requirement, the scope of that relief is the measure of what you owe. A variance that is narrower than you think, or that has lapsed, leaves the underlying duty in place.

Cautious course, and state it to yourself rather than to the tenant: for the Administrative Code and your local health and housing codes, do not assume there is no applicable requirement or no disclosure rule in them. If a variance, waiver or exception applies to your property, keep the written grant with its conditions and expiry, give it to the tenant voluntarily where the condition affects how they live in the unit (for example a restriction on occupancy, water use or a bedroom count), and do not rely on it to answer a habitability complaint without checking that it is still in force. Never write a lease term in which the tenant accepts a code deficiency: § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable rental agreement provision or an unconscionable settlement waiving a right under §§ 47-16-13.1 to 47-16-13.6, and North Dakota has no landlord-tenant non-waiver statute to soften the point either way.

title: Seasonal and Short-Season Rentals: North Dakota Has No Carve-Out, So State the Term
bodyText:
The default rule first, and this is the one that catches people out. North Dakota has not adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and it has no seasonal, transient, vacation-rental or resort exclusion anywhere in its leasing or eviction chapters. A seasonal letting is simply a lease: leasing is 'a contract by which one gives to another the temporary possession and use of real property for reward and the latter agrees to return such possession to the former at a future time' (N.D.C.C. 47-16-01). So the security-deposit limits, the landlord's maintenance duties and the eviction procedure all apply to a cabin let for a summer exactly as they do to a year-round apartment.

What a seasonal letting really needs is an express term, because three presumptions will otherwise fill the gap and none of them is what a seasonal landlord wants. A lease of real property other than lodgings, where there is no usage on the subject, is PRESUMED TO BE FOR ONE YEAR from its commencement unless otherwise expressed in the lease (47-16-05). For lodgings let for an unspecified term, the term is presumed to be the period the parties adopt for estimating the rent - a weekly rate presumes a week - and in the absence of any agreement on length, the leasing is presumed monthly (47-16-19). And if the tenant stays on after the term expires and you accept rent, the parties are presumed to have renewed on the same terms for the same time not exceeding one year, except that for residential property the presumed renewal is a MONTH-TO-MONTH TENANCY (47-16-06).

Two more traps. If a lease of residential property for a specified term of two months or more contains an automatic renewal clause, you may not enforce it unless you notified the tenant in writing of the automatic renewal provision, personally or by first-class mail, not less than thirty days before the current lease expires; without that notice the lease expires and its terms convert to a month-to-month tenancy (47-16-06.1). And once a tenancy is month-to-month, ending it takes at least one calendar month's written notice from either side, with rent due to and including the termination date - which for a season that ends in September means you cannot clear the unit on a week's notice (47-16-15(2) and (5)).

Do this. State the exact start and end dates in the lease, say in terms that the tenancy ends on the end date without further notice and that the lease is not renewed by any holding over, and say expressly that no automatic renewal applies - or, if one does, calendar the thirty-day notice under 47-16-06.1. Describe the premises and which seasonal amenities are and are not included, and if any utility or service is turned off out of season, say so, remembering that in a building other than a single-family residence you must supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat and cannot shift that duty by agreement (47-16-13.1(1)(f) and (5)). Do not write the lease as though it sits outside the statutes: it does not, and a term saying the tenant waives protections because the letting is seasonal is empty, because North Dakota created no seasonal exception to waive out of.

title: Where the Deposit Must Sit, and What You May Not Do Instead
bodyText:
Default rule in North Dakota: the holding method is not your choice. A lessor who requires money as a security deposit, however denominated, shall deposit the money in a federally insured interest-bearing savings or checking account for the benefit of the tenant, and the deposit together with any interest accruing on it must be paid to the tenant on termination of the lease (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1)).

Three things follow. First, there is no alternative to holding the money: North Dakota gives you no escrow option, no trust-account option and no surety or guarantee bond you can post in place of the cash. Second, the interest is the tenant's, not yours - there is no annual landlord fee to deduct and no interest-free starting period, and the only relief is that you need not pay interest at all if the period of occupancy was under nine months (§ 47-16-07.1(3)). Third, there is no small-landlord escape hatch: the section applies by its own terms to the state and its political subdivisions as landlords (§ 47-16-07.1(6)), and nothing in it turns on how many units you own.

North Dakota does not require you to tell the tenant the name or address of the bank or the account number, so the lease need not carry a depository statement - but keep the deposit money separate from your operating cash anyway, because if you cannot show what accrued you cannot defend the figure you return, and money withheld without reasonable justification exposes you to treble damages (§ 47-16-07.1(4)).

On a sale, the deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to the buyer, and you are not relieved of liability until you transfer it (§ 47-16-07.1(5)).

CAUTION, A REAL CONFLICT IF A BROKER HOLDS THE MONEY: a licensed broker or property manager must put "all funds not the broker's own" into a "separate, noninterest-bearing trust account" (N.D.C.C. § 43-23-14.1; N.D. Admin. Code § 70-02-01-15(1)(h): "All trust accounts must be noninterest bearing"). That cannot also be the interest-bearing account § 47-16-07.1(1) requires, and no statute says which rule gives way. You, as owner, are exempt from broker licensing when managing your own property (§ 43-23-07(1)(a)), so the conflict arises only when a licensed manager collects the deposit. Cautious course: have the deposit paid straight into a federally insured interest-bearing account held for the tenant's benefit that the manager never takes into its trust account, and if it does pass through the trust account, make sure the tenant still receives the interest the deposit would have earned.

The same caution applies to the new Uniform Special Deposits Act (chapter 6-08.6, created 2025), which names 'a security deposit of a tenant' as a permissible purpose for a special deposit but requires at least two beneficiaries and a contingency; it is opt-in and it does not displace § 47-16-07.1, so do not treat it as a substitute for a plain federally insured interest-bearing savings or checking account held for the tenant's benefit.

title: The Deposit Rules Carry No Non-Waiver Clause
bodyText: North Dakota's security-deposit section says what you may demand, that the money goes into a federally insured interest-bearing account for the tenant's benefit, what it may be applied to, the thirty-day itemisation, and treble damages for withholding without reasonable justification - but it contains no provision making any of that non-waivable (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1). That is not permission to write around it. A clause by which the tenant gives up the interest, the itemisation or the treble-damages remedy is a candidate for being refused enforcement as unconscionable (§ 47-16-13.3), and the deposit section applies by its own terms to the state and its political subdivisions as landlords, which shows it was written as a standard rather than a default. The practical answer is that the absence of a non-waiver clause gives you nothing to rely on, and a court asked to enforce such a waiver has § 47-16-13.3 ready to hand.

title: No Duty to Publish How You Set Deposit Amounts
bodyText: Default rule in North Dakota: there is none. No statute requires you to post, publish, hand over or otherwise disclose the standards, criteria or formula you use to decide how large a security deposit to ask for - not before signing, not on request, and not if you own more than four adjoining units and apply different standards to different applicants. What North Dakota regulates is the amount, not the explanation: a lessor may not demand or receive security, however denominated, in excess of one month's rent, with two narrow exceptions - you may accept up to two months' rent from an applicant convicted of a felony as an incentive to rent to them, and you may demand up to two months' rent from an applicant with a judgment against them for violating a previous rental agreement (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1)(a)-(b)). A pet security deposit is separate and capped at the greater of $2,500 or two months' rent (§ 47-16-07.1(2)). The real limit on using differing standards is not a disclosure statute, it is § 14-02.5-02(2), which forbids discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of race, colour, religion, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin, or status with respect to marriage or public assistance. What to do: keep one written internal standard, apply it to every applicant alike, and record the reason whenever you go above one month's rent under (a) or (b), because that reason is the only thing that makes the higher figure lawful. Do not print a deposit-standards disclosure in the lease; North Dakota does not ask for one and a printed disclosure invites an argument about whether you followed a standard you were never required to publish.

title: No Lock, Deadbolt, Peephole or Rekey-at-Turnover Duty in the Century Code
bodyText: Default rule: no North Dakota statute makes you install any security device in a rental dwelling. The words deadbolt, peephole, door viewer, window latch and keyless bolting device appear in no section name anywhere in the Century Code, and neither does any rekeying provision. There is no Texas-style security-device schedule, no peephole requirement for multi-unit buildings triggered by a construction date, no duty to rekey between tenancies, no tenant right to demand a lock change and no cost allocation for one. Chapter 47-16 says nothing about locks at all, and North Dakota has not adopted the URLTA, so there is no "provide and maintain locks and furnish keys" clause of the kind most URLTA states have. Your duties are the general ones and they still reach locks. Section 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes you comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and section 47-16-13.1(3) says that where that duty is greater than any other it measures your obligation -- so a lock requirement in the local code is your duty through that subdivision even though no statute names one. Section 47-16-13.1(1)(b) requires you to make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises fit and habitable, section 47-16-13.1(1)(d) puts every facility you supply -- which includes the locks you installed -- in good and safe working order, and section 47-16-08 binds you to secure the tenant's quiet possession. A broken exterior lock is therefore a repair you owe, whatever the statute books are silent about. Cautious course: treat working, keyed locks on every exterior door and openable ground-floor window as your baseline, check your municipality's building and housing code rather than the Century Code for a hardware list, rekey at every turnover as a matter of practice, and fix a reported lock failure as a habitability repair rather than as a tenant charge. One statute does mandate locks, for lodging only: section 23-09-08 requires sleeping-room doors in a "lodging establishment" to have bolts or locks the occupant can secure from within, on pain of a class B misdemeanor. Section 23-09-01(9) defines a lodging establishment as a place furnishing sleeping accommodations "to transient guests for a charge", excluding a building or group with five or fewer guest rooms and ten or fewer occupants. An ordinary lease is not lodging; a larger short-stay operation is.

title: No Work Card for 55+ Housing Staff -- the Real Duty Is the Exemption Test
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has no work card. There is no sheriff's card, no state permit, no registration and no fingerprint or background-check requirement imposed by statute on the staff of 55+ or 62+ housing, or on the staff of any other rental housing. The phrase 'work card' does not appear anywhere in the North Dakota Century Code, including in the section headings of titles this review could not open. So there is nothing to apply for, nothing to post and nothing to renew.

What North Dakota does require of senior housing is an exemption test, not a staffing test, and that is the thing to get right. § 14-02.5-11(1) exempts housing from the fair housing chapter's familial status and age provisions only if it is housing the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development determines is specifically designed and operated to assist elderly individuals under a federal programme; or the department determines is specifically designed and operated to assist elderly individuals under a state programme; or is intended for and SOLELY occupied by individuals sixty-two or older; or is intended and operated for occupancy by at least one individual fifty-five or older per unit as determined by department rules. For the 55+ route the statute itself names the minimum factors the department's rules must require: that at least EIGHTY PER CENT of the units are occupied by at least one individual fifty-five or older, and 'the publication of, and adherence to, policies and procedures which demonstrate an intent by the owner or manager to provide housing for individuals fifty-five years of age or older'. § 14-02.5-11(2) protects the status in two situations: residents in place as of 1 October 1999 who do not meet the age requirement, provided new occupants do; and unoccupied units, provided they are reserved for occupancy by people who do meet it.

What to do. Do not promise or demand a credential that does not exist, and do not import another state's work card form into a North Dakota employment file. Put your effort where the statute puts the risk: publish the age policy, follow it, and keep the occupancy records that prove the eighty per cent figure, because the exemption is what stands between an age-restricted community and a familial-status or age discrimination charge under § 14-02.5-02 -- and a charge is expensive (§ 14-02.5-32 allows administrative civil penalties of up to $11,000, $27,000 or $55,000 depending on history, plus damages, fees and costs; § 14-02.5-41 allows actual and punitive damages in court). Screen staff because it is good practice and because you are liable for what they do, not because a statute makes you. One caveat on the 55+ route: the eighty per cent test and the policy requirement come from the statute, but the department's implementing rules sit in the N.D. Administrative Code, which this review could not read -- check the current rule before relying on the percentage alone.

title: No Fixed Fine for Denying an Assistance Animal -- but Fair-Housing and Criminal Exposure
bodyText:
Default rule first, because the answer is the opposite of what landlords expect. North Dakota's landlord-tenant chapter imposes NO criminal penalty and no fixed statutory fine on a landlord for refusing a service or assistance animal in housing (but see chapter 25-13 below). The penalty provisions North Dakota actually wrote into its landlord-tenant chapter run the OTHER way -- against the tenant. Under § 47-16-07.6(1) an individual is guilty of an infraction who, in an attempt to obtain a reasonable housing accommodation under § 47-16-07.5, knowingly makes a false claim of a disability requiring a service or assistance animal or knowingly provides fraudulent supporting documentation; and under (2), only if that individual pleads guilty or is convicted may the lessor evict and recover a damage fee of up to $1,000.

That does not mean a refusal is free. Refusing a reasonable accommodation is a discriminatory housing practice under North Dakota's fair housing chapter. § 14-02.5-06(2) bars discrimination in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental or in the provision of services or facilities because of a disability, and § 14-02.5-06(3)(b) states in terms that discrimination includes 'a refusal to make a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices, or services if the accommodation may be necessary to afford the individual equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling'. The exposure that follows is civil and administrative, and it is larger than a criminal fine would be: after a hearing the department may order actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, court costs and injunctive or equitable relief, and may assess a civil penalty of up to $11,000, rising to $27,000 for one other discriminatory housing practice in the preceding five years and $55,000 for two or more in the preceding seven years (§ 14-02.5-32); in a civil action a court may award actual AND PUNITIVE damages, fees, costs and injunctive relief (§ 14-02.5-41). The one criminal provision in the chapter, § 14-02.5-45, is a class A misdemeanour -- but it requires force or threat of force used to intimidate or interfere with a person because of disability (among other grounds) in connection with occupying or renting a dwelling. A bare refusal, however wrong, is not that offence; shoving a tenant or threatening them over the animal could be.

So the practical rule for North Dakota is: there is no fixed denial fine in the landlord-tenant chapter, there is a possible criminal limb in chapter 25-13, there is a large discrimination exposure to fear, and the state has given you a defined documentation process instead of a veto. Use it. § 47-16-07.5 lets you require reliable supporting documentation from a tenant of a dwelling subject to a no-pets policy who asserts a disability requiring a service or assistance animal; the documentation must come from a physician or medical professional who does not operate in North Dakota solely to provide certifications for service or assistance animals, and it must confirm both the disability and the relationship between the disability and the need for the animal. You may NOT require documentation where the disability or the disability-related need is readily apparent or already known to you. Decide in writing, decide on the documentation, and never charge a pet deposit for a qualifying animal (§ 47-16-07.1(2) excludes a service animal or companion animal required as a reasonable accommodation).

Chapter 25-13 adds a criminal limb. § 25-13-02 entitles an individual with a disability to be accompanied by a service animal -- 'any dog trained to do work, perform tasks, or provide assistance' for that individual (§ 25-13-01.1) -- in places of public accommodation and 'all places to which the public is generally invited'. § 25-13-04 makes it a class A misdemeanour to deny or interfere with admittance to those places 'or otherwise interfere[] ... with the rights of an individual who is accompanied by a service animal'. A leasing office open to the public is plausibly such a place. Whether 'otherwise interferes' reaches a refusal to let a tenant keep a trained service dog in the unit only case law could settle. Cautious course: treat a wrongful refusal of a trained service dog as potentially criminal, never turn a service-dog user away from your office or common areas, and do not deny any animal without going through the § 47-16-07.5 documentation process and documenting your decision. On the tenant's side, § 25-13-02.2 makes a knowingly false claim that a pet is a service animal, made to obtain an accommodation under § 47-16-07.5, an infraction.

title: No North Dakota statute makes a landlord disclose sex-offender registry information, but one unread section is titled that way
bodyText:
Default rule first: nothing in the North Dakota landlord-tenant statutes makes a landlord disclose, warn about, or inquire into whether any registered offender lives in or near the building. The registration scheme puts every duty on someone else.

N.D.C.C. 12.1-32-15 is the registration statute, as amended and reenacted by S.L. 2025, ch. 302 (S.B. 2037), section 8. In the whole section, the words "landlord", "lessor", "tenant" and "rental" do not appear once. The duties run to the registrant, to the official in charge of the place of confinement, to the department of corrections and rehabilitation, to the law enforcement agency with local jurisdiction and to the attorney general. N.D.C.C. 54-12-22, as amended and reenacted by S.L. 2025, ch. 339, requires the attorney general to give a law enforcement dispatch center electronic access to registration information - again, not a landlord duty, and not a duty to tell a tenant anything.

One related statute protects brokers, not owners. N.D.C.C. 43-23-08.3, in the real estate brokers chapter, says: "A licensee is not liable for any action resulting from any disclosure or nondisclosure relating to the registration of sexual offenders under section 12.1-32-15." It is an immunity for a licensed broker or salesperson, not a duty, and it does not cover an owner renting out their own property.

The cautious course, and what to do: do not volunteer registry information, and do not put a registry disclosure or a registry disclaimer in the lease - no statute requires either, and a disclaimer invites the tenant to think you knew something. If a prospective tenant asks you directly, answer truthfully to the extent you actually know, or say you do not know and point them to the public registry; do not refuse to answer in a way that could be read as a misstatement. A licensed broker or salesperson who lets the property for you has the 43-23-08.3 immunity; you do not, so the same care applies to you. Keep registry status out of your screening criteria: the public registry exists to inform the public, and there is no North Dakota statute authorising a landlord to use it as a rental standard.

title: North Dakota puts no residency restriction on a landlord: the only occupancy limit in the registration statute binds the offender
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute readable here forbids you from renting to a registered offender, requires you to screen for one, limits how close to a school or park a registrant may live in private rental housing, or makes it an offence to let a dwelling where two registrants live together. A waiver or a promise in the lease about any of that would be waiving a rule North Dakota does not have - which is empty, not protective, and tells the tenant they gave up something they did not.

The registration statute, N.D.C.C. 12.1-32-15, was read whole for this row as amended and reenacted by S.L. 2025, ch. 302 (S.B. 2037), section 8. It contains exactly one occupancy restriction, subsection 18, and it binds the registrant and concerns public land: a sexual offender currently assigned a moderate or high-risk level by the attorney general "may not use a state park of this state as a residence or residential address to comply with the registration requirements of this section", and must notify a parks and recreation department law enforcement officer before arriving for overnight lodging or camping. Nothing in the section addresses an owner, a landlord, a lessor or a lease, and nothing makes two registrants sharing a dwelling an offence by anyone.

N.D.C.C. 12.1-20-25, read whole, bars a registrant, or an offender convicted of a class A misdemeanor or felony sexual offence against a minor, from knowingly entering "the real property comprising a public or nonpublic elementary, middle, or high school" except as the school allows; a violation is the offender's class A misdemeanor. It says nothing about where a registrant may live or about anyone who rents to one. The one-city co-residence fine with a lease-statement safe harbour that some states have would be a municipal ordinance.

The cautious course, and what to do: do not write a registrant exclusion, a co-residence prohibition or a safe-harbour statement into the lease. There is no North Dakota statute to anchor any of them, no statutory safe harbour to earn, and a clause that bans a class of tenant can only create exposure for you, not reduce it - note that N.D.C.C. 14-02.5-02(4) carves out only a conviction for the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance from the fair housing bar, which tells you the legislature knew how to write a criminal-history carve-out and wrote just the one. Before you adopt any blanket policy, check the ordinances of the city the property sits in, because that is where a residency restriction would be if North Dakota has one at all. Apply your ordinary written screening criteria consistently to every applicant and keep the records.

title: No single-family-residence disclosure in North Dakota, but the single-family duty-shift must be in writing and is narrower than it looks
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has no statute requiring a lease to state that the dwelling is a single-family residence, that it is owner-occupied, that it contains fewer than some number of units, or that it is exempt from anything - and no statute prescribes a type size, a relative font size, or first-page placement for any statement in a residential lease. There is nothing in chapter 47-16 about how a lease must be laid out.

There is no exemption to disclose, either, because North Dakota has no rent cap and no just-cause eviction law for a single-family home to be exempt from. N.D.C.C. 47-16-02.1 prohibits a political subdivision from enacting, maintaining or enforcing an ordinance or resolution that would have the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged for private residential or commercial property. The one place the state's own fair housing law turns on single-family character is an exemption that operates by itself: N.D.C.C. 14-02.5-09(1) says sections 14-02.5-02 through 14-02.5-08 do not apply to the sale or rental of a single-family house sold or rented by the owner if the owner does not own more than three single-family houses at any one time. That exemption does not depend on your saying anything, and you should not print it: a lease clause announcing that you are exempt from fair housing law reads badly, may be wrong on your facts, and gains you nothing legally.

What single-family character really does change in North Dakota is who may be made responsible for maintenance, and here the lease does matter. N.D.C.C. 47-16-13.1(4) lets the landlord and tenant of a single-family residence agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant perform the landlord's duties specified in subdivisions e and f of subsection 1 - waste receptacles and removal, and running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat - plus specified repairs, maintenance, alterations and remodeling. For any dwelling unit other than a single-family residence, subsection 5 reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" and does not mention e or f at all, and it requires a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration, work that is not necessary to cure noncompliance with subdivision e, and no diminution of the landlord's obligation to other tenants. So in a multi-unit building the duty to supply water, hot water and heat and to handle waste cannot be shifted to the tenant by any agreement. Note a drafting defect: subsection 6 bars making performance of "the separate agreement described in subsection 4" a condition of the lease, but it is subsection 5 that describes a separate writing. Both readings are arguable and the landlord-safe course is to assume the bar applies to both - so do not make the tenant's maintenance agreement a condition of getting the lease.

What to do: do not add a single-family or exemption disclosure, and do not put a statement in large type or on the first page thinking a rule requires it. If the property is a single-family residence and you want the tenant to handle maintenance or utilities, use the written agreement 47-16-13.1(4) authorises, keep it separate from the lease, give real consideration for it, and do not condition the tenancy on signing it. The library's maintenance-duty-shift and tenant-repair-agreement rows carry the drafting.

title: North Dakota requires no shoreline or water-access disclosure to a tenant
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant anything about a shoreline, a lakeshore, a riverbank, public access to water, an ordinary high water mark, a dock, or the public's right to use the bank or the bed of an adjoining watercourse. The North Dakota statutes do not use the word "shoreline" anywhere.

North Dakota's water-and-land statutes are about who owns what, not about what a landlord must say. The only sections in title 47 that use the word shore are N.D.C.C. 47-06-05, which gives land formed by imperceptible accretion on the bank of a river or stream to the owner of the bank; 47-06-09, which gives an island or accumulation formed in a non-navigable stream to "the owner of the shore on that side where the island or accumulation is formed"; and 47-06-10, which gives an island formed when a stream divides and surrounds land to the owner of that shore. Those are rules of title between riparian owners. None of them speaks to a tenant, a lease or a disclosure.

What to do: do not print a shoreline-access disclosure as though a statute required it. If the property does adjoin water and the public can lawfully reach the bank, that is worth saying in the lease as a plain description of what the tenant is renting - along with any rules you want about docks, watercraft, swimming and guests - but say it as your own term, not as a state-mandated disclosure, and deal with it under the library's common-area-use and tenant-responsibilities rows rather than as a disclosure. Two things could matter on a waterfront property: the North Dakota Administrative Code, and city, county and township ordinances, including any shoreland or floodplain overlay. The State Engineer's and water resource districts' rules on navigable waters sit in the Administrative Code.

title: Showing Notice: Consent, Not a Fixed Period, and Nothing Says It Can Be Waived
bodyText: North Dakota sets no number of hours of notice before a showing. Showing the unit to an actual or potential purchaser, insurer, mortgagee, real estate agent, tenant, workman or contractor is one of the enumerated purposes for which you may enter during reasonable hours and in a reasonable manner, and unless it is impractical to do so you must first notify the tenant and receive consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold, identifying a time certain (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.3(2)). The statute then does the work a waiver clause would: consent is presumed from the tenant's failure to object after notice of intent to enter at a time certain has been given, and notice may be given by personal service, by posting it in a conspicuous place in or about the unit for a reasonable period, or by any other method resulting in actual notice. Nothing in North Dakota law says that regime can be waived in the lease, and nothing says it cannot. Because the presumption already turns on the tenant's silence, a clause asking the tenant to waive showing notice adds little and risks reading as an abuse of the right of access, which the same section forbids.

title: Government Shutdowns and Furloughs: No Rent Relief in North Dakota Law
bodyText:
The default rule first, and it is strict. Rent is payable when the lease says; absent a contract or usage to the contrary, rents of lodgings are payable monthly at the end of each month and other rents quarterly at the end of each quarter (N.D.C.C. 47-16-20). An eviction lies where the tenant 'fails to pay rent for three days after the rent is due' (47-32-01(4)), and three days' written notice of intention to evict must be given before proceedings are instituted (47-32-02). North Dakota gives the tenant no statutory right to cure by paying within those three days - the notice states your intention to evict, it is not a pay-or-quit notice.

Against that, North Dakota has no shutdown or furlough protection of any kind. No statute delays rent, suspends a late fee, bars an eviction or creates a payment plan for a federal or state employee who is furloughed or working unpaid during a lapse in appropriations, and there is no general hardship, unemployment or loss-of-income rent protection either. There is also no statutory grace period before rent is late: any grace period in North Dakota is the one your lease gives.

Three points that do bear on a hardship case. First, the courts have one narrow lever: on a showing that immediate restitution of the premises would work a substantial hardship on the defendant or the defendant's family - except where the eviction judgment rests in whole or in part on a disturbance of the peace - the court may stay the special execution for a reasonable period not exceeding five days (47-32-04). Five days, not a month. Second, a local government cannot rescue the tenant either: a political subdivision may not enact, maintain or enforce an ordinance or resolution having the effect of controlling the amount of rent charged for leasing private residential or commercial property (47-16-02.1), so there is no room for a local shutdown rent ordinance. Third, in a mobile home park the rule is expressly the other way: if an action between landlord and tenant is commenced under 47-10-28, 'the tenant shall continue paying rent and comply with all park rules and regulations in effect at the time the action was commenced' (47-10-28(14)), and park tenants keep occupancy during a licence suspension (47-10-28(13)).

Do this. Decide your own policy and write it down, because the law will not supply one: a stated grace period, a written short-term payment agreement, or nothing. Keep two cautions in mind when you do. A fixed late fee has to survive the rules that penalties imposed by contract are void (9-08-03) and that damages fixed in advance are void to that extent unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (9-08-04); and you may not charge any fee for accepting cash, a check or a money order for rent or for any other payment required under the lease (47-16-20.1, effective August 1, 2025), so do not turn a hardship into an electronic-payment surcharge. In a mobile home park a monthly late fee may not exceed ten per cent of the monthly rent and a daily late fee may not exceed five dollars (47-10-28(11)). Finally, do not write a lease term saying the tenant waives a shutdown or hardship protection: North Dakota has none to waive, so the term is empty and it suggests to the tenant that they gave something up.

title: No State Limit on Renting in a Single-Family Zone -- Check the Local Ordinance
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute limits renting out a house in a single-family zone, and none conditions a rental on the owner living on the lot. There is no owner-occupancy requirement, no cap on the number of rentals in a residential district, no state rental licence or registration, no short-term-rental statute, and no county-specific rule of the kind Kentucky enacted for Jefferson County. The phrases 'short-term rental' and 'owner-occupied' return nothing in North Dakota's statutes.

Where the restriction can come from instead is local. North Dakota delegates zoning to cities (ch. 40-47), counties (ch. 11-33) and townships (ch. 58-03), which may regulate "the location and use of buildings, structures, and land for trade, industry, residence, or other purposes" (§ 40-47-01). None of those chapters limits rentals or says anything about owner occupancy. So a single-family-zone limit on rentals in North Dakota, if it exists for your property, is a city, county or township ordinance, or a private covenant in the chain of title -- not a statute. Two more provisions confirm the local picture rather than displacing it: §§ 40-47-05.1, 11-33-17.1 and 58-03-14.1 (all amended and reenacted in full in 2025) let a nonconforming residential structure in a residential zoning district be repaired or rebuilt even if damaged beyond fifty per cent of value, subject to conditions including that the new structure not violate existing building and fire codes or 'existing sanitary or health standards imposed by the local health district', and subject to the zoning authority's power to adopt a LESS restrictive ordinance; and § 23-10-03(2)(a) requires a mobile home park licence application to include 'evidence of approval from local officials as to the proposed mobile home park, recreational vehicle park, or campground applicant's compliance with local zoning laws, ordinances, or regulations for the physical address for its intended use'. Both assume a local zoning authority that the state does not second-guess.

Two state-law limits on such an ordinance are worth knowing. Under § 14-02.5-27, if the department handling a fair housing complaint determines the matter involves the legality of a state or local zoning or other land use law or ordinance, it may not issue a charge and must refer the matter immediately to the attorney general -- so a discriminatory zoning rule is challenged through the attorney general, not through an ordinary housing charge. And under § 14-02.5-12(1) the fair housing chapter 'does not affect a reasonable local or state restriction on the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling or a restriction relating to health or safety standards' -- note that this saves a restriction imposed by LOCAL OR STATE LAW. Your own occupancy cap is not a local or state restriction and gets no shelter from it; peg an occupancy clause to the applicable local code or health standard and say so, rather than picking a number.

What to do: check the zoning ordinance and the recorded covenants for the specific property before you advertise it, because the consequence of getting this wrong is not a lease dispute but an enforcement action against the use. Do not put a representation in the lease that the property is lawfully rentable under local zoning unless you have checked -- § 47-16-07.4 lets a party fraudulently induced into a lease terminate it AND recover the security deposit with accrued interest. And do not rely on the single-family language in § 47-16-13.1(4): that subsection uses 'single-family residence' only to mark where a landlord and tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant perform the landlord's waste-removal and water-and-heat duties under subdivisions (e) and (f) plus specified repairs -- an allocation rule for duties, not a zoning or licensing rule, and in any other dwelling subsection (5) reaches only specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, and only in a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration.

title: Smart Locks and App-Based Entry Are Unregulated -- and That Is the Problem
bodyText: Default rule: North Dakota has no smart-access law. There is no provision on smart locks, electronic or keyless locks, app-based or mobile-credential entry, key fobs or biometrics in a residential rental; no notice or consent requirement before you install one; no duty to offer a physical-key alternative; no limit on what entry data you may keep or how long; and no delayed effective date to plan around, so there is nothing here resembling Washington's RCW 59.18.750 to 59.18.760. The only electronic-access provision in the entire Century Code is section 54-21-17.1, which puts the issuance and return of keys and electronic card access to the state capitol buildings in the construction superintendent's hands. Nothing reaches rental housing. The practical consequence is the opposite of freedom: because no statute supplies any of the terms, every one of them has to come from your lease, and the existing North Dakota rules still apply to the new hardware. Section 47-16-07.3 governs when you may enter, and a remote unlock is an entry: you may enter at any time only in an emergency or on a reasonable belief of abandonment or substantial lease violation, and otherwise only during reasonable hours, in a reasonable manner, for an enumerated purpose, after notice and consent that may not be unreasonably withheld; the section says plainly that you may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass or intimidate the tenant. An audit log that shows every coming and going, or a credential you can revoke at will, is how that line gets crossed. Section 47-16-08 binds you to secure the tenant's quiet possession, so switching off a credential for unpaid rent is a lockout, not a remedy -- the remedy is an eviction under chapter 47-32. Section 47-16-13.1(1)(d) puts the lock system, as a facility you supply, in good and safe working order at your cost, and sections 9-08-03 and 9-08-04 mean a lost-fob or replacement-credential charge must be your actual cost, not a stated fee. What to do: put in the lease what the system is and where it controls, how many credentials the tenant gets, who may hold one, what happens if one is lost, whether a physical key is available and how to get it, that you will not use remote unlock except as section 47-16-07.3 allows, what entry data the system records, who can see it and when it is deleted, and what happens to access if the system or the tenant's phone fails. Offer a physical-key fallback even though nothing makes you, and never use credential revocation as a collection tool.

title: No Unit-to-Unit Smoke-Drift Rule, but Common Areas Are Smoke-Free by Law
bodyText:
North Dakota has no statute about smoke drifting between dwelling units and no duty to disclose a smoking policy in a lease.

It does have a smoke-free law that reaches rental buildings. Smoking is banned in the enclosed common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums, mobile home parks and other multi-unit residential buildings (N.D.C.C. §§ 23-12-09(11), 23-12-10(1)). It is also banned within twenty feet of their entrances, exits, operable windows and air intakes (§ 23-12-10(2)). The units themselves, as private residences, are exempt (§ 23-12-10(3)(a)).

You must post no-smoking signs, including at every entrance, and remove ashtrays (§ 23-12-10.4(1)). You must also tell a smoker to stop, ask them to leave if they refuse, and report a refusal. Willful failure is an infraction with fines of up to $500 per violation, and each day counts separately (§ 23-12-11). You may not retaliate against anyone for asserting these rights or reporting a violation; that is a class B misdemeanor (§ 23-12-10(5)).

A clause in which the tenant waives a claim for secondhand smoke from a neighbouring unit therefore waives no statutory right - though it cannot defeat a claim built on something else, such as the tenant's statutory duty not to disturb the neighbours' peaceful enjoyment (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.2(7)) running the other way, or your own duty to keep the premises fit and habitable (§ 47-16-13.1(1)(b)). A building-wide no-smoking policy, applied to every tenant alike and justified by odour, damage and fire risk, is the stronger ground than a waiver.

title: A late benefit or voucher payment is no defence to nonpayment, but you may not treat subsidised tenants differently
bodyText:
Default rule first: in North Dakota rent is rent, and a late government payment is not a statutory excuse. N.D.C.C. § 47-32-01(4) makes it a ground for eviction when a lessee "fails to pay rent for three days after the rent is due", and § 47-32-02 requires three days' written notice of intention to evict before proceedings may be instituted in that case. Nothing in either section, and nothing anywhere in chapter 47-32 or chapter 47-16, gives the tenant a continuance, a reinstatement, an abatement or any grace period because a social security payment, a housing voucher, a rent supplement or any other benefit arrived late. There is no North Dakota equivalent of the Massachusetts continuance-and-reinstatement rule.

The one thing close to it is narrow. N.D.C.C. § 47-32-04 provides that "[u]pon a showing by the defendant that immediate restitution of the premises would work a substantial hardship on the defendant or the defendant's family, except in cases in which the eviction judgment is based in whole or in part on a disturbance of the peace, the court may stay the special execution for a reasonable period, not to exceed five days." That is a discretionary five-day stay of the writ after judgment, not a defence and not a right to cure. The same section bars joining other actions and allows no counterclaim "except as a setoff to a demand made for damages or for rents and profits", so a tenant cannot turn a benefit delay into a counterclaim either.

Now the part that matters more to you, and that most landlords get wrong. North Dakota protects subsidised tenants as a class. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-02(1) and (2) make it unlawful to refuse to rent, to refuse to negotiate, to make a dwelling unavailable, or to "discriminate against an individual in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling or in providing services or facilities", because of "status with respect to marriage or public assistance". And § 14-02.5-01 says the definitions in § 14-02.4-02 "may be used to supplement the definitions in this chapter" — where § 14-02.4-02(19) defines "Status with regard to public assistance" as "the condition of being a recipient of federal, state, or local assistance, including medical assistance, or of being a tenant receiving federal, state, or local subsidies, including rental assistance or rent supplements." A voucher holder is squarely inside that. Separately, § 14-02.5-02(3) provides that an applicant for or tenant of "housing that is part of a state housing program" may not be denied admission or evicted on the basis that the person is or has been a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking, if otherwise qualified.

What to do. (1) You may enforce the rent. Serve the three-day notice under § 47-32-02 and proceed on § 47-32-01(4) exactly as you would for any tenant — that is not discrimination. (2) But treat the subsidised tenant identically to every other tenant in writing and in practice: same due date, same notice, same grace, same screening criteria. A rule, a fee or a notice practice applied only to assistance recipients is a § 14-02.5-02(2) problem even if the rent really is late. (3) Never say, write or email that the problem is the voucher, the subsidy or the housing agency; say the rent is unpaid, because that is the ground the statute gives you. (4) Where the delay is the housing agency's, call the agency before you file — the five-day stay in § 47-32-04 is all the cushion the court can give, and a filing you withdraw costs more than a phone call. (5) If the tenancy is federally subsidised, check the federal rules and your housing assistance payments contract as well; federal law can impose cause requirements and notice periods that North Dakota law does not. (6) Put no benefit-delay clause in the lease: North Dakota supplies no rule for one to carry, and a clause promising extra time to assistance recipients only is itself a difference in terms.

title: No special-district statement is required, but a public-body landlord still owes the deposit rules
bodyText:
Default rule first: a North Dakota residential lease does not have to say anything about special districts. There is no North Dakota statute requiring a landlord to state, represent or disclose that the property lies inside a special district, a special assessment district, an improvement district or any similar taxing body, and no statute makes such a statement a condition of the lease or gives the tenant a remedy for its absence. North Dakota does have bodies of this kind — the Century Code's own index lists ch. 11-28.1, County Special Service Districts, and ch. 11-28.2, recreation service districts, and title 40 (ch. 40-22 to ch. 40-24) carries the municipal special assessment machinery — but it runs against the land, through an assessment and a lien, and none of those chapters mentions a lease, a lessee or a tenant. One narrow exception reaches an occupant: where land is exempt from special assessments, N.D.C.C. § 40-23-08 lets the assessment "be levied against the occupant or beneficial user of the property and collected by suit" from that person. That matters only if a tax-exempt owner is the landlord. The phrase "special district" appears in none of those chapters and nowhere in title 47.

What North Dakota does say about a public landlord is worth knowing, and it cuts the other way from what landlords often assume. Two sections apply:
• N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(6) — the security deposit section "applies to the state and to political subdivisions of the state that lease real property or dwellings and require money as a security deposit." A district, authority or other political subdivision that rents out housing is held to the same deposit rules as a private owner, including the treble-damages exposure in § 47-16-07.1(4). Being a public body is not an exemption.
• N.D.C.C. § 47-16-02.1 — after forbidding a political subdivision to control the rent charged for private property, it adds that the section "does not impair the right of a political subdivision to manage and control residential property in which the political subdivision has a fee title interest." So a district may set the rent on, and make the rules for, housing it actually owns.

What to do. (1) Do not add a special-district representation or disclosure sentence to the lease because another state's form has one — North Dakota does not require it, and a statement you are not obliged to make is a statement you can get wrong. (2) Do check the local ordinance before you assume nothing is required: special assessments are a municipal subject in North Dakota. (3) If the landlord is itself a district or other political subdivision, treat § 47-16-07.1 as binding and hold deposits in a federally insured interest-bearing account for the tenant's benefit exactly as a private lessor must. (4) Who may appear in court for a district is a separate question. N.D.C.C. § 11-16-01(1)(e)-(f) has the state's attorney defend suits against the county and prosecute actions to recover debts owed to it, but that section does not say whether a district may appear through its own officer. Only case law could settle that — see the entity-representation entry; the safe course is counsel.

title: No sprinkler disclosure in the North Dakota statutes - and the building code that could require one was unreadable
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a lease, or a landlord, to tell a tenant whether the building has an automatic fire sprinkler system, whether it lacks one, when it was last inspected or serviced, or what the tenant should do if it is out of service. There is no state disclosure form, no bolded notice, no acknowledgment and no penalty. No statute or rule read uses "sprinkler" in a disclosure rule.

Where "sprinkler" does appear in North Dakota statutes, it is not a rental disclosure. 18-12-17, "Sprinklers", in the school-building fire code, was "Repealed by S.L. 1985, ch. 257, § 4." 23-09-06 says standpipe and sprinkler systems "must be installed as required by the state building code and state fire code" in a lodging establishment - a place furnishing sleeping accommodations "to transient guests for a charge" (23-09-01(9)), not an ordinary residential rental. And 54-21.3-03(4) says the state building code or a local code "may not include a requirement that fire sprinklers be installed in a single family dwelling or a residential building that contains no more than two dwelling units."

Now the caveat, and it changes the answer so do not read past it. 47-16-13.1(1)(a) requires the landlord to "comply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and 47-16-13.1(3) says that where that duty is greater than any other duty in the subsection, "the landlord's duty shall be determined by reference to" it. A sprinkler requirement, a service interval or an impairment-notification requirement living in the State Building Code is therefore a binding lease obligation even though ch. 47-16 never says the word. The State Building Code under ch. 54-21.3 is the international building, residential, mechanical and fuel gas codes adopted by Department of Commerce rule (54-21.3-03(1)); a city, township or county that elects to enforce it does so under 54-21.3-05, may amend it locally (54-21.3-03(6)), and 54-21.3-04 lists exemptions. The State Fire Code is separate: N.D. Admin. Code § 10-07-01-04 adopts the 2018 International Fire Code with state changes. Those model codes, incorporated by reference, decide when a building of three or more units must be sprinklered and how a system is maintained. No North Dakota statute or rule read turns any of it into a tenant disclosure. 47-16-13.2(1) puts the mirror duty on the tenant - comply with code obligations "primarily imposed upon tenants" - which is how a no-tampering rule reaches an occupant.

The enforcement machinery that does exist is in ch. 18-01, the State Fire Marshal Department chapter: 18-01-04 (rules for prevention of fires to be issued), 18-01-14 (abatement of fire hazards), 18-01-15 (abatement of conditions dangerous to persons - order - failure to comply - penalty), 18-01-16 (order of abatement - to whom directed - contents - how served - service by publication), 18-01-17 and 18-01-18 (appeals), 18-01-19 to 18-01-26 (court proceedings and judgment) and 18-01-27 (costs and the lien for them). So North Dakota's answer to a dangerous fire condition is a fire marshal's abatement order against the property, enforceable in district court with a cost lien - a regulatory route, not a lease term and not a disclosure. Read whole: under 18-01-15, an owner, agent or occupant served with an order to correct a condition that is "a danger or a menace to the safety of life and limb of the occupants" who fails to comply is guilty of a class B misdemeanor; under 18-01-27, enforcement costs are "a lien against the premises".

What to do: do not print a sprinkler disclosure as a North Dakota requirement. If the building is sprinklered, a short factual statement plus a no-obstruction and no-tampering rule is worth having, but take it as a house rule you chose, not a statute you obeyed (though tampering with or disabling fire suppression equipment in a "place of abode" so as to endanger person or property is itself a class B misdemeanor under 12.1-21-09(2)) - and check the locally enforced building code and your municipal fire ordinance first, because that is where a real requirement would be. Where a sprinkler system is out of service, treat it as a repair duty under 47-16-13.1(1)(a) and (b) and remember the tenant's remedies if you do not act after notice: 47-16-13 gives uncapped repair-and-deduct, recovery in any other lawful manner, or the right to vacate and stop paying rent.

title: A lease over one year must be in writing and signed by the landlord or a written-authority agent
bodyText:
Default rule first: in North Dakota an oral lease can be perfectly good, and the cut-off is ONE YEAR — not five, not seven. Two sections set the baseline. N.D.C.C. § 47-09-04: "A transfer may be made without writing in every case in which a writing is not required expressly by statute." And the section that supplies the express requirement, § 47-10-01: "An estate in real property, other than an estate at will or for a term not exceeding one year, can be transferred only by operation of law or by an instrument in writing, subscribed by the party disposing of the same or by the party's agent thereunto authorized by writing. This does not abridge the power of any court to compel the specific performance of any agreement for the sale of real property in case of part performance thereof."

Unpack that, because every word of it does work:
• A tenancy at will, and any lease for a term NOT EXCEEDING one year, needs no writing at all. A twelve-month lease is on the safe side of the line; thirteen months is not. One catch: the general statute of frauds, § 9-06-04(1), also makes invalid an unwritten "agreement that by its terms is not to be performed within a year from the making thereof", so a twelve-month lease agreed today to start next month needs a writing too.
• A lease for MORE than one year must be in writing and "subscribed by the party disposing of the same" — that is the LANDLORD, the party disposing of the estate — or by an agent whose authority is itself in writing. So if a manager signs a two-year lease for you, their authority needs to be in writing too. A tenant's signature is not what § 47-10-01 demands, but get it anyway: § 9-06-04(3) separately makes "[a]n agreement for the leasing for a longer period than one year" invalid unless in writing "subscribed by the party to be charged", which is whichever party you need to enforce it against, and an agent signing for that party needs written authority.
• Part performance is preserved as an escape hatch, but only for "any agreement for the sale of real property" — the section does not extend it to leases in terms.

Two interactions are worth holding together. § 47-16-05 provides that "[a] lease of real property, other than lodgings, in places where there is no usage on the subject, is presumed to be for one year from its commencement, unless otherwise expressed in the lease." So an oral lease that says nothing about its length is presumed to run one year — which is exactly at, and not over, the § 47-10-01 threshold, so the presumption and the writing rule fit together rather than colliding. And § 47-16-02 caps the other end: no lease of agricultural land reserving rent or service for longer than ten years is valid, and no lease of a city lot for longer than ninety-nine years. That is a maximum-term cap and nothing more — it is not a list of prohibited lease terms and should not be cited as one.

Is the one-year threshold a validity rule or a recording rule? In North Dakota it is a VALIDITY rule: § 47-10-01 says the estate "can be transferred only by" a writing. Recording is a separate and entirely optional matter — § 47-19-01 says any instrument affecting title or possession "may be recorded", and § 47-19-46 confirms an unrecorded instrument "is valid as between the parties thereto and those who have notice thereof." If you do want to record a lease, § 47-19-03 requires the execution to be established by acknowledgment and requires the document and any acknowledgment to be "executed with an original signature" — so an ordinary e-signed lease is not recordable, and notarisation is about recording, not about validity.

What to do. (1) Put every lease in writing regardless. The threshold is a floor on what the law demands, not advice — and several North Dakota rules only operate off a writing: § 47-32-01(8) makes violating "a material term of the written lease agreement" an eviction ground, § 47-16-15(2) lets the parties agree in writing to a longer notice period, and § 47-16-15(4)'s initialling rule assumes a written lease. (2) For any lease longer than a year, make sure the person signing for the landlord is the owner or holds written authority — a verbal authorisation to an agent does not satisfy § 47-10-01. (3) For a renewal or extension that carries the total beyond a year, get it in writing and signed; do not rely on a conversation. (4) Treat an assignment or a surrender of a lease longer than a year as needing a signed writing, even though none of the sections above says so expressly — see the caution below. (5) Do not look for a five-year or seven-year rule; North Dakota has neither.

title: Every Money Limit in North Dakota Tenancy Law, and What Each One Actually Does
bodyText: North Dakota's money figures do five different jobs, and reading one as another is the commonest way landlords get this wrong. CAPS ON CONDUCT: a lessor 'may not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's rent' (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1)) - it bites on the asking as well as the taking, it aggregates everything you hold as security whatever you call it, and it is measured as a multiple of rent rather than in dollars. PERMISSIONS, NOT ENTITLEMENTS: you may accept up to two months' rent from an applicant convicted of a felony as an incentive to rent to them, and you may demand up to two months' rent from an applicant with a judgment against them for violating a previous rental agreement (§ 47-16-07.1(1)(a)-(b)). A WHICHEVER-IS-GREATER CEILING: a pet security deposit 'may not exceed the greater of two thousand five hundred dollars or an amount equivalent to two months' rent' (§ 47-16-07.1(2)), so for a $900 unit the ceiling is $2,500 and for a $1,500 unit it is $3,000. A THRESHOLD ON A POWER, not a cap on money: abandoned property of 'total estimated value of not more than two thousand five hundred dollars' may be retained and disposed of without legal process after twenty-eight days (§ 47-16-30.1) - above that figure you need legal process, and you may recover storage and moving expenses above the sale proceeds from the deposit.
