A MULTIPLIER ON YOUR LIABILITY: treble damages for security deposit money withheld without reasonable justification (§ 47-16-07.1(4)). FLAT SUMS SET BY STATUTE: a damage fee 'not to exceed one thousand dollars' where a tenant is convicted of furnishing fraudulent disability documentation (§ 47-16-07.6(2)); a tenant terminating under the domestic-violence section owes the full month plus an amount equal to one month's rent (§ 47-16-17.1(5), (7)); and a court may award that tenant statutory damages of one thousand dollars if you retaliate (§ 47-16-17.1(11)). MOBILE HOME PARKS ARE DIFFERENT, and this is the trap: a park owner may not charge a monthly late fee of more than ten percent of the monthly rent, may not charge a daily late fee of more than five dollars a day, and may not add more than a three dollar administrative fee to a utility charge (§ 47-10-28(8), (11)); violating that section exposes the owner to a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and not more than the greater of $10,000 or actual damages (§ 47-10-28(12)) and is a defence to the eviction itself (§ 47-32-01.1). INTEREST: six percent a year on any legal indebtedness unless a different rate is contracted for in writing, up to the usury ceiling, which is the six-month treasury-bill average plus five and one-half percent but in any event never below seven percent (§§ 47-14-05, 47-14-09(1)). WHAT HAS NO CAP: outside mobile home parks, late fees, application and screening fees, pet rent, parking and storage charges and administrative fees are uncapped by statute, and the rent itself is uncapped - a political subdivision may not control it (§ 47-16-02.1). Uncapped is not unlimited: §§ 9-08-03 and 9-08-04 void penalties and damages fixed in advance, and § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision. And one figure is not a cap at all but a flat ban: you may not charge any fee to accept cash, a cheque or a money order for rent or any other payment required under the lease (§ 47-16-20.1).

title: No Radiator Cover Duty and No Mandatory Rider — But a Dangerous Radiator Is Still Your Problem
bodyText:
Some jurisdictions require a landlord to install a steam radiator cover on a tenant's request and to attach a prescribed rider to the lease saying so. North Dakota has nothing of the kind. The word "radiator" does not appear anywhere in North Dakota's statutes. There is no cover, guard, shield or enclosure requirement, no request procedure, and no rider.

The rider half of the question is settled twice over. Beyond the absence of any radiator provision, North Dakota prescribes no residential lease content at all — chapter 47-16 contains no provision telling you what a lease must contain, state or disclose — so no mandatory lease rider on this or any other subject exists under state law. Do not add one. A rider announcing a right North Dakota does not grant invites the tenant to believe it does.

That said, do not conclude that a scalding or leaking radiator is not your responsibility, because it reaches you through the general duties. Under N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(d) you must maintain in good and safe working order and condition all heating, ventilating and air-conditioning facilities and appliances you supply or are required to supply — a steam radiator is squarely within that, and the words are "good and safe," not merely functional. Under § 47-16-13.1(1)(b) you must make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition. And under § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) you must comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, with § 47-16-13.1(3) measuring your duty by the code wherever the code is greater — so if a city you operate in has adopted a housing code with a radiator guard provision, that becomes your duty even though the Century Code is silent. This research pass could not read the State Building Code or any municipal code, so check the codes applicable to your property.

If you do not address a dangerous radiator after notice, the ordinary consequences follow: under § 47-16-13 the tenant may repair it and deduct the expense from rent, recover the expense in any other lawful manner, or vacate and be discharged from further rent; under § 47-16-17(1) they may terminate the lease; and under §§ 47-16-13.5 and 47-16-13.6 they may recover appropriate damages by action with discretionary attorney's fees to the prevailing party. A burn injury would also sit outside the lease altogether as a personal injury claim, and § 9-08-02 means you cannot contract your way out of responsibility for your own willful injury or violation of law.

What to do: if a unit has exposed steam radiators and a tenant has young children or a mobility or cognitive impairment, fit covers when asked. Nothing compels it, it is inexpensive, and it removes a foreseeable burn risk from a facility you are already required to keep in good and safe working order. Document the request and what you did. Do not promise covers in a lease rider; handle it as a maintenance item, which is what it is under North Dakota law.

title: North Dakota has no stigmatized-property disclosure duty, and the material-fact duty it does have belongs to a seller
bodyText:
Default rule first: in North Dakota a residential landlord owes a prospective tenant no statutory duty to disclose anything about a death, suicide, homicide, crime, illness or other event on the property, and no statute makes such an event a defect the landlord must reveal. There is no stigmatized-property statute and no psychological-impact statute in the North Dakota statutes.

The trap to avoid is the one duty that looks like it fits. N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.1 ("Property disclosure - Requirements - Exceptions") requires a written disclosure of "all material facts the seller is aware could adversely and significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment of the property" - but it binds "the seller" in a "transaction for the sale, exchange, or purchase of real property", and runs to a "prospective buyer". So do N.D.C.C. 47-10-02.2 (radon) and 47-10-02.3 ("Required disclosures - Seller to provide"), both created in 2025; 47-10-02.2(1)(a) defines a "buyer" as a person negotiating or offering to acquire real property for value or legal or equitable title, or the right to acquire it. A tenant is not a buyer, and letting a tenant rent is not a sale or exchange. Do not convert any of these into a landlord duty. If you add a purchase option to the lease, the transaction may become a sale and these seller duties may then apply to you - get that reviewed before you sign.

On the HIV question other states raise: North Dakota has no HIV bill of rights, and the word does not appear in these statutes. What does bind you is ordinary fair housing. N.D.C.C. 14-02.5-02 and 14-02.5-06 forbid refusing to rent, or discriminating in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, because of disability, and 14-02.5-01(6) defines disability as a mental or physical impairment that substantially limits at least one major life activity, a record of the impairment, or being regarded as having it. So the practical answer is the opposite of a disclosure duty: do not condition a tenancy on a health status, do not ask about one, and do not repeat a diagnosis you learn to anyone.

What to do: say nothing about prior deaths or events on the property unless a prospective tenant asks a direct question, and then answer truthfully rather than evasively - there is no statute requiring the disclosure, but an affirmative misstatement is a different problem and could be argued to engage N.D.C.C. 51-15-02, which forbids a misrepresentation in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise and defines merchandise in 51-15-01(3) to include real estate. Do not print a stigma disclaimer in the lease: there is no rule to disclaim, and printing one invites the tenant to believe something was concealed. The separate question whether you must pass on sex-offender registry information when asked is covered separately; see the sex-offender-disclosure row.

title: North Dakota does not make you supply a stove or a fridge - but supplying one creates a duty
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota's landlord duties are a closed list in N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1), and the only things a landlord must actually supply are in subdivision (1)(f): "running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat", subject to that subdivision's own three exceptions. Subdivision (1)(e) adds waste receptacles and arranging removal. Cooking and food storage appear nowhere in the list.

THE ANSWER. There is no provision in the North Dakota statutes requiring a landlord to provide a stove, a cooking range, an oven or a refrigerator. The open-textured duty in § 47-16-13.1(1)(b) - to "[m]ake all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition" - is never linked in statute to a kitchen, a stove or a refrigerator.

BUT SUPPLY FLIPS IT. If you do supply a stove or a refrigerator, § 47-16-13.1(1)(d) requires you to "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, supplied or required to be supplied by the landlord." That duty is implied into every lease the moment the appliance is supplied, so there is nothing to print about it - the lease work is the inventory, not the duty. Two consequences follow. First, in anything other than a single-family residence you cannot hand that maintenance back to the tenant casually: § 47-16-13.1(5) requires good faith plus "a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration", bars work needed to cure a subdivision (e) failure, and bars diminishing your duty to other tenants; § 47-16-13.1(6) says you may not make the tenant's performance of that separate agreement a condition of the lease. In a single-family residence § 47-16-13.1(4) is looser, but it still requires a written, good-faith agreement. Second, § 47-16-13.1(2) gives you "a reasonable time" to remedy a (1)(b)-(f) failure, and § 47-16-13.6 makes these rights "enforceable by action" with fees to "the prevailing party" - which cuts both ways and favours a landlord who fixed a stove promptly.

WHAT THE LANDLORD SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. Decide whether the stove and fridge are yours or the tenant's, and write it down in both places: on the lease and on the statement of condition of the facilities that § 47-16-07.2 already makes mandatory ("[a] landlord shall provide the tenant with a statement describing the condition of the facilities in and about the premises", signed by both, and "prima facie proof of the condition of the facilities and the premises at the beginning of the rental agreement"). Use the appliances-excluded clause for the list. Do not advertise a unit as having a kitchen appliance you are not supplying. If the tenant brings their own, remember § 47-06-04: the tenant may remove anything affixed "for the purpose of trade, manufacture, ornament, or domestic use" at any time during the term where removal causes no injury and it has not become an integral part of the premises.

CAUTIOUS COURSE on the code. Section 47-16-13.1(1)(a) requires compliance with "applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and § 47-16-13.1(3) makes that duty controlling wherever it is greater than any other subdivision's. North Dakota's State Building Code, ch. 54-21.3, consists of the international building, residential, mechanical and fuel gas codes, applied where a city, township or county elects to enforce it and amendable locally (§ 54-21.3-03(1), (6)); no housing or property-maintenance code is adopted statewide. The model codes' text is published by the International Code Council, not the state, and codes elsewhere commonly require cooking facilities in a dwelling unit. So the honest answer is: nothing in the North Dakota statutes requires a stove or refrigerator, but an adopted code might, and if it does § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) with (3) makes it binding and controlling through the lease statute. Treat a code-required cooking facility as your duty and check the code adopted in your city before letting a unit with no means of cooking.

title: Student Rentals Get No Special Treatment in North Dakota
bodyText:
The default rule first: North Dakota's leasing chapter applies to every lease of real property for reward (N.D.C.C. 47-16-01), and it contains no exclusion for student housing. Many states carve dormitories, residence halls and institutional housing out of their landlord-tenant act; North Dakota has not adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and has no exclusions section at all, so there is nothing to carve anything out of.

That means a student rental is an ordinary residential tenancy. The security-deposit limits and accounting rules in 47-16-07.1 apply, including the pet-deposit cap and the treble-damages exposure in 47-16-07.1(4). Your maintenance duties under 47-16-13.1 apply in full, and in any building other than a single-family residence you cannot shift the waste-removal duty or the running-water, hot-water and heat duty to the tenant by any agreement (47-16-13.1(1)(e) and (f), with (5) omitting both). The condition statement must accompany the rental agreement (47-16-07.2). Entry rules (47-16-07.3), the notice rules (47-16-15), and the eviction grounds and three-day notice of intention to evict (47-32-01, 47-32-02) are the same as for any other tenant. There is no student exemption and no student protected class.

Two North Dakota points that matter for an academic-year letting. First, the term: a lease of real property other than lodgings is presumed to be for one year unless otherwise expressed (47-16-05), and if a student holds over after the term and you accept rent, a residential lease is presumed renewed as a month-to-month tenancy (47-16-06) - which then takes a full calendar month's written notice to end (47-16-15(2) and (5)). An automatic renewal clause in a residential lease of a specified term of two months or more is unenforceable unless you gave written notice of the renewal provision, personally or by first-class mail, at least thirty days before expiry; without it the lease expires and converts to month-to-month (47-16-06.1). A nine-month academic lease therefore needs its end date stated in terms. Second, if you require the lessee to give more than one calendar month's notice from the end of a month to terminate, the lease must state that requirement and provide space for the lessee to initial next to it; unless the lessee initials it at signing, the lessee may terminate on the last day of a month with one calendar month's notice (47-16-15(4)).

Do this. Treat the lease as a full residential lease, not a housing contract. Decide and write down whether each student is jointly and severally liable for the whole rent or liable per bed, and whether a guarantor signs - North Dakota supplies no rule, so silence will be read against the drafter. State the academic-year dates and whether the unit must be vacated over a break. And be careful how you apply any student-only or age-related rule: age and familial status are protected classes in the rental of a dwelling under 14-02.5-02, so a policy aimed at students that in fact falls on households with children or on older applicants is exposed, even though no statute sets the policy. Nothing in North Dakota law lets you refuse to rent to a student as such; note separately that 14-02.5-02(5) says nothing in that chapter prevents a person from refusing to rent a dwelling to two unrelated individuals of opposite gender who are not married to each other.

title: Subsidised-unit inspections: a federal duty, not a North Dakota one — what to do if the tenant refuses
bodyText:
The default rule: North Dakota has nothing on this. No provision in the North Dakota statutes requires a subsidised or assisted unit to be inspected, tells you what to do when the tenant refuses to let the inspector in, makes refusal a ground of eviction, or lets you pass the lost subsidy on to the tenant. The inspection obligation in a voucher or assisted-housing tenancy is a FEDERAL one — it comes from the programme's own rules and from your contract with the housing authority, not from North Dakota law. Do not let anyone tell you a North Dakota statute requires it, and do not look for one. Equally, do not treat the federal requirement as optional — it is simply not a state-law duty.

The two North Dakota rules that do bite on subsidised tenancies are worth knowing precisely. First, N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-02(1) and (2) make 'status with respect to ... public assistance' a protected characteristic: you may not refuse to rent to, refuse to negotiate with, or discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges offered to someone because their rent is paid with public assistance. A policy of 'no vouchers' is a discriminatory housing practice in North Dakota, and so is giving a voucher tenant worse terms. Second, § 14-02.5-02(3) protects an applicant for or tenant of housing that is part of a STATE housing programme from being denied admission or assistance, terminated from participation or evicted 'on the basis that the applicant or tenant is or has been a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking', if they otherwise qualify. Note the limit: that subsection reaches state housing programmes, so check whether yours is one.

The cautious course when a subsidised tenant will not admit the inspector. (1) Give notice the way § 47-16-07.3 describes — your own notice, of a time certain, personally delivered or conspicuously posted in or about the unit or by any method that actually reaches the tenant, keeping a dated copy. Consent is presumed if the tenant does not object, and a tenant who merely fails to respond has consented, which usually ends the problem. (2) Tell the housing authority in writing, promptly, and let it run its own process against the tenant; that is where the programme's leverage sits, not in your lease. (3) Do not force entry. § 47-16-07.3(2) gives you entry 'for the purpose of inspecting the premises' during reasonable hours after notice, and § 47-16-07.3(1) gives you entry at any time only on an emergency, a reasonable belief the tenant has abandoned the premises, or a reasonable belief the tenant is in substantial violation of the lease — a single missed appointment is unlikely to support the third. (4) Make your own lease require the tenant to permit an inspection required by law or by a housing assistance contract, because § 47-32-01(8) makes 'The lessee violates a material term of the written lease agreement' a ground of eviction; without that written term the refusal breaches nothing. If you use that ground, § 47-32-02 requires a three-day notice of intention to evict. (5) Do not charge the tenant the subsidy you lost. A fixed sum for a missed inspection is a contractual penalty, and § 9-08-03 makes penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance void outright.

title: No rent abatement for a bad unit in North Dakota, and no subsidy-inspection proration -- what the tenant gets instead
bodyText: Default rule first, and it is the opposite of what landlords in most states expect: North Dakota has NO rent abatement. There is no statute reducing or abating rent for a period in which the dwelling was uninhabitable, no statute prorating rent for days the tenant could not use the unit, no rent escrow and no rent-into-court procedure -- and nothing at all written for a subsidised tenancy, so no state rule prorates or suspends rent for a period in which the unit failed a housing-authority inspection or the subsidy payment was abated. What the tenant has instead, if you fail a repair duty, is N.D.C.C. Section 47-16-13: after notice from the tenant of dilapidations you ought to repair and a reasonable time to do them, the tenant may repair and deduct the expense from the rent (with no dollar cap and no cost threshold), recover it in any other lawful manner, or vacate -- and on vacating 'the lessee shall be discharged from further payment of rent or performance of other conditions'. That is all-or-nothing: the tenant either leaves and owes nothing more, or stays and owes the full rent less any repair actually paid for. Separately, if the tenancy ends before the agreed time, Section 47-16-21 makes the tenant pay 'the due proportion of the lease for such use as the lessee actually has made of the property unless such use is merely nominal and of no benefit to the lessee' -- so a tenant who never got beneficial use of the unit owes nothing for the period, which is the closest thing North Dakota has to an abatement and it only works on an ended tenancy, not a continuing one. What to do: for a subsidised tenancy, the rules that actually prorate or abate anything come from the federal programme -- the housing assistance payments contract and the HUD tenancy addendum you sign with the housing authority -- not from North Dakota law; read them, because when the authority abates its own payment that is a reduction in what the authority owes you, not a reduction in what the tenant owes, and only those documents say whether you may collect the difference from the tenant. Do not write a lease term charging the tenant the authority's abated share. And do not write a lease term abolishing the tenant's Section 47-16-13 options: the habitability duties in Section 47-16-13.1 can be shifted only on that section's own narrow terms, and Section 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision. Fix the condition promptly instead; a repair bill is cheaper than a tenant who vacates and stops paying.

title: Late fees when the tenant has a voucher or subsidy: North Dakota has no special rule, so the lease and the subsidy contract decide
bodyText: Default rule first: North Dakota sets no cap and no grace period for late fees in ANY tenancy, and it has no rule at all written for subsidised housing. There is no statute limiting a late fee in a housing choice voucher tenancy, none barring a late fee on the housing authority's portion of the rent, none requiring a separate written late-fee term in a subsidised lease, and no state administrative-charge rule for a subsidy tenancy. So nothing in North Dakota law is special here -- but three things still bind you. First, two general contract sections reach every late fee: penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (N.D.C.C. Section 9-08-03), and a clause fixing damages in advance is void unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (Section 9-08-04). A late fee has to look like a recovery of your real cost of a late payment, not a round punishment. Second, the fee can only be measured by what the TENANT owes. If your lease makes the tenant responsible only for the tenant's share of the rent, a late fee calculated on the full contract rent charges the tenant for money the tenant never owed, which is exactly the shape Section 9-08-03 voids; and a fee charged because the housing authority paid its own share late is not a charge for the tenant's nonperformance at all. Compute the fee on the tenant's share and on nothing else. Third, if the dwelling is in a mobile home park, there ARE hard caps and they apply whether or not the tenant has a subsidy: a park may not charge a monthly late fee of more than ten per cent of the monthly rent, and in addition may not charge a daily late fee of more than five dollars per day (Section 47-10-28(11)); a violation carries a civil penalty of not less than two thousand five hundred dollars (Section 47-10-28(12)) and is a defence to the eviction (Section 47-32-01.1). What to do: the real limits on a voucher tenancy come from the federal programme documents -- the HUD tenancy addendum and the housing assistance payments contract you sign with the housing authority -- not from North Dakota law, and those documents control over your own lease language for the assisted tenancy. Read them, and if they bar or limit a late fee, follow them. Put the late-fee term in writing in the lease, state the amount, the day it attaches and that it is charged on the tenant's share only, and charge it consistently. Separately, you may not refuse an applicant because they will pay with a subsidy -- see the source-of-income row.

title: Two 2025 Receivership Regimes -- Park Receivership, UCRERA, and No Conditions-Based Route
bodyText:
Default rule first, and it is not the usual one: North Dakota has NO habitability or code-enforcement receivership for ordinary rental housing. No statute lets a tenant, a city or a health authority ask a court to put an apartment building into receivership because it is substandard. The word 'substandard' appears only in a city's power to demolish, repair or remove 'Substandard buildings or structures' (§ 40-05-01(23)), which is not a receivership. What North Dakota does have, both of it new in 2025, is a park receivership and a general real-estate receivership act -- and the second one reaches rental property on grounds that have nothing to do with conditions.

MOBILE HOME PARKS -- a real receivership, but only the department can start it. Chapter 23-10.1, created by S.B. 2385, S.L. 2025, ch. 238 (effective 1 August 2025), works like this: when the department of health and human services REVOKES a park's licence, the department may petition the district court to place the park under a receiver 'for repeated or serious violations of chapter 23-10 or the administrative rules of the department, or to protect health or safety'. The court may grant the petition on finding either repeated or serious violations committed or continuing, or that 'health or safety would be seriously threatened if a condition existing at the time the petition was filed continues'. The court appoints the COMMISSIONER as receiver, who may designate a qualified individual or a non-profit organisation (not a state or political-subdivision employee) to execute it. The receiver uses the park's income and assets to maintain and operate the park and to try to correct the violations, and MAY NOT liquidate the park's assets. The receivership ends when the receiver and the court certify the conditions are corrected, the licence is restored, a new licence is issued, or the owner discontinues operation and the residents have secured other appropriate housing; the receiver then accounts to the court, which directs the disposal of surplus funds. Note the trigger: licence revocation first, department petition second. A tenant cannot start it. Alongside it, § 47-10-28(13) lets the district court suspend the park licence for a violation of that section, with a daily civil penalty equal to half the monthly rent roll divided by the days in the month, all tenants allowed to remain throughout, and no rule changes, rental changes, rent increases or no-cause terminations during the suspension.

ALL OTHER RENTAL PROPERTY -- the Uniform Commercial Real Estate Receivership Act, chapter 32-10.1, created by S.B. 2122, S.L. 2025, ch. 325 (effective 1 August 2025, and not applying to a receivership whose receiver was appointed before then). Do not be misled by the word 'commercial'. § 32-10.1-03(1) applies the chapter to a receivership for an interest in real property generally; subsection (2) excludes property improved by ONE TO FOUR DWELLING UNITS -- but not if, among other things, 'the owner is collecting or has the right to collect rents or other income from the property from a person other than an affiliate of the owner'. A rented duplex or single-family house is therefore back inside the chapter, and a building of five or more units was never outside it. Subsection (3) keeps the chapter out of a receivership authorised by other law where the receiver is a governmental unit, which is how the park receivership above stays separate, and subsection (4) preserves a court's authority to appoint a receiver under any other law. What the chapter does NOT do is give anyone a conditions-based ground: § 32-10.1-05 allows appointment before judgment to protect a party with an apparent right, title or interest in the property where the property or its revenue-producing potential is being subjected to or is in danger of waste, loss, dissipation or impairment, or has been or is about to be the subject of a voidable transaction; after judgment to carry it into effect or preserve non-exempt property; on equitable grounds; during a redemption period; and in connection with a mortgage foreclosure where appointment is necessary to protect the property from waste, loss, transfer, dissipation or impairment, or the mortgagor agreed to it in a signed record. Those are creditor-and-owner grounds, not tenant grounds.

THE PART THAT MATTERS MOST TO A LANDLORD AND TO A RESIDENT TENANT. Chapter 32-10.1 treats a lease as an executory contract (§ 32-10.1-01(4): 'The term includes a lease'), and § 32-10.1-16(2) lets a receiver adopt or reject an executory contract with court approval -- a rejection is a breach effective immediately before the receiver's appointment, and if the receiver does not seek approval within a reasonable time the contract is deemed rejected. But § 32-10.1-16(8) carves residents out: 'A receiver may not reject an unexpired lease of real property under which the owner is the landlord if: a. The tenant occupies the leased premises as the tenant's primary residence' -- or if the receiver was appointed at the request of someone other than a mortgagee, or at a mortgagee's request where the lease is senior to the mortgage, the tenant has an enforceable non-disturbance agreement, the mortgagee consented to the lease in a signed record or by failing to object timely that it violated the mortgage, or the lease terms were commercially reasonable when agreed and the tenant neither knew nor had reason to know the lease violated the mortgage. Any one of those is enough. So a residential tenant's lease survives a receivership. And § 32-10.1-16(4) kills the usual drafting reflex: a provision requiring or permitting forfeiture, modification or termination of the contract because a receiver was appointed or because of the owner's financial condition does not affect the receiver's power to adopt it. A 'this lease terminates on receivership' clause does not work.

What to do. If you own a park, treat the licence as the asset at risk: receivership follows revocation, and § 47-10-28(12) already carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and not more than the greater of $10,000 or actual damages plus actual fees and costs for a violation of that section, with § 47-32-01.1 making a violation a defence to an eviction. For other rentals, the realistic risks are a mortgagee-driven receivership and local code enforcement rather than a tenant-driven one -- and remember that § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) with (3) makes applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety binding and controlling on you through the lease statute, enforceable under § 47-16-13.6 with attorney's fees to the prevailing party. The local limb is real, but it is not a receivership. Under § 40-58-18 a city that adopts the ordinances names a public officer who, on his own motion or a petition by 'at least five residents of the municipality', may find a dwelling 'unfit for human habitation' after notice and a hearing, and order you to repair it, to 'vacate and close' it, or to demolish it. If you do not comply, the city may do the work, and its cost 'constitutes a lien against the real property'. § 40-05-01(23) gives every city a similar demolition and repair power, and under ch. 18-01 the state fire marshal can order a dangerous condition corrected, with costs a lien (§§ 18-01-15, 18-01-27). Check your city's ordinances before telling anyone it has no such power. Note also that 'condemnation' in the North Dakota Century Code means eminent domain, not a declaration that a building is unfit -- do not read a condemnation statute as a code-enforcement power.

title: Cable, satellite and internet in a North Dakota rental: no state tenant-access statute, no rent-differential rule, and federal law is the thing that actually limits you
bodyText:
Default rule: North Dakota has no tenant telecommunications-access statute. Nothing in the Century Code gives a tenant a right to obtain cable television, video, internet or telephone service in a multifamily building; nothing requires you to let a provider into the building or to grant it an easement; nothing bars you from charging a subscriber a different rent from a non-subscriber; and nothing regulates a bulk or exclusive marketing arrangement with a single provider. A sweep of every section heading in the entire Century Code found no access provision at all: the only cable-television chapter in North Dakota law is ch. 12.1-23.1, Theft of Cable Television, whose three sections are a criminal penalty, civil penalties and an action for injunction and forfeiture -- a chapter that protects the provider from theft, not the tenant from the landlord.

So what actually constrains you is not state law. It is federal, and it is real. The FCC's over-the-air reception devices rule limits a landlord's power to prohibit a tenant from installing a small satellite dish or antenna in an area within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a balcony or a patio, and the FCC also regulates exclusive access and bulk-billing arrangements in multiple-dwelling-unit buildings. None of that is North Dakota law and none of it was within the scope of this research pass, which read the Century Code only. Do not read this row as saying you may prohibit a dish: it says only that North Dakota has no statute on the subject.

Two North Dakota points that do bear on it. First, sec. 47-06-04 gives your tenant a statutory removal right: anything the tenant affixes "for the purpose of trade, manufacture, ornament, or domestic use" may be removed at any time during the term if it can be done without injury to the premises, unless it has become an integral part. A tenant-installed dish, antenna or router mount is the tenant's to take, and your clause should say so rather than claim it. Second, sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(d) requires you to maintain in good and safe working order all the facilities and appliances you supply -- so if you supply building wiring, a distribution system or a bulk service, you own the maintenance of it.

What ch. 49-21 says. North Dakota's telecommunications chapter, ch. 49-21, regulates telecommunications companies, not buildings. Its section indexed as "Telecommunications - Connections", sec. 49-21-09, lets the Public Service Commission require "a connection ... between the facilities of two or more telecommunications companies" -- carrier interconnection, not a right of entry into a multiple-dwelling building. Nothing in ch. 49-21 mentions a tenant, a landlord, a lease or a residential building's owner, so the absence stated above holds for the statutes.

The cautious course. Do not write a lease term that flatly prohibits a tenant from obtaining television, internet or telephone service, or from installing a reception device -- against the FCC rule such a term is likely void as to a tenant's exclusive-use area, and under sec. 9-08-01 a term contrary to express law is unlawful. Instead regulate the manner: require written approval before any penetration of the building envelope, roof, or a common element; specify where a device may go; require professional installation and removal and repair at the tenant's expense at the end of the term; and require insurance if the installation is on a balcony or rail. Do not charge a subscriber-only surcharge or differential rent -- North Dakota does not forbid it, but the FCC rules in this area and sec. 47-16-13.3 unconscionability both make it a poor risk for very little money. And if a provider asks for access, negotiate the terms; nothing in North Dakota law compels you to give it for nothing, but nothing establishes that you may refuse it either.

title: Tenancies at Will in North Dakota: One Month's Notice, and the Form Is Prescribed
bodyText: North Dakota has a dedicated chapter for this -- chapter 47-17, Termination of Estates -- and it is five short sections. Section 47-17-01: 'A tenancy or other estate at will, however created, may be terminated by the landlord's giving notice to the tenant in the manner prescribed by section 47-17-02 to remove from the premises within a period specified in the notice of not less than one month.' Note 'however created' -- it does not matter whether the at-will tenancy came from an oral agreement, a lapsed written lease or sufferance. Section 47-17-02 prescribes the form and it is the whole form: the notice 'must be in writing and must be served by delivering the same to the tenant or to some person of discretion residing on the premises', and if neither can be found with reasonable diligence it 'may be served by affixing it on a conspicuous part of the premises where it may be read conveniently'. No reason, no magic words, no filing. Section 47-17-03 is the timing discipline: only after that notice has been served as directed and the period in it has expired, 'but not before', may the landlord re-enter or proceed according to law to recover possession. Sections 47-17-04 and 47-17-05 deal with a reserved right of re-entry -- three days' previous written notice of intention to re-enter, served the 47-17-02 way, or an action for possession without that notice. How you end up with a tenancy at will, or something treated like one, is worth knowing. A lease of real property other than lodgings, where there is no usage on the subject, is presumed to be for one year unless the lease says otherwise (section 47-16-05). Lodgings for an unspecified term are presumed to run for whatever period the parties use to reckon the rent -- weekly rent, weekly term -- and in the absence of any agreement about length, monthly (section 47-16-19). If a residential lessee stays after the lease expires and you accept rent, the lease is presumed renewed as a month-to-month tenancy (section 47-16-06), and the same conversion happens if you fail to give the thirty days' written notice section 47-16-06.1 requires before enforcing an automatic renewal clause. Once it is month-to-month, section 47-16-15(2) governs: either party may terminate with at least one calendar month's written notice at any time, rent due through the termination date, unless the parties agreed in writing to a longer period or a different notice time -- and section 47-16-15(4) makes a longer tenant-side notice unenforceable unless the lease states it and the tenant initials next to it. One last point, because it decides holdover arguments: section 47-16-27 gives a tenant for years or at will the right to occupy the buildings and take the annual products of the soil 'unless the tenant is a wrongdoer by holding over'. North Dakota has no tenancy-at-sufferance category; a holdover is simply a wrongdoer, and section 47-32-01(4) makes the eviction maintainable.

title: A tenant bankruptcy stops you, and North Dakota law adds nothing you can use
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota's lease statutes do not mention a tenant's bankruptcy at all, and the two sections that say when a lease ends are closed lists that leave it out. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-14 says "[t]he leasing of real property terminates: 1. At the end of the term agreed upon; 2. By the mutual consent of the parties; 3. By the lessee's acquiring title to the property leased superior to that of the lessor; or 4. By the destruction of the property leased." N.D.C.C. § 47-16-16 says the lessor may terminate early and reclaim the property when the lessee "[u]ses or permits a use of the property leased in a manner contrary to the agreement of the parties" or "[d]oes not make such repairs as the lessee is bound to make within a reasonable time after a request is made." Insolvency, bankruptcy, a receivership and an assignment for the benefit of creditors are on neither list. Nor is bankruptcy a ground for eviction: the eight grounds in § 47-32-01 do not include it, and § 47-32-01.1, the only defence the eviction chapter creates, is about mobile home parks.

So the answer is that bankruptcy is a federal subject and North Dakota adds nothing to it. You must assume federal law governs, and two of its features matter: the filing of a petition stops an eviction in its tracks until the bankruptcy court lifts the stay, and a lease term that purports to terminate the tenancy, or to forfeit it, merely because the tenant filed is the kind of term federal bankruptcy law does not honour. The one North Dakota statute in title 47 that mentions bankruptcy, § 47-19-53, is a recording provision: it lets "the bankrupt, trustee, receiver, custodian, referee, or any creditor" record a certified copy of the petition, decree of adjudication or order approving the trustee's bond in the county where the bankrupt's real property lies. It says nothing about leases, and its own text still refers to "the Federal Bankruptcy Act of 1898, as amended by the Bankruptcy Act of 1938".

What to do. (1) The moment you learn a tenant has filed, stop. Do not serve a notice, do not file, do not proceed with a pending eviction, do not apply the security deposit and do not send a collection letter until you have advice — acting after a filing can expose you to sanctions in the bankruptcy court, and no North Dakota statute protects you from that. (2) Do not put a bankruptcy-or-insolvency termination clause in the lease. It has no support in § 47-16-14 or § 47-16-16, it is not an eviction ground under § 47-32-01, and federal law will not enforce it — so it buys you nothing and makes the lease look as though it is trying to take away a protection the tenant has. (3) Rely instead on the grounds you actually have. Unpaid rent that fell due before the filing is a claim in the bankruptcy; rent for the period after the filing is a different matter and is the point to raise with counsel first. (4) Keep enforcing the lease for reasons unconnected with the filing — a material breach of a written lease term is § 47-32-01(8) and remains available — but get the stay dealt with before you act on it. (5) Remember § 47-16-13.7: a lessee evicted according to law stays liable for rent for the remainder of the term, subject to your duty to mitigate, so the money question survives the possession question and is worth pleading properly.

title: Domestic violence papers you may never share — and the tenant information North Dakota lets you disclose
bodyText:
The default rule first: North Dakota has no general statute making tenant information confidential. No provision in the North Dakota statutes stops a landlord telling a prospective landlord, an employer, a debt collector or anyone else what the tenant paid, how they behaved or why they left, and none requires the tenant's consent before you do. If your lease promises confidentiality, that promise is yours alone and the tenant can enforce it against you as a contract term — so be deliberate about whether you want to make it.

There is one hard exception and it is absolute. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-17.1(4): 'A landlord may not disclose information provided to the landlord by a tenant documenting domestic violence under this section. The information may not be entered into any shared database or provided to any person, but may be used as evidence in an eviction proceeding, in a claim for unpaid rent or damages arising out of the tenancy, or as otherwise required by law.' Read what is not there: no consent exception. You cannot get the tenant to sign this away, and a lease clause purporting to authorise the disclosure is worthless — worse than worthless, because it will look like you planned the breach. The three carve-outs are the only ones: evidence in an eviction, evidence in a claim for unpaid rent or damages arising out of the tenancy, or where the law otherwise requires it.

It has teeth. § 47-16-17.1(11): 'In an action for a violation of this section, the court may award statutory damages of one thousand dollars. The court also may award actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, costs, and disbursements.' And § 47-16-17.1(10) separately bars refusing to rent to, refusing to negotiate with, making unavailable to, denying a dwelling to or otherwise retaliating against an applicant or tenant — or a household member — solely because the right to terminate for domestic violence was exercised. A note on a screening file saying 'left early, DV' is capable of breaching subsection 4, subsection 10 and § 14-02.5-02(3) all at once.

What to do. (1) Keep any domestic violence documentation physically and logically separate: a sealed file or an access-restricted folder, not the tenancy file, not your property management system's notes field, and above all not any shared or multi-property database — the statute names shared databases expressly. (2) Train anyone who answers a reference call. The rule that is easy to follow is: confirm only tenancy dates, the rent and whether the account is current, and say nothing about the reason for an early termination. (3) Ask for a written authority before releasing anything beyond that, not because a statute makes you but because it is the only record you will have if the tenant later says you harmed them. (4) Do not promise confidentiality in the lease unless you mean to be held to it. (5) Remember the direction of travel on eviction records: § 47-32-05, new on August 1, 2025, lets a tenant move to seal eviction court records, including on the ground that the eviction followed a domestic violence incident. Repeating a sealed eviction to a third party is exactly the kind of disclosure to take advice on first.

In a mobile home park the disclosure duties run the other way: § 47-10-28(1)(g) and (h) require you to give each tenant the name, address and telephone number of the legal entity that owns the park and the telephone number of any property manager or site agent, and (1)(c)(4) the contact details of the individual authorised to make decisions. Those are disclosures about you, not about the tenant, and a violation carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and is a defence to an eviction under § 47-32-01.1.

Two other chapters, and what they do. The Data Processing Information Confidentiality chapter bars disclosure without written consent, but only by a 'business entity which charges a fee for data processing services performed', such as bookkeeping or data storage for others (N.D.C.C. §§ 51-22-01(2), 51-22-02). A landlord keeping its own tenant files is not one. A manager who charges owners for bookkeeping might be, and whether that reaches tenant records only a court could say, so a fee-charging manager should get the tenant's written consent before sharing a file. The security-breach chapter does reach you. If you keep tenant names on computer with a social security number, driver's licence number, date of birth, account number with its access code, or electronic signature, and that data is acquired by someone unauthorised, you must tell each affected North Dakota resident without unreasonable delay, and the attorney general if more than 250 people are affected (§§ 51-30-01(4), 51-30-02). A violation is treated as consumer fraud under chapter 51-15 (§ 51-30-07). Encrypting that data takes it outside the duty.

title: Housing an Employee: Ending the Job Does Not End the Tenancy
bodyText:
The default rule first, and it is the point most employers get wrong. North Dakota's leasing chapter has no exclusion for employee housing and no special employee-housing regime. Leasing is 'a contract by which one gives to another the temporary possession and use of real property for reward' (N.D.C.C. 47-16-01) - and where occupancy is part of what the employee is paid, that is reward. So a caretaker's apartment, a farm or ranch house provided with a job, and a unit let to a staff member at a discount are all ordinary leases, with the full security-deposit rules (47-16-07.1), the condition statement (47-16-07.2), your maintenance duties (47-16-13.1), the entry limits (47-16-07.3) and the eviction procedure (47-32-01 and 47-32-02) applying.

Now the consequence. Ending the employment does not of itself end the tenancy. The list of ways a leasing of real property terminates is closed - end of the agreed term, mutual consent, the tenant acquiring superior title, or destruction of the property (47-16-14) - and ending a job is none of them. Your statutory grounds for terminating early are only that the tenant uses the property contrary to the agreement or does not make repairs the tenant is bound to make within a reasonable time after request (47-16-16). You therefore cannot treat a dismissed employee as a trespasser. To recover possession you must either let the term expire, or end a month-to-month tenancy on at least one calendar month's written notice (47-16-15(2)) or an estate at will by notice to remove from the premises within not less than one month (47-17-01, served under 47-17-02), and then use the eviction grounds with the three days' written notice of intention to evict that 47-32-02 requires for a holdover or a material lease breach. Self-help is not authorised anywhere in North Dakota law.

There is also no employee-housing disclosure duty. No statute requires a signed statement of the conditions of occupancy and of vacating, and none requires you to offer a rental agreement when the job ends. No statute makes an employer or sponsor answerable for an employee's rent or utilities, and the eviction chapter does not name caretakers or others placed on the property by the owner as a separate category.

Do this. Tie the two agreements together expressly in the lease, because the statutes will not do it for you. Define the term so that it ends on a stated date or on a stated number of days after the employment ends - that works through 47-16-14(1), 'at the end of the term agreed upon', which is the only lever you have - and reserve a right of re-entry, which North Dakota recognises and for which it supplies the procedure (three days' previous written notice of intention to re-enter under 47-17-04, or an action for possession without that notice under 47-17-05). State the rent in money even where occupancy is part of the pay, so a deposit, a proration and a damages claim can all be calculated. Record the position, the duties and the consideration for the housing. And take care with two statutory limits: in any building other than a single-family residence you cannot make the employee responsible for waste removal or for running water, hot water and heat, and any shift of other repairs or maintenance tasks needs good faith, a separate writing signed by the parties and adequate consideration, must not be necessary to cure a waste-receptacle failure, and must not affect your obligations to other tenants (47-16-13.1(1)(e) and (f), (4) and (5)); and you may not treat performance of that separate agreement as a condition of the lease (47-16-13.1(6)). The cautious course, since subsection (6) refers to subsection 4 while subsection 5 is the one describing a separate writing, is to apply that bar to both.

title: Your tenant must forward any notice of a proceeding against the property, and cannot attorn to a stranger
bodyText:
North Dakota is one of the states that already gives you this, and it gives you both halves of it, so there is nothing for the lease to add.

The default rule is N.D.C.C. § 47-16-25, "Notice of adverse proceedings to landlord", and it applies to every tenancy whether or not the lease mentions it. In full: "Every tenant who receives notice of any proceeding to recover the real property occupied by the tenant, or the possession thereof, must: 1. Inform the tenant's landlord immediately of the notice; and 2. Deliver the notice to the landlord. The tenant shall be responsible to the landlord for all damages which the landlord may sustain by reason of any omission by the tenant to inform the landlord of the notice or to deliver it to the landlord, if such notice is in writing. The attornment to a stranger is void unless made with the consent of the landlord or in consequence of a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction."

Three things follow, and they are worth reading closely because the section is compressed:
• The duty is the tenant's, it is owed to you, and it is immediate. It covers "any proceeding to recover the real property... or the possession thereof" — so a foreclosure, a contract-for-deed cancellation, a tax proceeding, a quiet title action, a condemnation, anything aimed at the property or at possession of it, not merely a suit naming you.
• The damages remedy is conditional. The tenant answers for "all damages which the landlord may sustain", but only "if such notice is in writing." If what the tenant got was oral, the duty to inform you still reads as absolute, but the damages sentence does not reach it.
• Attornment to a stranger is void — your tenant cannot switch allegiance and start paying rent to someone who claims the property, unless you consent or a court of competent jurisdiction has given judgment. The companion provision is § 47-10-20, "Attornment - When unnecessary": grants of rents, reversions or remainders "are good and effectual without attornments of the tenants, but no tenant, who before notice of the grant shall have paid rent to the grantor, must suffer any damage thereby." So if you sell or assign the rents, you do not need the tenant to attorn; but a tenant who pays the old landlord before being told is protected. And § 47-16-28 gives a transferee or devisee of the property, or of the rent, "the same remedies for recovery of rent, for nonperformance of any of the terms of the lease or for any waste or cause of forfeiture" as the grantor had.

What to do. (1) Do not add a forward-notices clause. The statute already binds every tenant and a clause cannot improve on it; restating it only invites an argument that your version, not the statute's, is the measure of the duty. (2) Do make sure the tenant can actually comply: keep a current notice address for you in the lease and update it when it changes, because "inform the tenant's landlord immediately" is hard to do against a stale address, and a tenant who tried will be a sympathetic defendant on the damages point. (3) If you want the damages limb to bite, you want the notice in writing — nothing you can control, but it tells you to ask the tenant for the paper, not just the story. (4) If you sell the property or assign the rents, tell the tenants promptly in writing: § 47-10-20 means you do not need their attornment, but until they have notice of the grant a tenant who pays the wrong party is protected and you will be arguing with your buyer about it. (5) Note what North Dakota does NOT give the tenant in return: there is no statutory duty on a landlord, a lender or a purchaser to notify a tenant of a foreclosure or sheriff's sale. Do not assume someone else will have told your tenant anything.

title: North Dakota requires no rent ledger — but five records duties will cost you if you miss them
bodyText:
The default rule first, because it is the opposite of what most landlords expect: North Dakota imposes no general recordkeeping duty on a landlord at all. No provision in the North Dakota statutes requires you to keep a rent ledger, to give the tenant a rent statement, to produce your file on request, or to keep anything for any particular number of years. One general rule does reach rent: a debtor 'has a right to require from the debtor's creditor a written receipt for any property delivered in performance of the debtor's obligation' (N.D.C.C. § 9-12-22), so give a written receipt whenever a tenant asks. There is no tenant right of access to a landlord's records and no retention period.

Five specific duties do exist, and they are the ones to get right.
1. The move-in condition statement is mandatory. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.2: you 'shall provide the tenant with a statement describing the condition of the facilities in and about the premises to be rented at the time of entering a rental agreement', it 'shall be agreed to and signed by the landlord and tenant', and it then 'constitute[s] prima facie proof of the condition of the facilities and the premises at the beginning of the rental agreement'. Keep the signed original; without it you are arguing about move-in condition from memory.
2. The deposit paper trail. § 47-16-07.1(1) requires the deposit to sit in a federally insured interest-bearing savings or checking account for the tenant's benefit. Subsection 3 requires that any part of the deposit you keep 'must be itemized', and the itemization 'together with the amount due must be delivered or mailed to the lessee at the last address furnished lessor, along with a written notice within thirty days after termination of the lease and delivery of possession', stating any amount still due you or the refund due the tenant. Subsection 4: you are 'liable for treble damages for any security deposit money withheld without reasonable justification'. Amounts the tenant does not claim within a year become unclaimed property reportable under § 47-30.2-04. So: keep the account statements, the itemization, proof of delivery and the date possession came back.
3. Domestic violence documentation is the one record you must NOT file normally. § 47-16-17.1(4): 'A landlord may not disclose information provided to the landlord by a tenant documenting domestic violence under this section. The information may not be entered into any shared database or provided to any person', except as evidence in an eviction proceeding or a claim for unpaid rent or damages arising out of the tenancy, or as otherwise required by law. Subsection 11 lets a court award statutory damages of one thousand dollars plus actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, costs and disbursements. Keep that documentation out of any shared or multi-property system and out of any screening file — in a separate, access-restricted place.
4. In a mobile home park you must hand over the lease on request. § 47-10-28(1)(f): the park owner shall 'Provide to each tenant, upon a written request by the tenant or the tenant's agent, a copy of the existing lease terms along with any modifications or amendments, within ten business days of receipt of a written request'. Subsection 8 also requires you to 'provide the tenant access to the records of meter readings taken at the mobile home lot of the tenant', and subsection 9 to give the tenant a summary of the lease and of both parties' rights and obligations. These are North Dakota's only tenant records-access rights, and they apply only in a park. A violation of § 47-10-28 carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and up to the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, and is a defence to an eviction under § 47-32-01.1. Diarise the ten business days.
5. Eviction court records can now be sealed. § 47-32-05, new on August 1, 2025, lets a person evicted for nonpayment or damage who has resolved all those claims move to seal the court records seven years after the order was satisfied, if not evicted elsewhere in those seven years; and lets a tenant evicted because of a domestic violence incident move to seal on the assailant's conviction or on a restraining or protection order. Those are court records, not yours — but it means an old eviction may lawfully disappear from the record you would have screened on.

What to do about applicant data, and this is where to be careful. Because no statute tells you to hold applicants' social security numbers, bank details or credit reports, nothing tells you how long to keep them either, and holding them is pure downside. Collect the minimum, keep it encrypted or locked, give access only to people who need it, and destroy it on a fixed schedule once the application is decided. North Dakota's security-breach chapter covers you. If you hold names on computer with a social security number, driver's licence or ID card number, date of birth, account number with its access code, or other listed data, unencrypted, and it is acquired by someone unauthorised, you must notify each affected North Dakota resident without unreasonable delay, and the attorney general if more than 250 people are affected (N.D.C.C. §§ 51-30-01(4), 51-30-02). A violation is treated as consumer fraud (§ 51-30-07). Encryption takes the data outside the duty, which is one more reason to encrypt. The data-processing confidentiality chapter applies only to a business that charges a fee for data processing services (§ 51-22-02), not to a landlord keeping its own files.

title: North Dakota gives tenants no right to organize -- and gives you no general retaliation exposure either
bodyText:
THE DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota confers NO statutory right on a tenant to form or join a tenant organization, to hold meetings, to canvass or distribute literature in the building, or to use the common areas for that purpose -- and it imposes NO duty on a landlord to permit any of it. There is no tenant-organizing statute, no tenant-association statute, and no anti-retaliation protection for organizing. In North Dakota's statutes, the vocabulary of this topic -- tenants' association, tenant organization, tenant union, tenant council, resident association, resident council, right to organize, concerted activity, collective action -- appears only in provisions that are not about rental housing: a collective bargaining reference in the employment part of the Human Rights Act (s 14-02.4-19), a licensed long-term-care facility's 'resident council meeting' (s 50-10.2-02(10)), and index headings for chapter 34-12, the LABOR relations chapter.

THE OTHER HALF, AND IT IS THE HALF THAT MATTERS TO YOU: NORTH DAKOTA HAS NO GENERAL LANDLORD RETALIATION STATUTE AT ALL. There is no provision making it unlawful to raise the rent, refuse to renew, change terms or evict because a tenant complained, organized, called a code inspector, or joined with other tenants. Four statutes speak to retaliation; one of them does not reach housing. The fair-housing bar never uses the word 'retaliate'.
- s 47-16-17.1(10): you may not refuse to rent, refuse to negotiate, make unavailable, deny a dwelling, 'or otherwise retaliate in the rental of a dwelling solely because a tenant or applicant or a household member ... exercised the right to terminate a lease under this section' -- i.e. the DOMESTIC-VIOLENCE termination right, and nothing else. s 47-16-17.1(11) backs it with statutory damages of one thousand dollars plus actual damages, reasonable attorney's fees, costs and disbursements.
- s 14-02.4-18 ('Retaliation prohibited') in the Human Rights Act. Do NOT rely on this for housing: all three of chapter 14-02.4's housing sections are REPEALED (while keeping their headings, which is the trap), so the chapter reaches employment, public accommodations and credit -- not housing.
- s 14-02.5-45(2) in the fair-housing act: 'It is a discriminatory practice to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with any individual in the exercise or enjoyment of, or on account of the individual having exercised or enjoyed, or on account of the individual having aided or encouraged any other individual in the exercise or enjoyment of, ANY RIGHT GRANTED OR PROTECTED BY THIS CHAPTER.' This is the one real limit, and note how narrow and how wide it is at once: narrow because the right exercised must be a FAIR-HOUSING right, wide because it covers the tenant who merely AIDED OR ENCOURAGED another tenant. So a group of tenants acting together on a discrimination complaint IS protected, and so is the one who helped them. s 14-02.5-45(1)(a) goes further where force or threat of force is used because of a protected ground and because the individual is 'applying for or participating in a service, ORGANIZATION, or facility relating to the business of selling or renting dwellings' -- a CLASS A MISDEMEANOR under s 14-02.5-45(3).
- s 23-12-10(5) in the state smoke-free law: no person may 'in any manner retaliate against ... [any] other person because that person asserts or exercises any rights afforded by this section or reports or attempts to prosecute a violation of this section' -- a class B misdemeanor. The smoke-free law covers the enclosed common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums, mobile home parks and other multi-unit residential buildings (s 23-12-09(11)), so a tenant who reports smoking in a hallway or lobby is protected.

THE CONSTITUTION WILL BE QUOTED AT YOU AND DOES NOT APPLY. N.D. Const. art. I, s 5: 'The citizens have a right, in a peaceable manner, to assemble together for the common good, and to apply to those invested with the powers of government for the redress of grievances.' Like every constitutional right, that restrains GOVERNMENT. A private landlord's lease is not state action, so art. I, s 5 does not give your tenants a right to meet in your community room. (A HOUSING AUTHORITY or other public landlord is in a different position and needs separate advice -- as is any federally subsidised property, where a federal organizing right may well apply.)

WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY DO -- AND THE ADVICE IS NOT 'DO AS YOU LIKE'. (1) Do NOT print a clause in which the tenant waives a right to organize. North Dakota confers no such right, so the waiver is EMPTY rather than lawful -- and it tells your tenant they surrendered something they never had, which is the fastest way to turn an organizing question into a grievance. (2) Do not write a clause forbidding tenants to talk to each other, to complain, or to contact a code official. It buys you nothing North Dakota law gives you anyway, and it looks exactly like the coercion s 14-02.5-45(2) makes a discriminatory practice. (3) If you set rules for the COMMON AREAS, set them about the SPACE -- booking, hours, numbers, noise, deposit for damage -- and apply them without regard to who is meeting or why. A neutral room-booking rule is defensible; refusing the room to the tenants who complained is not. (4) Remember that s 47-16-13.6 lets the court award reasonable attorney's fees to 'THE PREVAILING PARTY' in an action to enforce ss 47-16-13.1 to 47-16-13.6. That cuts both ways -- it favours you against a weak habitability claim, and against you if an organized group of tenants is right. (5) In a MOBILE HOME PARK you have real, affirmative duties that are the closest thing North Dakota has to an organizing regime: s 47-10-28(1)(e) requires you to acknowledge receipt of 'tenant inquiries or complaints regarding the park' within TWO BUSINESS DAYS; s 47-10-28(9) requires a summary of the tenant's lease and of both parties' rights and obligations; and during a pending action under the section s 47-10-28(14) forbids you to 'modify the park rules or regulations, modify the tenant's rental arrangement, increase a tenant's monthly rental rate, or terminate a tenant's lease without cause' -- a statutory freeze that functions as anti-retaliation protection while a dispute is live. Breach carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 (s 47-10-28(12)) and is a defence to the eviction (s 47-32-01.1).

title: No North Dakota agency statement of tenant rights, no signed acknowledgment, and nothing that must be the first page of a lease
bodyText:
Default rule first: no North Dakota statute requires a landlord to give a tenant a state agency's statement of tenant rights, to attach one as the first page of a lease or renewal, to have the tenant sign each page, or to obtain a signed acknowledgment of receipt. No North Dakota statute conditions a landlord's right to sue, or to bring an eviction, on having provided a tenant-rights statement first. No state agency is charged with producing such a statement, and no form exists to attach.

This is one of four topics that ask the same question at different scales. The full inventory of what a North Dakota landlord must give or tell a tenant is in the required-disclosures row ("The complete list of what a North Dakota landlord must give or tell a tenant - and it is short"); read that row rather than rebuilding the list. Two specific points worth knowing. First, nothing in the North Dakota statutes prescribes the position, order, type size or font of anything in a residential lease - chapter 47-16 was read heading by heading and contains no layout rule at all, and the only first-page requirement anywhere in these statutes is N.D.C.C. 11-18-05, which reserves three inches across the top of the first page of a recorded instrument for the county recorder's information. Second, North Dakota does know how to require prescribed wording when it wants to - it just has never done so for a residential lease. The places it has: N.D.C.C. 47-10-28(10), which requires a mobile home park's notice of intent to evict to include clear boldfaced language stating verbatim "You do not have to vacate immediately. You have the right to remain until a court issues an eviction order."; N.D.C.C. 47-15.1-03(2), which requires a ten-point boldface "NOTICE TO CONSUMER - READ BEFORE SIGNING" in a consumer rental purchase agreement for goods; N.D.C.C. 17-04-06, which requires a wind easement or wind energy lease to be delivered with a sixteen-point type cover page urging the property owner to hire a lawyer; N.D.C.C. 47-33-05, which requires a "Notice of Private Transfer Fee Obligation" in at least fourteen-point boldfaced type; and N.D.C.C. 47-18-05.1, which requires a conspicuous homestead-waiver statement. Not one of them is a residential lease.

What to do: do not attach a document described as a state tenant-rights statement, and do not represent that the tenant's signature on one affects their rights. If you want the tenant to acknowledge receiving something, the acknowledgment North Dakota actually cares about is the condition statement under N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.2, which the statute says "shall be agreed to and signed by the landlord and tenant" and which is prima facie proof of the condition of the premises - get that one right, because it protects you at move-out. If you operate a mobile home park, the summary duty under N.D.C.C. 47-10-28(9) is a real obligation and is covered on the rights-responsibilities-guide row, which is marked for review because the statute does not say what the summary must contain.

title: Screening applicants in North Dakota: no screening statute, one closed list of protected classes, and a bigger deposit instead of a refusal
bodyText:
The default rule first: North Dakota does not regulate tenant screening. No provision in the North Dakota statutes requires a conditional offer before you look at criminal history, sets a look-back period for convictions, caps an application or screening fee, limits a minimum-income test to the tenant's share of the rent, gives you a negligence shield for renting to someone with a record, bars reliance on erased or sealed records, or tells you what to disclose when you turn an applicant down. Those are all real rules in other states. They are not North Dakota law, so do not import them — and do not assume the reverse either, because the one body of law that does control your screening is fair housing, and in North Dakota that is chapter 14-02.5.

The protected characteristics, and they are a closed list. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-02(1) and (2): you may not refuse to rent, refuse to negotiate, make a dwelling unavailable, or give different terms, conditions or privileges because of 'race, color, religion, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin, or status with respect to marriage or public assistance'. Two consequences people get wrong. 'Status with respect to public assistance' is in the list, so a no-vouchers or no-benefits policy is a discriminatory housing practice in North Dakota. And the list does not include sexual orientation or gender identity — indeed § 14-02.5-01(6) expressly says 'disability' 'does not apply to an individual because of an individual's sexual orientation or because that individual is a transvestite'. That is what the statute says; it does not make such screening a good idea, and federal law and local ordinances may reach it.

Criminal history. Nothing in North Dakota's fair housing chapter protects it, and § 14-02.5-02(4) goes further: the section 'does not prohibit discrimination against an individual because the individual has been convicted under federal law or the law of any state of the illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance'. Note the narrowness — manufacture or distribution, not possession, and not crime in general. So a specific manufacture-or-distribution screen is expressly blessed by statute; a broad criminal screen is simply unregulated by North Dakota, which is not the same as safe. Blanket criminal bans attract federal disparate-impact claims under the federal Fair Housing Act, and that is federal law, not North Dakota law, so take advice on it rather than relying on this row. The practical course: write down your criteria in advance, apply them to everyone identically, look at the offence and how long ago it was rather than the mere existence of a record, and keep the decision notes.

North Dakota's real alternative to refusing a risky applicant is a bigger deposit, and this is the useful thing to know. § 47-16-07.1(1) caps security at one month's rent, with two exceptions: '(a) A lessor may accept an amount or value up to two month's rent, as security, from an individual convicted of a felony offense as an incentive to rent the property to the individual' and '(b) A lessor may demand an amount or value up to two months rent, as security, from an individual who has had a judgment entered against that individual for violating the terms of a previous rental agreement.' The statute is built on the assumption that you will screen for felony convictions and for prior rental judgments, and it gives you a priced way to say yes instead of no. Watch the difference in verbs: in (a) you may 'accept' two months as an incentive to rent; in (b) you may 'demand' it.

Four more limits to respect at the application stage. (1) § 14-02.5-06(3)(b) makes it disability discrimination to refuse 'a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices, or services' — your screening criteria are policies and practices, so be ready to consider a guarantor, a co-signer or alternative proof of income where a credit score alone would exclude a disabled applicant; § 14-02.5-06(6) does not require you to house an individual whose tenancy 'would constitute a direct threat to the health or safety of other individuals' or would result in substantial physical damage to others' property. (2) § 14-02.5-02(3) bars denying admission to housing that is part of a state housing programme on the basis that the applicant is or has been a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking. (3) § 47-16-17.1(10) bars refusing to rent to, refusing to negotiate with, making unavailable to, denying a dwelling to or otherwise retaliating against an applicant or a household member solely because the right to terminate a lease for domestic violence was exercised — with statutory damages of one thousand dollars plus actual damages and fees under (11). (4) § 14-02.5-03 bars an advertisement that 'indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination' on the protected grounds, so clean up your listings as well as your decisions.

Two things that change what you will even see. § 47-32-05, new on August 1, 2025, lets a tenant move to seal eviction court records seven years after a satisfied nonpayment or damage eviction, and lets a tenant evicted because of a domestic violence incident move to seal on the assailant's conviction or on a protection order — so an absent eviction record may be a sealed one, and acting on knowledge of a sealed record is a matter for advice. And the adverse-action notice you give when you reject someone on a credit or background report is a FEDERAL requirement under the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, not a North Dakota one; the federal regulations were not readable for this row, so comply with them and do not look for a North Dakota statute on the point.

Finally, check whether the chapter applies to you at all before you rely on any of this. § 14-02.5-09(1) exempts an owner of not more than three single-family houses renting without a broker, agent or realtor and without a prohibited advertisement, and then only for one rental in a twenty-four-month period if the owner was not the most recent resident; § 14-02.5-09(2) disapplies § 14-02.5-02 and §§ 14-02.5-04 to 14-02.5-08 to rooms or units in a dwelling of not more than four families living independently where the owner occupies one of them; and § 14-02.5-11 disapplies the familial-status and age provisions to qualifying housing for the elderly. If you are not exempt, the exposure is serious: § 14-02.5-32 lets the department assess civil penalties up to $11,000, $27,000 or $55,000 depending on your history, on top of actual damages, fees and costs; § 14-02.5-37 lets the attorney general seek up to $50,000 for a first and $100,000 for a later violation in a pattern-or-practice case; and § 14-02.5-45(3) makes intimidation or interference by force or threat of force a class A misdemeanour.

title: The seven duties North Dakota puts on every tenant -- and why 'guest' is the wrong word to use
bodyText:
THE DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota imposes tenant duties by statute, so they apply to every residential tenancy whether or not your lease says a word about them. You do not have to print them to rely on them. North Dakota has NOT adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and it has NO landlord-tenant non-waiver statute -- but the duties below are the tenant's by operation of law, and nothing in them depends on your lease.

THE SPINE: N.D.C.C. s 47-16-13.2 ('Tenant obligations - Maintenance of dwelling unit'). 'A tenant of a residential dwelling unit shall:'
1. 'Comply with all obligations primarily imposed upon tenants by applicable provisions of building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety.'
2. 'Keep that part of the premises that the tenant occupies and uses as clean and safe as the condition of the premises permit.'
3. 'Periodically remove all ashes, garbage, rubbish, and other waste from the tenant's dwelling unit, and dispose of them in a clean and safe manner.'
4. 'Keep all plumbing fixtures in the dwelling unit or used by the tenant as clean as their condition permits.'
5. 'Use in a reasonable manner all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, and other facilities and appliances including elevators in the premises.'
6. 'Not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair, or remove any part of the premises or knowingly permit any person to do so.'
7. 'Conduct oneself and require other persons on the premises with the tenant's consent to conduct themselves in a manner that will not disturb the tenant's neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises.'
Read subsections 2 and 4 closely: each duty is measured against 'the condition of the premises' or 'their condition' AS IT IS. A tenant is not obliged to make a dirty or unsafe unit clean or safe -- only to keep it as clean and safe as its own condition permits.
