That is a real limit on what you can demand, and it is in the statute's own words.

THREE MORE DUTIES THAT SIT OUTSIDE s 47-16-13.2 AND ARE EASY TO MISS.
- s 47-16-09: 'The lessee of real property must use ordinary care to preserve such property in safety and to keep it in good condition.'
- s 47-16-10: 'The lessee of real property must repair all deteriorations or injuries thereto occasioned by the lessee's ORDINARY NEGLIGENCE.' Note the standard -- ordinary negligence, not deliberate damage. This is broader than s 47-16-13.2(6) and is the section to cite for careless damage.
- s 47-16-11: where the property is leased for a particular purpose, 'the lessee must not use it for any other purpose', and on breach you 'may hold the lessee responsible for the safety of the property during such use in all events or may treat the contract as rescinded'. THIS ONE ONLY WORKS IF YOUR LEASE STATED THE PURPOSE -- see the prohibited-acts-renter clause row.

AND THE WORD THAT MATTERS MOST: DO NOT WRITE 'GUEST'. s 47-16-13.2(7) says the tenant must require 'other persons on the premises with the tenant's consent' to behave. Its eviction counterpart, s 47-32-01(7), says an eviction lies where 'A lessee or a person on the premises with the lessee's consent acts in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment of the premises.' NEITHER SECTION USES 'GUEST' OR 'VISITOR'. The statutory phrase is wider: it catches an unauthorised occupant, a partner who moved in, a relative staying for a month, a contractor the tenant let in -- anyone there by the tenant's leave. If you draft 'Tenant is responsible for Tenant's guests', you have given yourself a narrower rule than North Dakota already gives you. Use the statute's phrase.
The one place 'guest' does appear in North Dakota's statutes is the SECURITY DEPOSIT section: s 47-16-07.1(3)(a) lets you apply the deposit to 'damages the lessor has suffered by reason of deteriorations or injuries to the real property or dwelling by the lessee's pet or through the negligence of the lessee or the lessee's guest.' So for deposit purposes 'guest' is the statute's own word -- and that is the only context in which to use it.

HOW THESE DUTIES ARE ENFORCED. s 47-32-01(7) gives you an eviction for the disturbance duty directly, and because s 47-32-02 requires the three-day notice of intention to evict only 'in all cases arising under subsections 4, 5, 6, and 8', GROUND 7 NEEDS NO PRE-SUIT NOTICE. The other duties in s 47-16-13.2 have NO eviction ground of their own: to evict for a breach of subsections 1 to 6 you must go through s 47-32-01(8) ('violates a material term of the WRITTEN lease agreement'), which does require three days' notice -- and which requires that your written lease actually contain the term. That is the practical reason to restate these duties in the lease even though the statute already imposes them: not to create the duty, but to make it an evictable material term. s 47-16-13.7 keeps the tenant liable for rent during the term of the lease after an eviction, and s 47-16-13.5 imposes a duty to mitigate damages.

WHAT YOU SHOULD ACTUALLY DO. (1) Do not rely on the lease to create these duties -- they exist without it. (2) DO restate the ones you might evict on, in the statute's words, so ground 8 is available: see the prohibited-acts-renter clause row. (3) Never write a clause purporting to waive a tenant duty in exchange for something, or to shift a landlord duty to the tenant, without reading s 47-16-13.1(4)-(6) first: in anything other than a single-family residence the duty to provide waste receptacles and arrange removal, and to supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat, CANNOT be shifted to the tenant by any agreement, and a duty-shift needs a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration. (4) In a MOBILE HOME PARK, s 47-10-28(9) requires you to 'provide a tenant with a summary outlining the tenant's lease and the rights and obligations of the tenant and mobile home park owner under state law' -- a positive disclosure duty about duties, with a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 under s 47-10-28(12) and a defence to the eviction under s 47-32-01.1 if you skip it.

title: No Landlord Towing Statute, and the Gap Is Not in Your Favour
bodyText:
North Dakota gives a landlord no statutory authority to tow a vehicle from the leased premises, imposes no signage condition on doing so, and places no duty on the towing carrier in that situation - there is simply no provision about it in the landlord-tenant chapter or anywhere in the property title. That absence cuts against you rather than for you: towing someone's car is an interference with their property, and without a statute to point to you are relying entirely on what the lease says and on the vehicle owner having agreed to it.

Two things follow. Put the parking terms and the consequence in the lease, and get them signed, because that agreement is all the authority you have. And if what you are dealing with is a genuinely abandoned vehicle rather than a badly parked one, the route is the public abandoned-motor-vehicle procedure in chapter 23.1-15 rather than a private tow, since that chapter is where North Dakota put removal, disposal and the reimbursement of commercial towing services.

title: No tenant-purchase exemption notice in North Dakota - and why you should not recite one anyway
bodyText:
This one is empty in North Dakota, and it is worth saying why rather than leaving you to wonder.

An exemption notice is a creature of a tenant-purchase statute. In the states that have a Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act, the Act typically exempts certain sales - a transfer to a family member, a foreclosure, a transfer between co-owners, a building under a size threshold - and then requires the landlord who relies on an exemption to say so: to file, record or serve a notice certifying which exemption applies, often before the sale can close. North Dakota has no Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act, so there is nothing to be exempt from, no list of exemptions, and no exemption notice to give. See the row on tenant purchase notices: there is no tenant right of first refusal, no right of first offer, no opportunity-to-purchase notice and no duty even to tell a sitting tenant that the property is being sold.

So the default rule, stated first: you may sell your North Dakota rental to anyone, at any time, without offering it to your tenant, without telling your tenant, and without certifying to anybody that you are entitled to do so. There is no form, no filing, no recording, no waiting period and no penalty, because there is no scheme.

Two traps follow from that, and they are the practical point of this row.

First, do not put an exemption recital in your lease or in your purchase documents. A clause saying something like 'this sale is exempt from any tenant opportunity to purchase' or 'the tenant waives any right of first refusal' is empty in North Dakota, not protective - there is no right to waive and no exemption to claim. Worse, it is affirmatively unhelpful: it tells your tenant that a category of right exists and that they have given it up, which invites an argument you would otherwise never have had. The same goes for a recital borrowed from a District of Columbia, Maryland or Massachusetts form.

Second, do not let the absence of an exemption notice distract you from the notices and transfers North Dakota DOES require on a sale. Those are real and enforceable, and they are set out on the tenant purchase notice row: section 47-16-07.1(5) transfers the security deposit and its accrued interest to the buyer and keeps you liable until it actually moves, against section 47-16-07.1(4)'s treble damages; section 47-10-20 makes the sale good without the tenant's attornment but protects a tenant who paid rent to you before having notice of it; and if the property is a mobile home park, section 47-10-28 requires written notice of the change of ownership to every tenant within five business days, among nine other change-of-ownership duties, backed by a civil penalty of not less than two thousand five hundred dollars and by section 47-32-01.1's defence to an eviction.

What to do. Nothing, as far as exemption notices go - and specifically, nothing in the lease. Spend the attention instead on documenting the deposit transfer and on giving the tenant prompt written notice of the sale and of where rent now goes.

title: Selling a rented North Dakota property: no tenant right of first refusal, but the deposit must move with it
bodyText:
The default in North Dakota is that your rental property is yours to sell, to whom you like, when you like, and you owe the sitting tenant nothing by way of first refusal, first offer or advance notice of the sale. North Dakota has no Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act. There is no tenant right of first refusal, no right of first offer, no opportunity-to-purchase notice, no tenant-organization purchase right, no waiting period before you may accept a third party's offer, and no requirement that you even tell the tenant the property is on the market or has been sold. The only rights of first refusal in North Dakota property law belong to somebody else entirely - a public charter school over unused state-owned facilities, and the holders of options and refusal rights that the private-transfer-fee chapter happens to mention in passing. None of them is a tenant.

So do not go looking for a tenant purchase notice, and do not copy one from another state's lease. But the sale of an occupied rental does trigger real North Dakota duties, and they are the ones to get right.

THE SECURITY DEPOSIT MUST MOVE WITH THE PROPERTY, AND YOU STAY ON THE HOOK UNTIL IT DOES. Section 47-16-07.1(5): 'Upon a transfer in ownership of the leased real property or dwelling, the security deposit and accrued interest shall be transferred to the grantee of the lessor's interest. The grantor shall not be relieved of liability under this section until transfer of the security deposit to the grantee. The holder of the lessor's interest in the real property or dwelling at the termination of a lease shall be bound by this section even though such holder was not the original lessor who received the security deposit.' Three things follow. If you are selling, hand over the deposit AND the interest that has accrued on it, and get a written receipt - a credit on the settlement statement is not the same as a transfer and you remain liable until the money actually moves. Remember that the deposit has had to sit in a federally insured interest-bearing savings or checking account for the tenant's benefit, so the interest figure is real and must go too. And if you are buying, you are bound by section 47-16-07.1 at the end of the tenancy even though you never took the deposit - which means you need the money, the interest and the paperwork from the seller before you close, because section 47-16-07.1(4) makes a lessor liable for TREBLE DAMAGES for any deposit withheld without reasonable justification, and 'the seller never gave it to me' will not be a reasonable justification.

THE TENANT DOES NOT HAVE TO AGREE, BUT TELL THEM ANYWAY. Section 47-10-20: 'Grants of rents, reversions, or remainders are good and effectual without attornments of the tenants, but no tenant, who before notice of the grant shall have paid rent to the grantor, must suffer any damage thereby.' The sale works without the tenant's consent or acknowledgment - but until the tenant has notice of it, rent paid to the old owner is good payment and the tenant cannot be prejudiced for having paid it. There is no statutory notice to give and no form for it; the buyer simply has a strong practical reason to give prompt written notice of the sale and of where rent now goes, because every rent payment the tenant makes to the seller before that notice is a payment the buyer cannot recover from the tenant.

IF IT IS A MOBILE HOME PARK, THE RULES ARE ENTIRELY DIFFERENT AND SUBSTANTIAL. Section 47-10-28 is a separate and much stricter regime, and its heading is literally 'Mobile home park - Ownership - Transfer of ownership - Tenant rights - Penalty'. A person who owns or purchases an existing park must: obtain an annual licence under section 23-10-03; designate an official local office operational by the fifth business day after the change of ownership, unless the park has fewer than twenty-six lots; keep a telephone number manned weekdays from eight to five and an emergency number manned at all times; name at least one individual with authority to make and direct decisions, and give each tenant that person's contact details; give each tenant WRITTEN NOTICE OF THE CHANGE OF OWNERSHIP WITHIN FIVE BUSINESS DAYS of it taking effect, including those contact details; acknowledge a tenant complaint within two business days; supply a copy of the lease and any amendments within ten business days of a written request; and give each tenant the name, address and telephone number of the owning legal entity and the telephone number of any property manager or site agent. Two more that bite on a purchase: section 47-10-28(2) forbids requiring a tenant who owns their mobile home to sell or transfer it to the park owner, and section 47-10-28(7) stops a purchaser increasing the monthly rent for SIX MONTHS if the rent was raised in the sixty days before the purchase, and requires ninety days' notice of any rent increase in a month-to-month tenancy. The teeth are real: section 47-10-28(12) carries a civil penalty of not less than two thousand five hundred dollars and not more than the greater of ten thousand dollars or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs; subsection (13) lets the district court suspend the park licence with a daily penalty of half the month's rent roll divided by the days in the month; and section 47-32-01.1 makes a violation a defence to an eviction.

What to do. Sell freely, but put the deposit transfer in the purchase agreement as a condition and document the handover of both principal and interest. Give the tenant prompt written notice of the sale and the new rent address. Do not insert a clause purporting to give the tenant a right of first refusal unless you actually mean to grant one - in North Dakota that would be a right you created, not one the statute gave, and you would be bound by it. And if the property is a mobile home park, work through section 47-10-28 line by line before closing.

title: No North Dakota landlord-tenant statute is on a sunset clock - watch for amendments and repealed headings instead
bodyText:
The default, and the reassuring answer: no North Dakota landlord-tenant statute is on a repeal clock. Nothing in chapter 47-16 (landlord and tenant), chapter 47-17 (estates at will), chapter 47-32 (eviction), chapter 47-10 (conveyances, including section 47-10-28 on mobile home parks) or chapter 14-02.5 (fair housing) expires, sunsets or is repealed on a future date. None of these rules is going to lapse underneath your lease.

This is not an assumption, because North Dakota genuinely does use sunset clocks and uses them often. The usual form is a section at the end of an Act reading 'EXPIRATION DATE. This Act is effective through June 30, 2029, and after that date is ineffective', and the Legislative Council's index of the Century Code marks the affected sections with bracketed notes - '(Effective through June 30, 2029)', '(Expired effective August 1, 2031)', '(Repealed effective December 31, 2027)', '(Contingent expiration date - See note)'. There are 144 such markers across the Century Code. Not one of them is on a title 47 section. The ones nearest to property and land are a hunting provision on supplemental feed, which expires 31 July 2029, and a limitation on the liability of charitable organizations, effective through 30 June 2029; the rest cluster in the courts, insurance, tax, water, education, fire and consumer-email titles. Fair housing has no marker; neither does the consumer-fraud chapter.

There is also no Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act in North Dakota to be on a clock in the first place, so if you have come to this topic looking for a TOPA sunset date, there is none because there is no Act. See the rows on tenant purchase notices and exemption notices.

Two cautions, because 'no sunset' is not the same as 'nothing changes'.

First, North Dakota repeals and amends landlord-tenant provisions in the ordinary way, without a clock, and it has done so recently. In 2025 alone the legislature created section 47-16-20.1 (no fee for accepting cash, a cheque or a money order), created section 47-32-05 (sealing eviction records), created section 47-32-01.1 and amended section 47-10-28 (the mobile-home-park regime, including new late-fee caps), and amended section 47-16-17.1(2)(a) while creating a whole new chapter 14-07.7. The risk to your lease is not a sunset date you could diary; it is an amendment you did not notice. Review your form after each biennial legislative session rather than waiting for a date.

Second, and this is the trap that catches people reading the statute books: a repealed North Dakota section KEEPS ITS HEADING. Eighty-five sections in the chapters that bear on leasing are repealed but still carry their old headings in the chapter PDFs and in the official index, with nothing but 'Repealed by S.L. ...' in the body. Section 47-16-24 still reads 'Lessee must give written notice before removal of property from premises' and has no content at all; section 47-16-12, the old lessor repair duty, was repealed in 1977; all three housing sections of chapter 14-02.4 were repealed in 1999 and 2001 while keeping their headings, which is why fair housing lives in chapter 14-02.5. So a section heading, an index line or a search hit on a section number proves the number exists, not that it has any text. If you or your adviser relies on a North Dakota section, read the body of the section, every time.

What to do. Nothing needs to go in the lease. Do not write an expiry or a sunset reference into your form, and do not include a clause saying the lease survives the repeal of any statute - repeal and amendment take effect by force of law whatever your lease says. Diary a review of your lease form after each biennial session instead, and when you check a statute, read the section's body rather than its heading.

title: North Dakota imposes no lease translation duty and no type-size floor - and in 2025 wrote a customer's-language duty for crypto kiosks instead
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota requires no translation of a residential lease. There is no duty to provide the lease in a tenant's language, no duty triggered by having advertised or negotiated in another language, no duty to supply an interpreter, no verbatim statutory lease text a landlord must reproduce, and no minimum type size for anything in a residential lease. A lease that recites a translation right is creating one by contract, not reflecting a statute.

In the North Dakota statutes, the only language duties belong elsewhere. N.D.C.C. 47-19-36 lets an officer taking proof of a recorded instrument "employ and swear interpreters" - a procedural power in a recording proceeding. The master index names chapter 28-33 "Interpreters for Deaf Persons" and chapter 43-52 "Interpreters", both court-and-licensing chapters; neither could plausibly be a landlord duty. And in 2025 the legislature wrote precisely the duty this topic describes, for someone else: S.L. 2025, ch. 143 (H.B. 1447) created N.D.C.C. 13-09.1-51, requiring a virtual-currency kiosk operator to disclose all relevant terms "in a clear, conspicuous, and easily readable manner in the chosen language of the customer", to obtain acknowledgment of receipt by confirmation of consent, and to post a prescribed bold warning. That is a sibling proving the negative: North Dakota knows how to impose a customer's-language duty and has not imposed one on a landlord.

On type size and verbatim text the picture is the same. North Dakota dictates the words or the typography of a document in five places and a residential lease is not one of them: N.D.C.C. 17-04-06 requires a wind easement or wind energy lease to be delivered with a cover page in at least sixteen-point type carrying a prescribed "Special message to property owners" that urges the owner to hire a lawyer, and forbids execution for ten business days after delivery; N.D.C.C. 47-15.1-03(2) requires a ten-point boldface "NOTICE TO CONSUMER - READ BEFORE SIGNING" in a rent-to-own agreement for goods, with other disclosures in at least eight-point type; N.D.C.C. 47-33-05 requires a "Notice of Private Transfer Fee Obligation" in at least fourteen-point boldfaced type; N.D.C.C. 47-10-28(10) requires a mobile home park's notice of intent to evict to include clear boldfaced language stating verbatim "You do not have to vacate immediately. You have the right to remain until a court issues an eviction order."; and N.D.C.C. 47-18-05.1 requires a conspicuous homestead-waiver statement. Note the wind-lease provision in particular - it is a lease, it is in the statutes, and the legislature gave the property owner a sixteen-point warning and a ten-day cooling-off period. It chose not to do that for the tenant of a home.

What to do: if you advertise or negotiate in a language other than English, do not assume a statute forces you to produce a translated lease - but do recognise the practical exposure. A tenant who signed an English lease after an entirely Spanish-language negotiation has an obvious argument about what was actually agreed, and North Dakota has two tools that could bite: N.D.C.C. 47-16-13.3 makes an unconscionable lease unenforceable, and N.D.C.C. 51-15-02 forbids a deceptive act or misrepresentation in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise, which 51-15-01(3) defines to include real estate - though whether ch. 51-15 reaches a lease at all is itself unsettled, and the plain-language-consumer-statement row carries that open question. The cheap protection is to have the lease walked through in the language you negotiated in, give the tenant a translated summary of the money terms and the termination terms as a courtesy you are choosing to provide, and keep a note that you did. Do not print a clause stating that the tenant has read and understood the lease in English, or waiving any translation right: there is no right to waive, and the clause reads as an attempt to paper over exactly the problem it describes. If a tenant is deaf or hard of hearing, treat communication access as a fair housing reasonable-accommodation question under N.D.C.C. 14-02.5-06(3)(b), not as a translation question.

title: Barring a non-tenant in North Dakota: no statutory barment procedure, so build the record yourself
bodyText:
The default rule: nothing in North Dakota's landlord-tenant statutes lets a landlord bar a person from the property. The criminal trespass statute supplies only the notice method (see the posting rules at the end). No provision in the North Dakota statutes gives a landlord a notice-against-trespass procedure for a rental property, says what a no-trespassing notice must contain or how it must be served, sets how long a bar lasts, or spells out what defences a barred person has. The North Dakota statutes do not use the phrase 'no trespassing' at all. North Dakota's criminal trespass offence sits in § 12.1-22-03. It sets how notice against trespass is given, but no landlord barment procedure, so treat the cautious course below as the answer.

What the landlord-tenant statutes actually give you, and it is a lot less than a trespass bar.
• You control the common areas and you owe a duty over them. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(c): you must 'Keep all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition.' That duty is the real reason to deal with a person causing trouble in them — your other tenants can enforce it against you.
• Your tenant's rights are narrow and defined. § 47-16-27: a tenant for years or at will may occupy the buildings, take the annual products of the soil, work mines and quarries open at the start of the tenancy, and cultivate and harvest crops growing at the end — and 'The tenant has no rights to the property other than such as are given the tenant by the agreement or instrument by which the tenant's tenancy is acquired or by the provisions of this section.' So whatever right a tenant's guest has, they get it through the tenant, and the tenant's own right comes only from the lease and that section.
• Against the tenant you owe quiet possession. § 47-16-08 binds you 'to secure to the lessee the quiet possession of such property during the term of the lease against all persons lawfully claiming the same'. Barring a tenant's regular guest or carer from the building is the kind of act a tenant will frame as a breach of that, so do it on a written record and a stated reason, not on a conversation.
• Your lever against the person causing the problem is the tenant who lets them in. § 47-16-13.2(7) requires the tenant to 'Conduct oneself and require other persons on the premises with the tenant's consent to conduct themselves in a manner that will not disturb the tenant's neighbors' peaceful enjoyment of the premises.' And § 47-32-01(7) makes it a ground of eviction where 'A lessee or a person on the premises with the lessee's consent acts in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment of the premises' — note that the ground is against the LESSEE, for what their guest does. § 47-32-01(8), violation of a material term of the written lease, is the other route. Ground 7 needs no notice of intention to evict. Ground 8 needs three days' written notice of intention to evict before proceedings (§ 47-32-02).
• Against a person with no tenancy at all you already have a route that needs no notice. § 47-32-01's grounds 1 to 3 — a party who 'by force, intimidation, fraud, or stealth, has entered upon the prior actual possession' and detains it; who 'after peaceably entering upon real property, turns out by force, threats, or menacing conduct the party in possession'; or who 'by force or by menaces and threats of violence, unlawfully holds and keeps the possession' — require no notice at all under § 47-32-02, which lists only subsections 4, 5, 6 and 8. If someone has moved into a vacant unit, that is the route: an eviction action, not a lockout.

The cautious course for barring a non-tenant. (1) Put it in writing, to the person, naming the property, saying they may not enter or remain and why, dated and signed, and keep proof of delivery — a notice you can prove is the foundation of any trespass complaint you later make, and § 12.1-22-03(4) accepts notice by actual communication from the owner or someone the owner authorizes. (2) Post the common areas and entrances with clear signs, and keep a photograph of the posting with its date. (3) Tell the tenant whose guest it is, in writing, and tell them § 47-16-13.2(7) makes them responsible for the conduct of people on the premises with their consent. (4) Do not bar someone from a unit you have leased, and do not change a tenant's lock to exclude their guest — that is a step against your own tenant and runs into § 47-16-08 and the entry limits in § 47-16-07.3. (5) Call law enforcement to deal with the person rather than removing them yourself; the officer, not you, applies the criminal trespass statute. (6) Expect the guest, invitee and open-to-the-public arguments to be made against you and to carry weight in a building the public can walk into, and get advice before relying on a bar in a property with a public lobby, a leasing office or a shop.

Mobile home parks. § 47-10-28 contains no trespass or exclusion power, and the park rule-change machinery is slow and tenant-protective: subsection 3 requires thirty days' advance written notice of any modification to park rules and then, for a tenant who owns a home that fails to comply, written notice of the failure plus three months to remedy or vacate before an eviction can even be started, extendable where a relocator certifies the home cannot be moved in time. So you cannot create a guest-exclusion rule and enforce it quickly. A violation of § 47-10-28 carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 and up to the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, and is a defence to the eviction under § 47-32-01.1. The park licensing chapter also lets a park owner or manager 'eject any person from the premises' for nonpayment of charges for accommodations, a violation of law, disorderly conduct, a violation of a department regulation, or a violation of a reasonable rule publicly posted in the park (N.D.C.C. § 23-10-11). Use it for a visitor, not a tenant. Whether it can be used against a park tenant or the tenant's household instead of an eviction is unsettled; the cautious course is to evict a tenant only under chapter 47-32. The posting rules are specific. Under section 12.1-22-03(4), notice against trespass may be given by actual communication or "by posting in a manner reasonably likely to come to the attention of intruders", and "[t]he name of the person posting the premises must appear on each sign in legible characters" - so an unsigned no-trespassing sign may not do the work you think it does. Substantial compliance is enough where notice against trespass is clear from the circumstances. Note the carve-out in subsection 3(b): a licensed hunter or angler lawfully hunting or fishing is outside the fenced-land offence.

title: North Dakota has no truth-in-renting act and no state renting handbook you must deliver
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has no truth-in-renting statute. The phrase appears nowhere in the North Dakota statutes, and there is no state-published renting handbook, pamphlet, brochure or booklet that a landlord of ordinary rental housing must give a tenant, attach to the lease, post on the property, or get signed for. There is also no statute prohibiting a lease from containing a misleading statement of law - North Dakota has no prohibited-lease-provisions list in chapter 47-16 or chapter 47-32, and no landlord-tenant non-waiver statute anywhere.

This is one of four topics that ask the same question at different scales. The full inventory of what a North Dakota landlord must give or tell a tenant is in the required-disclosures row ("The complete list of what a North Dakota landlord must give or tell a tenant - and it is short"); read that row rather than rebuilding the list. The short version: the only document every North Dakota residential landlord must hand over is the condition statement under N.D.C.C. 47-16-07.2, signed by both parties; everything else is an event-driven notice. Mobile home parks are different and do carry a rights-summary duty - see the rights-responsibilities-guide row for N.D.C.C. 47-10-28(9), which is marked for review because the statute does not say what the summary must contain.

What to do: do not print a statement that the lease complies with a North Dakota truth-in-renting act, and do not attach a document described as a state-required renting guide - there is no act and no guide, and describing your own material as state-required is the kind of misstatement that could be argued to engage N.D.C.C. 51-15-02, which forbids a deceptive act or misrepresentation in connection with the sale or advertisement of merchandise, defined in 51-15-01(3) to include real estate. If you want to give tenants a plain-English summary of their rights, that is a good practice and nothing stops you - label it as your own summary, keep it accurate, and do not suggest that signing it waives anything. Because North Dakota has no non-waiver statute, a waiver you print is not automatically void, but N.D.C.C. 9-08-05 voids any stipulation restricting a party from enforcing their rights by the usual legal proceedings or limiting the time to do so, and 47-16-13.3 makes an unconscionable lease or settlement unenforceable - so an aggressive waiver buys you less than it looks like.

title: Squatters and People Who Were Never Your Tenant: Use Grounds 1 to 3, Which Need No Notice
bodyText: The default rule is that North Dakota has no squatter statute, no transient-occupant affidavit procedure and no route by which a sheriff or the police remove an unauthorised occupant on your sworn complaint outside the eviction process. The word squatter does not appear anywhere in the North Dakota statutes. What North Dakota gives you instead is better than it first looks, because the eviction chapter was written to reach exactly these people and to reach them fast. Section 47-32-01 makes an eviction action maintainable when: (1) 'A party, by force, intimidation, fraud, or stealth, has entered upon the prior actual possession of real property of another and detains the same'; (2) a party, after peaceably entering, 'turns out by force, threats, or menacing conduct the party in possession'; and (3) a party 'by force or by menaces and threats of violence, unlawfully holds and keeps the possession of any real property, whether the possession was acquired peaceably or otherwise'. Ground 1 is the squatter ground: entry by stealth, and detention of what was your prior actual possession. And here is the part that matters most -- section 47-32-02 attaches the three days' written notice of intention to evict only to grounds 4, 5, 6 and 8. Grounds 1, 2 and 3 are not on that list, so you serve no notice and file immediately, with an appearance date not fewer than three nor more than fifteen days out. If the person cannot be found in the county and you have tried service at least once between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m., you can post the summons on the door after filing an affidavit and mailing a copy to the last known address -- which is how you reach someone who will not answer. Section 47-32-04 then gives you judgment for immediate restitution, and the five-day hardship stay is unavailable where the judgment rests in whole or in part on a disturbance of the peace. Two other things to know. An occupant who is there with your tenant's consent is NOT a stranger to the tenancy: section 47-32-01(7) makes the tenancy itself evictable where 'a lessee or a person on the premises with the lessee's consent acts in a manner that unreasonably disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment', and that ground also needs no notice. And whoever the occupant is, you may not remove them yourself -- grounds 2 and 3 are grounds the person you turned out can use against you. Criminal trespass is a separate matter from possession and lives in section 12.1-22-03 (see the update below). Chapter 32-17, the quiet-title action, is a second and slower civil route: it lets you recover possession and the value of use and occupation from a trespasser (section 32-17-02). The cautious course is to call the police if a crime is in progress and, separately and at the same time, file the chapter 47-32 eviction on grounds 1 to 3 -- do not wait for a criminal outcome, and do not assume a police response gets you possession. UPDATE, and it is good news for you: North Dakota criminalised squatting in 2025. Section 12.1-22-03(2) now makes an individual who unlawfully detains, occupies or trespasses upon a residential dwelling guilty of a class C felony on the first offence, and a class B felony on a second or later offence at the same dwelling. Section 12.1-22-03(1) separately makes entering or remaining in a dwelling without licence or privilege a class C felony. So where the occupant is a genuine stranger rather than a holdover tenant, a criminal complaint is now a real route alongside the eviction, and grounds 1, 2, 3 and 7 of section 47-32-01 need no notice of intention to evict at all. None of this lets you remove anyone yourself - do not change locks or remove belongings; call law enforcement or file, or do both.

title: Charging Separately for Parking
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota has no parking statute for rental housing at all. In the statutes searched, the word "parking" appears in only one place in the whole of title 47 - N.D.C.C. § 47-04.1-16, the condominium electric-vehicle-charging section, which is about a unit OWNER'S designated parking space and an association's bylaws, not about a landlord and a tenant. There is no rule requiring parking to be offered separately from rent, none forbidding it, no cap on a parking charge, no permit-term rule and no landlord towing procedure. So the lease decides everything - and a tenant has no parking right at all unless the lease gives one, because N.D.C.C. § 47-16-27 provides that "[t]he tenant has no rights to the property other than such as are given the tenant by the agreement or instrument by which the tenant's tenancy is acquired or by the provisions of this section", and that section's own list is occupying the buildings, taking the annual products of the soil, working open mines and harvesting growing crops.

THE TRAP THAT MATTERS MOST - YOUR DEPOSIT CAP. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1) bars a lessor from demanding or receiving "security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's rent", with only the two exceptions in (1)(a) (a felony conviction, as an incentive to rent) and (1)(b) (a judgment for violating a previous rental agreement), each up to two months. North Dakota does not define "rent", and whether a separately charged parking fee counts towards it is a question no statute answers and only a court could settle. Take the cautious course: calculate the one-month cap on the dwelling rent ALONE, excluding the parking charge. Getting this wrong is expensive - § 47-16-07.1(4) makes a lessor "liable for treble damages for any security deposit money withheld without reasonable justification."

TWO MORE LIMITS ON THE MONEY. Keep the parking charge a straight rent for the space, measured by what you are letting, and not a penalty: § 9-08-03 provides that "[p]enalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance thereof are void", and § 9-08-04 voids an amount of damages fixed in advance "to that extent" unless "it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage". A flat $100 for parking in the wrong space is a penalty. And you may not surcharge the payment method: § 47-16-20.1, created by S.L. 2025, ch. 423 (H.B. 1610) and effective August 1, 2025, forbids a fee for accepting cash, a check or a money order.

ACCESSIBILITY IS NOT OPTIONAL. N.D.C.C. § 14-02.5-06(3)(b) makes it discrimination to refuse "a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices, or services" where it may be necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling - which reaches assigning an accessible or closer space, and reaches waiving a parking charge where the accommodation requires it. Section 14-02.5-06(3)(c) requires covered multifamily dwellings to be designed so "the public use and common use portions" are readily accessible. Section 14-02.5-02(2) bars discrimination "in providing services or facilities in connection with a sale or rental of a dwelling" on grounds that in North Dakota include age and familial status.

DO NOT TOW ON YOUR OWN AUTHORITY, and do not write a self-help towing clause. North Dakota's abandoned-vehicle machinery is ch. 23.1-15. A vehicle "located on private property without consent of the person in control of the property" is an "abandoned motor vehicle" (§ 23.1-15-01(1)), and "[i]f requested by an owner, lessee, tenant, or occupant of private property, a commercial towing service may remove and take into custody" it (§ 23.1-15-03). The towing service, not you, then gives the notices (§ 23.1-15-05), the owner may reclaim within thirty days on paying towing and storage, with storage capped at fifty dollars a day for an ordinary vehicle (§ 23.1-15-06), and only then may the towing service "obtain a release from the department of transportation which is sufficient title to dispose of the vehicle" (§ 23.1-15-07(2)). The statute therefore routes removal and disposal through a commercial towing service, not through the landlord. Separately, § 47-16-30.1 lets a lessor retain and dispose of property left on the premises without legal process only where it has "a total estimated value of not more than two thousand five hundred dollars", and only twenty-eight or more days after actual notice that the lessee has vacated or after it reasonably appears so - a figure most vehicles exceed. Use a licensed tow operator and keep the records.

CAUTIOUS COURSE on zoning. Whether you may let the space at all, or must keep a minimum number of spaces, is a zoning question. North Dakota delegates zoning to cities (ch. 40-47), counties (ch. 11-33) and townships (ch. 58-03), and none of those chapters sets a parking minimum; that is left to the local ordinance. The only off-street-parking text in them is a rebuild condition: §§ 40-47-05.1(1)(d)(4) and 11-33-17.1(1)(d)(4), created by S.L. 2025, ch. 112 (H.B. 1500), allow a damaged residential nonconforming structure to be rebuilt only if the new structure will not "[d]iminish the number of off-street parking spaces located on the property from the number of spaces before the damage". Check with the zoning office before letting spaces to anyone other than your own tenants.

title: North Dakota has a real unconscionability statute for residential leases -- and it reaches your move-out settlements too
bodyText: Default rule first: a North Dakota residential lease term is not void merely because it is one-sided. It has to be unlawful, and a provision is unlawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law, contrary to the policy of express law though not expressly prohibited, or 'otherwise contrary to good morals' (N.D.C.C. Section 9-08-01) -- the three limbs that, with Sections 9-08-02 to 9-08-05, do most of the work on exculpation, penalties, liquidated damages and clauses restricting the usual legal proceedings. See the prohibited-lease-terms and exculpatory-clauses rows for those. On top of that, North Dakota has a genuine unconscionability statute written for residential tenancies, and it is more useful to a tenant than most landlords expect. Under Section 47-16-13.3(1)(a), if a court of competent jurisdiction finds AS A MATTER OF LAW that a residential dwelling unit rental agreement, or any provision of it, was unconscionable WHEN MADE, the court may refuse to enforce the agreement, enforce the rest of it without the unconscionable provision, or limit the application of the provision to avoid an unconscionable result. Three features matter. The test is unconscionability at the time of making, so a term that merely turns out badly later is not caught -- North Dakota has nothing like the laws of some jurisdictions that let a court revise or end a running lease because performance has become excessively onerous. The remedy is flexible rather than all-or-nothing: the usual outcome is that your one bad clause is struck or read down and the rest of the lease stands, which is a reason to keep each term independently defensible. And under Section 47-16-13.3(2), once unconscionability is put in issue BY A PARTY OR BY THE COURT ON ITS OWN MOTION, both sides must be given a reasonable opportunity to present evidence about 'the setting, purpose, and effect' of the agreement -- so the judge may raise it even if the tenant's papers never do, and the evidence will be about how the lease came to be signed, not just what it says. The part most often missed: Section 47-16-13.3(1)(b) applies the same power to a SETTLEMENT in which a party waives or agrees to forego a claim or right under Sections 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 or under the rental agreement. Those are the habitability, entry, unconscionability, post-termination remedy and enforcement sections. So a move-out agreement, a mutual release, a 'sign here and we will not report the balance' deal, or a deposit compromise can itself be reviewed and refused. What to do: keep a signing file showing the setting -- that the tenant had the lease in advance and time to read it, what was explained, what was negotiable, what alternatives were offered, and any addendum the tenant chose. Make every clause defensible on its own so severance leaves you intact. Give real consideration for any settlement or waiver, put it in writing, state what each side is giving up, and never take a waiver of habitability rights for nothing. And drop the terms that only work as leverage: unlimited landlord discretion over a money term, round sums untied to any actual cost, and waivers of statutory rights.

title: There is no usufruct in North Dakota - what to do if your own interest in the property is limited
bodyText:
The default in North Dakota is that renting out property is a contract, not a carved-up ownership right. Section 47-16-01 defines the whole institution: 'Leasing is a contract by which one gives to another the temporary possession and use of real property for reward and the latter agrees to return such possession to the former at a future time.' Your tenant gets temporary possession and use, and owes you the property back.

North Dakota has no usufruct. The words 'usufruct', 'usufructuary', 'naked owner', 'civil fruits' and 'fructuary' do not appear anywhere in the North Dakota Century Code, the 2025-26 session laws or the state constitution. There is no North Dakota lessor who holds a usufruct rather than an estate, no naked owner sitting behind one, and no rule about who takes the fruits when a usufruct ends. That is a Louisiana and civil-law structure; North Dakota is a common-law state and has instead a leasehold under chapter 47-16 carved out of an estate in land. So if a form, a title company or an out-of-state adviser asks you to identify yourself as a 'usufructuary lessor', the honest answer in North Dakota is that the category does not exist here - and do not sign a document that says it does, because you would be describing your interest in words North Dakota law gives no content to.

What North Dakota has instead, and it answers the real question underneath. The practical worry behind this topic is a landlord whose own interest in the land is limited and may end before the lease does - most often a life tenant. North Dakota handles that in four readable sections, none of them in the landlord-tenant chapter:

- Section 47-02-33: the owner of a life estate 'may use the land in the same manner as the owner of a fee simple, except that the owner of a life estate must do no act to the injury of the inheritance.' So a life tenant may let the property - renting it out is an ordinary use - but may not do so in a way that injures the inheritance.
- Section 47-02-34: the owner of a life estate 'must keep the buildings and fences in repair from ordinary waste and must pay the taxes and other annual charges and a just proportion of extraordinary assessments benefiting the whole inheritance.' A life-tenant landlord carries repair and tax burdens in their own right, on top of the chapter 47-16 habitability duties owed to the tenant.
- Section 47-10-09, which is the key one: 'A grant made by the owner of an estate for life or years, purporting to transfer a greater estate than the owner could transfer lawfully, does not work a forfeiture of the owner's estate but passes to the grantee all the estate which the grantor could lawfully transfer.' So a lease granted for longer than your own interest is not void and does not cost you your interest - it simply gives the tenant as much as you had and no more. It is good as far as it goes, and no further.
- Section 47-04-22: the person in fee, remainder or reversion may sue for an injury done to the inheritance even though a life or term estate sits in between. The remainderman is not powerless while your tenancy runs.

Note what is not on the list in section 47-16-14. A lease of real property terminates at the end of the agreed term, by mutual consent, by the lessee acquiring title superior to the lessor's, or by destruction of the property. The ending of the lessor's own estate is not one of the four. Chapter 47-16 simply does not address it, so the answer comes from section 47-10-09 and the general law of estates rather than from the lease statute.

What to do. If your interest in the property is anything less than a fee simple - a life estate, a term, an interest held with others whose consent you need - say so in the lease and set the lease term so it cannot outlast your interest. Do not grant a longer term and rely on section 47-10-09 to tidy it up: it protects your estate from forfeiture, but it leaves your tenant holding a tenancy that ends early with no remedy you have agreed, and that is where disputes come from. Put in the lease what happens if your interest ends during the term - who the tenant then pays, what notice is given, and how the deposit is dealt with - and remember that under section 47-16-07.1(5) a security deposit transfers to the grantee on a transfer of ownership and the grantor is not relieved of liability until it does. And do not use the civil-law vocabulary in a North Dakota lease at all; describe your estate in the terms chapter 47-02 uses.

title: North Dakota caps what you may charge a tenant for a utility only in a mobile home park -- and there, the cap is actual cost plus three dollars
bodyText:
Default rule: outside mobile home parks, North Dakota does not cap a utility charge, does not require a utility allowance, and does not force master-metered service to be recovered through a fixed rent. There is no utility allowance statute in the Century Code -- the phrase appears nowhere in it. Whatever you and the tenant agree the tenant will pay for utilities is what governs, subject only to the general contract limits and to the landlord duties below.

The answer where it matters most. If you rent mobile home lots, N.D.C.C. sec. 47-10-28(8) is a hard cap and it is the only utility money cap in the entire North Dakota statutes. A park owner may buy utility service for a tenant and either include it in rent or bill it as a separate charge based on actual usage, but the owner "may not charge a tenant more than the actual cost per unit amount paid by the landlord to the utility service provider, except for a reasonable administrative fee that may not exceed three dollars." If the tenant pays utilities as part of rent, the owner may not charge or back charge for them at all unless the owner's own cost increases, and then only a reasonable amount to cover the increase. And the owner may not charge a utility fee at all unless every mobile home has an individual meter. A violation draws a civil penalty of at least $2,500 under sec. 47-10-28(12) and is a complete defence to an eviction under sec. 47-32-01.1.

What still limits you outside a park. Two things. First, a round-number "utility fee" untied to cost is exposed: N.D.C.C. sec. 9-08-03 makes contractual penalties void outright and sec. 9-08-04 voids an amount of damages fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. A charge measured by your actual cost sits outside both; a flat monthly figure invites the argument. Second, you cannot charge for utilities you are required to supply: sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(f) obliges you to supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat unless one of that subdivision's own exceptions applies, and in anything other than a single-family residence that duty cannot be shifted to the tenant by agreement at all.

What to do. Set the tenant's utility charge by actual cost, not a round number: state the source (the provider invoice, the meter reading) and pass it through. Keep any administrative charge separate, modest and disclosed -- and if the property is a mobile home park, at or under three dollars. Keep the provider invoices and meter readings; they are your evidence that the charge is a cost pass-through and not a penalty.

title: A Utility Deposit You Collect Is a Security Deposit
bodyText: Default rule in North Dakota: there is no separate utility-deposit statute for landlords, and that is why the general deposit section swallows the money. A lessor who requires money as a security deposit, however denominated, must put it in a federally insured interest-bearing savings or checking account for the tenant's benefit, and it and any interest must be paid to the tenant on termination of the lease (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1)). Money you collect against unpaid water, sewer, electricity, gas or heat is security however you label it, so three things follow. It counts in the aggregate against the one-month-rent ceiling - a one-month deposit plus a separate utility deposit is more than one month's security, and you may only go to two months for an applicant convicted of a felony or an applicant with a judgment for violating a previous rental agreement (§ 47-16-07.1(1)(a)-(b)). It must be held and accounted for like any deposit, with itemisation and written notice within thirty days of termination and delivery of possession (§ 47-16-07.1(3)). And here is the trap: the deposit may be applied only to pet or negligence damage, any unpaid rent, and cleaning or repairs that were the tenant's responsibility - an unpaid utility bill is not on that list. North Dakota has no statute deeming a charge to be rent, so unless your lease genuinely makes the tenant's utility charges payable as rent, deducting a final utility bill from the deposit is money withheld without reasonable justification and carries treble damages (§ 47-16-07.1(4)). What to do: do not take a separate utility deposit at all. Have the tenant put the utilities in their own name with the provider, so the provider holds any deposit and returns it under the rules that govern utilities; or, if you must bill utilities yourself, make them payable as rent in the lease so an arrear is 'unpaid rent' within subsection 3(b). A deposit the tenant pays to the utility company itself is governed by utility law, not by chapter 47-16. A public utility may take a deposit 'in accordance with commission rules' and must pay interest on it at a rate the commission sets (N.D.C.C. § 49-04-02.1). The commission's rules cap an electric deposit at about sixty days' estimated charges and a gas deposit at one and a half times an average month's bill, with yearly interest at the Bank of North Dakota six-month certificate rate (N.D. Admin. Code §§ 69-09-02-04, 69-09-01-17). Those rules bind the utility, not you, so for when a provider-held deposit comes back, point the tenant to the provider.

title: North Dakota requires no utility disclosure attachment with a lease -- but it does require two other documents, and a mobile home park owes a third
bodyText:
Default rule: North Dakota requires no utility disclosure, addendum, attachment, schedule or separate signed page with a residential lease. There is no prescribed form, no list of utilities you must disclose, no average-bill or high-and-low-bill statement, and no type-size or separate-page rule anywhere in the Century Code.

What North Dakota does require with a lease. Two documents, neither about utilities. First, N.D.C.C. sec. 47-16-07.2 requires you to give the tenant, at the time of entering the rental agreement, a statement describing the condition of the facilities in and about the premises; it must be agreed to and signed by both of you, and it is prima facie proof of the condition of the facilities at the start of the tenancy. "Facilities" is the same word sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(d) uses for the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems -- so this is the document in which you should record the condition of the furnace, water heater, meters and plumbing. Second, if you are shifting any duty to the tenant in a dwelling that is not a single-family residence, sec. 47-16-13.1(5) requires a SEPARATE WRITING signed by both parties and supported by adequate consideration, and sec. 47-16-13.1(6) forbids making the tenant's performance of it a condition of the lease. That separate writing is a genuine attachment requirement, and it is the one most landlords get wrong.

Mobile home parks. If you rent mobile home lots, sec. 47-10-28(9) requires you to give each tenant "a summary outlining the tenant's lease and the rights and obligations of the tenant and mobile home park owner under state law", and sec. 47-10-28(1)(f) requires you to give a tenant a copy of the existing lease terms with any modifications within ten business days of a written request. Failure draws a civil penalty of at least $2,500 under sec. 47-10-28(12) and is a defence to an eviction under sec. 47-32-01.1.

What to do. Do not attach a utility disclosure because you think North Dakota requires one -- it does not, and a document labelled as a required disclosure when none is required is a representation you will have to stand behind. Put the utility allocation in the lease itself, in the utilities clause. Use the sec. 47-16-07.2 condition statement to record the state of the heating, water-heating and metering equipment, since that statement is prima facie proof and is your best protection in a later dispute about a utility bill or a failed furnace. If you are shifting a duty in a multi-unit building, draft the separate signed writing sec. 47-16-13.1(5) requires, recite the consideration, and do not condition the lease on it.

title: North Dakota has no utility-shutoff statute -- which does not make shutting off a submetered tenant safe, and for heat and water it is a breach of your own statutory duty
bodyText:
Default rule, and it surprises people: North Dakota has no statute prohibiting a landlord from interrupting a tenant's utility service. There is no essential-services provision, no self-help or lockout statute, and no statutory damages award for a shutoff. If you were told N.D.C.C. sec. 47-16-13.6 is North Dakota's unlawful-interruption section, that is wrong: sec. 47-16-13.6 is captioned "Enforcement of sections 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6" and does nothing but make those rights enforceable by action, with attorney's fees to the prevailing party at the court's discretion.

The answer. The absence of a shutoff statute does not make a shutoff lawful; it means the consequences come from elsewhere, and for heat and water they are serious. Under sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(f) you must supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat, unless that subdivision's own exception applies -- the building is not required by law to be equipped for the purpose, the installation is within the tenant's exclusive control and on a direct public utility connection, or the public utility itself has failed. If the duty applies and you cut the service off, you have breached it, and sec. 47-16-13 lets the tenant repair at your expense and deduct it from rent, recover it in any other lawful manner, or vacate and be discharged from further rent. Sec. 47-16-13.5 lets the aggrieved party recover appropriate damages and sec. 47-16-13.6 adds attorney's fees. A deliberate shutoff is also a "violation of law" for the purposes of sec. 9-08-02, so any lease term exempting you from responsibility for it is contrary to the policy of express law under sec. 9-08-01, and the shutoff is material to unconscionability under sec. 47-16-13.3.

Submetered electricity is the weaker case, and you should not rely on that. Sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(f) covers water, hot water and heat but not electricity as such; sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(d) requires you to keep electrical facilities in good and safe working order, which is about the equipment rather than the supply. So cutting submetered electricity is not as cleanly a breach of a named statutory duty. It will still usually breach the covenant of quiet possession in sec. 47-16-08, and in practice cutting electricity to a dwelling in a North Dakota winter disables the heating system and so breaches (1)(f) anyway.

Mobile home parks. If you rent mobile home lots the exposure is much larger and much more certain. Sec. 47-10-28(12) imposes a civil penalty of not less than $2,500, up to the greater of $10,000 or actual damages, plus actual attorney's fees and costs, for violating any provision of sec. 47-10-28 -- including the subsection 8 utility rules. And sec. 47-32-01.1 lets the tenant raise the violation as a defence in your eviction, and provides that if the court finds a violation it "may not order an eviction".

What to do. Never interrupt, shut off or reduce a utility to collect money or to make a tenant leave, whether the service is submetered, master-metered or in your own name. Collect an unpaid utility charge the way you collect rent: bill it as additional rent and, if it is not paid, use the eviction procedure in ch. 47-32. If you must interrupt service for genuine repair or safety work, give notice, keep it as short as possible, document it, and restore it promptly -- sec. 47-16-13.1(2) allows a reasonable time to remedy a non-compliance, which is a repair allowance, not a licence to leave a unit without heat.

title: Utilities in the landlord's name in North Dakota: no pay-and-deduct statute, no rent receiver, no master-meter notice duty -- and no protection if you stop paying
bodyText:
Default rule: North Dakota has no statute about landlord-held utility accounts. There is no provision letting tenants pay the utility and deduct it from rent as such, no liquidated damages for failing to identify your tenants to the provider, no duty on a master-meter owner to notify the utility of anything, and no procedure by which tenants petition a court to appoint a receiver to collect rents and pay the utility. North Dakota has not adopted the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and none of the URLTA machinery other states use here exists.

The answer, which is that the general law is quite enough to hurt you. If the account is in your name and you stop paying it, you have not escaped liability -- you have breached sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(f), which requires you to supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water at all times and reasonable heat, and sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(d), which requires you to maintain the heating, plumbing and electrical facilities in good and safe working order. Sec. 47-16-13 then gives the tenant three choices on notice of something you ought to repair and have not: repair it and deduct the expense from rent, recover it from you in any other lawful manner, or vacate, in which case the tenant "shall be discharged from further payment of rent or performance of other conditions". That third option is the real risk: a tenant whose heat is cut off because you did not pay the gas bill can walk away from the lease entirely. Sec. 47-16-13.5 adds appropriate damages and sec. 47-16-13.6 adds attorney's fees to the prevailing party. In a dwelling other than a single-family residence you cannot contract out of the (1)(f) duty at all: sec. 47-16-13.1(5) does not permit it, and sec. 47-16-13.1(4) permits it only for a single-family residence, in writing and in good faith.

Mobile home parks. Sec. 47-10-28(8) assumes the park owner holds the account -- it expressly lets the owner buy utility service, including water and sewer, on the tenant's behalf -- and then controls what the owner may charge: no more than actual cost per unit plus an administrative fee capped at three dollars, nothing at all without an individual meter for each mobile home, and the tenant must be given access to the meter readings for the lot. A violation draws a civil penalty of at least $2,500 under sec. 47-10-28(12) and bars the eviction under sec. 47-32-01.1.

What the utility must do. The Public Service Commission's rules answer the shutoff question for electric and gas service from a public utility. A utility must give its customer notice before disconnecting for nonpayment, in line with the commission's rules (N.D.C.C. § 49-04-20(1)). And where a customer with tenants includes the cost of utilities in the rent and the bill becomes delinquent, the utility 'must also notify the tenants in writing at least ten days prior to the proposed termination date'. It must let each tenant apply to become the customer in the tenant's own name, keep or restore service, and pay 'the pro rata share of future bills' (N.D. Admin. Code §§ 69-09-02-05.1(9), 69-09-01-18.1(9)). A utility also may not cut a customer off for a previous occupant's bill (subsection 6 of each rule). So your tenants will hear about your arrear from the utility, and can take the account over.

The cautious course. Keep the accounts you hold current, and treat a utility arrear as more dangerous than a mortgage arrear because it can discharge your tenants from rent. Tell your tenants in writing which utilities are in your name, name the provider and give a contact, so a tenant who gets a shutoff notice calls you rather than a lawyer. Give the provider the occupant information it asks for. If you include utilities in the rent, expect the utility to write to your tenants ten days before any shutoff for your arrear. And if a shutoff is threatened, pay it -- the sec. 47-16-13 remedies are far more expensive than the bill.

title: Submetering and utility charge-backs in North Dakota: no disclosure rule, no billing limits, no late-fee cap -- unless you rent mobile home lots
bodyText:
Default rule: North Dakota has no submetering law. The word "submeter" appears nowhere in the North Dakota Century Code -- not in any section and not in any section heading in the Legislative Council master index. So for an ordinary residential tenancy, every one of the things other states regulate here is simply absent: there is no prescribed disclosure and no required wording; no type-size rule and no separate-signed-page rule; no unit threshold distinguishing water from electric submetering; no cap on what you may bill; no late-fee cap on a utility bill; no bar on disconnection, late fees or eviction for non-payment of a landlord-billed utility; no exclusion for ratio billing or for third-party submetering; and no distinction by building size. There is also no requirement that you have a written agreement or utility-regulator authority before billing a utility.

The answer where North Dakota does regulate it. Mobile home lots, under N.D.C.C. sec. 47-10-28(8), and there the rules are strict. A park owner may buy utility service for a tenant and either include it in rent or bill it as a separate charge based on actual usage. The owner may not charge more than the actual cost per unit it paid the provider, except a reasonable administrative fee that may not exceed three dollars. If the tenant pays utilities as part of rent the owner may not charge or back charge for them unless the owner's own cost increases, and then only a reasonable amount to cover the increase. A park "may not charge a fee for a utility without an individual meter for each mobile home" -- which bans ratio and square-footage billing outright. And the owner must give the tenant access to the meter readings for that lot. Separately, sec. 47-10-28(11) caps a park's late fees at ten percent of monthly rent per month plus no more than five dollars a day. A violation of any of this draws a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 under sec. 47-10-28(12) and bars the eviction under sec. 47-32-01.1.

Adding a charge-back mid-tenancy. North Dakota has no opt-in mechanism and no ninety-day notice rule. What it has is sec. 47-16-07: in a month-to-month tenancy the landlord may change the terms of the lease to take effect at the expiration of the month on at least thirty days' written notice before the end of that month, served in any reasonable manner that actually informs the tenant, and the new terms bind the tenant if the tenant holds over. Under a fixed-term lease you cannot impose a utility charge-back mid-term at all without the tenant's agreement.

What still limits you. A flat utility fee untied to cost has to survive sec. 9-08-03, which makes contractual penalties void outright, and sec. 9-08-04, which voids an amount of damages fixed in advance unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. A charge measured by actual cost is outside both. And you cannot bill the tenant for a utility you are obliged to supply -- see the utility-apportionment row on sec. 47-16-13.1(1)(f).

What to do. Put the billing method in the lease, because nothing supplies one by default. State the measure (meter reading, or the provider invoice), state the rate source, and keep any administrative charge separate and modest. Give the tenant the meter reading and the invoice on request -- North Dakota does not make you, but it is what sec. 47-10-28(8) would require in a park and it is the cheapest way to defend the charge. Bill the charge as additional rent so it is collectible like rent and so the security-deposit provision in sec. 47-16-07.1(3), which reaches "[a]ny unpaid rent" but says nothing about utility arrears, can reach it.

title: Veteran and military rental discounts in North Dakota: none required, none regulated, and the one thing you must not get wrong
bodyText: Default rule first: North Dakota requires nothing of a landlord because a tenant is a veteran or a servicemember. There is no statutory rent discount, no deposit waiver, no application-fee waiver, no priority or preference in letting a dwelling, no tax credit or state reimbursement for giving one, and no statute regulating a veterans' incentive you choose to offer. North Dakota's statutes contain no provision connecting veteran or military status to rent, a dwelling or a lease at all. So an incentive is yours to offer or not: you may give a veteran a rent discount, waive a fee, or hold a unit, and the lease is where it has to be written to operate -- use the library's rent concession clause and state the amount and the periods it covers. Two cautions. Veteran and military status are NOT protected classes under North Dakota's fair housing law: the protected grounds are race, color, religion, sex, disability, age, familial status, national origin, and status with respect to marriage or public assistance (N.D.C.C. Section 14-02.5-02). So a veterans-only incentive is not a fair-housing violation on its face -- but age IS a protected ground in North Dakota, unusually, so do not let an incentive operate as an age screen, and a veteran with a service-connected disability has the same reasonable-accommodation and reasonable-modification rights as any other tenant with a disability whether or not you offer an incentive. The one statutory veterans' savings clause in the Human Rights Act, Section 14-02.4-11, preserves veterans' preferences only against Sections 14-02.4-03 through 14-02.4-06, which are the employment provisions -- it does not reach housing, and the housing sections of that chapter are repealed. The thing you must not get wrong is unrelated to incentives: North Dakota DOES have a state military civil relief act. Section 37-01-43 gives an individual called or ordered to active service for thirty consecutive days or longer all of the protections of the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act as that Act stood on December 31, 2024 -- which includes the right to end a residential lease on military orders. Treat a servicemember tenant's termination notice as valid under state law as well as federal, and do not tell a tenant that North Dakota adds nothing.

title: Taking Rent After a Breach: No Statute, One Presumption to Watch
bodyText: North Dakota has no statute saying that accepting rent waives a breach, and none saying it does not. The one acceptance rule in the chapter runs to renewal rather than waiver: if a tenant stays on after the lease expires and you accept rent, the parties are presumed to have renewed on the same terms for the same time, not exceeding one year - and for a residential tenancy, except where the lease has an automatic renewal clause, the presumption is a month-to-month tenancy (N.D.C.C. § 47-16-06). So accepting rent after the term ends has a defined statutory consequence, while accepting rent after some other breach does not, and whether it waives your right to act on that breach is a common-law question North Dakota's statutes do not answer. If you take rent while a breach is live and you mean to keep your remedies, say so in writing when you take it.

title: No Statutory Water Heater Setting — But Check the Building Code and Set It Yourself
bodyText:
Some states put this duty squarely on the landlord: Wisconsin requires a unit-only water heater to be set to a maximum temperature before each new tenant moves in, and Washington does something similar through an energy statute rather than its landlord-tenant act. North Dakota's landlord-tenant law contains no equivalent. There is no maximum water heater temperature, no required setting, no at-each-new-occupancy duty, no thermostat or tempering-valve requirement, and no scald-protection provision anywhere in chapter 47-16.

What North Dakota does require is the supply itself and the working order of the equipment. Under N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(f) you must supply running water and "reasonable amounts of hot water at all times" — an adequacy standard about quantity and availability, with no word about temperature. Subdivision (f)'s three exceptions apply here as they do to heat: the duty does not apply if the building is not required by law to be equipped for the purpose, or if the unit is so constructed that hot water is generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control supplied by a direct public utility connection, or if the water is unavailable due to supply failure by a public utility. And under § 47-16-13.1(1)(d) you must maintain the water heater itself, as a plumbing facility you supply, "in good and safe working order and condition." A water heater delivering scalding water is not in safe working order, so the safety point reaches you through subdivision (d) even though no statute names a number.

There is one more channel. Section 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes compliance with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety your duty, and § 47-16-13.1(3) measures your duty by the code where the code asks more. North Dakota's State Building Code consists of the international building, residential, mechanical and fuel gas codes, and it leaves the State Plumbing Code out (N.D.C.C. §§ 54-21.3-03(1), 54-21.3-04(1)(b)). The plumbing code is the 2018 Uniform Plumbing Code, adopted by the state plumbing board for chapters 1 to 4, 6 to 11 and 17 only, and 'all plumbing', including its maintenance, must meet it (N.D. Admin. Code § 62-03.1-01-01; N.D.C.C. § 43-18-01(5)). Neither chapter 43-18, chapter 54-21.3 nor the board's own rules sets a water heater temperature or a setting duty at each new tenancy. The model code's text is published by its private author, not the state. If it limits delivered temperature at a fixture, § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) and (3) make that limit binding on you through the lease.

CAUTIOUS COURSE, and do this regardless of how the code question resolves: set the water heater thermostat to about 120 degrees Fahrenheit before each new tenancy, record the date and the setting on your move-in checklist, and check it at turnover. That is the widely used safe setting, it reduces scald risk to children and older tenants, and it is comfortably consistent with supplying "reasonable amounts of hot water at all times." Do not set it lower than the point at which the supply stops being reasonable in amount, because the supply duty is the one North Dakota actually imposes. Have a licensed plumber install or replace water heaters and shower or tub valves to the plumbing code. Cities may amend the building code and apply their own ordinances (N.D.C.C. § 54-21.3-03(6); N.D. Admin. Code § 62-03.1-02-01), so check your city's code before you treat 120 as a legal ceiling rather than a practical one.

What not to do: do not write a lease clause making the tenant responsible for the water heater's temperature setting in a multi-unit building. Section 47-16-13.1(5) lets a tenant in anything other than a single-family residence agree only to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodelling, and the water and hot water duty in subdivision (f) is not on that list, so it cannot be shifted there. In a single-family residence it can be, by a good-faith writing under § 47-16-13.1(4).

title: Waterbeds
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. North Dakota has no waterbed statute of any kind. So there is no tenant right to keep a waterbed, no landlord duty to permit one, no statutory insurance requirement and no statutory floor-load rule. A landlord may simply prohibit a waterbed, and does so by writing it in the lease.

ONE HARD LIMIT, AND IT IS EASY TO BREACH. You may not take extra deposit money for a waterbed. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1) bars a lessor from demanding or receiving "security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of one month's rent", with only two exceptions - up to two months' rent from an applicant convicted of a felony offence as an incentive to rent, and up to two months' rent from one with a judgment for violating a previous rental agreement. Subsection 2 creates a separate allowance for a PET security deposit of up to the greater of $2,500 or two months' rent. There is no waterbed equivalent. "However denominated" means calling it a waterbed deposit, a liquid-furniture deposit or a flotation deposit does not get you out of the one-month cap, and § 47-16-07.1(4) makes a lessor "liable for treble damages for any security deposit money withheld without reasonable justification."

WHAT THE LEASE SHOULD CARRY. The lease clause offers a prohibition and a permission on conditions; use one and delete the other.

WHY CONDITION (c) OF THE PERMISSION MATTERS. Without it, a landlord's claim for water damage runs only through N.D.C.C. § 47-16-10 ("[t]he lessee of real property must repair all deteriorations or injuries thereto occasioned by the lessee's ordinary negligence"), § 47-16-09 (ordinary care) and § 47-16-13.2(6) (not deliberately or negligently damage the premises) - all of which require fault. A seam that fails without anyone's fault falls outside them. The deposit section only reaches "deteriorations or injuries to the real property or dwelling... through the negligence of the lessee or the lessee's guest" under § 47-16-07.1(3)(a), or "repairs which were the responsibility of the lessee" under § 47-16-07.1(3)(c). Clause (c) is what puts a no-fault leak inside (3)(c).

CAUTIOUS COURSE on floor loading. Floor loading is a building-code question. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes the landlord comply with "applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety" and § 47-16-13.1(3) makes that duty controlling where it is greater than any other, and North Dakota's State Building Code consists of the international building, residential, mechanical and fuel gas codes (§ 54-21.3-03(1)). Do not rely on a tenant's promise to carry the weight: if you have any doubt about an older wood-framed upper floor, prohibit the waterbed rather than permit it.
