Charging a non-refundable waterbed fee instead of a deposit is also unsafe - North Dakota has no statute authorising non-refundable fees, and a fixed sum not measured by actual cost has to survive § 9-08-03 ("[p]enalties imposed by contract for any nonperformance thereof are void") and § 9-08-04 (damages fixed in advance void except where actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix). Require insurance, not money.

title: No window-guard duty and no window-guard notice in North Dakota law
bodyText:
DEFAULT RULE FIRST. A North Dakota landlord's duties are the closed list in N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.1(1): comply with applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition; keep all common areas clean and safe; maintain the facilities and appliances supplied; provide waste receptacles and arrange removal; and supply running water, hot water and reasonable heat. Nothing in that list names a window, a guard, a railing or a balcony.

THE ANSWER. There is no provision in the North Dakota statutes requiring a landlord to install window guards, and none requiring a window-guard notice in a lease - in bold type or at all. The phrases "window guard", "window bars", "window stop" and "fall prevention" appear nowhere in the North Dakota Century Code; "railing", "banister" and "balcony" appear nowhere in it either. In the Century Code, every occurrence of "window" is a motor-vehicle, school-security, cigar-lounge or arrest-entry provision, and every "guardrail" is a highway one. So a lease that recites a window-guard notice is reciting a rule North Dakota does not have, and a lease in which the tenant "waives" window guards is waiving nothing - which is worse than silence, because it invites the tenant to believe they gave something up.

WHERE A DUTY COULD STILL COME FROM. Two routes, and both lead outside the statutes. First, § 47-16-13.1(1)(a) makes the landlord "[c]omply with the requirements of applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety", and § 47-16-13.1(3) provides that where the (1)(a) duty "is greater than any duty imposed by any other subdivision of that subsection, the landlord's duty shall be determined by reference to subdivision a" - so a code requirement is imported into the lease statute and becomes binding and controlling. North Dakota's State Building Code, ch. 54-21.3, consists of the international building, residential, mechanical and fuel gas codes, applied where a city, township or county enforces it; the chapter itself says nothing about windows, and the model codes' text is published by the International Code Council, not the state. Second, § 47-16-13.1(1)(b)'s "fit and habitable condition" is open-textured and undefined, and a broken or unsecured window in a unit with small children is the kind of thing it could be held to reach.

CAUTIOUS COURSE, which is what this row is for. Treat it as if a duty exists. Where children live above the ground floor, fit guards or limiting stops at your own cost, keep the written record that you did, and never charge for them. Where a tenant asks to install their own, consent in writing and say who restores the frame - and note that if the request comes from or for a person with a disability, § 14-02.5-06(3)(a) makes refusing "a reasonable modification of existing premises" at the tenant's own expense a discriminatory practice, though you may reasonably condition consent on the tenant "agreeing to restore the interior of the premises to the condition that existed before the modification, reasonable wear and tear excepted". Remember that a tenant who installs a guard may be entitled to take it with them: § 47-06-04 lets a tenant remove anything affixed "for the purpose of trade, manufacture, ornament, or domestic use" at any time during the term if removal causes no injury and the thing has not become an integral part of the premises. And do not try to push a window-safety duty onto the tenant in a multi-unit building without complying with § 47-16-13.1(5) - a separate writing signed by both parties and supported by adequate consideration - because § 47-16-13.1(6) also bars making the tenant's performance of it a condition of the lease.

THE ONE THING TO AVOID. Do not write a clause disclaiming liability for a window fall. N.D.C.C. § 9-08-02 makes contracts whose object is "the exempting of anyone from responsibility for that person's own fraud or willful injury to the person or property of another, or violation of law, whether willful or negligent" against the policy of the law, and § 9-08-01 turns that into unlawfulness; a breach of the § 47-16-13.1 duties is a violation of law, so a negligent habitability failure sits inside it. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.3 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable provision outright.

title: Which North Dakota notices must be in writing, and the ones that need not be
bodyText:
Default rule first: North Dakota has no general rule that lease notices must be in writing. It requires writing notice by notice, and the pattern is uneven — so the right question is never "must notice be written?" but "which notice is this?" Here is the whole inventory, from the sections themselves.

WRITING IS REQUIRED:
- § 47-16-15(2) — terminating a month-to-month tenancy: "either party may terminate the tenancy by giving at least one calendar month's written notice at any time." Rent is due to and including the termination date.
- § 47-16-07 — a landlord changing the terms of a month-to-month tenancy: "notice in writing at least thirty days before the expiration of the month." Served notice becomes part of the lease if the tenant holds over. Service may be "in any reasonable manner which actually informs the tenant".
- § 47-16-06.1 — enforcing an automatic renewal clause in a residential lease of a specified term of two months or more: the lessor must have "notified the lessee in writing, delivered personally or by first-class mail", not less than thirty days before expiry. Miss it and the lease expires and converts to month-to-month.
- § 47-17-02 — the notice terminating a tenancy at will under § 47-17-01 "must be in writing and must be served by delivering the same to the tenant or to some person of discretion residing on the premises. If neither can be found with reasonable diligence, the notice may be served by affixing it on a conspicuous part of the premises where it may be read conveniently." The period is not less than one month.
- § 47-17-04 — exercising a reserved right of re-entry: "three days' previous written notice of intention to re-enter served in the mode prescribed by section 47-17-02."
- § 47-32-02 — "three days' written notice of intention to evict", but ONLY "[i]n all cases arising under subsections 4, 5, 6, and 8 of section 47-32-01" — that is nonpayment or holdover (4), possession after a judicial or contract-for-deed sale (5), possession after partition or decree (6), and violation of a material term of the written lease (8). Grounds 1, 2, 3 and 7 need no such notice. Service is as a summons, or by posting conspicuously if the party cannot be found.
- § 47-16-07.1(3) — the deposit itemisation and "a written notice within thirty days after termination of the lease and delivery of possession".
- § 47-16-17.1(2)-(3) — a domestic-violence termination: "advance written notice" stating the three listed matters, "delivered by mail, facsimile communication, or in person before the termination of the tenancy."
- § 47-10-28(1)(d), (3), (4), (5), (7) — in a mobile home park, written notice of a change of ownership within five business days, thirty days' advance written notice of rule changes, and ninety days' notice before a rent increase on a month-to-month agreement; § 47-10-28(10) requires a notice of intent to evict a park tenant to carry boldfaced wording that the tenant need not leave immediately.

WRITING IS NOT REQUIRED — and these are the ones that catch people out:
- § 47-16-15(1) — notice of intention to terminate a lease for an unspecified term: the section says "gives notice" and does not say written.
- § 47-16-15(3) — the tenant's response to a § 47-16-07 change of terms: "the tenant may terminate the lease at the end of the month by giving at least twenty-five days' notice." Not written. Note it is twenty-five days, not a month, and note that your thirty-day change notice therefore gives the tenant a shorter exit than the ordinary month.
- § 47-16-15(4) and (5) — the fallback terminations each read "with at least one calendar month's notice". Not written. So within one section, subsection (2) says "written notice" and subsections (3), (4) and (5) say only "notice" — do not assume the word carries across.
- § 47-16-13 — repair-and-deduct: the tenant need only give "notice from the lessee of dilapidations which the lessor ought to repair". No writing, no form, no dollar threshold, and the remedy is uncapped. An oral complaint can start the clock.
- § 47-16-25 — the tenant must inform you of any proceeding against the property and deliver the notice; the duty is unqualified, but the tenant is answerable in damages only "if such notice is in writing".
- § 47-16-30.1 — abandoned property: the twenty-eight days run from when "the lessor received actual notice that the lessee has vacated" or from when it "reasonably appears" so. No written notice is needed either way.

One rule about the lease itself, and it is the one most often missed. § 47-16-15(4): "Any agreement that requires a lessee to give notice that exceeds one month from the end of a month to terminate a lease of real property for residential purposes must state the notice requirement and provide space for the lessee to initial next to the notice requirement. If the notice is not initialed by the lessee at the time of executing the lease, the lessee may terminate the lease on the last day of a month with at least one calendar month's notice." So a longer tenant-notice period is available under § 47-16-15(2) only by written agreement, and under (4) only if the lease states it and gives the tenant a line to initial, initialled at signing. Get either wrong and the requirement collapses to one calendar month.

What to do. (1) Put every notice you give in writing, date it, and keep proof of how it was delivered — the statute's minimum is not your best practice, and three of the sections above prescribe a delivery method you must actually follow. (2) Never rely on an oral notice from a tenant being ineffective: under §§ 47-16-13, 47-16-15(3), (4) and (5) and 47-16-30.1 it can be perfectly good. Log oral complaints the day you get them. (3) If your lease asks the tenant for more than one month's notice, check it states the requirement and carries an initial line, and check the tenant actually initialled it at signing. (4) Before serving a three-day notice, identify which § 47-32-01 ground you are on; on grounds 1, 2, 3 or 7 the notice is not required, and on 4, 5, 6 or 8 it is. (5) For a tenancy at will use the § 47-17-02 form and method, not a generic letter.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: North Dakota follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (N.D.C.C. § 41-03-37). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (N.D.C.C. § 41-01-22(2)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. North Dakota's general contract law adds that part performance of an obligation, expressly accepted by the creditor in writing in satisfaction, extinguishes it (N.D.C.C. § 9-13-07). The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: North Dakota's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (N.D.C.C. chs. 47-16 and 47-32 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how North Dakota's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Tenant Work and Construction Liens
bodyText: When one person improves another's land, everyone interested in the land is "deemed to have authorized the improvements" (N.D.C.C. § 35-27-07(1)). If a tenant orders improvements, "no lien is allowed unless the legal or equitable owner has actual or constructive notice of the improvements and fails to object" (§ 35-27-07(3)). You object by serving written notice on the person making the improvements within five days after you learn of them, or by posting and keeping posted a notice of objection in a conspicuous place on the premises (§ 35-27-07(2)). A lien is also not allowed if a valid lien waiver signed by the person who did the work has been received (§ 35-27-02(3)). Whether approving an alteration in writing counts as failing to object only case law could settle, so when you approve work, also collect lien waivers before it starts; when you have not approved it, object in writing within five days.

title: Guaranties and Renewals
bodyText:
North Dakota's lease law contains no guaranty provision at all, so the lease's guaranty clause is the only thing that makes a guarantor answerable for a renewal.

The guaranty rules are in N.D.C.C. ch. 22-01. A guaranty must be "in writing and signed by the guarantor" (§ 22-01-04). The guarantor's obligation may not be "larger in amount, nor in other respects more burdensome, than that of the principal" (§ 22-01-12). A guarantor is exonerated if the landlord alters the tenant's obligation "without the consent of the guarantor" (§ 22-01-15), which is why the clause records that consent in advance. A continuing guaranty "may be revoked at any time by the guarantor in respect to future transactions" unless there is a continuing consideration the guarantor does not renounce (§ 22-01-14).

Whether a renewal is such a future transaction only case law could settle, so the clause requires any revocation to be written and delivered, as § 22-01-14 allows. Have the guarantor sign the lease itself or a writing that refers to it by date and address; always fill in both the maximum amount and the end date; and do not add a term saying the guaranty is irrevocable.

title: Environmental Covenants and Your Lease
bodyText: North Dakota does not require a lease to give notice of an environmental covenant recorded under N.D.C.C. ch. 47-37. The lease's environmental covenant clause is there because the covenant binds the tenant's use whether or not the lease mentions it, and only the lease can make a breach of the covenant a default under the lease.

title: Ending a Fixed-Term Lease So the Owner Can Move In
bodyText: Sections 47-17-01 and 47-17-02 govern terminating an estate at will, so they do not themselves prescribe how an owner-occupancy termination notice under a fixed-term lease is served; the lease's owner occupancy clause adopts the section 47-17-02 manner by agreement. Section 47-17-04 does reach the clause once the termination date has passed: a right of re-entry reserved in a lease may be exercised on three days' previous written notice of intention to re-enter, served in the mode section 47-17-02 prescribes. Section 47-17-05 lets you bring an action for possession without that notice. If the tenant stays past the termination date, recover possession by an eviction action, not by changing the locks.

title: Rules and Regulations in a Mobile Home Park
bodyText: If the property is a mobile home park, do not use the lease's rules and regulations clause as drafted. Section 47-10-28(3) requires thirty days' advance written notice of a rule change and then, for a tenant who owns the dwelling unit, written notice of the failure to comply and three months to remedy it or vacate before an eviction may be started, during which the tenant complies with the pre-change rules. The three months are extended, by up to two more months, if the tenant gives the owner a mobile home relocator's signed declaration that the home cannot be relocated within them. A violation carries a civil penalty of not less than $2,500 (section 47-10-28(12)) and is a defence to the eviction (section 47-32-01.1). The three-month period does not apply to rules and regulations under section 47-10-28(4) and (5).
